======================================================================
WIKIPEDIA ARTICLE: Dom Casmurro
======================================================================

{{short description|1899 novel by Machado de Assis}}
{{Use dmy dates|date=July 2024}}
{{Infobox book
| name              = Dom Casmurro
| image             = DomCasmurroMachadodeAssis.jpg
| author            = [[Machado de Assis]]
| language          = Portuguese
| country           = Brazil
| genre             = [[literary realism|Psychological realism]], [[impressionism]]
| published         = 1899 (1st Brazilian edition), [[Livraria Garnier]], Rio de Janeiro
| caption           = Title page of the first edition of ''Dom Casmurro'', 1900.
}}

'''''Dom Casmurro''''' is an 1899 novel written by Brazilian author [[Machado de Assis|Joaquim Maria Machado de Assis]]. Like ''[[The Posthumous Memoirs of Brás Cubas]]'' and ''[[Quincas Borba]]'', both by Machado de Assis, it is widely regarded as a masterpiece of [[literary realism|realist]] literature. It is written as a fictional memoir by a distrusting, jealous husband. The narrator, however, is not a [[Unreliable narrator|reliable conveyor]] of the story as it is a dark comedy. Dom Casmurro is considered by critic [[Afrânio Coutinho]] "a true Brazilian masterpiece, and perhaps Brazil's greatest representative piece of writing" and "one of the best books ever written in the [[Portuguese language]], if not the best one to date." The author is considered a master of Brazilian literature with a unique style of realism.<ref>{{cite web |author=Jackson |first=K. David |date=22 February 1998 |title=Madness in a Tropical Manner |url=https://www.nytimes.com/books/98/02/22/reviews/980222.22jacksot.html |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181006112318/https://archive.nytimes.com/www.nytimes.com/books/98/02/22/reviews/980222.22jacksot.html |archive-date=6 October 2018 |access-date=5 January 2014 |website=[[The New York Times]]}}</ref>

Its protagonist is Bento Santiago, the narrator of the story which, told in the first person, aims to "tie together the two ends of life",<ref name="de assis">{{Cite book |last=de Assis |first=Machado |url=https://archive.org/details/in.ernet.dli.2015.149403/mode/2up?view=theater |title=Dom Casmurro |publisher=W. H. Allen |year=1953 |location=London |pages= |translator-last=Caldwell |translator-first=Helen}}</ref>{{Rp|page=7}} in other words, to bring together stories from his youth to the days when he is writing the book. Between these two moments, Bento writes about his youthful reminiscences, his life at the [[seminary]], his affair with Capitu and the jealousy that arises from this relationship, which becomes the main plot of the story.<ref name="guilhermino">{{Cite book |last=Guilhermino |first=Almir |title=Dom Casmurro: A Encenação De Um Julgamento Na Adaptação Cinematográfica De Moacyr Góes E De Paulo César Saraceni |date=2008 |publisher=Edufal |isbn=978-85-7177-427-8 |pages=21; 22; 25–28 |language=pt-BR |trans-title=Dom Casmurro: The Staging Of A Trial In The Film Adaptation By Moacyr Góes And Paulo César Saraceni}}</ref> Set in [[Rio de Janeiro]] during the [[Second reign (Empire of Brazil)|Second Reign]], the novel begins with a recent episode in which the narrator is nicknamed "Dom Casmurro", hence the title of the novel. Machado de Assis wrote it using literary devices such as [[irony]] and [[intertextuality]], making references to [[Arthur Schopenhauer|Schopenhauer]] and, above all, to Shakespeare's ''[[Othello]]''.

Over the years, ''Dom Casmurro'' has been the subject of numerous studies, adaptations to other media and interpretations throughout the world, from psychological and psychoanalytical in [[literary criticism]] in the 1930s and 1940s, through [[feminist literary criticism]] in the 1970s, to sociological in the 1980s and beyond, with its themes of jealousy, Capitu's ambiguity, the moral portrait of the time and the character of the narrator. Credited as a forerunner of [[Modernism]]<ref name="guilhermino" /> and of ideas later written by the father of psychoanalysis [[Sigmund Freud]],<ref name="andrade">{{Cite journal |last=Andrade |first=Fernando Teixeira de |year=2001 |title=Dom Casmurro |journal=Os Livros da FUVEST |language=pt-BR |location=São Paulo |publisher=Sol |volume=1}}</ref>{{Rp|page=144}} the book influenced writers such as [[John Barth]], [[Graciliano Ramos]] and [[Dalton Trevisan]], and is considered by some to be Machado's [[masterpiece]], on a par with ''The Posthumous Memoirs of Brás Cubas''.<ref name="petronio; alvarenga">{{Cite book |last1=Petronio |first1=Rodrigo |title=Dom Casmurro |last2=Alvarenga |first2=Luis Fernando Ribeiro |publisher=Editora Escala Educacional |year=2008 |isbn=978-85-377-0632-9 |language=pt-BR |chapter=Foreword}}</ref>{{Rp|page=6}} ''Dom Casmurro'' has been translated into several languages and remains one of his most famous books and is considered one of the most fundamental works in all of [[Brazilian literature]].<ref name="saraiva">{{Cite book |last=Saraiva |first=Juracy Assmann |title=Nos labirintos de Dom Casmurro: ensaios críticos |date=2005 |publisher=EDIPUCRS |isbn=978-85-7430-524-0 |series=Coleção Literatura brasileira |location=Porto Alegre |language=pt-BR |trans-title=In the labyrinths of Dom Casmurro: critical essays}}</ref>{{Rp|page=7}}

== Plot ==
The story is told in the first person and the main character is 54-year-old Bento de Albuquerque Santiago, a solitary, well-established lawyer from Rio de Janeiro who, after having rebuilt his childhood house "in the old Rua de Matacavalos" (now {{Ill|Rua do Riachuelo|pt}}) in [[Engenho Novo]], wants to "tie together the two ends of life and restore his adolescence in old age", in other words, recount his youthful moments in middle age. In the first chapter, the author explains the title: it's a tribute to a "train poet" who once pestered him with his verses and called him "Dom Casmurro" because, according to Bento, he "closed his eyes three or four times" during the recitation.<ref name="de assis" />{{Rp|pages=5–6}} His neighbours, who found his "taciturn, recluse-like habits" strange, and also his close friends, popularised the nickname. He was inspired to write the book by medallions of [[Julius Caesar|Caesar]], [[Augustus]], [[Nero]] and [[Masinissa]]: Roman emperors who killed their adulterous wives.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Petry |first=Adalberto José |title=Ecos e Reflexos de Dom Casmurro |trans-title=Echoes and Reflections of Dom Casmurro |url=http://www.diaadiaeducacao.pr.gov.br/portals/pde/arquivos/838-2.pdf |language=pt-BR}}</ref>

In the following chapters Bento begins his recollections. He recounts the experiences he had when his mother, the widowed D. Glória, sent him to the seminary. Glória sent him to the seminary to fulfil a promise she had made: if she were to conceive a second child after her first, who died in childbirth, she would send it to the seminary. The idea was revived by the dependent José Dias, who tells Uncle Cosme and D. Glória about Bentinho's flirtation with Capitolina, the poor neighbour with whom Bentinho was in love. At the seminary, Bentinho meets his best friend, Ezequiel de Sousa Escobar, the son of a lawyer from [[Curitiba]]. Bentinho left the seminary and studied law in São Paulo, while Escobar became a successful businessman and married Sancha, Capitu's friend. In 1865 Capitu and Bentinho get married; Sancha and Ezequiel have a daughter they name Capitolina, while the protagonist and his wife conceive a son named Ezequiel. Bento's companion Escobar, who was an excellent swimmer, paradoxically drowns in 1871, and at the funeral both Sancha and Capitu stare at the deceased: "There was a moment when Capitu's eyes gazed down at the dead man as the widow's had, [...] like the swollen wave of the sea beyond, as if she too wished to swallow up the swimmer of that morning."<ref name="de assis" />{{Rp|page=210}} according to him.

Soon the narrator starts to suspect that his best friend and Capitu were secretly cheating on him. Dom Casmurro also begins to doubt his own paternity. He says in the last lines: "[...] were destined to join together and deceive me..."<ref name="de assis" />{{Rp|page=240}} The book ends with the ironic invitation "Let's go to the ''History of the Suburbs''",<ref name="de assis" />{{Rp|page=240}} a book he would have thought of writing at the beginning of the novel, before the idea of ''Dom Casmurro'' occurred to him. The novel takes place from approximately 1857 to 1875, and the narrative, although set in [[Time perception|psychological time]], allows us to perceive certain units: Bento's childhood in Matacavalos; Dona Glória's house and the Pádua family, with relatives and dependents; his acquaintance with Capitu; the seminary; married life; the intensification of jealousy; the psychotic outbursts of jealousy and aggression; the break-up.<ref name="andrade" />{{Rp|page=163}}

== Characteristics ==

=== Genre ===
After ''[[The Posthumous Memoirs of Brás Cubas]]'' (1881), Machado de Assis wrote books with different themes and styles from his earlier novels, such as ''[[Ressurreição|Resurrection]]'' and ''[[A Mão e a Luva|The Hand and the Glove]]''. These new novels – which include, in addition to ''the Posthumous Memoirs'', ''[[Quincas Borba]]'' (1891) and ''Dom Casmurro'' – are labeled as [[Literary realism|realist]] because of their critical attitude, [[Subjectivity and objectivity (philosophy)|objectivity]] and contemporaneity.<ref name="andrade" />{{Rp|page=134}} Some critics prefer to call this genre "psychological realism",<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Coutinho |first1=Afrânio |title=Enciclopédia de literatura brasileira |last2=Sousa |first2=José Galante de |date=1990 |publisher=Fundação de assistência ao estudante |others=Oficina literária Afrânio Coutinho |isbn=978-85-222-0241-6 |location=Rio de Janeiro |language=pt-BR |trans-title=Encyclopaedia of Brazilian literature}}</ref>{{Rp|page=1098}} because it presents the interior, the thought, the absence of action combined with psychological and philosophical density.<ref name="andrade" />{{Rp|page=87}} However, there are also romantic residues in ''Dom Casmurro'', such as the [[Eroticism|erotic]] metaphor in relation to Capitu, described with "gipsy's eyes, oblique and sly."<ref name="andrade" />{{Rp|page=134}} [[Ian Watt]] has stated that realism refers to the [[Empiricism|empirical]] experiences of men,<ref>{{Cite book |last=Watt |first=Ian |title=The rise of the novel: studies in Defoe, Richardson and Fielding |date=1957 |publisher=University of California press |isbn=978-0-520-01318-6 |location=Berkeley (Calif.) Los Angeles (Calif.)}}</ref>{{Rp|page=12}} but the recreation of the past through Bentinho's memory, his "stains" of recollections, brings the book closer to an [[Impressionism|impressionist]] novel.<ref name="andrade" />{{Rp|page=84}}

For {{Ill|John Gledson|pt|John Gledson}}, ''Dom Casmurro'' "is not a realist novel in the sense that it presents us with facts in an open and easily assimilated form. It presents them to us, but we have to read against the narrative to discover and connect them for ourselves. In doing so, we will learn more not only about the characters and the events described in the story, but also about the protagonist, Bento, the narrator himself."<ref name="gladson">{{Cite book |last=Gledson |first=John |title=The deceptive realism of Machado de Assis: a dissenting interpretation of 'Dom Casmurro' |date=1984 |publisher=Francis Cairns |isbn=978-0-905205-19-9 |series=Liverpool monographs in Hispanic studies |location=Liverpool}}</ref>{{Rp|page=14}} We can therefore conclude that ''Dom Casmurro'' is a realist novel that focuses on psychological analysis (or exposition) and ironically criticises society, in this case the elite of Rio de Janeiro, through the behaviour of certain characters.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Terra |first1=Ernani |title=Português: de olho no mundo do trabalho |last2=Nicola |first2=José de |publisher=Scipione |year=2006 |location=São Paulo |language=pt-br |trans-title=Portuguese: with an eye on the world of work}}</ref>{{Rp|page=419}} Critics have also noted certain elements of modernism in ''Dom Casmurro''. Some, such as [[Roberto Schwarz]], even go so far as to call it "the first Brazilian modernist novel",<ref name="guilhermino" /> mainly because of its short chapters, its fragmentary, non-linear structure, its penchant for the allusive, the [[Metalanguage|metalinguistic]] attitude of those who write and those who see themselves as writers, the interruption of the narrative and the possibility of multiple readings or interpretations; "anti-literary" elements that would only be popularised by modernism decades later.<ref name="andrade" />{{Rp|page=134}}

Others see it as a detective novel, where the reader would have to investigate the details of the actions, distrusting the narrator's point of view to reach a conclusion about the authenticity of the adultery.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Braslauskas |first=Ligia |date=2 July 2008 |title=Abertura da Flip vira aula com leitura de Schwarz sobre Machado de Assis |trans-title=Flip opening turns into a lesson with Schwarz reading about Machado de Assis |url=http://www1.folha.uol.com.br/folha/ilustrada/ult90u418653.shtml |access-date=2010-10-29 |website=Folha de S.Paulo |language=pt-br}}</ref> because "from the beginning there are inconsistencies, obscure steps, disconcerting emphases, which form an enigma."<ref name="schwarz">{{Cite book |last=Schwarz |first=Roberto |title=Duas meninas |publisher=Companhia das Letras |year=1997 |location=São Paulo |language=pt-Br |trans-title=Two girls}}</ref>{{Rp|page=9}} Among these clues are the metaphor of the "eyes like the tide" and the "gipsy's eyes, oblique and sly", the parallel with the Shakespearean drama of [[Othello (character)|Othello]] and [[Desdemona]], the closeness to the opera of [[tenor]] Marcolini (the duet, the [[Trio (music)|trio]] and the [[quartet]]), the "strange resemblances", the relationship with Escobar at the seminary, Capitu's lucidity and Bentinho's obscurantism, the ex-seminarian's delirious and perverse imagination, the biblical precept from [[Ecclesiastes]] at the end of the book.<ref name="andrade" />{{Rp|page=129}}

=== Themes ===
The main theme of the novel is jealousy and Bentinho's marital tragedy. From quoting the emperors [[Julius Caesar|Caesar]], [[Augustus]], [[Nero]] and [[Masinissa]], who killed their wives accused of adultery, to quoting Shakespeare's ''[[Othello]]'', the Moor who killed his wife for the same reason. His first hint of jealousy appears in chapter 62, when he asks José Dias, a dependent at his mother's house, when the latter goes to visit him at the seminary, "She's gay and happy as ever. What a giddy creature! Just waiting to hook some young buck of the neighbourhood and marry him."<ref name="de assis" />{{Rp|page=115}} For Bentinho, the answer was a shock, as he writes: "[..] and it was accompanied by such a violent beating of my heart that even now I seem to hear it."<ref name="de assis" />{{Rp|page=116}} According to Roberto Schwarz, in ''Dom Casmurro'' "the most dramatic instance lies in jealousy, which had been one of the boy's many imaginative outbursts, and now, associated with the authority of being the landowner and husband, it becomes a force for devastation".<ref name="schwarz" />{{Rp|page=29}} In ''Dom Casmurro'', however, the theme of jealousy is presented from the point of view of a husband who suspects that he has been betrayed, with no room for the other characters' versions.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Kosovski |first=Ester |title=O "crime" de adultério |date=1997 |publisher=MAUAD |isbn=978-85-85756-58-1 |series=Série jurídica |location=Rio de Janeiro, RJ |language=pt-br |trans-title=The "crime" of adultery}}</ref>{{Rp|page=127}}

[[File:Rio_de_janeiro_1889_01.jpg|thumb|300x300px|Rio de Janeiro in 1889.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Lago |first=Pedro Correa do |title=Coleção [[Isabel, Princess Imperial of Brazil|Princesa Isabel]]: Fotografia do século XIX. |publisher=Capivara |year=2008 |language=pt-br |trans-title=Princess Isabel Collection: 19th century photography}}</ref>]]
Another very clear theme of the book is its setting – [[Rio de Janeiro]] during the [[Second reign (Empire of Brazil)|Second Reign]], in the house of a member of the elite. Critics have written that, at the time of its publication, it was the book that "made the most intense psychological exploration of the character of Rio de Janeiro's society".<ref name="faraco; moura">{{Cite book |last1=Faraco |first1=Carlos Emílio |title=Português Projetos |last2=Moura |first2=Francisco Mato |publisher=Ática |year=2009 |location=São Paulo |language=pt-br |trans-title=Portuguese Projects}}</ref>{{Rp|page=231}} Bento is a landowner who went to university and became a lawyer, and represents a different class from Capitu, who is intelligent but from a lower-class family.<ref name="faraco; moura" />{{Rp|page=231}} The narrator uses French and English quotations throughout the book, a common practice among 19th-century aristocrats in Brazil.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Faoro |first=Raimundo |author-link=Raymundo Faoro |title=Machado De Assis: A Piramide E O Trapezio |publisher=Globo |year=2001 |isbn=978-85-250-3430-4 |language=pt-BR |trans-title=Machado De Assis: The Pyramid And The Trapezium}}</ref>{{Rp|page=181}} The contrast between the two characters has given rise to interpretations that Bentinho destroyed his wife's [[persona]] because he was a member of the elite and she was poor (see [[Dom Casmurro#Interpretations|Interpretations]]). In ''Dom Casmurro'', the man is the result of his own duality and is incoherent within himself, while the woman is sly and charming.<ref name="guilhermino" /> Thus, it is a book that represents the politics, ideology and religion of the Second Reign.<ref name="gladson" />{{Rp|page=13}}

[[File:Almeida_Júnior_-_Cena_de_Família_de_Adolfo_Augusto_Pinto,_1891.JPG|left|thumb|327x327px|Common ''[[carioca]]'' family scene from the time of Dom Casmurro, 1891 (''Family Scene'' by Adolpho Augusto Pinto; artist: [[Almeida Júnior]])<ref name="faraco; moura" />{{Rp|page=265}}]]
According to Eduardo de Assis Duarte, "the universe of the white, noble elite is the setting through which thenarrator character distils his resentment and distrust of the alleged [[adultery]]".<ref>{{Cite book |last=Machado de Assis |title=Machado de Assis afro-descendente: escritos de caramujo (antologia) |publisher=Pallas |year=2007 |isbn=978-85-347-0408-3 |editor-last=Duarte |editor-first=Eduardo de Assis |location=Rio de Janeiro |language=pt-br |trans-title=Machado de Assis of African descent: writings of caramujo (anthology) |oclc=ocm86122054}}</ref>{{Rp|page=215}} Schwarz states that the novel represents the social relations and behaviour of the Brazilian elite of the time: [[Progressivism|progressive]] and [[Social liberalism|liberal]] on the one hand, [[Patriarchy|patriarchal]] and authoritarian on the other.<ref name="schwarz" />{{Rp|page=29}} Another point that has been studied is that Dom Casmurro is almost non-communicative with Capitu – hence the fact that only the girl's gestures and glances (and not her words) indicate that she may have cheated on him.<ref name="maguina">{{Cite book |last=Maguiña |first=Carlos García-Bedoya |title=Memorias de JALLA 2004 Lima: sextas jornadas andinas de literatura latinoamericana |publisher=Universidad Nacional Mayor de San Marcos |year=2005 |isbn=9799972463036 |edition=2 |location=Lima |language=es |trans-title=Memories of JALLA 2004 Lima: Sixth Andean Conference on Latin American Literature}}</ref>{{Rp|page=1081}} Bento is a quiet man who keeps to himself. One of his friends once sent him a letter that said: "I am going to my old place at [[Petrópolis]], Dom Casmurro. See if you can't tear yourself away from the cave in [[Engenho Novo]] and come spend a couple of weeks with me."<ref name="de assis" />{{Rp|page=5}} This isolation, which becomes a reason for him to "tie together the two ends of his life", is also one of the themes of the novel.<ref name="maguina" />{{Rp|page=1081}} The critic Barreto Filho, for example, noted that it was "the tragic spirit that would shape Machado's entire work, leading destinies towards madness, absurdity and, in the best of cases, solitary old age."<ref>{{Cite book |last=Bosi |first=Alfredo |title=Machado de Assis |publisher=[[Publifolha]] |year=2002 |series=Folha Explica |language=pt-br |trans-title=Machado de Assis – Folha Explains}}</ref>{{Rp|page=12}}

One of the central problems in all of Machado's work, and also in this book, is the question of "to what extent do I exist only through others?", since Bento Santiago becomes Dom Casmurro, influenced by the events and actions of those close to him.<ref name="andrade" />{{Rp|page=135}} Eugênio Gomes observes that the theme of the son's physical resemblance, resulting from the mother's "impregnation" by the characteristics of a beloved man, without the latter having conceived the son (as happens between Capitu, her son Ezequiel and his possible father Escobar), was a hot topic in ''Dom Casmurro''<nowiki/>'s time.<ref name="marquior">{{Cite book |last=Merquior |first=José Guilherme |title=De Anchieta a Euclides: breve história da literatura brasileira |publisher=Olympio |year=1977 |edition=1 |series=Brazilian Documents Collection |volume=182 |language=pt-br |trans-title=From Anchieta to Euclides: a brief history of Brazilian literature}}</ref>{{Rp|page=181}} [[Antonio Candido]] has also written that one of the main themes of ''Dom Casmurro'' is the assumption that an imagined fact is real, an element that is also present in Machado's short stories:<ref name="franca">{{Cite book |last1=França |first1=Eduardo Melo |url=https://www.worldcat.org/title/440712558 |title=Ruptura ou amadurecimento? uma análise dos primeiros contos de Machado de Assis |last2=Vieira |first2=Anco Márcio Tenório |publisher=[[Federal University of Pernambuco|UFPE]] |year=2008 |isbn=978-85-7315-551-8 |location=Recife |language=pt-br |trans-title=Rupture or maturity? an analysis of Machado de Assis' first short stories |oclc=440712558}}</ref>{{Rp|page=190–192}} the narrator, through himself, would tell the facts through a certain [[Insanity|madness]] that would make his [[Fantasy (psychology)|fantasies]], expressed in exaggerations and deceptions, come [[Reality|true]].<ref name="franca" />{{Rp|page=190–192}}

=== Style ===
With ''Dom Casmurro'', Machado maintains the style he had been developing since ''[[The Posthumous Memoirs of Brás Cubas]]''. The language is highly cultured, full of references, but informal, in a conversational tone with the reader, almost [[Modernism|proto-modernist]], filled with [[intertextuality]], [[metalanguage]] and irony. It is considered to be the last novel in his "realist trilogy".<ref name="andrade" />{{Rp|page=3}} However, in ''Dom Casmurro'' the author also uses features reminiscent of [[romanticism]] (or "conventionalism", as some modern critics prefer).<ref name="andrade" />{{Rp|page=79}} Bentinho's relationship with Capitu, his jealousy and possible adultery are examples of this. Moreover, there is always a romantic streak, with ''[[Ressurreição|Resurrection]]'', where he describes the "graceful bust" of the character Lívia, and in his realist phase, where there is a fixation on Capitu's dubious "gipsy's eyes, oblique and sly".<ref>{{Cite magazine |last=Teixeira |first=Jerônimo |date=24 September 2008 |title=Machado: Um Verdadeiro Imortal |trans-title=Machado: A True Immortal |magazine=[[Veja (magazine)|Veja]] |language=pt-br}}</ref>{{Rp|page=166}} Capitu is able to drive the action, even though the dominance of the Romanesque plot has not diminished.<ref>{{Cite magazine |last=Rangel |first=Maria Lúcia Silveira |date=1 June 2000 |title=As Personagens Femininas em Machado de Assis |trans-title=Female Characters in Machado de Assis |url=http://kplus.cosmo.com.br/materia.asp?co=53&rv=Literatura |magazine=Revista Literária Brasileira |language=pt-br |volume=17 |issue=10|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20051110060608/http://kplus.cosmo.com.br/materia.asp?co=53&rv=Literatura |archive-date=2005-11-10 }}</ref>

{| class="toccolours" style="float: right; margin-left: 1em; margin-right: 2em; font-size: 85%; background:#c6dbf7; color:black; width:30em; max-width: 25%;" cellspacing="0"
| style="text-align: left;" |"The restrained, 'lean', sober style and the short chapters, arranged in harmonious blocks, blend perfectly into the plot's inverted, fragmented setting. Nothing escapes the narrator's reflection, not even his own account, which is also plagued by the demon of analysis, by the "underground man", who relativises any sentimental outpouring with irony and scepticism."
|-
| style="text-align: right;" |—Fernando Teixeira Andrade.<ref name="andrade" />{{Rp|page=154}}
|}
However, as in the previous novel, in ''Dom Casmurro'' there is the same break with the realists who followed [[Gustave Flaubert|Flaubert]], whose narrators disappeared behind narrative objectivity, and also with the [[Naturalism (literature)|naturalists]] who, like [[Émile Zola|Zola]], narrated every detail of the plot; the author chooses to abstain from both methods to cultivate fragmentation and to create a narrator who intervenes in the narrative to communicate with the reader, commenting on his own novel with philosophy, [[intertextuality]] and [[metalanguage]].<ref name="andrade" />{{Rp|page=81}} An example of this is found in the one-paragraph chapter 133, in which the narrator writes "You must already understand. Now read another chapter".<ref name="de assis" />{{Rp|page=221}} As a lawyer, Bento also makes use of [[rhetoric]] to present his version of the facts;<ref name="franca" />{{Rp|page=192}} his narrative, in psychological time, follows the shifts of his memory in a less random way than in ''The Posthumous Memoirs of Brás Cubas'', but just as fragmentarily.<ref name="andrade" />{{Rp|page=163}} However, some themes are noticeable: his childhood in Matacavalos; Dona Glória's house and the Pádua family, relatives and households; his acquaintance with Capitu; the seminary; married life; the intensification and outbursts of jealousy; the separation, etc.<ref name="andrade" />{{Rp|page=163}}

In fact, the book's style is very close to that of [[Impressionism (literature)|associative impressionism]], with a break in the [[Story structure|linear narrative]], so that the actions do not follow a logical or [[Chronology|chronological]] thread, but are told as they emerge from Bento Santiago's memory and will.<ref name="andrade" />{{Rp|page=84}} [[José Guilherme Merquior]] noted that the style of the book "remains in line with the two previous novels, with short chapters, marked by appeals to the reader in a more or less humorous tone and by digressions between seriousness and humour".<ref>{{Cite book |last=Machado de Assis |title=Dom Casmurro |publisher=Novo Século |year=2001 |isbn=8586880191 |editor-last=Araújo |editor-first=Homero |language=pt-br |editor-last2=Gonzaga |editor-first2=Sergius}}</ref>{{Rp|page=7}} [[Digression]]s are "intrusions" of elements that seem to deviate from the central theme of the book and which Machado uses as interpolations of episodes, memories or thoughts, often quoting other authors or works or commenting on chapters, sentences or the organisation of the whole book itself.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Achcar |first=Francisco |title=Contos de Machado de Assis |publisher=Sol |year=1999 |language=pt-br |chapter=Introdução a Machado de Assis |trans-chapter=An Introduction to Machado de Assis}}</ref>{{Rp|page=10–12}}

=== Literary influences ===
Out of all Machado's novels ''Dom Casmurro'' is probably the work with the most [[Theology|theological]] influence. There are references to [[James the Great|St James]] and [[Saint Peter|St Peter]], mainly because the narrator Bentinho studied at a [[seminary]]. In addition, in chapter 17<ref name="de assis" />{{Rp|page=34–35}} the author alludes to a [[Paganism|pagan]] [[oracle]] from the myth of [[Achilles]] and to Jewish beliefs.<ref name="faraco; moura" />{{Rp|page=232–233}} At the end of the novel, he also uses the biblical precept of Jesus, son of [[Book of Sirach|Sirach]], as an [[Epigraph (literature)|epigraph]]: "Be not jealous of thy wife lest she set herself to deceive thee with the malice that she learnt from thee".<ref name="de assis" />{{Rp|page=240}}

[[File:Page_004_(Faust,_1925).png|left|thumb|In the book, Bento alludes to [[Johann Wolfgang von Goethe|Goethe]]'s [[Faust]] to evoke his memories. (Illustration: [[Harry Clarke]], 1925).]]

The theological influence is not limited to the facts, it is also found in the names of the characters: Ezequiel – [[Ezekiel|biblical name]]; Bento Santiago – Bento (saint), Bentinho (diminutive for saint), Santo + Iago (mix of good and evil, from "saint" and [[Iago]], the evil character in [[William Shakespeare|Shakespeare]]'s ''[[Othello]]''); Capitu – suggests numerous derivations: from ''caput'', ''capitis'' which in Latin means "head", in an allusion to intelligence or cleverness (phonetically, it's similar to ''capeta'' (devil), an image of vivacity, or of the malice and treachery with which the jealous narrator infuses it); "Capitolina" is also reminiscent of the verb "[[Capitulation (surrender)|capitulate]]" (to renounce), the resigned attitude of the wife who has been insulted by her husband, and who capitulates and renounces any reaction.<ref name="andrade" />{{Rp|page=161}}

To evoke his memories, Bento quotes [[Faust]], by [[Johann Wolfgang von Goethe]] (1749–1832), transcribing: "Ah there, are you come again, restless shades?".<ref name="de assis" />{{Rp|page=8}} Faust is the main character in the play who sells his soul to the demon [[Mephistopheles]] so he can be given [[immortality]], eternal youth and wealth.<ref name="andrade" />{{Rp|page=163}} The "restless shades" are, in this case, the memories of people and incidents from the past, dormant but still disturbing.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Ribeiro |first=Luis Filipe |title=Mulheres de papel: um estudo do imaginário em José de Alencar e Machado de Assis |date=1996 |publisher=[[Fluminense Federal University]] Press |isbn=978-85-228-0187-9 |location=[[Niterói]] |language=pt-br |trans-title=Women on paper: a study of the imaginary in José de Alencar and Machado de Assis}}</ref>{{Rp|page=236}} For American critic [[Helen Caldwell]], this quote is the one that sets Bento's memory in motion: "closely followed by the allegory of the 'opera', with its colloquies in heaven between God and Satan, gives the impression that Santiago perhaps identified himself with Faust and felt he had sold his soul to the devil".<ref name="caldwell">{{Cite book |last=Caldwell |first=Helen |url=https://archive.org/details/brazilianothello0000cald/mode/2up |title=The Brazilian Othello of Machado de Assis: A Study of Dom Casmurro |publisher=University of California Press |year=1960 |edition=6 |series=Perspectives in criticism |location=Berkeley and Los Angeles |language=en}}</ref>{{Rp|page=131}} Critics note that the ancient and modern classics and the biblical quotations are never mere erudition in Machado; on the contrary, they enlighten the narratives and properly inscribe them in the great archetypes of universal literature.<ref name="andrade" />{{Rp|page=163}}

[[File:Oteloydesdemona_MuñozDegrain.jpg|thumb|''Othello and Desdemona'' by [[Antonio Muñoz Degrain|Muñoz Degrain]] (1881) is a portrait of Shakespeare's drama ''Othello'': an archetypal influence on the jealousy of Bentinho in ''Dom Casmurro''.]]

This is also the case with Shakespeare's ''Othello''. Othello is the archetype of jealousy. Bento interacts with the play three times in addition to chapter 62, in chapter 72 and chapter 135: his first remark is on the relationship between Desdemona and her Moorish husband, while in the second mention he watches the play and says that, although he "had never seen or read ''Othello''", he realised the similarity to his own relationship with Capitu when he arrived at the theatre.<ref name="andrade" />{{Rp|page=165}} [[Helen Caldwell]] strongly supported the thesis that ''Dom Casmurro'' was influenced by ''Othello'' not only in the theme of jealousy but also in the characters; for her, Bento is the "Iago of himself" and José Dias (who loved superlatives) a typical Shakespearean character who devotes his energies to counselling (like ''[[Hamlet]]''<nowiki/>'s [[Polonius]], who gives advice to his son and exaggerates the facts when he talks to the king).<ref name="caldwell" />{{Rp|page=3–4}}

Other sources refer to the physical resemblance of the son (in this case, Ezequiel) as a result of the mother being "impregnated" with the features of a beloved man, without the latter having conceived him, a theme already used earlier by [[Émile Zola|Zola]] in his ''[[Madeleine Férat]]'' (1868) and also in [[Johann Wolfgang von Goethe|Goethe]]'s earlier ''[[The Elective Affinities]]'' (1809), where Eduard and Charlotte's son has the eyes of Ottilie, with whom Eduard is in love, and the features of the captain, loved by Charlotte;<ref name="marquior" />{{Rp|page=181}} Bento's pessimistic philosophy, where critics have noted the direct influence of [[Arthur Schopenhauer|Schopenhauer]], for whom "the pleasure of existence does not rest in living, but is only achieved in contemplating what has been lived" (hence Bento's aim to portray his past),<ref name="marquior" />{{Rp|page=182}}<ref name="gladson" />{{Rp|page=148}} and Pascal, as Bentinho's Christianity is analogous to the [[Jesuits|Jesuit]] casuistry attacked by him and the [[Jansenism|Jansenists]].<ref>{{Cite book |last=Maia Neto |first=José Raimundo |title=O Ceticismo Na Obra De Machado De Assis |date=30 August 2007 |publisher=Annablume |isbn=978-85-7419-739-5 |language=pt-BR |trans-title=Scepticism in the Works of Machado De Assis}}</ref>{{Rp|page=160}}

== Influence and dialogue ==
''Dom Casmurro'', just as ''The'' ''Posthumous Memoirs of Brás Cubas'', has its own style and "anti-literary" elements that would only be popularised by [[modernism]] decades later – short chapters, a fragmentary, non-linear structure, a tendency towards the allusive, a [[Metalinguistics|metalinguistic]] stance of the writer and of those who see themselves as writers, interferences in the narrative and the possibility of multiple readings and interpretations.<ref name="andrade" />{{Rp|page=134}}

[[Oswald de Andrade]], a leading figure in the important 1922 [[Modern Art Week]], whose literary style, similar to [[Mário de Andrade]]'s, was part of the experimental, metalinguistic and city-based tradition that was somewhat comparable to the work of Machado de Assis and had ''Dom Casmurro'' as one of his favourite books and saw the writer as a master of the Brazilian novel.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Martins |first=Cláudia Mentz |title=Oswald de Andrade e sua crítica literária |publisher=Federal University of Rio Grande |pages=106–107 |language=pt-br |trans-title=Oswald de Andrade and his literary criticism}}</ref> The book's most direct influence, however, is foreign; [[John Barth]] wrote ''[[The Floating Opera]]'' (1956) which, in [[David Morrell (writer)|David Morrell]]'s comparison, has similar traits to the plot of ''Dom Casmurro'', such as the fact that the main characters in both books are lawyers, even consider suicide and compare life to an opera, and live in a [[love triangle]].<ref>{{Cite book |last=Morrell |first=David |title=John Barth: an introduction |publisher=Pennsylvania State University Press |year=1976 |isbn=978-0-271-01220-9 |location=University Park |language=en}}</ref>{{Rp|page=127}} In fact, all of Barth's early works were strongly influenced by Machado de Assis's book, especially his technique for writing the novel and the plot of ''Dom Casmurro''.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Bellei |first=Sérgio Luís Prado |date=July 1979 |title=Machado de Assis nos Estados Unidos: A Influência de Dom Casmurro nos Romances Iniciais de John Barth |trans-title=Machado de Assis in the United States: Dom Casmurro's Influence on John Barth's Early Novels |journal=Ciências Humanas |language=pt-br |location=Rio de Janeiro |volume=3 |issue=10 |pages=30–44}}</ref> ''Dom Casmurro'' is also linked to ''[[The Devil to Pay in the Backlands]]'' (1956), in which [[João Guimarães Rosa|Guimarães Rosa]] takes up the "journey of memory" found in Machado's book.<ref name="lucas">{{Cite magazine |last=Lucas |first=Fábio |date=2008 |title=A Condição Feminina de Capitu |trans-title=Capitu's Female Status |magazine=Revista da Academia Brasileira de Letras |pages=9–23 |language=pt-br |volume=50 |issue=85}}</ref>{{Rp|page=82}}

Bentinho's challenge to attract and win Capitu over to achieve his goal of being interested in his girlfriend's gifts – an attitude identified as a "lordly and possessive model that dispenses with greater subtleties" – indirectly influenced [[Graciliano Ramos]] when he wrote one of his most famous modernist novels of the 20th century, ''{{Ill|S. Bernardo (novel)|lt=São Bernardo|pt|S. Bernardo (romance)}}'' (1934), portraying Paulo Honório's direct action in capturing Madalena.<ref name="lucas" />{{Rp|page=11}} ''Dom Casmurro'' also influenced, only this time explicitly, [[Dalton Trevisan]]'s short story "''Capitu Sou Eu"'', published in a book of short stories of the same name in 2003, in which a teacher and a rebellious student have a sordid affair and discuss the personality of the character.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Estação Veja – livros |trans-title=Estação Veja – books |url=https://veja.abril.com.br/idade/estacao/veja_recomenda/151003/capitu.html |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090318124333/http://veja.abril.com.br/idade/estacao/veja_recomenda/151003/capitu.html |archive-date=2009-03-18 |access-date=2010-10-31 |language=pt-br}}</ref>

Modern critics also attribute to ''Dom Casmurro'' ideas and concepts that would later be developed by [[Sigmund Freud]] and his [[psychoanalysis]] projects. Machado's book was published in the same year as Freud's ''[[The Interpretation of Dreams]]'', and Dom Casmurro had already written sentences such as "I think that I learned the taste of her felicity in the milk with which she gave me suck",<ref name="de assis" />{{Rp|page=143}} an allusion to what Freud later called the [[Oral stage|oral phase]] in [[psychoanalysis]], in relation to the mouth–breast, in what some call a "Freudian premonition".<ref name="andrade" />{{Rp|page=144}} The boy Bentinho was introspective and his daydreams replaced part of reality: "Daydreams are like other dreams, they weave themselves on the pattern of our inclinations and memories"<ref name="de assis" />{{Rp|page=55}} wrote Dom Casmurro when he was older, in an anticipation of the Freudian concept of the unity of psychological life in dreams and waking life.<ref name="andrade" />{{Rp|page=144}}

The subsequent adaptations of ''[[Dom Casmurro#Adaptations|Dom Casmurro]]'', in countless media and forms, also prove the dialogue and influence that the novel still has in many different areas, whether in cinema, theatre, popular and classical music, television, comics, literature itself, etc.

== Critic ==

=== Introduction ===
{| class="toccolours" style="float: right; margin-left: 1em; margin-right: 2em; font-size: 85%; background:#c6dbf7; color:black; width:30em; max-width: 25%;" cellspacing="0"
| style="text-align: left;" |"''Dom Casmurro'' is a work open to so many interpretations, some of which have already been made and published, especially in the last fifty years, and many others which are undoubtedly yet to be made. I don't think any Brazilian novel has been reinterpreted in such a comprehensive way."
|-
| style="text-align: right;" |—[[David Haberly]]<ref name="saraiva" />{{Rp|page=43}}
|}
In short, one could say that criticism of ''Dom Casmurro'' is relatively recent. It was endorsed by Machado's contemporaries and the criticism that followed his death tried to analyse the character Bento and his psychological situation. ''Dom Casmurro'' has also been analysed in studies of [[Human sexuality|sexuality]] and the [[Psyche (psychology)|human psyche]], and [[existentialism]], so that in recent times Machado's work has been commonly attributed an open range of interpretations.<ref name="andrade" />{{Rp|page=82}}

However, the first study that reinvigorated the role of the novel, written by [[Helen Caldwell]] in the 1960s, didn't make an impact in Brazil.<ref name="saraiva" />{{Rp|page=128}} It was only recently, through [[Silviano Santiago]] in 1969 and especially Roberto Schwarz in 1991, that Caldwell's book was discovered and opened up new possibilities for Machado's work.<ref name="saraiva" />{{Rp|page=128}} This was also the decade when Machado de Assis received the most critical attention in France, and the novel received important commentary from French translators; Dom Casmurro's book was of interest mainly to literary journals of psychology and [[psychiatry]], which also recommended reading ''L'Aliéniste'', "''[[O alienista|The Psychiatrist]]''", to their readers.<ref>{{Cite book |title=Recortes machadianos |publisher=PUC-SP |year=2003 |isbn=978-85-283-0282-0 |editor-last=Mariano |editor-first=Ana Salles |location=São Paulo |language=pt-br |trans-title=Snippets of Machado |oclc=ocm52875129 |editor-last2=Oliveira |editor-first2=Maria Rosa Duarte de}}</ref>{{Rp|page=129}}

Modern critics, strongly influenced by the history of interpretations of the novel, which will be discussed below, identify three successive readings of ''Dom Casmurro'', namely:
# Romanesque, it's the story of the rise and fall of a love, from the idyll of youth, through marriage, to the death of a partner and a questionable child.<ref name="andrade" />{{Rp|page=129}}
# Close to the psychoanalytic and detective novel, it is the accusatory libel of the husband-lawyer, who looks for signs and proofs of adultery, which he takes as undeniable.<ref name="andrade" />{{Rp|page=129}}
# It must be carried out against the current, by reversing the course of suspicion, turning the narrator into the defendant and the accuser into the accused.<ref name="andrade" />{{Rp|page=129}}

The history of interpretations in the next section, focusing on criticism from the 1930s and 40s to the 1980s, shows the turn that has been taken in the different interpretations of ''Dom Casmurro'', supported not only by Brazilian critics, but also, and considerably, by international ones.<ref name="schwarz" />{{Rp|page=228}} The majority of interpretations of the novel are influenced by sociology, [[feminism]] and [[psychoanalysis]],<ref name="saraiva" />{{Rp|page=7}} and most also refer to the theme of the narrator's jealousy, Dom Casmurro; some arguing that there was no [[adultery]] and others that the author left the question open to the reader.<ref name="caldwell" />{{Rp|page=vi}}

===Interpretations===
Among the themes interpreted over the years by critics and essayists were Capitu's possible [[adultery]], a socio-psychological analysis of the characters and the character of the narrator-character. Critics in the 1930s and 40s wrote that Bento Santiago suffered from [[dysthymia]] and linked his quiet and solitary personality to the author himself, who supposedly suffered from [[epilepsy]].<ref name="teive etal">{{Cite journal |last1=Teive |first1=Hélio A. G. |last2=Paola |first2=Luciano De |last3=Cardoso |first3=Francisco |date=2007 |title=A neuro-psiquiatria em Machado de Assis. |trans-title=Neuropsychiatry in Machado De Assis |url=https://www.actamedicaportuguesa.com/revista/index.php/amp/article/view/860 |journal=Acta Médica Portuguesa |language=pt |volume=20 |issue=4 |pages=385–92 |doi=10.20344/amp.860  |doi-access=free|doi-broken-date=4 May 2026 |pmid=18198085 |issn=1646-0758}}</ref>{{Rp|pages=386–387; 390}} His friend Escobar is said to suffer from [[Obsessive–compulsive disorder|obsessive-compulsive disorder]] and [[Tic|motor tics]], with possible control over them.<ref name="teive etal" />{{Rp|pages=|page=390}} These considerations played some of a [[psychologism]] role regarding ''Dom Casmurro'' and Machado de Assis. Modern critics see this interpretation as the fruit of the psychologism of the time, which exaggerated his sufferings and gave no importance to his career rise (as a journalist and [[Civil service|public employee]]).<ref name="andrade" />{{Rp|page=76}} [[Psychiatrist]]s such as José Leme Lopes noted Bentinho's developmental inhibitions and his "delay in affective development and [[neurosis]]".<ref name="andrade" />{{Rp|page=145}} The Bentinho that Dom Casmurro evokes would have "late [[Human sexuality|sexuality]]" and "a predominance of [[Fantasy (psychology)|fantasy]] over reality, with [[anguish]]".<ref name="andrade" />{{Rp|page=146}}

According to the psychiatric interpretation, this is one of the reasons for his insane jealousy.<ref name="franca" />{{Rp|page=190}} [[Psychoanalytic literary criticism|Psychoanalytic critics]] believe that Bento was "born without the power to have his own desires".<ref name="franca" />{{Rp|page=190}} The character was born to "take the place of a stillborn brother", to which psychoanalyst [[Arminda Aberastury]] writes that "he always drew attention to the difficulties that children who are predestined, who come in place of another, will have in their psychological development".<ref>{{Cite book |last=Freitas |first=Luiz Alberto Pinheiro de |title=Freud e Machado de Assis: uma interseção entre psicanálise e literatura |publisher=Mauad |year=2001 |isbn=978-85-7478-607-0 |language=pt-BR |trans-title=Freud and Machado de Assis: an intersection between psychoanalysis and literature}}</ref>{{Rp|page=130}} Dom Casmurro was a boy who obeyed his mother's every wish: he entered the seminary, became a priest, and so some see him as an insecure and spoiled man.<ref name="franca" />{{Rp|page=190}} Bentinho is seen as a typical 19th century Brazilian man from Rio's high society, with no historical perspective (hence his desire to write ''History of the Surburbs'' but then choosing to first recount the memories of his youth), [[Pessimism|pessimistic]] and elusive.<ref name="petronio; alvarenga" />{{Rp|page=7}} Others, such as [[Millôr Fernandes]], also believe that Bentinho had a tendency towards homosexuality and that he was somewhat fond of Escobar.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Fernandes |first=Millôr |date=26 January 2005 |title=Coluna do Millôr |trans-title=Millôr's column |url=https://veja.abril.com.br/260105/millor.html |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090202064401/https://veja.abril.com.br/260105/millor.html |archive-date=2009-02-02 |access-date=2010-10-31 |website=[[Veja (magazine)|Veja]] |language=pt-br}}</ref>

Over the years, ''Dom Casmurro'' has been perceived from two main points of view: one, the oldest, of trusting the words written by Bento Santiago, without further questioning ([[José Veríssimo]], Lúcia Miguel Pereira, [[Afrânio Coutinho]], [[Erico Verissimo|Érico Veríssimo]] and especially [[Dom Casmurro#Reception|Machado's contemporaries]] are part of this group);<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Ellis |first=Keith |date=1962 |title=Technique and Ambiguity in "Dom Casmurro" |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/337406 |journal=Hispania |volume=45 |issue=3 |pages=436–440 |doi=10.2307/337406 |jstor=337406 |issn=0018-2133|url-access=subscription }}</ref>{{Rp|pages=76–81}} and the other, latest, that Machado de Assis leaves it up to the reader to come to their own conclusions about the characters and the plot, which is one of the most frequent characteristics of his literature.<ref name="petronio; alvarenga" />{{Rp|page=7}} Advocates of this approach often shy away from the issues of the novel and see ''Dom Casmurro'' as an open-ended work.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Décio |first=João |title=Retorno ao romance eterno: Dom Casmurro de Machado de Assis e outros ensaios |publisher=Editora da FURB |year=1999 |isbn=978-85-7114-083-7 |location=Blumenau |language=pt-br |trans-title=Return to the eternal novel: Machado de Assis' Dom Casmurro and other essays}}</ref>

{| class="toccolours" style="float: right; margin-left: 1em; margin-right: 2em; font-size: 85%; background:#c6dbf7; color:black; width:30em; max-width: 25%;" cellspacing="0"
| style="text-align: left;" |"The conclusion to which Santiago gradually leads the reader is that the deceit perpetraded against him by his dearly loved wife and dearly loved friend wrought upon him and changed him from the kind, loving, ingenuous Bento into the hard, cruel and cynical Dom Casmurro."
|-
| style="text-align: right;" |—[[Helen Caldwell]],<ref name="caldwell" />{{Rp|page=10}} one of the key authors in changing the common interpretation and judging the narrator instead of Capitu.
|}
The interpretative criticism negatively directed at the narrator and Capitu's salvation, arguing that she didn't betray him, has only recently been made, since the [[feminist movement]] of the 1960s and 1970s and above all by the American essayist [[Helen Caldwell]]. In ''The Brazilian Othello of Machado de Assis'' (1960), she argues that the character Capitu did not betray Bentinho, thus changing the prevailing perception of the novel,<ref name="gladson" />{{Rp|page=7}} and that she is the victim of a cynical Dom Casmurro who actually misleads the reader with words that are not true.<ref name="candido">{{Cite book |last=Candido |first=Antonio |title=Vários escritos |publisher=Duas Cidades |year=1995 |isbn= |location=São Paulo |language=pt-BR |trans-title=Many writings}}</ref>{{Rp|pages=30–31}} Caldwell's main evidence is the author's clear and frequent [[intertextuality]] with Shakespeare's ''[[Othello]]'', whose protagonist kills his wife mistakenly thinking that she has betrayed him. The author writes her thesis from the main perspective that Machado's narrator is autonomous enough to give his own unique version of the facts.<ref name="candido" />{{Rp|pages=30–31}} For the critic, Bentinho doesn't do it on purpose, but out of madness, since he is, in her words, the "[[Iago]] of himself".<ref name="caldwell" />{{Rp|pages=3–4}} Caldwell also revalidated the role of Capitu, who was supposed to be prettier and have better dreams than her husband.<ref name="caldwell" />{{Rp|page=94}} Other foreign critics, such as John Gledson, from the 1980s onwards hypothesised social interests related to the organisation and crisis of the [[Patriarchy|patriarchal]] order during the [[Second reign (Empire of Brazil)|Second Reign]]. For Dona Glória's carrion, mouldy and repressed universe, with its widowers, servants and slaves, the energy and freedom of opinion of the modern, poor girl, daring and irreverent, lucid and active, would become intolerable.<ref name="andrade" />{{Rp|page=130}} One of the evidences of Gledson's argument can be found in chapter 3, which he considers to be the "foundation of the novel", in José Dias' motivation when talking about Capitu's family and reminding Mrs Glória of the promise she made to put Bentinho in the seminary, in other words, treating the "Pádua people" as inferior and their daughter as a dissimulated and poor girl who could corrupt the boy.<ref name="gladson" />{{Rp|pages=26;165}}

Thus, the jealousy of Bentinho, a rich boy from a decaying family, of the typical bachelor of the Second Reign, would condense a broad social problem behind this "new Othello who slanders and destroys his beloved".<ref name="andrade" />{{Rp|page=130}} This sociological interpretation is still preserved today, as we read in the words of the Portuguese essayist [[Hélder Macedo]] who made a statement regarding the theme of jealousy:

: "In the destruction of Capitu, in the neutralisation of the challenge to the alternative way of being that she represents, lies the fundamental purpose of the restoration sought by Bento Santiago through the writing of his memoir. [...] She was a stranger, an intruder, a threat to the ''[[status quo]]'', an undesirable trace of union with a lower social class, thus also implicitly representing the potential emergence of a new political order that threatened the established power. [...] Class and gender are thus fused in the same threat represented by Capitu's supposedly dubious morality."<ref name="saraiva" />{{Rp|page=130}}
From this perspective, the narrator, a [[Stereotype|stereotypical]] tool used by the author to criticise a certain social class of his time,<ref name="andrade" />{{Rp|page=130}} is able to use the [[prejudice]]s of Brazilians to induce them in his argument against Capitu.<ref name="gomes jr">{{Cite magazine |last=Gomes Jr. |first=Luiz Carlos |date=2009 |title=Uma análise do conhecimento casmurro |trans-title=An analysis of casmurro knowledge |magazine=A Palo Seco |publisher=[[Federal University of Sergipe]] |pages=55–67 |language=pt-br |volume=1 |issue=1}}</ref>{{Rp|page=66}} These prejudices include the physical resemblance and mannerisms that a son inherits from his real father, a prejudice that would be common to Brazilian culture, and which Bento uses when talking about how Ezequiel was like Escobar.<ref name="gomes jr" />{{Rp|page=66}}

Aware of the discomfort that the critical debate on the theme of jealousy has caused since then, authors such as {{Ill|José Aderaldo Castello|pt|José Aderaldo Castello}} have claimed that ''Dom Casmurro'' is not a novel about jealousy, but about doubt: "it is par excellence the novel that expresses the atrocious and insoluble conflict between subjective truth and insinuations of high infiltration power, generated by coincidences, appearances and misunderstandings, immediately or belatedly fuelled by intuitions".<ref>{{Cite book |last=Castello |first=José Aderaldo |title=Realidade & Ilusão em Machado de Assis |publisher=Ateliê Editorial |year=1969 |isbn=978-85-7480-410-1 |language=pt-BR}}</ref> The previously mentioned hypotheses that Bento Santiago was really telling the truth and that Capitu had cheated on him and that Machado wanted to leave the truth up to the reader are not disregarded.

The writer [[Lygia Fagundes Telles]], who studied the novel to write the screenplay for the film ''Capitu'' (1968), said in a recent interview that she was the reader who judged Capitu and then Bentinho: "I don't know anymore. My last version is this one, I don't know. I think I've finally stopped judging. In the beginning she was a saint, in the second she was a monster. Now, in my old age, I don't know. I think ''Dom Casmurro'' is more important than ''[[Madame Bovary]]''. In ''Dom Casmurro'' there is doubt, whereas Bovary has it written on her forehead that she's an adulteress".<ref>{{Cite news |date=27 February 2008 |title=Capitu traiu Bentinho? Lygia Fagundes Telles dá sua opinião |trans-title=Did Capitu cheat on Bentinho? Lygia Fagundes Telles gives her opinion |url=https://www.estadao.com.br/cultura/literatura/capitu-traiu-bentinho-lygia-fagundes-telles-da-sua-opiniao/ |url-access=subscription |work=[[O Estado de S. Paulo]] |language=pt-br}}</ref>

== Reception ==
{| class="toccolours" style="float: right; margin-left: 1em; margin-right: 2em; font-size: 85%; background:#c6dbf7; color:black; width:30em; max-width: 25%;" cellspacing="0"
| style="text-align: left;" |"Dom Casmurro came out in 1900. Machado died in 1908. No critic in those eight years ever dared to deny Capitu's adultery."
|-
| style="text-align: right;" |—[[Otto Lara Resende]]<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Resende |first1=Otto Lara |title=Bom dia para nascer: crônicas |last2=Suzuki Jr. |first2=Matinas |publisher=Companhia das Letras |year=1993 |isbn=978-85-7164-313-0 |location=São Paulo |language=pt-br |trans-title=A good day to be born: chronicles}}</ref>
|}
At the time of its publication, ''Dom Casmurro'' was praised by the author's close friends. [[Medeiros e Albuquerque]], for example, said it was "our ''Othello''".<ref>{{Cite book |last=Trevisan |first=Dalton |author-link=Dalton Trevisan |title=Dinorá |publisher=Editora Record |year=1994 |isbn=978-85-01-07830-8 |language=pt-BR}}</ref>{{Rp|page=29}} His friend [[Graça Aranha]] commented on Capitu: "While married, she had her husband's closest friend for a lover".<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Callado |first1=Antônio |title=Crônicas de fim do milênio |last2=Vianna |first2=Martha |publisher=F. Alves |year=1997 |isbn=978-85-265-0384-7 |location=Rio de Janeiro |language=pt-br |trans-title=End of the millennium chronicles}}</ref>{{Rp|page=254}} The first critics seem to have believed the narrator's words, comparing the book to [[Eça de Queiroz]]'s ''[[Cousin Bazilio]]'' (1878) and [[Gustave Flaubert|Flaubert]]'s ''[[Madame Bovary]]'', novels about adultery.<ref>{{Cite journal |year=2004 |title=Dom Casmurro e a colonização |trans-title=Dom Casmurro and colonisation |url=https://doi.org/10.26300/z60b-at72 |journal=Brasil/Brazil: A Journal of Brazilian Literature |language=pt-br |publisher=Brown University, EdiPUCRS, and Pontifícia Universidade Católica do Rio Grande do Sul |volume=17 |issue=31 |doi=10.26300/z60b-at72 |last1=Vieira |first1=Nelson H. |last2=Zilberman |first2=Regina |last3=Valente |first3=Luiz Fernando |last4=Bordini |first4=Maria Da Glória }}</ref>

[[José Veríssimo]] wrote that "''Dom Casmurro'' is about an undoubtedly intelligent man, but a simple one, who from an early age let himself be deceived by the girl he had loved as a child, who had bewitched him with her calculated cheekiness, with her deep innate science of dissimulation, to whom he had given himself with all the fervour compatible with his quiet temperament".<ref>{{Cite book |last=Veríssimo |first=José |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=mk4tAAAAYAAJ |title=História da literatura brasileira de Bento Teixeira (1601) a Machado de Assis (1908) |publisher=University of Brasília Press |year=1981 |language=pt-BR |trans-title=History of Brazilian literature from Bento Teixeira (1601) to Machado de Assis (1908)}}</ref>{{Rp|page=286}} Veríssimo also drew an analogy between ''Dom Casmurro'' and the narrator of [[The Posthumous Memoirs of Brás Cubas|''The'' ''Posthumous Memoirs of Brás Cubas'']]: "Dom Casmurro is the twin brother, albeit with great differences in features if not in character, of Brás Cubas".<ref>{{Cite news |last=Veríssimo |first=José |date=19 March 1900 |title=Novo livro do Sr. Machado de Assis |trans-title=New book by Mr Machado de Assis |url=https://memoria.bn.gov.br/docreader/DocReader.aspx?bib=364568_09&pagfis=177 |work=[[Jornal do Commercio]] |location=Rio de Janeiro |at=Columns 2–5 |language=pt-br}}</ref>

[[File:Machado de Assis 57 years.jpg|thumb|upright|[[Machado de Assis]], c. 1896.|left]]
[[Sílvio Romero|Silvio Romero]] had not accepted Machado's break with narrative linearity and the nature of the traditional plot for some time, and he belittled his prose.<ref name="guilhermino" /> As we know, however, Livraria Garnier published Machado's volumes both in Brazil and in Paris, and with the new book, international critics were already questioning whether Eça de Queiroz was still the best Portuguese language novelist.<ref name="guilhermino" /> [[Artur Azevedo|Artur de Azevedo]] praised the work twice, in one of which he wrote: "''Dom Casmurro'' is one of those books that is impossible to summarise, because it is in the inner life of Bento Santiago that all its charm, all its strength lies",<ref name="pujol">{{Cite book |last=Pujol |first=Alfredo |title=Machado de Assis: curso literário em sete conferências na Sociedade de Cultura Artística de São Paulo |collaboration=Alberto Venancio Filho |publisher=[[Academia Brasileira de Letras]] |year=2007 |isbn=978-85-7440-097-6 |edition=2 |language=pt-BR |trans-title=Machado de Assis: literary course in seven lectures at the Artistic Culture Society of São Paulo}}</ref>{{Rp|page=152}} and concluded that "What is everything, however, in this dark and sad book, where there are pages written with tears and blood, is the fine psychology of the two main characters and the noble and superb style of the narrative".<ref name="pujol" />{{Rp|page=152}}

Machado de Assis sent letters to his friends expressing his satisfaction with the comments published about his book.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Guimarães |first=Hélio |title=Os leitores de Machado de Assis: o romance machadiano e o público de literatura no século 19 |publisher=edusp |year=2004 |isbn=978-85-86372-70-4 |location=São Paulo |language=pt-br |trans-title=The readers of Machado de Assis: the Machado novel and the literary public in the 19th century}}</ref>{{Rp|page=237}} ''Dom Casmurro'' has received countless other criticisms and interpretations over the years; it is now considered one of the greatest contributions to the [[Impressionism (literature)|impressionist novel]] and is considered by some to be one of the greatest exponents of [[Brazilian literature#Realism|Brazilian realism]].<ref name="petronio; alvarenga" />{{Rp|page=7}}

== Publications ==

=== Editions ===
Published by Livraria Garnier in 1900, although the imprint on the title page shows the previous year, ''Dom Casmurro'' was written to be published directly as a book, unlike ''[[The Posthumous Memoirs of Brás Cubas]]'' (1881) and ''[[Quincas Borba]]'' (1891), which were published as pamphlets prior to publication in book format. ''Quincas Borba'' appeared in chapters in the magazine ''A Estação'' from 1886 to 1891 before finally being published in 1892, and ''The Posthumous Memoirs of Brás Cubas'' was in ''[[Revista Brasileira]]'' from March to December 1880 until it was published by Tipografia Nacional in 1881.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Freitas |first=Bruna Canellas de |year=2017 |title=Quincas Borba, o folhetim e livro: uma análise comparada das versões do romance machadiano |trans-title=Quincas Borba, the pamphlet and the book: a comparative analysis of the versions of Machado's novel |url=https://ojs.latic.uerj.br/ojs/index.php/aproximando/issue/view/1 |journal=Revista Aproximando |language=pt-br |volume=3 |issue=4 |pages=1–2}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Facioli |first=Valentim |title=Um Defunto Estrambótico: análise e interpretação das Memórias póstumas de Brás Cubas |date=1 April 2008 |publisher=Edusp |isbn=978-85-314-1083-3 |language=pt-BR |trans-title=A Strange Dead Man: analysing and interpreting The Posthumous Memoirs of Brás Cubas}}</ref>{{Rp|page=56}}

Garnier, which published Machado's works both in Brazil and in Paris (under the name Hippolyte Garnier), received a letter in French from the author on 19 December 1899, complaining about the delay in publication: "We expect ''Dom Casmurro'' on the date you announced. I ask you, with all our interests, that the first batch of copies be large enough, because it could run out quickly, and the delay of the second batch will affect sales", to which the publisher replied on 12 January 1900: "Dom Casmurro did not leave this week, it is a delay of one month due to causes beyond our control [...]".<ref name="magalhaes jr">{{Cite book |last=Magalhães Júnior |first=R. |title=Aprendizado – Vida E Obra De Machado De Assis |publisher=Editora Record |year=2008 |isbn=978-85-01-07653-3 |edition=2 |volume=1 |location=Rio de Janeiro |language=pt-br |trans-title=Learning - Life And Work Of Machado De Assis}}</ref>{{Rp|page=104}}

The first edition was limited, but the novel was kept in stock to be reprinted as soon as the initial 2,000 copies were sold out.<ref name="magalhaes jr" />{{Rp|page=105}}

==Adaptations==

=== Cinema ===
The two [[Cinematography|film]] adaptations of the novel are different. The first, ''Capitu'' (1968), directed by [[Paulo César Saraceni]], with a screenplay by Paulo Emílio Sales Gomes and [[Lygia Fagundes Telles]], and performances by Isabella, [[Othon Bastos]] and [[Raul Cortez]], is a faithful reading of the book,<ref name="petronio; alvarenga" />{{Rp|page=13}} while the latest, ''Dom'' (2003), directed by [[Moacyr Góes]], with [[Marcos Palmeira]] and [[Maria Fernanda Cândido]], shows a contemporary approach to jealousy in relationships.<ref name="petronio; alvarenga" />{{Rp|page=13}}

=== Theatre ===
The novel also received relevant theatre adaptations, such as the play ''Capitu'' (1999), directed by Marcus Vinícius Faustini, awarded and praised by the [[Academia Brasileira de Letras|Brazilian Academy of Letters]],<ref name="petronio; alvarenga" />{{Rp|page=13}} and ''Criador e Criatura: o Encontro de Machado e Capitu'' (2002), a free adaptation by [[Flávio Aguiar]] and [[Ariclê Perez]], directed by [[Bibi Ferreira]].<ref name="petronio; alvarenga" />{{Rp|page=13}} Before these two productions, ''Dom Casmurro'' was adapted into an opera, with a [[libretto]] by Orlando Codá and music by [[Ronaldo Miranda]], which premiered at the [[Theatro Municipal (São Paulo)|Theatro Municipal de São Paulo]] in 1992.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Ronaldo Miranda |url=http://www.abmusica.org.br/acad13nov.html |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20101030013945/http://www.abmusica.org.br/acad13nov.html |archive-date=2010-10-30 |access-date=2010-10-31 |language=pt-br}}</ref>

=== Music ===
Luiz Tatit composed "Capitu", a song performed by singer [[Ná Ozzetti]].<ref>{{Cite book |last=Paschoal |first=Marcio |title=Os atalhos de Samanta |publisher=Ed. Record |year=2004 |isbn=978-85-01-06846-0 |location=Rio de Janeiro, São Paulo |language=pt-br |trans-title=Samanta's shortcuts}}</ref>{{Rp|page=176}} Composer [[Ronaldo Miranda]] wrote an opera with a libretto by Orlando Codá, which premiered in May 1992 at the [[Theatro Municipal (São Paulo)|Theatro Municipal de São Paulo]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Dom Casmurro |url=http://www.patriciaendo.com/003-D.Casmurro.htm |access-date=2017-04-03 |website=www.patriciaendo.com |language=pt-br}}</ref>

=== Literature ===

In 1998, Fernando Sabino published the novel ''Amor de Capitu''. In this version, the narrative was rewritten in [[Third-person narrative|third person]].<ref>{{cite web |title=O universo machadiano em novos livros |trans-title=Machado's universe in new books |url=https://www1.folha.uol.com.br/fsp/mais/fs22119807.htm |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170812023144/https://www1.folha.uol.com.br/fsp/mais/fs22119807.htm |archive-date=12 August 2017 |website=folha.uol.com.br |language=pt-br}}</ref>

=== Television ===
In 2008, to celebrate 100 years since the death of Machado de Assis, [[TV Globo|Rede Globo]] produced a [[micro-series]] called ''[[Capitu]]'', directed by [[Luiz Fernando Carvalho]], written by Euclydes Marinho, starring [[Eliane Giardini]], [[Maria Fernanda Cândido]] and Michel Melamed; combining period elements such as [[costume]]s with modern elements ranging from the soundtrack, with songs by the band [[Beirut]], to scenes in which [[MP3]]s were shown.<ref>{{Cite web |date=7 December 2008 |title=Obra-prima de Machado de Assis volta modernizada na microssérie 'Capitu' |trans-title=Machado de Assis' masterpiece returns modernised in the 'Capitu' micro-series |url=https://oglobo.globo.com/cultura/revista-da-tv/obra-prima-de-machado-de-assis-volta-modernizada-na-microsserie-capitu-3603811 |access-date= |website=O Globo |language=pt-BR}}</ref>

=== Comic books ===
A comic book adaptation was made in 2012 by [[Mario Cau]] and Felipe Greco. This comic won the 2013 [[Prêmio Jabuti]] (the most traditional Brazilian literary award) in "best illustration" and "best school related book" categories, and the HQ Mix Trophy in 2014 (in the "Comic book adaptation" category).<ref>{{cite web |author=Assis |first=Érico |date=18 October 2013 |title=Jabuti premia quadrinistas na categoria "Ilustração" |trans-title=Jabuti honours comic artists in the "Illustration" category |url=http://omelete.uol.com.br/quadrinhos/jabuti-premia-quadrinistas-na-categoria-ilustracao/#.U5X-3y_-vUU |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230421182917/https://omelete.com.br/quadrinhos/jabuti-premia-quadrinistas-na-categoria-ilustracao/ |archive-date=21 April 2023 |website=omelete.com.br |publisher=Omelete |language=pt}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Naranjo |first=Marcelo |date=24 January 2013 |title=Devir lança adaptação em quadrinhos de Dom Casmurro |trans-title=Devir launches comic book adaptation of Dom Casmurro |url=https://universohq.com/noticias/devir-lanca-adaptacao-em-quadrinhos-de-dom-casmurro/ |access-date= |website=UNIVERSO HQ |language=pt-br}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Naliato |first=Samir |date=8 September 2014 |title=A lista dos vencedores do 26° Troféu HQ Mix |trans-title=List of winners of the 26th HQ Mix Trophy |url=https://universohq.com/noticias/lista-dos-vencedores-26-trofeu-hq-mix/ |access-date= |website=UNIVERSO HQ |language=pt-br}}</ref>

Other comic book adaptations of ''Dom Casmurro'' have also been published by Ática (authors: Ivan Jaf and Rodrigo Rosa) and Nemo (authors: Wellington Srbek and José Aguiar).<ref>{{Cite web |title='Dom Casmurro', de Machado de Assis, ganha nova versão em HQ; veja outras adaptações |trans-title=Machado de Assis' 'Dom Casmurro' gets new comic book version; see other adaptations |url=https://entretenimento.uol.com.br/noticias/redacao/2012/05/29/dom-casmurro-de-machado-de-assis-ganha-nova-versao-em-hq-veja-outras-adaptacoes.htm |access-date=2024-07-23 |website=entretenimento.uol.com.br |language=pt-br}}</ref>
