| width1            = 200
| alt1              = The Great Gatsby dust jacket art drafts
| image2            = Celestial eyes-The Great Gatsby cover-Francis Cugat-1925.tif
| width2            = 100
| alt2              = The Great Gatsby 1925 dust jacket without the title or author superimposed.
| footer            = Drafts of the dust jacket by artist [[Francis Cugat]] juxtaposed with the final version. In one draft (''first''), a single eye loomed over [[Long Island Sound]]. In a subsequent draft (''second''), Cugat expanded upon this concept to feature two eyes gazing over the New York cityscape. In the final draft (''third''), the shadowy cityscape was replaced by carnival lights evoking [[Coney Island]].
| footer_align      = left
}}

<!--Do not change "artwork" or "imagery" to "cover" or "painting". It was the preliminary drafts, not the final painting, that influenced Fitzgerald.-->The artwork for the first edition of ''The Great Gatsby,'' known as ''[[Celestial Eyes]],'' is among the most celebrated in American literature and represents a unique instance in literary history in which a novel's commissioned artwork directly influenced the composition of the text.{{sfn|Scribner|1992|pp=141–155}} Rendered in an [[Art Deco]] visual style,{{sfn|Scribner|1992|p=141}} the artwork depicts the disembodied face of a Jazz Age flapper with celestial eyes and rouged mouth over a dark blue skyline.{{sfn|Bruccoli|2002|p=202}} A little-known [[Barcelona]]n painter named [[Francis Cugat]]—born Francisco Coradal-Cougat—was commissioned by an unknown individual in Scribner's art department to illustrate the cover while Fitzgerald was composing the novel.{{sfn|Scribner|1992|pp=140–155}}

In a preliminary sketch, Cugat drew a concept of a dismal gray landscape inspired by Fitzgerald's original title for the novel, ''Among Ash Heaps and Millionaires''.{{sfn|Scribner|1992|p=146}} Discarding this gloomy concept, Cugat next drew a divergent study which became the prefiguration to the final cover: A pencil and crayon drawing of a flapper's half-hidden visage over Long Island Sound with scarlet lips, one celestial eye, and a single diagonal tear.{{sfn|Scribner|1992|pp=148–149}} Expanding upon this study, his subsequent drawing featured two bright eyes looming over a shadowy New York cityscape.{{sfn|Scribner|1992|pp=149–151}} In later iterations, Cugat replaced the shadowy cityscape with dazzling carnival lights evoking a [[Ferris wheel]] and likely referencing the glittering amusement park at New York's [[Coney Island]].{{sfn|Scribner|1992|pp=149–153}} Cugat affixed reclining nudes within the flapper's irises and added a green tint to the streaming tear.{{sfn|Scribner|1992|p=154}} Cugat's final cover,{{efn|name=Final Cover|Many years after ''The Great Gatsby''{{'}}s publication, Francis Cugat's original painting for the book cover was presumed forever lost until it was found in a trash can at Scribner's and donated to the Princeton University Libraries for its Graphic Arts Collection.{{sfn|Scribner|1992|pp=145, 154}}}} which Max Perkins hailed as a masterpiece, was the only work he completed for Scribner's and the only book cover he ever designed.{{sfn|Scribner|1992|pp=143, 154}}

Although Fitzgerald likely never saw the final [[gouache]] painting prior to the novel's publication,<ref>{{harvnb|Scribner|1992|p=145}}: "It is entirely conceivable that Fitzgerald had never seen Cugat's final, finished artwork".</ref> Cugat's preparatory drafts influenced his writing.<ref name="Preparatory Drafts" />{{sfn|Scribner|1992|p=141}} Upon viewing Cugat's drafts before sailing for France in April–May 1924,<ref name="Preparatory Drafts">{{Harvnb|Scribner|1992|pp=145–146}}: "Since there were at most a couple of weeks between the commission and Fitzgerald's departure for France, it is likely that what he had seen—and "written into the book"—was one or more of Cugat's preparatory sketches which were probably shown to him at Scribners before he set sail".</ref>{{sfn|Scribner|1992|pp=143–144}} Fitzgerald was so enamored that he later told editor Max Perkins that he had incorporated Cugat's imagery into the novel.{{sfn|Scribner|1992|p=142}} This statement has led many to analyze interrelations between Cugat's art and Fitzgerald's text.{{sfn|Scribner|1992|p=142}} One popular interpretation is that the celestial eyes are reminiscent of those of optometrist T. J. Eckleburg depicted on a faded commercial billboard near George Wilson's auto repair shop.<ref>{{harvnb|Scribner|1992|pp=140–155}}: "We are left then with the enticing possibility that Fitzgerald's arresting image was originally prompted by Cugat's fantastic apparitions over the [[Flushing Meadows–Corona Park|valley of ashes]]; in other words, that the author derived his inventive metamorphosis from a recurrent theme of Cugat's trial jackets, one which the artist himself was to reinterpret and transform through subsequent drafts".</ref> Author [[Ernest Hemingway]] supported this latter interpretation and claimed that Fitzgerald had told him the cover referred to a billboard in the valley of the ashes.{{sfn|Hemingway|1964|p=176|ps=: "Scott brought his book over. It had a garish dust jacket and I remember being embarrassed by the violence, bad taste, and slippery look of it. It looked like the book jacket for a book of bad science fiction. Scot told me not to be put off by it, that it had to do with a billboard along a highway in Long Island that was important in the story. He said he had liked the jacket and now he didn't like it. I took it off to read the book".}} Although this passage has some resemblance to the imagery, a closer explanation can be found in Fitzgerald's explicit description of Daisy Buchanan as the "girl whose disembodied face floated along the dark cornices and blinding signs".{{sfn|Scribner|1992|pp=140–155}}

== Critical reception ==
=== Initial reviews ===
[[Charles Scribner's Sons]] published ''The Great Gatsby'' on April 10, 1925.{{sfn|Bruccoli|2002|p=217}} Fitzgerald cabled Perkins the day after publication to monitor reviews: "Any news?"{{sfn|Bruccoli|2002|p=217}} "Sales situation doubtful [but] excellent reviews", read a telegram from Perkins on April 20.<ref name="O'Meara 2002 49">{{harvnb|O'Meara|2002|p=49}}; {{harvnb|Bruccoli|2002|p=217}}.</ref> Fitzgerald responded on April&nbsp;24, saying the cable dispirited him, closing the letter with "Yours in great depression".<ref name="O'Meara 2002 49" /> Fitzgerald soon received letters from contemporaries [[Willa Cather]], [[Edith Wharton]], and poet [[T. S. Eliot]] praising the novel.{{sfn|Bruccoli|2002|p=218}} Although gratified by such correspondence, Fitzgerald sought public acclaim from professional critics.<ref>{{harvnb|Mizener|1960}}; {{harvnb|Quirk|1982|p=576}}.</ref>

[[File:H-L-Mencken-1928.jpg|thumb|right|upright=0.7|alt=Photographic portrait of H.L. Mencken |Although he praised the novel's style, [[H. L. Mencken]] criticized the plot as highly improbable—a criticism that Fitzgerald particularly resented.]]
''The Great Gatsby'' received generally favorable reviews from literary critics of the day.<ref>{{harvnb|Bruccoli|2002|p=217}}; {{harvnb|Mizener|1965|p=193}}.</ref> Edwin Clark of ''[[The New York Times]]'' felt the novel was a mystical and glamorous tale of the Jazz Age.{{sfn|Clark|1925}} Similarly, Lillian C. Ford of the ''[[Los Angeles Times]]'' hailed the novel as a revelatory work of art that "leaves the reader in a mood of chastened wonder".{{sfn|Ford|1925}} The ''[[New York Post]]'' described Fitzgerald's prose style as scintillating and genuinely brilliant.{{sfn|''New York Post''|1925}} The ''[[New York Herald Tribune]]'' was less impressed, referring to ''The Great Gatsby'' as "a literary lemon meringue" that nonetheless "contains some of the nicest little touches of contemporary observation you could imagine—so light, so delicate, so sharp".{{sfn|''New York Herald Tribune''|1925}} In ''[[Chicago Tribune|The Chicago Daily Tribune]]'', [[H. L. Mencken]] judged the work's plot to be highly improbable, although he praised the writing as elegant and the "careful and brilliant finish".<ref>{{harvnb|Mencken|1925|p=9}}: "''The Great Gatsby'' is in form no more than a glorified anecdote, and not too probable at that. The story for all its basic triviality has a fine texture; a careful and brilliant finish&nbsp;... What gives the story distinction is something quite different from the management of the action or the handling of the characters; it is the charm and beauty of the writing".</ref>

Several reviewers felt the novel left much to be desired following Fitzgerald's previous works and criticized him accordingly. Harvey Eagleton of ''[[The Dallas Morning News]]'' predicted that the novel signaled the end of Fitzgerald's artistic success.{{sfn|Eagleton|1925|ps=: "[Fitzgerald] is considered a [[Roman candle (firework)|Roman candle]] which burned brightly at first but now flares out".}} Ralph Coghlan of the ''[[St. Louis Post-Dispatch]]'' dismissed the work as an inconsequential performance by a once-promising author who had grown bored and cynical.{{sfn|Coghlan|1925}} Ruth Snyder of ''[[New York World|New York Evening World]]'' lambasted the book's style as painfully forced and declared the editors of her newspaper were "quite convinced after reading ''The Great Gatsby'' that Mr. Fitzgerald is not one of the great American writers of today".{{sfn|Snyder|1925}} John McClure of ''[[The Times-Picayune]]'' insisted the plot was implausible and the book itself seemed raw in its construction.{{sfn|McClure|1925}}

After reading these reviews, Fitzgerald believed that many critics misunderstood the novel.{{sfn|Eble|1974|p=37}} He despaired that "of all the reviews, even the most enthusiastic, not one had the slightest idea what the book was about".{{sfn|Fitzgerald|1945|loc=Letter to Edmund Wilson|p=270}} In particular, Fitzgerald resented criticisms of the novel's plot as implausible since he had never intended for the story to be realistic.{{sfn|Eble|1974|p=37}} Instead, he crafted the work to be a romanticized depiction that was largely scenic and symbolic.<ref>{{harvnb|Bruccoli|2002|p=219}}; {{harvnb|Flanagan|2000}}; {{harvnb|Leader|2000|pp=13–15}}.</ref> According to his friend [[John Peale Bishop]], Fitzgerald further resented the fact that critics failed to perceive the many parallels between the author's life and the character of Jay Gatsby; in particular, that both created a mythical version of themselves and attempted to live up to this legend.{{sfn|Kruse|2002|p=75}} Dispirited by critics failing to understand the novel, Fitzgerald remained hopeful that the novel would at least be a commercial success, perhaps selling as many as 75,000 copies.{{sfn|O'Meara|2002|p=49}}

To Fitzgerald's great disappointment, ''Gatsby'' was a commercial failure in comparison with his previous efforts, ''[[This Side of Paradise]]'' (1920) and ''[[The Beautiful and Damned]]'' (1922). By October, the book had sold fewer than 20,000 copies.{{sfn|Mizener|1960}}
Although the novel went through two initial printings, many copies remained unsold years later.{{sfn|Bruccoli|2000|p=175}} Fitzgerald attributed the poor sales to the fact that women tended to be the primary audience for novels during this time, and ''Gatsby'' did not contain an admirable female character.{{sfn|Bruccoli|2000|p=175}} According to his ledger, he earned only $2,000 from the book.<ref>{{harvnb|Howell|2013}}; {{harvnb|F. Scott Fitzgerald's ledger 1919–1938}}.</ref> Although [[Owen Davis]]' 1926 stage adaptation and the [[Paramount Pictures|Paramount]]-issued [[The Great Gatsby (1926 film)|silent film version]] brought in money for the author, Fitzgerald lamented that the novel fell far short of the success he had hoped for and would not bring him recognition as a serious novelist in the public eye.{{sfn|Mizener|1960}} With the onset of the [[Great Depression]], ''The Great Gatsby'' was regarded as little more than a nostalgic period piece.{{sfn|Mizener|1960}} By the time Fitzgerald died in 1940, the novel had fallen into near obscurity.{{sfn|Rimer|2008}}

=== Revival and reassessment ===
[[File:Edmund Wilson.jpg|thumb|upright=0.7|left|alt=A photographic portrait of Edmund Wilson|Fitzgerald's friend [[Edmund Wilson]] helped revive the author's posthumous reputation.]]
In 1940, Fitzgerald suffered a third and fatal heart attack and died believing his work forgotten.<ref>{{harvnb|Donahue|2013b}}: "When 'Gatsby' author F. Scott Fitzgerald died in 1940, he thought he was a failure".</ref> His obituary in ''The New York Times'' hailed him as a brilliant novelist and cited ''Gatsby'' as his greatest work.{{sfn|Fitzgerald's obituary|1940|ps=: "The best of his books, the critics said, was ''The Great Gatsby''. When it was published in 1925 this ironic tale of life on Long Island, at a time when [[Bathtub gin|gin]] was the national drink and sex the national obsession, it received critical acclaim. In it, Mr. Fitzgerald was at his best".}} In the wake of Fitzgerald's death, a strong appreciation for the book gradually developed in writers' circles. Future authors [[Budd Schulberg]] and [[Edward Newhouse]] were deeply affected by it, and [[John O'Hara]] acknowledged its influence on his work.<ref>{{harvnb|Mizener|1960}}: "Writers like John O'Hara were showing its influence and younger men like Edward Newhouse and Budd Schulberg, who would presently be deeply affected by it, were discovering it".</ref> By the time that ''Gatsby'' was republished in [[Edmund Wilson]]'s edition of ''The Last Tycoon'' in 1941, the prevailing opinion in writers' circles deemed the novel to be an enduring work of fiction.{{sfn|Mizener|1960}}

In the spring of 1942, mere months after the United States' entrance into [[World War II|World War&nbsp;II]], an association of publishing executives created the [[Council on Books in Wartime]] with the stated purpose of distributing paperback [[Armed Services Editions]] books to [[combat troops]]. ''The Great Gatsby'' was one of them.{{sfn|Cole|1984|p=25}} Within the next several years, 155,000 copies of ''Gatsby'' were distributed to U.S. soldiers overseas,<ref>{{harvnb|Cole|1984|p=26}}: "One hundred fifty-five thousand [[Armed Services Editions|ASE copies]] of ''The Great Gatsby'' were distributed-as against the twenty-five thousand copies of the novel printed by Scribners between 1925 and 1942".</ref> and the book proved popular among beleaguered troops, according to the ''[[Saturday Evening Post]]''{{'}}s 1945 report.{{sfn|Wittels|1945|ps=: "Troops showed interest in books about the human mind and books with sexual situations were grabbed up eagerly. One soldier said that books with 'racy' passages were as popular as 'pin-up girls'".}}

By 1944, a full-scale Fitzgerald revival had occurred.<ref>{{harvnb|Mizener|1960}}; {{harvnb|Verghis|2013}}.</ref> Full-length scholarly articles on Fitzgerald's works were being published in [[periodicals]] and, by the following year, the earlier consensus among professional critics that ''The Great Gatsby'' was merely a sensational story or a nostalgic [[period piece]] had effectively vanished.<ref>{{harvnb|Bruccoli|2002|p=217}}; {{harvnb|Mizener|1960}}.</ref> The tireless promotional efforts of literary critic Edmund Wilson, who was Fitzgerald's Princeton classmate and his close friend, led this Fitzgerald revival.{{sfn|Verghis|2013}} In 1951, three years after [[Zelda Fitzgerald#Hospital fire and death|Zelda's death]] in a hospital fire, Professor [[Arthur Mizener]] of [[Cornell University]] published ''[[The Far Side of Paradise]]'', the first biography of Fitzgerald.{{sfn|Mizener|1965}} Mizener's bestselling biography emphasized ''The Great Gatsby''{{'}}s positive reception by literary critics, which may have further influenced public opinion and renewed interest in it.{{sfn|Mizener|1965|p=183}}

By 1960—thirty-five years after the novel's original publication—the book was steadily selling 100,000 copies per year.{{sfn|Tredell|2007|p=90}} Renewed interest in it led ''The New York Times'' editorialist Mizener to proclaim the novel was a [[masterwork]] of 20th-century [[American literature]].{{sfn|Mizener|1960}} By 1974, ''The Great Gatsby'' had attained its status as a literary masterwork and was deemed a contender for the title of the "[[Great American Novel]]".<ref>{{harvnb|Eble|1974|pp=34, 45}}; {{harvnb|Batchelor|2013}}.</ref>

By the mid-2000s, many literary critics considered ''The Great Gatsby'' to be one of the greatest novels ever written,<ref>{{harvnb|Hogeback|2016}}; {{harvnb|Lacayo|Grossman|2010}}; {{harvnb|Burt|2010}}.</ref> and the work was part of the assigned curricula in the near majority of U.S. high schools.{{sfn|Rimer|2008}} As of early 2020, ''The Great Gatsby'' had sold almost 30 million copies worldwide and continues to sell an additional 500,000 copies annually.{{sfn|Italie|2020}} Numerous foreign editions of the novel have been published,{{sfn|Tredell|2007|pp=89–90}} and the text has been translated into 42 different languages.{{sfn|Donahue|2013b}} The work is Scribner's most popular title; in 2013, the [[e-book]] alone sold 185,000 copies.{{sfn|Donahue|2013b}} The [[American Library Association]] lists the book as among the most challenged classics in U.S. literature.{{sfn|American Library Association|2025}} The novel's U.S. copyright expired on January 1, 2021, when it, along with all the other [[1925 in literature|literature of 1925]], entered the [[public domain in the United States|public domain]].<ref>{{harvnb|Alter|2018}}; {{harvnb|Williams|2021}}.</ref> Since then, numerous altered and incomplete reprints have flooded the market.{{sfn|Alberge|2022}}

== Critical analysis ==
=== Major themes ===
==== The American Dream ====
[[File:EdwardMoran-UnveilingTheStatueofLiberty1886Large.jpg|thumb|right|upright=0.8|alt=A painting featuring the Statue of Liberty|The [[American Dream]], often represented by the [[Statue of Liberty]] signifying new opportunities in life, is a central theme underlying the novel.]]

Following the novel's revival, later critical writings on ''The Great Gatsby'' focused on Fitzgerald's disillusionment with the [[American Dream]] in the hedonistic Jazz Age,<ref>{{harvnb|Kazin|1951|p=189}}; {{harvnb|Bewley|1954|pp=223–224}}.</ref> a name for the era which Fitzgerald claimed to have coined.<ref>{{harvnb|Pearson|1970|p=638}}: "[Fitzgerald] was the self-appointed spokesman for the 'Jazz Age,' a term he takes credit for coining, and he gave it its arch-high priest and prophet, Jay Gatsby, in his novel ''The Great Gatsby''".</ref> In 1970, scholar [[Roger Pearson (literary scholar)|Roger L. Pearson]] asserted that Fitzgerald's work—more so than other twentieth century novels—is especially linked with this conceptualization of the American dream.{{sfn|Pearson|1970|p=638}} Pearson traced the literary origins of this dream to [[Colonial history of the United States|Colonial America]]. The dream is the belief that every individual, regardless of their origins, may seek and achieve their desired goals, "be they political, monetary, or social. It is the literary expression of the concept of America: The land of opportunity".{{sfn|Pearson|1970|p=638}}

However, Pearson noted that Fitzgerald's particular treatment of this theme is devoid of the discernible optimism in the writings of earlier American authors.{{sfn|Pearson|1970|p=638}} He suggests Gatsby serves as a false prophet of the American dream, and pursuing the dream only results in dissatisfaction for those who chase it, owing to its unattainability.{{sfn|Pearson|1970|p=645}} In this analytical context, the green light on the Buchanans' dock (visible across [[Long Island Sound]] from Gatsby's house) is frequently interpreted as a symbol of Gatsby's unrealizable goal to win Daisy and, consequently, to achieve the American Dream.{{sfn|Rimer|2008}}{{sfn|Bewley|1954|pp=235, 238|ps=: "For Gatsby, Daisy does not exist in herself. She is the green light that signals him into the heart of his ultimate vision&nbsp;... Thus the American dream, whose superstitious valuation of the future began in the past, gives the green light through which alone the American returns to his traditional roots, paradoxically retreating into the pattern of history while endeavoring to exploit the possibilities of the future".}} Also, scholar [[Sarah Churchwell]] points out that adultery in the novel is linked to the loss of faith and broken promises, which symbolizes the corruption of the American Dream.{{sfn|Churchwell|2012}}

==== Class permanence ====
Scholars and writers commonly ascribe Gatsby's inability to achieve the American Dream to entrenched class disparities in American society.<ref>{{harvnb|Churchwell|2013b}}; {{harvnb|Gillespie|2013}}; {{harvnb|Bechtel|2017|p=117}}.</ref> The novel underscores the limits of the American lower class to transcend their [[Social class in the United States|station of birth]].{{sfn|Churchwell|2013b}} Scholar Sarah Churchwell contends that Fitzgerald's novel is a tale of [[Class conflict|class warfare]] in a status-obsessed country that refuses to acknowledge publicly it even has a class system.{{sfn|Churchwell|2013b}}

Although scholars posit different explanations for the continuation of [[Social inequality|class differences]] in the United States, there is a consensus regarding the novel's message in conveying its underlying permanence.<ref>{{harvnb|Gillespie|2013}}; {{harvnb|Bechtel|2017|p=117}}; {{harvnb|Churchwell|2013b}}.</ref> Although ''Gatsby''{{'}}s fundamental conflict occurs between entrenched sources of socio-economic power and upstarts like Gatsby who threaten their interests,{{sfn|Gillespie|2013}} Fitzgerald's novel shows that a class permanence persists despite the country's capitalist economy that prizes innovation and adaptability.{{sfn|Gillespie|2013}} Dianne Bechtel argues Fitzgerald plotted the novel to illustrate that class transcends wealth in America. Even if the poorer Americans become rich, they remain inferior to those Americans with "old money".{{sfn|Bechtel|2017|p=120}} Consequently, Gatsby and other characters in the novel are trapped in a rigid American class system.{{sfn|Bechtel|2017|pp=117, 128}}

==== Gender relations ====
[[File:Saturday Evening Post cover 2-4-1922.jpg|thumb|left|upright=0.8|alt=A sketch of a flapper on the cover of an issue of the ''Saturday Evening Post''|An idealized depiction of a [[flapper]] as illustrated by [[Ellen Bernard Thompson Pyle|Ellen Pyle]] for the cover of ''[[The Saturday Evening Post]]'' (1922)]]
Besides exploring the difficulties of achieving the American dream, ''The Great Gatsby'' explores [[Gender polarization|societal gender expectations]] during the Jazz Age.{{sfn|Drudzina|2006|pp=17–20}} The character of Daisy Buchanan has been identified specifically as personifying the emerging cultural [[archetype]] of the flapper.<ref name="Daisy as Flapper Archetype"/> Flappers were typically young, [[Modernity|modern women]] who [[Bob cut|bobbed their hair]] and wore short skirts.<ref>{{harvnb|Conor|2004|p=209}}: "More than any other type of the Modern Woman, it was the Flapper who embodied the scandal which attached to women's new public visibility, from their increasing street presence to their mechanical reproduction as spectacles".</ref>{{sfn|Conor|2004|pp=210, 221}} They also drank&nbsp;alcohol and had [[premarital sex]].<ref>{{harvnb|Fitzgerald|1945|loc="Echoes of the Jazz Age"|p=16}}: The flappers, "if they get about at all, know the taste of [[gin]] or [[Corn liquor|corn]] at sixteen".</ref><ref name="Premarital sex" />

Despite the newfound societal freedoms attained by flappers in the 1920s,{{sfn|Conor|2004|p=209}} Fitzgerald's work critically examines the continued limitations upon women's [[Agency (sociology)|agency]] during this period.{{sfn|Person|1978|pp=250–257}} In this context, although early critics viewed the character of Daisy to be a "monster of [[Bitch (slang)|bitchery]]",{{sfn|Person|1978|p=253}} later scholars such as Leland S. Person Jr.<!--Please do not correct to Pearson. Roger L. Pearson and Leland S. Person are different scholars.--> asserted that Daisy's character exemplifies the marginalization of women in the elite social environment that Fitzgerald depicts.<ref>{{harvnb|Person|1978|pp=250–257}}; {{harvnb|Donahue|2013a}}.</ref>

Writing in 1978, Person noted Daisy is more of a hapless victim than a manipulative victimizer.{{sfn|Person|1978|p=250}} She is the target first of Tom's callous domination and next of Gatsby's dehumanizing adoration.{{sfn|Person|1978|p=250}} She involuntarily becomes the [[holy grail]] at the center of Gatsby's unrealistic quest to be steadfast to a youthful concept of himself.{{sfn|Person|1978|p=250}} The ensuing contest of wills between Tom and Gatsby reduces Daisy to a [[trophy wife]] whose sole existence is to augment her possessor's socio-economic success.{{sfn|Person|1978|p=256}}

As an [[upper-class]] white woman living in East Egg during this time period, Daisy must adhere to societal expectations and [[gender norms]] such as actively fulfilling the roles of dutiful wife, nurturing mother, and charming [[socialite]].{{sfn|Person|1978|pp=250–257}} Many of Daisy's choices—ultimately culminating in the fatal car crash and misery for all those involved—can be partly attributed to her prescribed role as a "beautiful little fool" who is reliant on her husband for financial and societal security.{{efn|name=Beautiful Little Fool|Daisy's statement that she hopes her daughter will be a "beautiful little fool" was said by [[Zelda Fitzgerald]] when their daughter Scottie was born on October 26, 1921, in a St. Paul hospital.<ref>{{harvnb|Bruccoli|2002|p=156}}; {{harvnb|Milford|1970|p=80}}; {{harvnb|Turnbull|1962|p=127}}.</ref>}}{{sfn|Person|1978|pp=253, 256}} Her decision to remain with her husband, despite her feelings for Gatsby, is because of the security that her marriage to Tom Buchanan provides.{{sfn|Person|1978|p=253}}

==== Race and displacement ====
[[File:Dust jacket, first edition of The Rising Tide of Color Against White World-Supremacy.jpg|thumb|right|upright=0.8|alt=Dust jacket of the book ''The Rise of the Colored Empires'' by Lothrop Stoddard| Fitzgerald's novel references a fictional book, Goddard's ''The Rise of the Colored Empires'', which is a parody of ''[[The Rising Tide of Color Against White World-Supremacy|The Rising Tide of Color]]'' (1920) by [[Lothrop Stoddard]].]]

Many scholars have analyzed the novel's treatment of race and displacement; in particular, a perceived threat posed by newer immigrants to older Americans, triggering concerns over a loss of [[socio-economic status]].<ref>{{harvnb|Slater|1973|p=55}}; {{harvnb|Pekarofski|2012|p=52}}; {{harvnb|Michaels|1995|pp=18, 29}}; {{harvnb|Vogel|2015|p=43}}; {{harvnb|Berman|1996|p=33}}.</ref> In one instance, Tom Buchanan—the novel's antagonist—claims that he, Nick, and Jordan are [[Nordicism|racially superior Nordics]]. Tom decries [[Immigration to the United States|immigration]] and advocates [[white supremacy]].<ref>{{harvnb|Slater|1973|p=54}}; {{harvnb|Michaels|1995|p=29}}.</ref> A fictional book alluded to by Tom is Goddard's ''The Rise of the Colored Empires'', which is a parody by Fitzgerald of [[Lothrop Stoddard]]'s ''[[The Rising Tide of Color Against White World-Supremacy|The Rising Tide of Color]],'' a 1920s [[bestseller]].<ref>{{harvnb|Slater|1973|p=54}}; {{harvnb|Vogel|2015|p=36}}; {{harvnb|Pekarofski|2012|p=52}}.</ref> Stoddard warned that immigration would alter America's racial composition and destroy the country.{{sfn|Michaels|1995|p=29}}

Analyzing these elements, [[Literary theory|literary theorist]] [[Walter Benn Michaels]] contends that Fitzgerald's novel reflects a historical period in American literature characterized by fears over the influx of [[Southern Europe|Southern]] and [[Eastern Europe]]an immigrants whose "[[Other (philosophy)|otherness]]" challenged Americans' sense of [[national identity]].<ref>{{harvnb|Pekarofski|2012|p=52}}; {{harvnb|Michaels|1995|pp=18, 29}}.</ref> Such anxieties were more salient in national discourse than the societal consequences of World War&nbsp;I,{{sfn|Berman|1996|p=33}}<ref>{{harvnb|Slater|1973|p=53}}: "An obsessive concern with ethnic differences has always been a part of American culture, but in some periods this concern has been more intense and explicit than in others. The 1920s, the time of the [[Second Ku Klux Klan|reborn Ku Klux Klan]], [[Immigration Act of 1924|immigration restriction legislation]], and the pseudo-scientific racism of [[Madison Grant]] and [[Lothrop Stoddard]] was one of the periods when concern about ethnicity was most evident on the surface of national life".</ref> and the defining question of the period was who constituted "a real American".{{sfn|Vogel|2015|p=38}}

In this context of immigration and displacement, Tom's hostility towards Gatsby, who is the embodiment of "latest America",{{sfn|Vogel|2015|p=45}} has been interpreted as partly embodying [[Status shift|status anxieties]] of the time involving anti-immigrant sentiment.{{sfn|Vogel|2015|p=45}} Gatsby—whom Tom belittles as "Mr. Nobody from Nowhere"<ref>{{harvnb|Vogel|2015|p=40}}; {{harvnb|Slater|1973|p=54}}.</ref>—functions as a cipher because of his obscure origins, his unclear ethno-religious identity and his indeterminate class status.{{sfn|Pekarofski|2012|p=52}} Although his ethnicity is vague, his last name Gatz and his father's adherence to the [[Lutheran]] religion indicate his family are recent German immigrants.{{sfn|Slater|1973|p=56}} This would preclude them from the coveted status of [[Old Stock Americans]].{{sfn|Slater|1973|p=56}} Consequently, Gatsby's socio-economic ascent is deemed a threat not only due to his status as ''nouveau riche'', but because he is perceived as an outsider.{{sfn|Vogel|2015|p=41}}

Because of such themes, ''The Great Gatsby'' captures the perennial American experience as it is a story about change and those who resist it—whether such change comes in the form of a new wave of immigrants, the ''nouveau riche'', or successful minorities.{{sfn|Gillespie|2013}} Since Americans living in the <!--Please do not change to the anachronistic and historically misleading term "Roaring Twenties" which typically refers to the second half of the 1920s decade.-->1920s to the present are largely defined by their fluctuating socio-economic circumstances and must navigate a society with entrenched racial and ethnic prejudices, Fitzgerald's depiction of resultant status anxieties and social conflict has been highlighted by scholars as still enduringly relevant nearly a hundred years after the novel's publication.{{sfn|Gillespie|2013}}<ref>{{harvnb|Vogel|2015|pp=29–30, 33, 38–40, 51}}: "''The Great Gatsby'' resonates more in the present than it ever did in the Jazz Age", and "the work speaks in strikingly familiar terms to the issues of our time", especially since its "themes are inextricably woven into questions of race, ethnicity, gender, and sexuality".</ref>

==== Sexuality and identity ====
[[File:F. Scott Fitzgerald circa 1915 (Retouched Oval Portrait Cropped).jpg|thumb|upright=0.8|alt=Photographic portrait of F. Scott Fitzgerald dressed as a woman circa 1915|A photo of Fitzgerald dressed as a woman circa 1915]]
Questions regarding the sexuality of characters have been raised for decades and—augmented by biographical details about the author—have given rise to [[Queering|queer readings]].{{sfn|Vogel|2015|pp=38–40}} During his lifetime, Fitzgerald's sexuality became a subject of debate among his friends and acquaintances.<ref>{{harvnb|Fessenden|2005|p=28}}: "Fitzgerald's career records the ambient, dogging pressure to repel charges of his own homosexuality".</ref><ref name="Sexuality Rumors">{{harvnb|Bruccoli|2002|p=284}}: According to biographer Matthew J. Bruccoli, author [[Robert McAlmon]] and other contemporaries in Paris publicly asserted that Fitzgerald was a homosexual, and Hemingway later avoided Fitzgerald due to these rumors.</ref>{{sfnm|Milford|1970|1p=154|Kerr|1996|2p=417}} As a youth, Fitzgerald had a close relationship with Father Sigourney Fay,<ref>{{harvnb|Fessenden|2005|p=28}}: "Biographers describe Fay as a '[[fin-de-siècle]] aesthete' of considerable appeal; 'a dandy, always heavily perfumed,' who introduced the teenaged Fitzgerald to [[Oscar Wilde]] and good wine".</ref> a possibly [[gay]] Catholic priest,<ref>{{harvnb|Fessenden|2005|p=28}}.</ref><ref>{{harvnb|Bruccoli|2002|p=275}}: "If Fay was a homosexual, as has been asserted without proof, Fitzgerald was presumably unaware of it".</ref> and Fitzgerald later used his last name for the idealized romantic character of Daisy Fay.{{sfn|Fessenden|2005|p=30}} After college, Fitzgerald [[cross-dressed]] during outings in Minnesota.<ref>{{harvnb|Mizener|1965|p=60}}: "In February he put on his Show Girl make-up and went to a [[Psi Upsilon|Psi U]] dance at the [[University of Minnesota]] with his old friend Gus Schurmeier as escort. He spent the evening casually asking for cigarettes in the middle of the dance floor and absent-mindedly drawing a small vanity case from the top of a blue stocking".</ref> Years later, while drafting ''The Great Gatsby'', rumors dogged Fitzgerald among the American expat community in Paris that he was gay.<ref name="Sexuality Rumors" /> Soon after, Fitzgerald's wife Zelda Fitzgerald likewise doubted his heterosexuality and asserted that he was a [[closeted homosexual]].{{sfn|Fessenden|2005|p=33}} She publicly belittled him with [[homophobic slurs]],{{sfn|Milford|1970|p=183}} and she alleged that Fitzgerald and fellow writer [[Ernest Hemingway]] engaged in homosexual relations.{{sfn|Fitzgerald|Fitzgerald|2002|p=65}}<ref>{{harvnb|Bruccoli|2002|p=275}}: "Zelda extended her attack on Fitzgerald's masculinity by charging that he was involved in a homosexual liaison with Hemingway".</ref> These incidents strained the Fitzgeralds' marriage at the time of the novel's publication.{{sfn|Fessenden|2005|p=33}}

Although Fitzgerald's sexuality is a subject of scholarly debate,{{efn|name=Fitzgerald's sexuality|Fessenden (2005) argues that Fitzgerald struggled with his sexual orientation.{{sfn|Fessenden|2005|pp=32–33}} In contrast, Bruccoli (2002) insists that "anyone can be called a latent homosexual, but there is no evidence that Fitzgerald was ever involved in a homosexual attachment".{{sfn|Bruccoli|2002|p=275}}}} such biographical details lent credence to critical interpretations that his fictional characters are either gay or bisexual surrogates.{{efn|name=Half-Feminine|Scholars have focused on Fitzgerald's statement in a letter that his mind was "half feminine".{{sfn|Kerr|1996|p=406}} In 1935, Fitzgerald wrote to Laura Guthrie: "I don't know what it is in me or that comes to me when I start to write. I am half feminine—at least my mind is".{{sfn|Turnbull|1962|p=259}}}}<ref>{{harvnb|Fessenden|2005|p=31}}: The novel "includes some queer energies, to be sure—we needn't revisit the more gossipy strains of Fitzgerald biography to note that it's Nick who delivers the sensuous goods on Gatsby from beginning to end".</ref>{{sfn|Kerr|1996|p=406}} As early as 1945, critics such as [[Lionel Trilling]] noted that characters in ''The Great Gatsby'', such as Jordan Baker, were implied to be "vaguely homosexual",{{sfn|Kazin|1951|p=202}}{{sfn|Paulson|1978|p=326}} and, in 1960, writer [[Otto Friedrich]] commented upon the ease of examining the thwarted relations depicted in Fitzgerald's fiction through a queer lens.{{sfn|Friedrich|1960|p=394}} In recent decades, scholarship has focused sharply on the sexuality of Nick Carraway.<ref>{{harvnb|Kerr|1996|p=406}}: "It was in the 1970s that readers first began to address seriously the themes of gender and sexuality in ''The Great Gatsby''; a few critics have pointed out the novel's bizarre homoerotic leitmotif".</ref> In one instance in the novel, Carraway departs a drunken orgy with a "pale, feminine" man named Mr. McKee and—following suggestive ellipses—Nick next finds himself standing beside a bed while McKee sits between the sheets clad only in his underwear.{{sfn|Vogel|2015|p=34}}{{sfn|Kerr|1996|pp=412, 414}} Such scenes have led scholars to describe Nick as possessing an overt queerness and prompted analyses about his emotional attachment to Jay Gatsby.{{sfnm|Kerr|1996|1pp=409–411|Vogel|2015|2p=34|Lisca|1967|3pp=20–21|Paulson|1978|4p=329|Wasiolek|1992|5pp=20–21}} For these reasons, the novel has been described as an exploration of sexual identity during a historical era typified by the societal transition towards [[modernity]].<ref>{{harvnb|Vogel|2015|pp=31, 51}}: "Among the most significant contributions of ''The Great Gatsby'' to the present is its intersectional exploration of identity.... these themes are inextricably woven into questions of race, ethnicity, gender, and sexuality".</ref><ref>{{harvnb|Paulson|1978|p=329}}: Commenting upon Nick's sexual confusion, A. B. Paulson remarked in 1978 that "the novel is about identity, about leaving home and venturing into a world of adults, about choosing a profession, about choosing a sexual role to play as well as a partner to love, it is a novel that surely appeals on several deep levels to the problems of adolescent readers".</ref>

==== Technology and environment ====
Technological and environmental criticisms of ''Gatsby'' seek to place the novel and its characters in a broader historical context.<ref>{{harvnb|Keeler|2018|pp=174–188}}; {{harvnb|Marx|1964|pp=358, 362–364}}; {{harvnb|Little|2015|pp=3–26}}.</ref> In 1964, [[Leo Marx]] argued in ''[[The Machine in the Garden]]'' that Fitzgerald's work evinces a tension between a complex [[Pastoralism|pastoral ideal]] of a bygone America and the societal transformations caused by [[Technological and industrial history of the United States|industrialization]] and [[machine technology]].{{sfn|Marx|1964|pp=358–364}} Specifically, the valley of the ashes, in between West Egg and New York, represents a man-made [[Barren vegetation|wasteland]] which is a byproduct of the industrialization that has made Gatsby's booming lifestyle, including his automobile, possible.{{sfn|Marx|1964|p=358}} Marx argues that Fitzgerald, via Nick, expresses a pastoral longing typical of other 1920s American writers like [[William Faulkner]] and Ernest Hemingway.{{sfn|Marx|1964|p=362}} Although such writers cherish the pastoral ideal, they accept that technological progress has deprived this ideal of nearly all meaning.<ref name="Leo Marx">{{harvnb|Marx|1964|pp=363–364}}</ref> In this context, Nick's repudiation of the <!--Please do not change to "East Coast" as "eastern United States" is conceptually distinct.-->[[eastern United States]] represents a futile attempt to withdraw into nature.<ref name="Leo Marx" /> Yet, as Fitzgerald's work shows, any technological demarcation between the eastern and the [[western United States]] has vanished,{{efn|name=East-West Theme|Throughout the novel, Fitzgerald identifies his native region of the [[Midwestern United States|Midwest]]—those "towns beyond [[Ohio River|the Ohio]]"—with the perceived virtuousness and rustic simplicity of the [[American frontier|American West]] and as culturally distinct from the decadent values of the eastern United States.{{sfnm|Mizener|1965|1p=190|Marx|1964|2p=363}}<ref>{{harvnb|Turnbull|1962|p=46}}: "In those days the contrasts between [[Eastern United States|East]] and [[American West|West]], between city and country, between prep school and high school were more marked than they are now, and correspondingly the nuances of dress and manners were more noticeable".</ref>}} and one cannot escape into a pastoral past.<ref name="Leo Marx" />

In 2018, scholar Kyle Keeler argued that the voracious pursuit of wealth as criticized in Fitzgerald's novel offers a warning about the perils of [[environmental destruction]] in pursuit of [[self-interest]].<ref name="Keeler 2018">{{harvnb|Keeler|2018|p=174}}.</ref> According to Kyle Keeler, Gatsby's quest for greater status manifests as self-centered, [[anthropocentric]] resource acquisition.<ref name="Keeler 2018" /> Inspired by the predatory [[Strip-mining|mining practices]] of his fictional mentor Dan Cody, Gatsby participates in extensive [[deforestation]] amid World War&nbsp;I and then undertakes bootlegging activities reliant upon exploiting [[Agriculture in South America|South American agriculture]].<ref name="Keeler 2018" /> Gatsby conveniently ignores the wasteful devastation of the valley of ashes to pursue a [[consumer culture|consumerist lifestyle]] and exacerbates the [[Wealth gap in the United States|wealth gap]] that became increasingly salient in 1920s America.<ref name="Keeler 2018" /> For these reasons, Keeler argues that—while Gatsby's socioeconomic ascent and self-transformation depend upon these very factors—each one is nonetheless partially responsible for the ongoing [[Global warming|ecological crisis]].<ref name="Keeler 2018" />


==== Time ====
Scholars have identified time as one of the novel's central preoccupations. Biographer [[Matthew J. Bruccoli]] states that the theme of the novel "can be expressed as Gatsby's struggle against time" and that Fitzgerald, who referred to the "hauntedness" in ''The Great Gatsby'', "was haunted by lost time and borrowed time".{{sfn|Bruccoli|2002|p=220}} From the novel's opening words ("In my younger and more vulnerable years") to its closing line ("borne back ceaselessly into the past"), the text contains at least 450 time words; excluding character names, "time" is the second most frequent noun in the novel, with 87 appearances.{{sfn|Bruccoli|2002|p=220}} Bruccoli traces the time imagery threaded through the narrative: the Buchanans' lawn "jumping over sun-dials" in the novel's first striking image, the list of Gatsby's guests that Nick records on a time-table, and the reunion scene in which Gatsby almost knocks the defunct clock off the mantel.{{sfn|Bruccoli|2002|p=220}} Time, he notes, is a concern in all of Fitzgerald's best writing, and [[Malcolm Cowley]] observed that Fitzgerald's work reads as though it was written in a room full of clocks and calendars.{{sfn|Bruccoli|2002|p=220}}

=== Antisemitism ===
{{CSS image crop | Image = Arnold Rothstein Chicago 1919.jpg | bSize = 190 | cWidth = 160 | cHeight = 200 | oTop = 0 | oLeft = 20 | Location = right |alt=Photograph of Arnold Rothstein | Description = Fitzgerald based the character of Meyer Wolfsheim on [[Jazz Age]] [[Racket (crime)|racketeer]] [[Arnold Rothstein]] (''pictured above'') who was murdered in 1928.}}
''The Great Gatsby'' has been accused of [[antisemitism]] because of its use of [[stereotypes of Jews]].{{sfn|Krystal|2015}} One of the novel's supporting characters is Meyer Wolfsheim,{{efn|name=Wolfsheim|The spelling "Wolfshiem" appears throughout Fitzgerald's original manuscript, while "Wolfsheim" was introduced by editor [[Edmund Wilson]] in the second edition.{{sfn|Fitzgerald|1991|p=liv}} This appears in later Scribner's editions.{{sfn|Fitzgerald|1991|p=148}}}} a [[Jewish]] friend and mentor of Gatsby. A corrupt profiteer who assists Gatsby's bootlegging operations and who [[1919 World Series#The fix|fixed the 1919 World Series]], he appears only twice in the novel, the second time refusing to attend Gatsby's funeral. Fitzgerald describes Wolfsheim as "a small, flat-nosed Jew", with "tiny eyes" and "two fine growths of hair" in his nostrils.{{sfn|Berrin|2013}} Evoking ethnic stereotypes regarding the [[Jewish nose]], he describes Wolfsheim's nose as "expressive", "tragic", and able to "flash&nbsp;... indignantly".{{sfn|Berrin|2013}} The fictional character of Wolfsheim is an allusion to real-life Jewish gambler [[Arnold Rothstein]],<ref>{{harvnb|Krystal|2015}}; {{harvnb|Bruccoli|2000|p=29}}; {{harvnb|Mizener|1965|p=186}}.</ref> a notorious New York [[Crime boss|crime kingpin]] whom Fitzgerald met once in undetermined circumstances.<ref>{{harvnb|Bruccoli|2002|p=179}}; {{harvnb|Mizener|1965|p=186}}</ref> Rothstein was blamed for match fixing in the [[Black Sox Scandal]] that tainted the [[1919 World Series]].{{sfn|Bruccoli|2000|p=29}}

Wolfsheim has been interpreted as representing the [[Economic antisemitism#Allegations of unethical business practices|Jewish miser stereotype]]. [[Richard S. Levy|Richard Levy]], author of ''Antisemitism: A Historical Encyclopedia of Prejudice and Persecution'', claims that Wolfsheim serves to link Jewishness with corruption.{{sfn|Berrin|2013}} In a 1947 article for ''[[Commentary (magazine)|Commentary]]'', Milton Hindus, an assistant professor of humanities at the [[University of Chicago]], stated that while he believed the book was a superb literary achievement, Wolfsheim was its most abrasive character, and the work contains an antisemitic undertone.{{sfn|Hindus|1947}} Hindus argued the Jewish stereotypes displayed by Wolfsheim were typical of the time when the novel was written and set and that its antisemitism was of the "habitual, customary, 'harmless,' unpolitical variety".<ref>{{harvnb|Hindus|1947}}; {{harvnb|Berrin|2013}}.</ref> A 2015 article by essayist [[Arthur Krystal]] agreed with Hindus' assessment that Fitzgerald's use of Jewish caricatures was not driven by malice and merely reflected commonly held beliefs of his time. He notes the accounts of [[Frances Kroll Ring|Frances Kroll]], a Jewish woman and secretary to Fitzgerald, who claimed that Fitzgerald was hurt by accusations of antisemitism and responded to critiques of Wolfsheim by claiming he merely "fulfilled a function in the story and had nothing to do with race or religion".{{sfn|Krystal|2015}}

== Adaptations ==
{{further|Adaptations of The Great Gatsby}}
=== Plays ===
[[File:James Rennie and Florence Eldridge in The Great Gatsby, 1926.jpg|thumb|upright=0.8|Florence Eldridge as Daisy and James Rennie as Gatsby in the first stage adaptation of ''The Great Gatsby'', 1926]]
The first stage adaptation was produced by [[William A. Brady|William Brady]], a veteran theatrical impresario and promoter of prize fights, who acquired the rights only a few days after first reading the novel in early 1925. The script was written by the American dramatist [[Owen Davis]], who had won a Pulitzer Prize in 1923 for his play, [[Icebound (play)|''Icebound'']].{{sfn|West|Daniel|2024|pp=xii–xiv}} Davis dramatically altered the structure of the novel, rearranging the action in chronological order, eliminating prominent elements such as the valley of ashes and the scene in the Plaza Hotel, and inventing minor characters.{{sfn|West|Daniel|2024|p=xxx}}

The play, directed by [[George Cukor]] and starring [[James Rennie (actor)|James Rennie]] as Gatsby and [[Florence Eldridge]] as Daisy, opened at the [[Ambassador Theatre (Broadway)|Ambassador Theatre]]<ref>"'Gatsby' Tonight", ''Daily News'' (New York), February 2, 1926, p.26</ref> 
on [[Broadway theatre|Broadway]] on February 2, 1926.<ref>"'Gatsby' Tonight", ''Daily News'' (New York), February 2, 1926, p.26</ref> It was well received by critics and the public, and the run was extended past the originally scheduled closing date, finally ending on May 22, after 112 performances.{{sfn|West|Daniel|2024|pp=xvi–xviii, xxvii–xxviii}} The production, with some changes in the cast, then moved to Chicago, where it opened on August 1. Its popularity again led to an extension of the run, which came to an end in late September.{{sfn|West|Daniel|2024|pp=xxviii–xxix}} A brief one-week return engagement at New York's [[Shubert Theatre (Broadway)|Shubert Theater]] began on October 4, after which a road production traveled to several other cities, including Baltimore, Philadelphia, Detroit, St. Louis, Denver, and Minneapolis.{{sfn|West|Daniel|2024|p=xxix}}

In July 2006, a stage adaptation written by [[Simon Levy]] and directed by [[David Esbjornson]] premiered at the [[Guthrie Theater]] in Minneapolis to celebrate the opening of its new building.{{sfn|Skinner|2006}} In 2010, critic [[Ben Brantley]] of ''[[The New York Times]]'' highly praised the debut of ''[[Gatz]]'', an [[Off-Broadway]] staging of the novel's full text by [[Elevator Repair Service]].{{sfn|Brantley|2010}} The [[Metropolitan Opera|New York Metropolitan Opera]] commissioned [[John Harbison]] to compose an [[opera]]tic treatment of the novel to commemorate the 25th anniversary of [[James Levine]]'s debut. The work, called ''[[The Great Gatsby (opera)|The Great Gatsby]]'', premiered on December 20, 1999.{{sfn|Stevens|1999}}

The novel has also been adapted for ballet performances. In 2009, [[BalletMet]] premiered a version at the Capitol Theatre in [[Columbus, Ohio]].{{sfn|Grossberg|2009}} In 2010, [[The Washington Ballet]] premiered a version at the [[Kennedy Center]]. The show received an encore run the following year.<ref>{{harvnb|Kaufman|2011}}; {{harvnb|Aguirre|2011}}.</ref>

=== Film ===
{{multiple image
| align             = right
| direction         = vertical
| width             = 280
| image1            = Great Gatsby lobby card.jpg
| alt1              = A lobby card advertising the lost 1926 Gatsby film version
| caption1          = A [[lobby card]] for the lost [[The Great Gatsby (1926 film)|1926 film adaptation]]
| image2            = The Great Gatsby trailer (1926).webm
| alt2              = A trailer advertising the 1926 Gatsby film
| caption2          = The 1926 film trailer—the only extant footage
}}

[[The Great Gatsby (1926 film)|The first film version of the novel]] appeared in 1926. A version of Owen Davis's Broadway play of the same year, it was directed by [[Herbert Brenon]] and starred [[Warner Baxter]], [[Lois Wilson (actress)|Lois Wilson]] and [[William Powell]]. It is a famous example of a [[lost film]]. Reviews suggest it may have been the most faithful adaptation of the novel, but a trailer of the film at the [[National Archives and Records Administration|National Archives]] is all that is known to exist.{{sfn|Dixon|2003}} Reportedly, Fitzgerald and his wife Zelda loathed the silent version. Zelda wrote to an acquaintance that the film was "rotten". She and Fitzgerald left the cinema midway through the film.<ref name="Howell 2013">{{harvnb|Howell|2013}}; {{harvnb|Hischak|2012|pp=85–86}}.</ref>

Following the 1926 film was 1949's ''[[The Great Gatsby (1949 film)|The Great Gatsby]]'', directed by [[Elliott Nugent]] and starring [[Alan Ladd]], [[Betty Field]] and [[Macdonald Carey]].<ref name="Dixon 2003">{{harvnb|Dixon|2003}}; {{harvnb|Hischak|2012|pp=85–86}}.</ref> Twenty-five years later in 1974, ''[[The Great Gatsby (1974 film)|The Great Gatsby]]'' appeared onscreen again. It was directed by [[Jack Clayton]] and starred [[Robert Redford]] as Gatsby, [[Mia Farrow]] as Daisy, and [[Sam Waterston]] as Nick Carraway.<ref name="Dixon 2003" /> Most recently, ''[[The Great Gatsby (2013 film)|The Great Gatsby]]'' was directed by [[Baz Luhrmann]] in 2013 and starred [[Leonardo DiCaprio]] as Gatsby, [[Carey Mulligan]] as Daisy, and [[Tobey Maguire]] as Nick.<ref name="Howell 2013" />

In 2021, visual effects company [[DNEG#Animation|DNEG Animation]] announced they would be producing an animated film adaptation of the novel directed by [[William Joyce (writer)|William Joyce]] and written by [[Brian Selznick]].{{sfn|Giardina|2021}}

=== Television ===
''Gatsby'' has been retold as a short-form television movie multiple times. The first was in 1955 as an [[NBC]] episode for ''[[Robert Montgomery Presents]]'' starring [[Robert Montgomery (actor)|Robert Montgomery]], [[Phyllis Kirk]], and [[Lee Bowman]]. The episode was directed by Alvin Sapinsley.{{sfn|Hyatt|2006|pp=49–50}} In 1958, [[CBS]] filmed another adaptation as an episode of ''[[Playhouse 90]]'', also titled ''[[The Great Gatsby (Playhouse 90)|The Great Gatsby]],'' which was directed by [[Franklin J. Schaffner]] and starred [[Robert Ryan]], [[Jeanne Crain]] and [[Rod Taylor]].{{sfn|Hischak|2012|pp=85–86}} Most recently, the novel was adapted as an [[A+E Global Media|A&E movie]] in 2000. ''[[The Great Gatsby (2000 film)|The Great Gatsby]]'' was directed by [[Robert Markowitz]] and starred [[Toby Stephens]] as Gatsby, [[Mira Sorvino]] as Daisy, and [[Paul Rudd]] as Nick.{{sfn|Howell|2013}}{{sfn|Hischak|2012|pp=85–86}}

=== Musicals ===
The [[Yale Dramatic Association]] performed the first musical production of ''The Great Gatsby'' in Summer 1956.<ref>{{harvnb|Tredell|2007|p=109}}: "It was adapted for a musical at Yale University in 1956".</ref>{{sfnm|''The New York Times''|1956|1p=21|''Wilmington News-Journal''|1956|2p=11|''The Reporter Dispatch''|1956|3p=6}} For the production, Aubrey L. Goodman adapted Fitzgerald's novel and wrote the lyrics for 14 songs by composer Robert E. Morgan. The show was performed in the [[University Theatre]] at [[Yale University]] to sold-out performances.{{sfnm|''The Waco Times-Herald''|1956|1p=24|''The Boston Globe''|1956|2p=127}} After the Yale production, a number of musical adaptations followed.

A second musical adaptation debuted in Spring 1998, undertaken by Stage One, with Colin Stevens as Gatsby and Ann Marcuson as Jordan Baker.{{sfn|''The Chronicle''|1999|p=100}} Directed by Phil Smith with an original score by Thomas Johnson, this jazz adaptation premiered at the Pavilion Theatre in [[Rhyl]], Wales. As a jazz adaptation, Johnson's original score emphasized saxophone and brass sextet instruments.{{sfn|''The Chronicle''|1999|p=100}}

In 2023, [[The Great Gatsby (musical)|the third musical adaptation]], with music and lyrics by [[Jason Howland]] and [[Nathan Tysen]] and a book by [[Kait Kerrigan]] began a one-month limited engagement at the [[Paper Mill Playhouse]].{{sfn|Heckmann|2023}} The Broadway tryout began its previews on October 12, 2023, followed by an official opening night scheduled for ten days later. The production concluded on November 12 of the same year. [[Jeremy Jordan (actor, born 1984)|Jeremy Jordan]] and [[Eva Noblezada]] starred as the leading roles of [[Jay Gatsby]] and [[Daisy Buchanan]], with [[Samantha Pauly]] and Noah J. Ricketts as Jordan Baker and Nick Carraway.{{sfn|Gordon|Stewart|2023}} The production transferred to [[Broadway theatre|Broadway]] for previews on March 29, 2024, and opened officially on April 25, 2024.{{sfn|Leavitt|2024}}{{sfn|Hall|2024}}

In Spring 2024, ''[[Gatsby: An American Myth]]'', a fourth musical adaptation with music and lyrics by [[Florence Welch]] and [[Doveman|Thomas Bartlett]] and a book by [[Martyna Majok]] premiered at the [[American Repertory Theater]]. The production starred [[Isaac Cole Powell]] as Jay Gatsby and [[Ben Levi Ross]] as Nick Carraway.{{sfn|American Repertory Theater|2023}} On May 25, 2024, the show began previews and opened officially on June 5 of the same year. It closed on August 3, 2024.

=== Literature ===
Since entering the public domain in 2021, retellings and expansions of ''The Great Gatsby'' have become legal to publish. ''[[Nick (novel)|Nick]]'' by [[Michael Farris Smith]] (2021) imagines the backstory of Nick Carraway.{{sfn|Flood|2020}} That same year saw the publication of ''[[The Chosen and the Beautiful]]'' by [[Nghi Vo]], a retelling with elements of the [[fantasy]] genre while tackling issues of race and sexuality,{{sfn|Wick|2021}} and ''The Pursued and the Pursuing'' by [[AJ Odasso]], a queer partial retelling and sequel in which Jay Gatsby survives.{{sfn|Grossman|2021}} [[Anna-Marie McLemore]]'s own queer retelling, ''Self-Made Boys: A Great Gatsby Remix'', was released in 2022 and was longlisted for the [[National Book Award for Young People's Literature]].{{sfn|Cerézo|2022}}

=== Radio ===
The novel has been adapted into a series of radio episodes. The first radio episode was a 1950 half-hour-long adaptation for CBS' ''[[Family Hour of Stars]]'' starring [[Kirk Douglas]] as Gatsby.{{sfn|Pitts|1986|p=127}} The novel was read aloud by the [[BBC World Service]] in ten parts in 2008. In a 2012 [[BBC Radio 4]] broadcast, ''[[Gaynor Macfarlane#The Great Gatsby|The Great Gatsby]]'' took the form of a [[Classic Serial]] dramatization. It was created by dramatist [[Robert Forrest (dramatist)|Robert Forrest]].{{sfn|White|2007}}{{sfn|Forrest|2012}}

In 2025, a radio adaptation entitled ''Gatsby in Harlem'' was broadcast on [[BBC Radio 3]]. The dramatisation was written by [[Roy Williams (playwright)|Roy Williams]], with [[Malachi Kirby]] starring as Nick Carraway, [[Ncuti Gatwa]] as Jay Gatsby, [[Gugu Mbatha-Raw]] as Daisy Buchanan, [[Chiké Okonkwo]] as Tom Buchanan.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Jones |first=Anna |title=Roy Williams on revamping The Great Gatsby with Ncuti Gatwa: 'I didn't want to repeat the same story' {{!}} Radio Times |url=https://www.radiotimes.com/audio/radio/gatsby-in-harlem/ |access-date=2026-07-07 |website=www.radiotimes.com |language=en-GB}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Drama On 3 - Gatsby In Harlem - part 1 |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/mediacentre/proginfo/2025/02/a-on-3 |access-date=2026-07-07 |website=www.bbc.co.uk |language=en}}</ref> The series won multiple awards at the inaugural British Audio Awards in 2025, including Audio of the Year, Best Audio Drama Adaptation, and Best Performance (won by Gatwa).<ref>{{Cite news |last=Loffhagen |first=Emma |date=2025-11-24 |title=Ncuti Gatwa leads star winners at first Speakies awards for audio storytelling |url=https://www.theguardian.com/books/2025/nov/24/ncuti-gatwa-leads-star-winners-at-first-speakies-awards-for-audio-storytelling |access-date=2026-07-07 |work=The Guardian |language=en-GB |issn=0261-3077}}</ref> It was also nominated for Best Adaptation in the [[BBC Audio Drama Awards]] 2026.<ref>{{Cite web |title=BBC Radio 4 - BBC Audio Drama Awards - The 2026 Finalists |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/programmes/articles/10RHpQPhRknkYxfFJSRDWgb/the-2026-finalists |access-date=2026-07-07 |website=BBC |language=en-GB}}</ref>

=== Video games ===
In 2010, Oberon Media released a casual [[hidden object game]] called ''Classic Adventures: The Great Gatsby''.{{sfn|Benedetti|2010}}{{sfn|Paskin|2010}} In 2011, developer Charlie Hoey and editor Pete Smith created an [[History of video game consoles (third generation)|8-bit-style]] online game of ''The Great Gatsby'' called ''The Great Gatsby for NES'';{{sfn|Bell|2011}}{{sfn|Crouch|2011}} in 2022, after the [[Adobe Flash#End of life|discontinuation of Adobe Flash]], they adapted this game to an actual [[NES]] [[ROM file]], which can also be played on their website.{{sfn|Smith|2022}} In 2013, ''[[Slate (magazine)|Slate]]'' released a short symbolic adaptation called ''The Great Gatsby: The Video Game''.{{sfn|Kirk|Morgan|Wickman|2013}}{{sfn|Sarkar|2013}}
