[[Hobey Baker|Hobey Amory Baker]] (third), a Princeton football hero, inspired the protagonist's name "Amory" and the character of Allenby. [[Zelda Sayre]] (fourth) inspired the cruel and selfish character of Rosalind Connage.
 | footer_align = left
}}
* '''Amory Blaine'''{{snd}} a handsome and egocentric young man, who has a series of unfulfilling romances with young women. Originally from the [[Midwestern United States|Midwest]], he attends Princeton and later fights in World War&nbsp;I. Ambitious in a undefined way "I was planning to be such an important finger" {{sfn|Fitzgerald|1921|p=229}}, he is compared to "Narcissus", is "completely lacking in all human sympathy"{{sfn|Fitzgerald|1921|p=276}}, "cynical" {{sfn|"I'm a cynical idealist." Fitzgerald|1921|p=93}}, and has a "tendency to pose".{{sfn|Fitzgerald|1921|p=35}} Amory spends much of his first two years at Princeton in a pursuit of a prestigious "club" (fraternity) membership. Courses do not interest him, except the "melancholy hexameters"{{sfn|Fitzgerald|1921|p=88}} and the "rigid clarity in solid geometry" {{sfn|Fitzgerald|1921|p=36}}. At the end of the sophomore year he is "conditioned" and fails in the fall an important exam on "conic sections" {{sfn|Fitzgerald|1921|p=104}}, which prevents his original plan "to be one of the gods of the class" {{sfn|Fitzgerald|1921|p=47}}. 

Fitzgerald based the character on an idealized version of himself and his disappointing romantic relationships.<ref>{{harvnb|Bruccoli|1981|p=127}}: "Amory Blaine is a rather idealized Fitzgerald".</ref>{{sfn|Tate|1998|p=22}} The name "Amory" derives from Fitzgerald's football hero at Princeton, [[Hobey Baker|Hobart Amory Baker]].<ref>{{harvnb|Bernstein|2009|p=40}}: "Fitzgerald called Hobart Amory Hare (Hobey) Baker 'an ideal worthy of everything in my enthusiastic imagination' and named the protagonist of his novel ''This Side of Paradise'' Amory in his honor".</ref>{{sfn|Salvini|2005|p=49}}

* '''Isabelle Borgé'''{{snd}}a wealthy and shallow debutante<!-- Isabelle is not a flapper. --> who is Amory's first love.{{sfnm|Smith|2003|1p=E1|Tate|1998|2p=24}} Amory wonders whether she may "prove not too exotic a bloom" {{sfn|Fitzgerald|1921|p=89}}, but he believes she is too beautiful to pass and starts a long-distance relationship, fueled by long love letters "in an eternal monotone" {{sfn|Fitzgerald|1921|p=91}} that required two "bulky envelopes".{{sfn|Fitzgerald|1921|p=89}} He then discovers that he has no real affection for her and that the liaison is only a pretense in a struggle for power "She mustn't lose the leadership a bit." {{sfn|Fitzgerald|1921|p=71}}

[[Ginevra King]], a socialite upon whom Fitzgerald developed a life-long romantic obsession, inspired the character.{{sfnm|Bruccoli|1981|1pp=125, 127|Noden|2003}}{{sfnm|Smith|2003|1p=E1|Tate|1998|2p=24}} Like Amory and Isabelle, an 18-year-old Fitzgerald fell in love with a 16-year-old King on Christmas break in Saint Paul, Minnesota, during his sophomore year at Princeton, and their relationship ended in a similar fashion.{{sfn|Smith|2003|p=E1}} Rumors circulated that Ginevra had kissed dozens of boys, all of whom fell in love with her.{{sfn|Donaldson|1983|p=48}} "I was too thoughtless in those days," Ginevra recalled, "and too much in love with love to think of consequences."{{sfn|Eble|1963|p=115}} Until his death, Fitzgerald remained forever in love with King and "could not think of her without tears coming to his eyes".<ref name="Lifelong Obsession">{{harvnb|Mizener|1972|p=28}}: "Ginevra gave substance to an ideal Fitzgerald would cling to for a lifetime; to the end of his days, the thought of her could bring tears to his eyes."</ref>{{sfnm|Stevens|2003|Noden|2003}}

* '''Rosalind Connage'''{{snd}}a cruel and selfish [[flapper]] whom Amory romances.{{sfn|Tate|1998|p=40}} Amory has real affection for her (unlike for Isabelle). She cultivates expensive habits "I don't even do my own hair, usually."{{sfn|Fitzgerald|1921|p=207}}, is uninterested in family or children "I want to worry whether my legs will get slick and brown when I swim in the summer." {{sfn|Fitzgerald|1921|p=210}}, and sets her own price "Fifty-one shares, name, good- will, and everything goes at $25,000 a year."{{sfn|Fitzgerald|1921|p=187}}.

Fitzgerald based Rosalind on 18-year-old [[Zelda Fitzgerald|Zelda Sayre]] and, to a lesser extent, on the fictional character of Beatrice Normandy in [[H. G. Wells]]' 1909 novel ''[[Tono-Bungay]]''.<ref>{{harvnb|Bruccoli|1981|p=127}}: "Rosalind is a combination of Zelda and Beatrice Normandy from Tono-Bungay."</ref>{{sfn|Tate|1998|p=40}} Mirroring Rosalind's materialistic relationship with Amory, Sayre ended her engagement with Fitzgerald due to his inability to support her privileged lifestyle as an idle<!-- See Wagner 2004 and Bruccoli 1981 citations for "idle". --> [[Southern belle]] of Montgomery's [[country club]] set.<ref name="Unwilling to wait"/><ref name="Idle Southern Belle"/> She resumed their engagement on the condition that he would provide her with luxury.<ref name="Affluent lifestyle"/>{{sfnm|Bruccoli|1981|1pp=100-110|Turnbull|1962|2p=102|Milford|1970|3p=57}}

* '''Eleanor Savage'''{{snd}}a beautiful and reckless atheist whom Amory meets in a haystack in rural Maryland.{{sfnm|Mizener|1951|1p=44|Tate|1998|2p=219}} She is exiled to rural MD by her Baltimore family and of "Bohemian naughtiness"{{sfn|Fitzgerald|1921|p=258}}, "Oh, just one person in fifty has any glimmer of what sex is" {{sfn|Fitzgerald|1921|p=255}}, she resents being "tied to the sinking ship of future matrimony".{{sfn|Fitzgerald|1921|p=255}} Amory and Eleanor recite Poe and Verlaine to each other, yet part "hating each other with a bitter sadness".{{sfn|Fitzgerald|1921|p=258}}

Fitzgerald partly based Eleanor on a purported love of his mentor Father Sigourney Fay,{{sfnm|Mizener|1951|1p=44|Bruccoli|1981|2p=127}}  and, to a lesser extent, on 18-year-old Elizabeth Beckwith MacKie, a romantic interest he briefly knew.{{sfnm|Tate|1998|1p=219|MacKie|1970|2pp=16–27}}<ref>{{harvnb|MacKie|1970|p=20}}: Scott "was always trying to see how far he could go in arousing your feelings, but it was always with words... This was his first exposure to southern girls, who in turn had been exposed to less timid southern boys. The southern boys I knew, despite their verbal lethargy, at least understood what it was all about, and were more aggressive and emotionally satisfying. In 1917, I'm afraid, Scott just wasn't a very lively male animal."</ref> MacKie commented that the character "reminded me of how little he really knew me. His Eleanor loved to sit on a haystack in the rain reciting poetry. Forgive me, Scott: if that is the way you wanted it, then you missed the whole idea of what can happen atop a haystack."{{sfn|MacKie|1970|p=23}} 

* '''Thayer Darcy'''{{snd}}a jovial and impious Catholic priest who serves as Amory's spiritual mentor.{{sfnm|Fitzgerald|1921|1p=26|Tate|1998|2p=53}} Father Sigourney Fay, a possibly [[gay]] Catholic priest with whom Fitzgerald had an intimate and ambiguous relationship,<ref name="Sigourney Fay"/><ref name="Fay Sexuality"/> inspired the character.{{sfn|Bruccoli|1981|p=127}}{{sfnm|Turnbull|1962|1p=39|Tate|1998|2p=53}} While writing ''This Side of Paradise'', Fitzgerald quoted verbatim entire letters sent to him by Fay.<ref>{{harvnb|Mizener|1951|p=44}}: "Fitzgerald used three of Fay's letters and one of his poems in ''This Side of Paradise''".</ref> In addition to using Fay's private correspondence, Fitzgerald drew on anecdotes that Fay had told him in confidence about his personal life, including his purported failed romances with women.{{sfn|Mizener|1951|p=44}} When reading ''This Side of Paradise'', Fay wrote to Fitzgerald that the unapproved use of these experiences told in confidence to the author "gave him a queer feeling."{{sfn|Mizener|1951|p=44}}
* '''Beatrice Blaine'''{{snd}}an aging and eccentric matron who is Amory's mother. Based on the mother of one of Fitzgerald's friends.{{sfn|Bruccoli|1981|p=127}}
* '''Clara Page'''{{snd}}a widowed older cousin for whom Amory has unrequited affection. Based on Fitzgerald's cousin Cecilia Delihant Taylor.{{sfn|Tate|1998|p=186}}
* '''Cecelia<!-- The character is named Cecelia, not Cecilia. --> Connage'''{{snd}}Rosalind's cynical younger sister who steals cigarettes and envies her sibling's popularity among young men.{{sfnm|Fitzgerald|1921|1pp=192-193|Tate|1998|2p=40}}

* '''[[Thomas Parke D'Invilliers]]'''{{snd}}a bespectacled and high-brow Princeton classmate who has a gift for poetry.{{sfn|Fitzgerald|1921|pp=55-57}} Fitzgerald based D'Invilliers on his Princeton friend, poet [[John Peale Bishop]].{{sfnm|Bruccoli|1981|1p=127|Tate|1998|2p=21}} D'Invilliers becomes Amory's close friend and confidante in various subjects, among which are literature, love for young beauties, politics, and the meaning of the self. He becomes a journalist, developing his own perspectives apart from those he shares with Amory. The character reappears as a fictitious poet quoted on the title page of Fitzgerald's 1925 novel ''[[The Great Gatsby]]''.{{sfn|Tate|1998|p=21}}

* '''Alec Connage'''{{snd}} Rosalind's older brother and classmate of Amory at Princeton. Met by Amory later in Atlantic City NJ, with a ``Miss Jill" (real name Stella Robbins from NH) who was known to the hotel staff.  
	
* '''Kerry Holiday'''{{snd}} classmate at Princeton, volunteers in an aviation unit and dies in the war
	
* '''Burne Holiday'''{{snd}} Kerry's younger brother, classmate at Princeton, becomes a pacifist

* '''Fred Sloane'''{{snd}} classmate at Princeton, plays pitcher, careless and relaxed 

* '''Dick Humbird'''{{snd}} classmate at Princeton, dies in a car accident due to own recklessness

* '''Allenby'''{{snd}}a heroic football captain at Princeton based on [[Hobey Baker]].{{sfn|Fitzgerald|1921|pp=41, 46}}{{sfnm|Tate|1998|1p=3|Mizener|1972|2p=9|Mizener|1951|3p=6}} The national press praised Baker as one of the greatest athletes of his time, and he embodied everything Fitzgerald aspired to be as a Princeton undergraduate.{{sfn|Salvini|2005|p=49}}{{sfnm|Tate|1998|1p=3|Mizener|1972|2p=9|Mizener|1951|3p=6}} He described Baker as "an ideal worthy of everything in my enthusiastic admiration, yet consummated and expressed in a human being who stood within ten feet of me."{{sfnm|Salvini|2005|1p=49|Bernstein|2009|2p=40}} After graduating from Princeton in 1914, Baker enlisted in the [[U.S. Army Air Service]] amid World War&nbsp;I and died in a plane crash in December 1918.{{sfn|''The New York Times''|1919}}{{sfn|Salvini|2005|pp=62, 94–101, 111–119}}

== Background and composition ==
=== Love, war, and novel ambitions ===
{{multiple image
 | perrow = 2
 | total_width = 300
 | align = left
 | image1 = F Scott Fitzgerald circa 1920.jpg
 | width1 = 150
 | image2 = Ginevra King.jpg
 | width2 = 150
 | footer = [[F. Scott Fitzgerald|Fitzgerald]] circa 1920, the year his novel debuted, and socialite [[Ginevra King]] circa 1918
 | footer_align = left
}}
Since childhood, F. Scott Fitzgerald aspired to become a famous novelist.{{sfn|Turnbull|1962|p=7}} "Three months before I was born," Scott later wrote, "my mother lost her other two children... I think I started then to be a writer."{{sfn|Turnbull|1962|p=7}} While attending Princeton University, his passion for writing literature began to solidify into a career choice, and he wrote fiction as an undergraduate for the [[Princeton Triangle Club]], the ''[[Princeton Tiger Magazine|Princeton Tiger]]'', and the ''Nassau Literary Review''.{{sfn|Bruccoli|1981|pp=44–45, 65–75, 102–106}}{{sfn|Turnbull|1962|p=73}}

During his sophomore year at Princeton, Fitzgerald returned home to [[Saint Paul, Minnesota]] during Christmas break where the 18-year-old aspiring writer fell in love with 16-year-old Chicago debutante [[Ginevra King]].<!-- The New York Times erroneously states Fitzgerald was 19 years old on January 4, 1915. --><ref name="Ginevra King">{{harvnb|Smith|2003|p=E1}}: Fitzgerald confided to [[Frances Scott Fitzgerald|his daughter]] that Ginevra King "was the first girl I ever loved" and that he "faithfully avoided seeing her" to "keep the illusion perfect".</ref>{{sfn|West|2005|p=21}} They began a passionate romantic relationship spanning several years.{{sfnm|Smith|2003|1p=E1|West|2005|2p=104}} Although Ginevra loved him,{{sfn|West|2005|p=35}} her upper-class family belittled Scott's courtship because of his lower-class status compared to her other wealthy suitors.{{sfn|West|2005|p=42}} Rejected by Ginevra as a suitable match, Fitzgerald enlisted in the United States Army amid World War&nbsp;I.{{sfn|Mizener|1951|p=70}}<ref name="Suicidal Urge">{{harvnb|Bruccoli|1981|p=84}}: "Like all infantry lieutenants at the time, Fitzgerald expected to be killed in battle. He began writing a novel in training camp, hoping to leave evidence of his genius."</ref>

In November 1917, hoping to have a novel published before his deployment to Europe and his anticipated death in the trenches of World War&nbsp;I,<ref name="Suicidal Urge"/> Fitzgerald began writing a 120,000-word manuscript titled ''The Romantic Egotist''.{{sfnm|Bruccoli|1981|1pp=83–87|Tate|1998|2p=281}} Having never before undertaken a novel, he relied upon [[H. G. Wells]]' 1909 novel ''[[Tono-Bungay]]'' and Sir [[Compton Mackenzie]]'s 1913 novel ''[[Sinister Street]]'' as his literary templates.{{sfnm|Wilson|1952|1p=32|Fitzgerald|2004|2pp=41, 83|Kazin|1951|3pp=29, 48, 78}} He sought to write the story of America's younger generation from the perspective of himself as a conscious observer.{{sfn|Bruccoli|1981|pp=84–85}} After obtaining a brief leave from the army in February 1918, Fitzgerald continued work on his unpublished manuscript at the [[University Cottage Club]]'s library in Princeton.{{sfnm|Bruccoli|1981|1p=86|Tate|1998|2p=251}} Eighty-one pages of this revised manuscript appeared in the final version of ''This Side of Paradise''.{{sfn|Bruccoli|1981|p=103}}
{{multiple image
 | perrow = 2
 | total_width = 300
 | align = right
 | image1 = Shane Leslie LCCN2014686812 (cropped).jpg
 | width1 = 150
 | image2 = For remembrance, soldier poets who have fallen in the war, Adcock, 1920 DJVU pg 10.jpg
 | width2 = 150
 | footer = Sir [[Shane Leslie]] (first), the first cousin of Sir [[Winston Churchill]], enclosed Fitzgerald's manuscript in a letter to [[Charles Scribner's Sons|Scribner's]], hailing Fitzgerald as the next [[Rupert Brooke]] (second). "Though Scott Fitzgerald is still alive it has a literary value," Leslie wrote in the letter, "Of course when he is killed, it will also have a commercial value."
 | footer_align = left
}}
In March 1918, Fitzgerald gave the revised manuscript to his acquaintance, Anglo-Irish journalist [[Shane Leslie]], to deliver to [[Charles Scribner's Sons]] in New York City.{{sfnm|Turnbull|1962|2p=82|Tate|1998|1p=251|Bruccoli|1981|3p=86}} Fitzgerald had met Leslie when the journalist visited America and toured the Newman School in New Jersey.{{sfn|Berg|1978|pp=12–13}} After proofreading ''The Romantic Egotist'', Leslie asked Scribner's to retain the manuscript no matter what they thought of it.{{sfn|Turnbull|1962|p=82}} He proclaimed that Fitzgerald, upon his presumed death in the trenches, would become the next [[Rupert Brooke]], a posthumously famous poet killed during World War&nbsp;I.{{sfn|Turnbull|1962|p=82}}{{sfn|Bruccoli|1981|p=86}} "Though Scott Fitzgerald is still alive it has a literary value," Leslie wrote to Scribner's on May 6, 1918, "Of course when he is killed, it will also have a commercial value."{{sfn|Bruccoli|1981|p=86}} 

Upon reading Fitzgerald's draft of ''The Romantic Egotist'', Scribner's editor [[Max Perkins]] urged his superiors to publish the manuscript, but senior editors [[Edward L. Burlingame]] and [[William C. Brownell]] disagreed with him regarding its quality and instructed him to reject the work.{{sfn|Bruccoli|1981|pp=88–89}} In an August 19, 1918 letter to Fitzgerald, Perkins turned down the manuscript but praised the writer's talent. Although he had been instructed to reject the work, Perkins provided detailed guidance on how to revise it, suggesting that Fitzgerald add more significance and details about Amory's "affairs with girls."{{sfn|Bruccoli|1981|pp=88–89}} Perkins encouraged Fitzgerald to resubmit the manuscript after making these revisions.{{sfn|Bruccoli|1981|pp=88–89}}

By June 1918, Fitzgerald served with the [[45th Infantry Regiment (United States)|45th]] and [[67th Infantry Regiment (United States)|67th Infantry Regiments]] at Camp Sheridan near Montgomery, Alabama.{{sfnm|Tate|1998|1pp=6, 32|Bruccoli|1981|p=86}} Attempting to rebound from Ginevra's rejection, a lonely Fitzgerald began courting young women, including [[Zelda Sayre Fitzgerald|Zelda Sayre]], an idle<!-- See Wagner 2004 and Bruccoli 1981 citations for "idle". --> [[Southern belle]],<ref name="Idle Southern Belle">Per {{harvnb|Wagner-Martin|2004|p=24}} and {{harvnb|Bruccoli|1981|pp=192–193, 440–441}}, during her idle youth as a Southern belle in the [[Jim Crow]] South, Zelda's affluent family employed half a dozen domestic servants, many of whom were [[African Americans|African-American]]. Consequently, Zelda was unaccustomed to responsibilities of any kind.</ref><ref>Per {{harvnb|Milford|1970|pp=3–4}}, "if there was a Confederate establishment in the [[Deep South]], [[Zelda Sayre]] came from the heart of it." Her grandfather, [[Willis B. Machen]], served in the [[Confederate Congress]]. {{harvnb|Milford|1970|p=5}} states her father's uncle was [[John Tyler Morgan]], a Confederate general and—according to {{harvnb|Davis|1924|pp=45, 56, 59}} and {{harvnb|Svrluga|2016}}—a [[Grand Dragon]] of the [[Ku Klux Klan]] in Alabama.</ref> who reminded him of Ginevra.<ref>{{harvnb|Piper|1965|p=40}}: "Zelda was attractive and vivacious and reminded him in many ways of Ginevra King".</ref>{{sfn|West|2005|pp=65–66, 73}} At their first meeting, Fitzgerald told Zelda that she reminded him of Isabelle, the free-spirited character based on Ginevra in his unpublished manuscript.{{sfn|Piper|1965|p=40}} After sharing his ambitions, Zelda dismissed Fitzgerald's remarks as mere boastfulness and concluded that he would never become a famous writer.{{sfn|Turnbull|1962|p=102}} A romance blossomed,{{sfn|Bruccoli|1981|pp=87–89}} although Fitzgerald continued secretly writing to Ginevra, hoping in vain for a chance to resume their relationship.{{sfn|West|2005|pp=65–66}} Three days after Ginevra's [[arranged marriage]] to a wealthy Chicago polo player, a heartbroken Fitzgerald professed his affection for Zelda in September 1918.{{sfn|West|2005|pp=66–70, 73}} In October 1918, Fitzgerald submitted a revised version of ''The Romantic Egoist'' to Scribner's, but the publisher rejected the work a second time, and he captioned their telegram in his scrapbook: "{{mono|The end of a dream}}."{{sfn|Tate|1998|p=251}}

=== Despair and manuscript revisions ===
After his army discharge in February 1919, Fitzgerald moved to New York City amid the onset of the [[Jazz Age]].{{efn|name=Jazz Age|Fitzgerald settled in New York City amid the societal transformations of the Jazz Age,{{sfn|Turnbull|1962|pp=92–93}} an era he described as racing "along under its own power, served by great filling stations full of money" and characterized by moral permissiveness, disillusionment with social norms, and an obsession with hedonism.<ref name="Filling stations">{{harvnb|Fitzgerald|1945|p=18}}: "In any case, the Jazz Age now raced along under its own power, served by great filling stations full of money".</ref><ref name="Hedonism">{{harvnb|Fitzgerald|1945|p=15}}: The Jazz Age represented "a whole race going hedonistic, deciding on pleasure".</ref>}}{{sfnm|Turnbull|1962|1pp=92–93|Fitzgerald|1945|2p=15}} While seeking a breakthrough as an author of fiction, he turned to writing advertising copy for [[Barron Collier]] to sustain himself but the vacuity of the work irritated him.{{sfn|Milford|1970|p=39}}{{sfn|Tate|1998|p=282}} "Advertising is a racket, like the movies and the brokerage business," Fitzgerald complained. "You cannot be honest without admitting that its constructive contribution to humanity is exactly minus zero."{{sfn|Fitzgerald|1966|p=108}} Although Fitzgerald had not intended to marry Zelda in December 1918,<ref>{{harvnb|Bruccoli|1981|p=94}}: Fitzgerald wrote on December 4, 1918, "My mind is firmly made up that I will not, shall not, can not, should not, must not marry".</ref> he changed his mind over the next three months, and the two became engaged by March 1919.{{sfnm|Milford|1970|1p=42|Turnbull|1962|2p=92}} As time passed, Fitzgerald continued living in poverty in New York City, and he could not convince Zelda that he could support her affluent lifestyle.<ref name="Affluent lifestyle">{{harvnb|Gallo|1978|p=6}}: "Even after Zelda fell in love with Scott, she would not settle for a marriage that promised only romance and poverty. She wanted luxury; and Scott would have to provide it."</ref> She broke off their engagement in June.<ref name="Unwilling to wait">{{harvnb|Tate|1998|p=82}}: "Unwilling to wait while Fitzgerald succeeded in the advertisement business and unwilling to live on his small salary, Zelda broke their engagement."</ref><ref name="Financial Success"/>{{sfn|Milford|1970|p=52}}
{{quote box | quote = <poem>Limbs that gleam and shadowy hair,
Or floating lazy, half-asleep.
Dive and double and follow after,
Snare in flowers, and kiss, and call,
With lips that fade, and human laughter
And faces individual,
Well this side of Paradise! . . .
There's little comfort in the wise.</poem> | source = —[[Rupert Brooke]], ''Tiare Tahiti'' (1914){{sfn|Brooke|1918|p=15}} | width = 22em | align = right | style = padding:1.5em}}
In the wake of Ginevra rejecting Fitzgerald two years prior, Zelda's rejection further dispirited him.{{sfn|Stern|1970|p=7}} Unable to earn a successful living in New York City, Fitzgerald carried a revolver while contemplating suicide,{{sfn|Turnbull|1962|pp=93–94}} and he threatened to jump to his death from a window ledge of the [[Yale Club of New York City|Yale Club]].<ref>{{harvnb|Bruccoli|1981|p=98}}: "When he climbed out on a window ledge and threatened to jump, no one tried to stop him."</ref> According to biographer [[Andrew Turnbull (biographer)|Andrew Turnbull]], "one day, drinking martinis in the upstairs lounge, [Fitzgerald] announced that he was going to jump out of the window. No one objected; on the contrary, it was pointed out that the windows were French and ideally suited for jumping, which seemed to cool his ardor."{{sfn|Turnbull|1962|pp=93–94}} Despite Zelda's rejection, Fitzgerald hoped that his success as an author might change her mind, and he told a friend, "I wouldn't care if she died, but I couldn't stand to have anybody else marry her."{{sfn|Bruccoli|1981|p=101}}

In July 1919, Fitzgerald quit his advertising job in New York and returned to St. Paul.{{sfn|Bruccoli|1981|pp=100–101}} Returning to his hometown as a failure, Fitzgerald became a recluse and lived on the top floor of his parents' home at [[F. Scott Fitzgerald House|599&nbsp;Summit Avenue]].{{sfn|Bruccoli|1981|pp=100–101}} He decided to make one last attempt to become a novelist and to stake everything on the success or failure of a book.{{sfn|Bruccoli|1981|pp=100–101}} Abstaining from alcohol,{{sfn|Bruccoli|1981|p=101}} he worked day and night to revise ''The Romantic Egotist'' as ''This Side of Paradise''—an autobiographical account of his Princeton years and his romances with Ginevra King, Zelda Sayre, and other young women.{{sfnm|Milford|1970|1p=55|West|2005|2pp=65, 74, 95}}{{sfnm|Tate|1998|1p=22|MacKie|1970|2p=23}} Fitzgerald chose the new title based on a line in [[Rupert Brooke]]'s poem ''Tiare Tahiti'', "Well this side of Paradise!... There's little comfort in the wise."{{sfnm|Tate|1998|1p=252|Shinn|1920|2p=8A|Brooke|1918|3p=15}}

While revising the manuscript, Fitzgerald drew upon the correspondence of friends and acquaintances.{{sfn|Mizener|1951|p=44}}{{sfn|Bruccoli|1981|p=95}} He quoted verbatim three letters and one poem by Father Sigourney Fay,{{sfn|Mizener|1951|p=44}} a possibly [[gay]] Catholic priest with whom Fitzgerald had a close relationship.<ref name="Sigourney Fay">{{harvnb|Fessenden|2005|p=28}}: "Biographers describe Fay as a '[[fin-de-siècle]] aesthete' of considerable appeal; 'a dandy, always heavily perfumed,' who introduced the teenaged Fitzgerald to [[Oscar Wilde]] and good wine".</ref><ref name="Fay Sexuality">{{harvnb|Bruccoli|1981|p=278}}: "If Fay was a homosexual, as has been asserted without proof, Fitzgerald was presumably unaware of it".</ref>{{sfnm|Turnbull|1962|1p=39|Tate|1998|2p=53}} He also used a quote from Zelda's letters for a [[soliloquy]] by the narrator in the final pages.{{sfn|Bruccoli|1981|p=95}} Zelda had written a letter eulogizing the [[Confederate States Army|Confederate soldiers]] who died during the [[American Civil War]]. "I've spent today in the graveyard," she wrote to Scott, "Isn't it funny how, out of a row of Confederate soldiers, two or three will make you think of dead lovers and dead loves—when they're exactly like the others, even to the yellowish moss."{{sfn|Fitzgerald|Fitzgerald|2002|p=96}} In the novel's final pages, Fitzgerald altered Zelda's [[neo-Confederate]]<!-- See Cline 2002 and Turnbull 1962 citations for Zelda's neo-Confederate views. --> sentiments to refer to [[Union Army|Union]] soldiers instead of Confederates.{{sfnm|Cline|2002|1p=65|Turnbull|1962|2p=102|Fitzgerald|1991|3p=vii}}<ref>Per {{harvnb|Cline|2002|p=13}}, Zelda claimed that she drew her strength from Montgomery's Confederate past.</ref>

[[File:Maxwell_Perkins_NYWTS_cropped.jpg|thumb|right|[[Max Perkins]] threatened to resign from [[Scribner's]] if the company did not publish Fitzgerald's novel. "If we're going to turn down the likes of Fitzgerald," Perkins stated, "I will lose all interest in publishing books."]]
Fitzgerald sent the revised manuscript to Scribner's on September 4, 1919.{{sfn|Tate|1998|p=252}} Although the manuscript again impressed Perkins who wished to publish the novel, senior executives at the publishing house again disagreed with Perkins and disliked the novel on the grounds of indecency.{{sfn|Berg|1978|pp=15–19}} At the monthly meeting of Scribner's editorial board, an elderly [[Charles Scribner II]], the company's president, grumbled that the work lacked "literary merit," and senior editor William C. Brownell dismissed it as "frivolous."{{sfnm|Berg|1978|1pp=15–22|Bruccoli|1981|2p=103|Turnbull|1962|3p=118|Tate|1998|4p=191}}<ref name="Editorial Insurrection">{{harvnb|Turnbull|1962|p=118}}: "Charles Scribner, Sr. had hesitated to put his imprint on ''This Side of Paradise'', which struck him as frivolous. When he yielded to the enthusiasm of Maxwell Perkins, his most far-seeing editor, the monarchy of Scribners went over to the revolution."</ref>

As the lone voice supporting the publication of Fitzgerald's novel at the editorial board meeting, a frustrated Perkins threatened to resign unless the company agreed to publish it.{{sfn|Berg|1978|pp=15–19}}{{sfn|Bruccoli|1981|p=103}} "My feeling is that a publisher's first allegiance is to talent. And if we aren't going to publish a talent like this, it is a very serious thing," Perkins declared at the meeting. "If we're going to turn down the likes of Fitzgerald, I will lose all interest in publishing books."{{sfn|Bruccoli|1981|p=103}} Despite the fact that Fitzgerald's manuscript repelled older employees at Scribner's, the executives relented out of fear of losing Perkins as a gifted editor and literary talent scout.{{sfnm|Berg|1978|1pp=15–22|Bruccoli|1981|2p=103|Turnbull|1962|3p=118|Tate|1998|4p=191}}<ref name="Editorial Insurrection"/>

On September 16, eight days before Fitzgerald's 23rd birthday, Scribner's accepted the novel for publication.{{sfn|Bruccoli|1981|p=103}}{{sfn|Tate|1998|p=252}} Now able to express their opinions, lower-ranking editors at Scribner's opined that they believed Fitzgerald's novel represented the "voice of a new age".{{sfn|Berg|1978|pp=15–22}} Soon after Scribner's decision, Perkins wrote a congratulatory letter to Fitzgerald that omitted his threat to resign if the company failed to publish the novel: "I am very glad, personally, to be able to write to you that we are all for publishing your book ''This Side of Paradise''... I think that you have improved it enormously... The book is so different that it is hard to prophesy how it will sell but we are all for taking a chance and supporting it with vigor."{{sfn|Berg|1978|pp=15–22}}

=== Publication and meteoric success ===
{{multiple image
 | perrow = 2
 | total_width = 300
 | align = right
 | image1 = F. Scott Fitzgerald (1929 photo portrait by Nickolas Muray) Cropped.jpg
 | width1 = 150
 | image2 = Zelda Fitzgerald circa 1919 Retouched.jpg
 | width2 = 150
 | footer = After F. Scott Fitzgerald informed Zelda Sayre of his novel's upcoming publication, she agreed to marry him. "I hate to say this," Zelda wrote contritely, "but I don't think I had much confidence in you at first... It's so nice to know you really ''can'' do things".
 | footer_align = left
}}
Upon receiving Perkins' letter and learning of his first novel's impending publication, Fitzgerald became euphoric.{{sfn|Tate|1998|p=252}} "The postman rang, and that day I quit work and ran along the streets, stopping automobiles to tell friends and acquaintances about it⁠—my novel ''This Side of Paradise'' was accepted for publication," he recalled, "I paid off my terrible small debts, bought a suit, and woke up every morning with a world of ineffable top-loftiness and promise."{{sfn|Tate|1998|p=252}} After Scott informed Zelda of his novel's upcoming publication, a shocked Zelda replied contritely: "I hate to say this, but I don't think I had much confidence in you at first.... It's so nice to know you really ''can'' do things".{{sfn|Turnbull|1962|p=102}} 

''This Side of Paradise'' debuted on March 26, 1920, with a dust jacket illustrated by [[William Ely Hill|W. E. Hill]].{{sfn|Bruccoli|1981|pp=136–137}} Advertised in newspapers with the slogan, "A Novel About Flappers Written For Philosophers,"{{sfn|Tate|1998|p=252}} the initial printing of 3,000 copies sold out in three days.{{sfn|Bruccoli|1981|pp=136–137}} Although not among the ten [[Publishers Weekly list of bestselling novels in the United States in the 1920s|best-selling novels]] of the year,{{sfn|Bruccoli|1981|pp=136–137}} the 23-year-old F. Scott Fitzgerald's first novel proved to be his most popular work and became a cultural sensation across the United States, making him a household name.<ref name="Household name">{{harvnb|Buller|2005|p=3}}: "The appearance of the novel... made him a household name".</ref>{{sfn|Bruccoli|1981|pp=136–137}}<ref name="Brilliant success">{{harvnb|Milford|1970|p=66}}: "''This Side of Paradise'' was... a brilliant success..."</ref> The book went through twelve printings in 1920 and 1921, totaling 49,075 copies.{{sfn|Bruccoli|1981|pp=136–137}} Despite this success, the novel provided only modest income for Fitzgerald.{{sfn|Mizener|1951|p=87}}<ref name="Novel income">{{harvnb|Bruccoli|1981|p=137}}: "The sales of ''This Side of Paradise'' did not make Fitzgerald rich."</ref> Copies sold for $1.75 ({{Inflation|US|1.75|1920|fmt=eq}}), and he earned 10% on the first 5,000 copies and 15% thereafter, totaling $6,200 in 1920 ({{Inflation|US|6200.00|1920|fmt=eq}}).{{sfn|Bruccoli|1981|p=137}}

Although Fitzgerald complained to his friend [[Burton Rascoe]] that ''This Side of Paradise'' didn't make him wealthy,<ref name="Not rich">{{harvnb|Mizener|1951|p=87}}: Fitzgerald complained that "the book didn't make me as rich as I thought it would".</ref> his new fame enabled him to earn much higher rates for his short stories,<ref name="Story Prices">{{harvnb|Fitzgerald|1945|p=89}}: "My story price had gone from $30 to $1,000. That's a small price to what was paid later in the Boom, but what it sounded like to me couldn't be exaggerated."</ref> and Zelda resumed their engagement as he could now afford her privileged lifestyle.<ref name="Financial Success">{{harvnb|Mizener|1951|pp=85, 89, 90}}: "Zelda would question whether he was ever going to make enough money for them to marry", and Fitzgerald was thus compelled to prove that "he was rich enough for her."</ref>{{sfnm|Bruccoli|1981|1pp=100–110|Turnbull|1962|2p=102|Milford|1970|3p=57}}<ref name="Idle Southern Belle"/> By the time of their wedding in April 1920, Fitzgerald claimed neither he nor Zelda still loved each other,<ref name="Ebb of Passion">{{harvnb|Bruccoli|1981|p=482}}: Fitzgerald wrote in 1939, "You [Zelda] submitted at the moment of our marriage when your passion for me was at as low ebb as mine for you.&nbsp;... I never wanted the Zelda I married. I didn't love you again till after you became pregnant."</ref><ref name="Lost Love">{{harvnb|Turnbull|1962|p=102}}: "Victory was sweet, though not as sweet as it would have been six months earlier before Zelda had rejected him. Fitzgerald couldn't recapture the thrill of their first love".</ref> and the early years of their marriage proved a disappointment.<ref name="Marriage Reservations">{{harvnb|Bruccoli|1981|p=441}}: In July 1938, Fitzgerald wrote to his daughter that, "I decided to marry your mother after all, even though I knew she was spoiled and meant no good to me. I was sorry immediately I had married her but, being patient in those days, made the best of it".</ref><ref name="Emotional distance">{{harvnb|Bruccoli|1981|p=133}}: Describing his marriage to Zelda, Fitzgerald said that—aside from "long conversations" late at night—their relations lacked "a closeness" which they never "achieved in the workaday world of marriage."</ref><ref>{{harvnb|Turnbull|1962|p=102}}: "Fitzgerald couldn't recapture the thrill of their first love".</ref> Despite his disappointing marriage, Fitzgerald had achieved the peak of his fame and cultural salience, and he recalled traveling in a taxi one afternoon through the streets of New York City and weeping when he realized that he would never be as happy again.{{sfn|Turnbull|1962|p=115}}

== Reception ==
=== Cultural sensation ===
{{Quote box | align = right | width = 26em | quote = ''This Side of Paradise'' was the flaming skyrocket of its season... [Fitzgerald's] photograph appeared in all of the exclusive journals as the picture of the hope of young America, the first person to turn the spotlight on the flapper in the back seat on a lonely road... | author = —Fanny Butcher | source = ''[[Chicago Tribune]]'', 1925{{sfn|Butcher|1925|p=11}}}}
{{Quote box | align = right | width = 26em | quote = ''This Side of Paradise'' focused the thought of the whole nation on the problems of 'flappers and parlor snakes' which it had known before simply as its daughters and sons. Some of the old-lady magazines are still debating these problems with tiresome gravity. | author = —Ralph Coghlan | source = ''[[St. Louis Post-Dispatch]]'', 1925{{sfn|Coghlan|1925|p=11}}}}
Upon its publication, Fitzgerald's ''This Side of Paradise'' caused a cultural sensation that sparked societal debate,{{sfnm|1a1=Butcher|1y=1925|1p=11|2a1=Coghlan|2y=1925|2p=11}} and, he became a national figure overnight.<ref name="National Figure">{{harvnb|Tate|1998|p=4}}: "With the publication of ''This Side of Paradise'' in 1920, F. Scott Fitzgerald became a national literary figure."</ref><ref name="Generational Consciousness">{{harvnb|Weaver|1922|p=3}}: "But what the first book principally did was to introduce new material; it made this wild, keen, enthusiastic younger generation self-conscious; it encourage them to self-expression; to open revolt against the platitudes and pollyannalysis {{sic}} of precedent. In a literary way, Fitzgerald's influence is so great that it cannot be estimated."</ref><ref name="Change in Social Mores">{{harvnb|Rascoe|1920|p=11}}: "As a picture of contemporary life and as an indication of codes of conduct obtaining among the American young, the novel is revelatory and valuable. It is a comment upon the times. It shows definitely that whatever the teachings of our elders, the [[Victorian morality|Victorian checks]], taboos, and reticences {{sic}} are no longer in force among the flappers, the debutantes, and the collegians of the present [Jazz Age] generation."</ref> He riveted the public's attention on the promiscuous activities of their sons and daughters cavorting in the [[rumble seat]]s of [[Stutz Bearcat|Bearcat roadsters]] and prompted a national conversation over the perceived immorality of this hedonistic younger generation.<ref name="Sons and Daughters">{{harvnb|Coghlan|1925|p=11}}: "''This Side of Paradise'' focused the thought of the whole nation on the problems of 'flappers and parlor snakes' which it had known before simply as its daughters and sons. Some of the old-lady magazines are still debating these problems with tiresome gravity".</ref><ref name="Spotlighting the Flappers">{{harvnb|Butcher|1925|p=11}}: ''This Side of Paradise'' made him "the first person to turn the spotlight on the flapper in the backseat on a lonely road".</ref><ref>{{harvnb|Fitzgerald|Fitzgerald|2002|p=184}}: "...where young men in [[Stutz Bearcat|bear-cat roadsters]] are speeding to whatever Genevra {{sic}} [King] Mitchell's dominate the day".</ref> Despite the fact that Fitzgerald had composed the work several years earlier and his novel chronicled the more restrained social milieu of pre-war 1910s America, the work became popularly and inaccurately associated with the wild carefree atmosphere of post-war 1920s America immortalized in [[John Held, Jr.]]'s satirical drawings.{{sfn|Bruccoli|1981|pp=83–84, 127}}

With this debut novel, critics touted Fitzgerald as the first writer to turn the national spotlight on the [[Greatest Generation|Jazz Age generation]],<ref name="Jazz Age Generation"/><ref name="Lost Generation As Younger"/><ref name="Post-War Generation">{{harvnb|Fitzgerald|2004|p=118}}: "The Post-War generation is an utterly disrupted one. Youth suffered with interrupted educations. Mr. Fitzgerald finds this generation essentially weak, and much inclined to be looking to the two older groups for guidance, without being certain of which to follow as a standard. There is no vitality in this group, and it is best described in fiction by books like ''[[The Plastic Age]]'' and ''[[Flaming Youth (novel)|Flaming Youth]]''."</ref> especially their young [[flapper]]s.<ref name="Sons and Daughters"/><ref name="Spotlighting the Flappers"/> In contrast to the older [[Lost Generation]] to which [[Gertrude Stein]] posited that [[Ernest Hemingway]] and Fitzgerald belonged,<ref name="Gray 1946">{{harvnb|Gray|1946|p=59}}: "They were the most conspicuous representatives of that 'lost generation,' fragments of which Gertrude Stein was forever stumbling upon in the byways of Paris."</ref><ref name="Lost Generation Label Rejected">{{harvnb|Bruccoli|1981|p=281}}: "...Fitzgerald's rebuttal to Gertrude Stein's 'lost generation' catch phrase that had achieved currency through Hemingway's use of it as an epigraph for ''The Sun Also Rises''. Whereas Stein had identified the lost generation with the war veterans, Fitzgerald insisted that the lost generation was the prewar group and expressed confidence in 'the men of the war.'"</ref> the Jazz Age generation were those Americans younger than Fitzgerald who had been adolescents during World War&nbsp;I and largely untouched by the conflict.{{efn|name=World War I and the Jazz Age|Fitzgerald argued that World War&nbsp;I neither created the Jazz Age nor influenced young Americans, asserting the conflict had no lasting impact.{{sfn|Fitzgerald|2004|pp=6–7}}}}<ref name="Jazz Age Generation">{{harvnb|Fitzgerald|1945|p=15}}: "The generation which been adolescent during the confusion of the War, brusquely shouldered my contemporaries out of the way and danced into the limelight. This was the generation whose girls dramatized themselves as flappers, the generation that corrupted its elders and eventually overreached itself less through lack of morals than through lack of taste."</ref><ref name="Lost Generation As Younger"/> Fitzgerald described this younger generation as the true "lost" generation which shouldered his generational contemporaries out of the way: "This was the generation whose girls dramatized themselves as flappers".{{sfn|Fitzgerald|1945|pp=14–15}}<ref name="Lost Generation As Younger">{{harvnb|Bruccoli|1981|p=451}}: Fitzgerald insisted "the real lost generation... were those who were young right after the war because they were the ones with infinite belief."</ref>

Due to its focus on liberated flappers and college life, Fitzgerald's novel became a cultural phenomenon among young Americans.{{sfnm|Bruccoli|1981|1pp=127–128|Kazin|1951|2p=119}}<ref>{{harvnb|Gallo|1978|p=16}}: "''This Side of Paradise'' was acclaimed as their book by Fitzgerald's enthusiastic youthful readers."</ref> According to writer [[John O'Hara]], half a million young men and women "fell in love with the book,"{{sfn|Bruccoli|1981|p=127}} and, according to essayist [[Glenway Wescott]], Fitgerald's novel became the rallying banner of the "youth movement".{{sfn|Kazin|1951|p=119}} The novel's immense popularity among American youth stemmed from its frank portrayal of their chafing under the outdated social mores of Wilsonian America.{{sfnm|Bruccoli|1981|1pp=127–128|Kazin|1951|2p=119}} Although earlier works about collegiate life had been published such as [[Owen Johnson (writer)|Owen Johnson]]'s ''[[Stover at Yale]]'' (1912), Fitzgerald's work became heralded as "the first realistic American college novel", and young American men viewed the novel as a guide for social conduct.{{sfnm|Bruccoli|1981|1pp=127–128|Rascoe|1920|2p=11}} Newspapers reported that young American women imitated the rebellious behavior of the novel's women characters, and some writers miscredited Fitzgerald's novel with creating the cultural archetype of the flapper.{{sfn|Bruccoli|1981|pp=127–128}}

=== Youth in revolt ===
{{CSS image crop|Image=Krazy Kat LOC npcc.04658.jpg|bSize=500|cWidth=300|cHeight=180|oTop=150|oLeft=90|Location=right|Description=A flapper and patrons in front of ''[[Krazy Kat Klub|The Krazy Kat]]'', a [[Jazz Age]] speakeasy, in 1921. Critics touted Fitzgerald's ''This Side of Paradise'' as turning the national spotlight on the [[Greatest Generation|Jazz Age generation]]⁠—those Americans younger than Fitzgerald who had been adolescents during World War&nbsp;I and whom Fitzgerald regarded as the true "lost" generation.}}
With his photograph appearing in many newspapers,{{sfn|Butcher|1925|p=11}}<ref>{{harvnb|Bruccoli|1981|p=119}}: "Fitzgerald's appearance accelerated his elevation to celebrity status. His striking good looks combined with his youth and brilliance to complete the image of the novelist as a romantic figure. He photographed handsomely, especially in profile; and, though never a dandy, he dressed well in Brooks Brothers collegiate style. During the Twenties he often carried a cane, as did many young men. It was frequently remarked that Fitzgerald looked like a figure in a collar ad."</ref> the national press depicted Fitzgerald as the standard-bearer for "youth in revolt".{{sfn|''The Montgomery Advertiser''|1922|p=25}}<ref name="Youth Movement">Per [[Glenway Wescott]]'s 1941 essay, collected in {{harvnb|Kazin|1951|p=119}}: "''This Side of Paradise'' haunted the decade like a song, popular but perfect. It hung over an entire youth movement like a banner, somewhat discolored and windworn now; the wind has lapsed out of it. But a book which college boys really read is a rare thing, not to be dismissed idly or in a moment of severe sophistication."</ref> "'Behold a new prophet is risen, who speaketh for Youth in Revolt!" wrote ''[[The Montgomery Advertiser]]'', describing the reaction to Fitzgerald's novel.{{sfn|''The Montgomery Advertiser''|1922|p=25}} "All things formerly held to be beautiful, good and true are now become futile, fatuous and fabulous, and worthy of respect no more. The bob-haired girl and the mop topped boy shall teach you the Facts of Life. Go to, ye elders, hearken unto them!'"{{sfn|''The Montgomery Advertiser''|1922|p=25}} Such articles fostered the widespread impression of Fitzgerald as championing the revolt by young Americans against traditional norms and as the outstanding aggressor in the rebellion of "[[Flaming Youth (film)|flaming youth]]" against the "old guard".<ref name="Outstanding aggressor"/>

Capitalizing on his new standing as a national figure with his finger on the pulse of young America, Fitzgerald gave interviews discoursing on the revolt by youth culture.{{sfn|Fitzgerald|2004|p=7}} Declaring that World War&nbsp;I "had little or nothing to do" with the change in morals among young Americans and did not leave "any real lasting effect,"{{sfn|Fitzgerald|2004|p=7}}{{sfn|Fitzgerald|1945|pp=14, 18}} Fitzgerald attributed the [[sexual revolution]]<!-- "Sexual revolution" is the correct phrase and later appropriated by 1960s writers for the so-called second sexual revolution. --> among young adults to a combination of popular literature by [[H. G. Wells]] and other intellectuals criticizing repressive social norms, [[Sigmund Freud]]'s sexual theories gaining salience, and the invention of the automobile allowing youths to escape parental surveillance in order to engage in [[premarital sex]].{{sfnm|Fitzgerald|1945|1pp=15, 18|Fitzgerald|2004|2p=7}}

As a result of Fitzgerald's new fame as a celebrated author chronicling young Americans' defiance towards traditional values, [[social conservatives]] attacked the author in newspaper columns. [[Heywood Broun]] decried Fitzgerald's use of modern slang and attempted to discredit him by claiming the author fabricated his novel's depiction of young people engaging in drunken sprees and premarital sex.{{sfn|Broun|1920|p=14}} An amused Fitzgerald ridiculed such allegations,{{sfnm|Wilson|1952|1pp=143–144|Fitzgerald|1945|2p=16}} and he opined that such critics wished to discredit his work in order to retain their outdated conceptions of American society.{{sfn|Fitzgerald|1945|pp=15–16}}

=== Critical reaction ===
{{multiple image
 | perrow = 2
 | total_width = 300
 | align = right
 | image1 = Burton Rascoe portrait.jpg
 | width1 = 150
 | image2 = H. L. Mencken - The Borzoi Cropped Retouched.jpg
 | width2 = 150
 | footer = Literary critics such as [[Burton Rascoe]] and [[H. L. Mencken]] hailed Fitzgerald's ''This Side of Paradise'' as an outstanding debut novel.
 | footer_align = left
}}

The majority of critics lauded Fitzgerald's debut novel with "wild enthusiasm",<ref name="Wild enthusiasm">{{harvnb|Wilson|1952|p=29}}: "...one can understand the wild enthusiasm with which ''This Side of Paradise'' was hailed."</ref> and the most enthusiastic reviewers went so far as to hail the young Midwestern writer as a literary genius.{{sfnm|Rascoe|1920|1p=11|Bryer|1978|2pp=xii-xiii}}{{sfnm|Bruccoli|1981|1pp=119–121|Mencken|1920|2p=140|Ford|1920|3p=52|Butcher|1920|4p=33}} In his April 1920 review, critic [[Burton Rascoe]] of ''[[The Chicago Tribune]]'' urged his readers to "make a note of the name, F. Scott Fitzgerald. It is borne by a 23 year old novelist who will, unless I am much mistaken, be much heard of hereafter."{{sfn|Rascoe|1920|p=11}} Rascoe asserted that Fitzgerald's first novel bore "the impress, it seems to me, of genius. It is the only adequate study that we have had of the contemporary American in adolescence and young manhood."{{sfnm|Rascoe|1920|1p=11|Bruccoli|1981|2p=120}} 

"The prize first novel of a decade is F. Scott Fitzgerald's ''This Side of Paradise''," critic [[Fanny Butcher]] raved in her June 1920 column for ''The Chicago Tribune'', singling out Fitzgerald for particular praise amid other competitors that included the U.S. publication of [[Virginia Woolf]]'s first novel ''[[The Voyage Out]]'' and [[Zane Grey]]'s novel ''A Man for the Ages''.{{sfn|Butcher|1920|p=33}}  Butcher declared Fitzgerald's book to be "the living, palpitant being of the youth of the hour, a book which, I haven't a doubt in the world, will have a serious and far reaching effect on American literature."{{sfn|Butcher|1920|p=33}} 

Perhaps the most influential review of Fitzgerald's novel came from critic [[H. L. Mencken]], the editor of the [[literary magazine]] ''[[The Smart Set]]''.{{sfnm|Kronenberger|1934|1p=50|Mizener|1951|2pp=112–113|Bruccoli|1981|3p=138}} Mencken's authoritative opinions on the latest literary endeavors often lifted their authors upward toward greater success or cast them down into cultural oblivion.{{sfnm|Kronenberger|1934|1p=50|Mizener|1951|2pp=112-113|Bruccoli|1981|3p=138}} In his August 1920 review of ''This Side of Paradise'', Mencken described Fitzgerald's work as an amazing debut and lavished praise on its author:

{{Quote|The best American novel that I have seen of late is also the product of a neophyte, to wit, F. Scott Fitzgerald... He offers a truly amazing first novel—original in structure, extremely sophisticated in manner, and adorned with a brilliancy that is as rare in American writing... The young American novelist usually reveals himself as a naive, sentimental and somewhat disgusting ignoramus—a believer in [[Prohibition in the United States|Great Causes]], a snuffler and eye-roller, a spouter of stale philosophies out of [[Kensington Palace|Kensington drawing rooms]], the doggeries of French [[Hackney carriage|hack-drivers]], and the lower floor of the [[Staatliches Hofbräuhaus in München|Munich Hofbräuhaus]]... Fitzgerald is nothing of the sort. On the contrary, he is... an artist—an apt and delicate weaver of words...{{sfn|Mencken|1920|p=140}}}}

Mencken declared the first half of ''This Side of Paradise'' to be superior to the second half, perceiving that Fitzgerald's novel became more "thin" as the young author followed less autobiographical plot strands.{{sfn|Mencken|1920|p=140}} Fitzgerald concurred with Mencken's low opinion of certain later chapters, particularly Amory's relations with Eleanor.{{sfn|Bruccoli|1981|p=125}} In his annotated copy of ''This Side of Paradise'', Fitzgerald deemed his Eleanor subplot to be unintentionally hilarious and admitted he could not "even bear to read it."{{sfn|Bruccoli|1981|p=125}} Believing that Fitzgerald's protagonist began to elude the author in the second half, Mencken criticized Fitzgerald for dropping "his Amory Blaine as [[Mark Twain]] dropped [[Huckleberry Finn]], but for a less cogent reason."{{sfn|Mencken|1920|p=140}} Despite this critique, he commended most of the novel, particularly up to and including the section detailing the love story with Rosalind.{{sfn|Mencken|1920|p=140}}

Whereas some critics praised the novel's form and structure as highly original, others criticized the work for the same reasons.{{sfnm|Wilson|1952|1p=28|Mencken|1925|2p=9|Ford|1920|3p=52}} Lillian C. Ford in ''[[The Los Angeles Times]]'' complained "the construction is odd and the book has two parts, the first with four chapters and the second with five. The chapters have unexpected topical divisions and when the author feels so inclined he throws his story into drama form and then again it jogs along as plain narrative."{{sfn|Ford|1920|p=52}} Similarly, many reviewers commented that Fitzgerald's structural craftsmanship left much to be desired.{{sfnm|Stagg|1925|1p=9|Mencken|1925|2p=9}} He could write entertainingly, they conceded, but he paid scant attention to form and construction.{{sfn|Mencken|1925|p=9}} Having read these criticisms of his debut novel, Fitzgerald sought to improve on his form and construction in his next work, ''[[The Beautiful and Damned]]'', and to venture into a new genre of fiction altogether.{{sfn|Wilson|1952|p=32}}

=== Princeton backlash ===
[[File:Portrait of John Grier Hibben.jpg|thumb|left|upright=0.9|[[John Grier Hibben]], the president of Princeton University, criticized the novel in a letter to Fitzgerald. "Very frankly," Hibben wrote, "your characterization of Princeton has grieved me."]]
Despite the novel's warm reception by critics and readers, many of [[Princeton University]]'s faculty and alumni reacted with hostility towards Fitzgerald's ''This Side of Paradise'', much to Fitzgerald's surprise and dismay.{{sfn|Fitzgerald|1945|pp=88–89}} Although Fitzgerald's mentor [[Christian Gauss]], a Professor of French Literature, lauded the novel as "a work of art,"{{sfn|Campus Critic|1920|p=2}} other Princetonians attacked the book in the pages of the ''[[Princeton Alumni Weekly]]'' and ''[[The Daily Princetonian]]''.{{sfnm|Fitzgerald|1945|1pp=88–89|Campus Critic|1920|2p=2|Kent|1920|3p=3}} They despised his popular novel for fostering an unfavorable impression of their school as a snobbish milieu focused on idle pleasures.{{sfnm|''The Daily Princetonian''|1922|1p=2|Bruccoli|1981|2p=128}} In a typical review, Ralph Kent, a senior editor of the ''Nassau Literary Review'', disparaged the work as impugning Princeton's reputation due to its superficial depiction of undergraduate life.{{sfn|Kent|1920|p=3}}

Fitzgerald's novel soon attracted the attention and displeasure of [[John Grier Hibben]], a [[Presbyterian]] minister and educational reformer who succeeded [[Woodrow Wilson]] as the president of Princeton University.{{sfnm|Bruccoli|1981|1p=128|''Time'' Magazine|1931}} In a private letter to Fitzgerald dated May 27, 1920, Hibben expressed his profound disappointment with Fitzgerald's depiction of the school and informed the young author that his novel had wounded him:{{sfn|Bruccoli|1981|p=128}}

{{Quote|It is because I appreciate so much all that is in you of artistic skill and [a] certain elemental power that I am taking the liberty of telling you very frankly that your characterization of Princeton has grieved me. I cannot bear to think that our young men are merely living for four years in a country club and spending their lives wholly in a spirit of calculation and snobbishness... I have always had a belief in Princeton and in what the place could do in the making of a strong vigorous manhood. It would be an overwhelming grief to me, in the midst of my work here and my love for Princeton's young men, should I feel that we have nothing to offer but the outgrown symbols and shells of a past whose reality has long since disappeared.{{sfn|Bruccoli|1981|p=128}}}}
{{quote box | quote = These weeks in the clouds ended abruptly a week later when Princeton turned on the book—not undergraduate Princeton but the [[black mass]] of faculty and alumni. There was a kind but reproachful letter from [[John Grier Hibben|President Hibben]], and a room full of classmates who suddenly turned on me with condemnation... The ''Alumni Weekly'' got after my book and only [[Christian Gauss|Dean Gauss]] had a good word to say or me. The unctuousness and hypocrisy of the proceedings was exasperating and for seven years I didn't go to Princeton. | author = —F. Scott Fitzgerald | source = "Early Success," October 1937{{sfn|Fitzgerald|1945|pp=88–89}} | width = 22em | align = right | style = padding:1.5em}}
In response to Hibben's chastising letter, Fitzgerald wrote a respectful but uncompromising reply that denied any attempt to disparage Princeton and defended his novel's depiction of the university.{{sfn|Bruccoli|1981|p=129}}{{sfn|Turnbull|1962|p=108}} "I have no fault to find with Princeton that I can't find with [[Oxford University|Oxford]] and [[Cambridge University|Cambridge]]," Fitzgerald explained. "I simply wrote out of my own impressions, wrote as honestly as I could a picture of its beauty. That the picture is cynical is the fault of my temperament.... I must admit however that ''This Side of Paradise'' does over accentuate the gaiety and country club atmosphere of Princeton. For the sake of the readers interest that part was much over-stressed, and of course the hero, not being average, reacted rather unhealthily I suppose to many perfectly normal phenomena. To that extent the book is inaccurate."{{sfn|Bruccoli|1981|p=129}}

As a result of this unexpected backlash by the faculty and alumni, Fitzgerald's joy at becoming a famous novelist proved short-lived.{{sfn|Fitzgerald|1945|pp=88–89}} Although undergraduates across the country touted the novel as a realistic portrayal of college life,{{sfn|Kazin|1951|p=119}}{{sfn|Bruccoli|1981|p=127}} Princeton alumni and former classmates continued to treat the author with contempt in social settings over the ensuing months.{{sfnm|Fitzgerald|1945|1pp=88–89|Turnbull|1962|2p=108}} In one instance, Fitzgerald visited Princeton's [[University Cottage Club]] and faced a room full of alumni and former classmates who condemned him for tarnishing their school's reputation.{{sfnm|Fitzgerald|1945|1pp=88–89|Turnbull|1962|2p=108}} After informing Fitzgerald that he had been suspended from the club, they symbolically ejected him from the building via a rear window.{{sfn|Turnbull|1962|p=108}} Exasperated by the contemptuousness and sanctimoniousness of Princeton's faculty and alumni, a dispirited Fitzgerald did not return to visit his alma mater for many years, presumably until their hostility had lessened.{{sfn|Fitzgerald|1945|pp=88–89}}

{{quote box | quote = When, shortly after his death, Zelda Fitzgerald attempted to sell her husband's papers to Princeton for $3,750, the librarian declined the offer. The university had no obligation, he commented, to support the widow of a second-rate Midwestern hack who'd been lucky enough to attend Princeton. | author = —Scott Donaldson | source = ''F. Scott Fitzgerald: Fool for Love'' (1983){{sfn|Donaldson|1983|p=40}} | width = 22em | align = left | style = padding:1.5em}}
After a 44-year-old Fitzgerald died of a heart attack due to occlusive [[coronary arteriosclerosis]] in December 1940, many Princeton staff and alumni continued to privately and publicly belittle the author and his literary oeuvre.{{sfn|Donaldson|1983|p=40}} According to biographer Scott Donaldson, after Fitzgerald's death, his widow Zelda Fitzgerald attempted to sell the entirety of her late husband's papers to Princeton University for the modest sum of $3,750 ({{Inflation|US|3750.00|1940|fmt=eq}}), but the Princeton librarian spurned the offer.{{sfn|Donaldson|1983|p=40}} The Princeton librarian explained that the university felt no obligation to pay such a sum for the papers of a mediocre author who had been fortunate enough to attend their prestigious institution.{{sfn|Donaldson|1983|p=40}}

One year later, in 1941, literary critic [[Edmund Wilson]], a close friend of Fitzgerald and a fellow Princetonian, attempted to use his considerable influence to persuade the university to publish a book honoring F. Scott Fitzgerald but proved unsuccessful.{{sfn|Donaldson|1983|p=40}} In 1956, when the [[Princeton University Library]] released a collection of Fitzgerald's writings titled ''Afternoon of an Author'', many alumni wrote letters of complaint arguing that Princeton should neither celebrate its connection to the author nor describe him as "most Princetonian."{{sfn|Donaldson|1983|p=40}}

== Critical analysis ==
=== Contemporary analysis ===
==== Innovative style ====
{{multiple image
 | perrow = 2
 | total_width = 300
 | align = right
 | image1 = H.G. Wells by Beresford.jpg
 | width1 = 150
 | alt1 = Photograph of H. G. Wells
 | image2 = Compton Mackenzie.jpg
 | width2 = 150
 | alt2 = Photograph of Compton Mackenzie.
 | footer = Fitzgerald used ''[[Tono-Bungay]]'' (1909) by [[H. G. Wells]] (first) and ''[[Sinister Street]]'' (1913) by Sir [[Compton Mackenzie]] (second) as templates for his novel.
 | footer_align = left
}}
For his first novel, Fitzgerald used as his literary templates [[H. G. Wells]]' 1909 realist work ''[[Tono-Bungay]]'' and Sir [[Compton Mackenzie]]'s 1913 novel ''[[Sinister Street]]'',{{sfnm|Wilson|1952|1p=32|Fitzgerald|2004|2pp=41, 83|Kazin|1951|3pp=29, 48, 78}} which chronicles a college student's [[coming of age]] at [[Oxford University]].{{sfn|Wilson|1952|pp=28–29}} The influence of these two particular novels upon ''This Side of Paradise'' proved apparent to perceptive readers such as Fitzgerald's friend Edmund Wilson who, upon finishing the novel, described Fitzgerald's work as "an exquisite burlesque of Compton Mackenzie with a pastiche of Wells thrown in at the end."{{sfn|Bruccoli|1981|p=105}}

Although Fitzgerald imitated these novels, his debut work differed due to its experimental style.{{sfnm|Milford|1970|1p=67|Weaver|1922|2p=3}} He discarded the traditional narrative of most novels and instead unspooled the plot in the form of intermingled textual fragments, letters, and poetry, even incorporating a [[Stream of consciousness|stream-of-consciousness]] passage.{{sfn|Berg|1978|p=14}} This approach resulted from combining ''The Romantic Egotist'', his earlier novel attempt, with various short stories and poems he had written but never published.{{sfn|Prigozy|2002|pp=48–56}} 

This atonal blend of different fictive<!-- Do not change "fictive" to "fictional" as "fictive" is the correct form in this instance. --> elements prompted critics to fête Fitzgerald as a trailblazer whose work modernized a staid literature that had fallen "as far behind modern habits as behind modern history."{{sfn|Kazin|1951|p=128}} "''This Side of Paradise'' may not seem like much now," writer [[Dorothy Parker]] attested decades later, "but in 1920 it was considered an experimental novel; it cut new ground."{{sfn|Milford|1970|p=67}}

==== Prose anomalies ====
More so than most contemporary writers of his era, Fitzgerald's authorial voice evolved and matured over time,{{sfnm|McCardell|1926|1p=6|Mencken|1925|2p=9|Butcher|1925|3p=11|Van Allen|1934|4p=83}} and each of his novels represented a discernible progression in literary quality.{{sfn|Van Allen|1934|p=83}} Although critics eventually regarded him as possessing "the best narrative gift of the century," they did not perceive this narrative gift as evident in ''This Side of Paradise''.{{sfn|Kazin|1951|pp=13, 122}} Believing that prose had a basis in [[Lyric poetry|lyric verse]],{{sfn|Wilson|1952|p=638}} Fitzgerald crafted his sentences by ear and, consequently, ''This Side of Paradise'' contains numerous malapropisms and descriptive [[Formal fallacy|non sequiturs]] which annoyed readers and reviewers.{{sfnm|Wilson|1952|1p=29|Wilson|1952|2p=638}} Reflecting on these copious defects, critic [[Edmund Wilson]] remarked that Fitzgerald's first novel exhibited nearly every possible fault and weakness a novel can possess.{{sfn|Wilson|1952|p=28}}

=== Posthumous analysis ===
{{quote box | quote = I don't want to repeat my innocence. I want the pleasure of losing it again. | author = —F. Scott Fitzgerald | source = ''This Side of Paradise'' (1920){{sfn|Fitzgerald|1921|p=278}} | width = 22em | align = right | style = padding:1.5em}}
In more recent years, the underlying themes of [[narcissism]] and [[feminism]] in the novel have been examined in a variety of scholarly essays.{{sfnm|Tanaka|2004|1pp=123–140|Riccardo|2012|2pp=26–57}}  Scholar Saori Tanaka's argues that "Amory comes to know himself through Beatrice and his four lovers, which are like five [[Plate glass|sheets of glass]]. They are his reflectors... reflecting his narcissism and the inner side."{{sfn|Tanaka|2004|p=126}}

The first three women in the book allow Amory to dream in a narcissistic way. After participating in the war and losing his financial foundation, the last two women he meets, Rosalind and Eleanor, "make him not dream but awake" in postwar America.{{sfn|Tanaka|2004|p=131}} "With Beatrice and Isabelle, Amory activates the grandiose self," Tanaka states, "with Clara and Rosalind, he restricts narcissism, and with Eleanor, he gains a realistic conception of the self."{{sfn|Tanaka|2004|p=134}}

Others have analyzed [[feminist]] themes in the work. Scholar Andrew Riccardo views several characters to be feminist templates.{{sfn|Riccardo|2012|pp=26–57}} Eleanor's character serves as a "love interest, therapeutic friend, and conversational other".{{sfn|Riccardo|2012|p=36}} Highly educated in discussing poetry and philosophy, "Eleanor not only posits her desires in juxtaposition to the lingering expectations of women in her day but also serves as soothsayer to the demands which would be placed on females".{{sfn|Riccardo|2012|p=36}}

== Legacy and influence ==
{{See also|Echoes of the Jazz Age}}
{{multiple image
 | perrow = 2
 | total_width = 300
 | align = right
 | image1 = John V. A. Weaver circa 1923.jpg
 | width1 = 150
 | alt1 = Photograph of John V. A. Weaver
 | image2 = Gertrude Stein 1935-01-04.jpg
 | width2 = 150
 | alt2 = Photograph of Gertrude Stein
 | footer = [[John V. A. Weaver]] (first) claimed the literary influence of Fitzgerald's ''This Side of Paradise'' on young writers to be inestimable, while [[Gertrude Stein]] (second) wrote that his novel created a new generation of young writers in the public's mind.
 | footer_align = left
}}
{{quote box | quote = [Fitzgerald] has been to post-war American letters what [[Victor Hugo]] was to his time; and ''This Side of Paradise''... was the manifesto of the 'younger generation'... It made this wild, keen, enthusiastic younger generation self-conscious; it encouraged innumerable beginners to open revolt against the platitudes and [[Pollyanna|pollyannalysis]] {{sic}} of precedent. In a literary way, Fitzgerald’s influence is so great that it cannot be estimated. | author = —[[John Van Alstyne Weaver|John V. A. Weaver]] | source = 1922{{sfn|Weaver|1922|p=3}} | width = 25em | align = right | style = padding:1.5em}}
As an experimental novel, ''This Side of Paradise'' influenced the next generation of upcoming American writers, and critics such as [[John Van Alstyne Weaver|John V. A. Weaver]] likened Fitzgerald's impact on post-war American literature to [[Victor Hugo]]'s vast influence on French letters.{{sfnm|Butcher|1920|1p=33|Weaver|1922|2p=3|Milford|1970|3p=67}}<ref name="Wilson Paraphrasing Weaver">{{harvnb|Wilson|1952|p=142}}: "There were a lot of people writing before ''This Side of Paradise''—but the Younger Generation never really became self-conscious till then nor did the public at large become conscious of it. My slogan is that I am the man who made America Younger-Generation-conscious {{sic}}."</ref> Within two years, in the wake of young imitators writing in more experimental styles and discarding the traditional story structure, Weaver declared Fitzgerald's influence on younger writers to be so great as to be inestimable.{{sfn|Weaver|1922|p=3}} In her memoir ''[[The Autobiography of Alice B. Toklas]]'', [[Gertrude Stein]] wrote that Fitzgerald's novel created this new generation of young writers in the public's mind.<ref name="Stein on This Side of Paradise">{{harvnb|Stein|1933|p=268}}: "Stein had been very much impressed by ''This Side of Paradise''. She read it when it came out and before she knew any of the young American writers. She said of it that it was this book that really created for the public the new generation."</ref>

In addition to its literary influence on young writers, social commentators credited Fitzgerald's novel with having a profound cultural impact, purportedly inspiring the younger generation of Americans to rebel against the social norms and cultural standards of their elders.{{sfnm|Kazin|1951|1p=119, 123|''The Montgomery Advertiser''|1922|2p=25}} Remarking upon the popular association between Fitzgerald and the [[Flaming Youth (film)|flaming youth]]<!-- Popularized by Colleen Moore's film of the same name, the phrase "flaming youth" refers to the Jazz Age generation and is used in many historical works. --> of the Jazz Age,  critic Burke Van Allen wrote in 1934 that "no generation of Americans has had a chronicler so persuasive and unmaudlin" as Fitzgerald, and no author became so closely identified with the generation he recorded.{{sfn|Van Allen|1934|p=83}}

The popular identification of Fitzgerald as the chronicler of carefree youth and proselytizer of Jazz Age hedonism earned him the enmity of reactionary societal figures.{{sfnm|Broun|1920|1p=14|Kazin|1951|2pp=123–124}}<ref name="Outstanding aggressor">Per [[Glenway Wescott]]'s 1941 essay, collected in {{harvnb|Kazin|1951|p=123}}: "Fitzgerald, the outstanding aggressor in the little warfare which divided our middle classes in the twenties—warfare of moral emancipation against moral conceit, flaming youth against old guard—definitely has let his side down. The champion is as dead as a doornail. Self-congratulatory moral persons may crow over him if they wish."</ref> When he died in 1940, social conservatives rejoiced over his death.{{sfn|Kazin|1951|pp=13, 123, 125}} Writing in ''[[The New York World-Telegram]]'', columnist [[Westbrook Pegler]] wrote that Fitzgerald's death a few weeks prior reawakened "memories of a queer bunch of undisciplined and self-indulgent brats who were determined not to pull their weight in the boat and wanted the world to drop everything and sit down and bawl with them. A kick in the pants and a clout over the scalp were more like their needing."{{sfn|Kazin|1951|p=125}} Due to this widespread perception of Fitzgerald and his literary works, the [[Roman Catholic Archdiocese of Baltimore|Baltimore Diocese]] denied him a Catholic burial and refused his family permission to intern him at [[Third Addition to Rockville and Old St. Mary's Church and Cemetery|St. Mary's Church]] in [[Rockville, Maryland]].{{sfn|Bruccoli|1981|pp=490–491}}<ref>{{harvnb|Turnbull|1962|p=321}}: "Fitzgerald had wanted to be buried with his family in the Catholic cemetery in Rockville, but since he had died a non-believer the Bishop raised objections, and he was buried in the Union Cemetery not far away."</ref><ref name="Denied Catholic burial">{{harvnb|Alexander|2025}}: "He was denied burial at the Catholic Church because he was not considered a good Catholic,” said [Jackson] Brier. "He was not thought of as the way he is now, he was remembered as a kind of radical writer... It was the novel he wrote in 1920 called ''This Side of Paradise'', which was all about the high jinks of young people, college age kids kissing and holding all sorts of liquor soaked parties, which was a big revelation in 1920."</ref>

Observing the joyful vitriol expressed by social conservatives after Fitzgerald's death, essayist [[Glenway Wescott]] opined that such persons could never erase the impact of Fitzgerald's ''This Side of Paradise'' on 1920s America and young Americans.{{sfn|Kazin|1951|pp=119–123}} "Self-congratulatory moral persons may crow over him if they wish," Wescott wrote in a February 1941 essay two months after Fitzgerald's death, but "''This Side of Paradise'' haunted the decade like a song, popular but perfect. It hung over an entire youth movement like a banner, somewhat discolored and windworn now; the wind has lapsed out of it. But a book which college boys really read is a rare thing, not to be dismissed idly or in a moment of severe sophistication."{{sfn|Kazin|1951|pp=119–123}}

The title was alluded to in the first major biography of Fitzgerald, ''[[The Far Side of Paradise]]'', by Arthur Mizener, first published in 1951.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Borne Back into the Past |url=https://www.commonwealmagazine.org/borne-back-past |first=Mike |last=St Thomas |date=2018-01-04 |url-status=live |website=Commonweal Magazine|access-date=2026-08-31}}</ref>

'''Ursula Kroeber Le Guin''' ({{IPAc-en|ˈ|k|r|oʊ|b|ər|_|l|ə|_|ˈ|ɡ|w|ɪ|n}} {{respell|KROH|bər|_|lə|_|GWIN}};<ref>{{Cite web |last=Le Guin |first=Ursula |title=How to Pronounce Me |url=http://www.ursulakleguin.com/Note-HowToPronounceMe.html |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140306133634/http://www.ursulakleguin.com/Note-HowToPronounceMe.html |archive-date=March 6, 2014 |access-date=March 22, 2014}}</ref> {{née}} '''Kroeber'''; October 21, 1929 – January 22, 2018) was an American author. She is best known for her works of [[speculative fiction]], including [[science fiction]] works set in her [[Hainish universe]] and the [[fantasy]] series ''[[Earthsea]]''. Her work was first published in 1959, and her literary career spanned nearly sixty years, producing more than [[Ursula K. Le Guin bibliography|twenty novels and more than a hundred short stories]], in addition to poetry, [[literary criticism]], translations, and children's books. Frequently described as an author of science fiction, Le Guin has also been called a "major voice in American Letters".{{sfn|White|1999|pp=1–2}} Le Guin said that she would prefer to be known as an "American novelist".<ref name="Phillips 2012">{{Cite news |last=Phillips |first=Julie |author-link=Julie Phillips |date=December 2012 |title=Ursula K. Le Guin, American Novelist |work=Bookslut |url=http://www.bookslut.com/features/2012_12_019664.php |url-status=live |access-date=September 13, 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170120151556/http://www.bookslut.com/features/2012_12_019664.php |archive-date=January 20, 2017}}</ref>

Le Guin was born in [[Berkeley, California|Berkeley]], California, to author and anthropologist [[Theodora Kroeber]] and anthropologist [[Alfred Louis Kroeber]]. Having earned a master's degree in French, Le Guin began doctoral studies but abandoned these after her marriage in 1953 to historian [[Charles Le Guin]]. She began writing full-time in the late 1950s, and she achieved major critical and commercial success with the novels ''[[A Wizard of Earthsea]]'' (1968) and ''[[The Left Hand of Darkness]]'' (1969); these have been described by [[Harold Bloom]] as her masterpieces.{{sfn|White|1999|p=2}} For the latter volume, Le Guin won both the [[Hugo Award for Best Novel|Hugo]] and [[Nebula Award for Best Novel|Nebula awards for best novel]], becoming the first woman to do so. Several more works set in Earthsea or the Hainish universe followed; others included books set in the fictional country of [[Orsinia]], several works for children, and many anthologies.

[[Cultural anthropology]], [[Le Guin and Taoism|Taoism]], [[feminism]], and the writings of [[Carl Jung]] all had a strong influence on Le Guin's work. Many of her stories used anthropologists or cultural observers as protagonists, and Taoist ideas about balance and equilibrium have been identified in several writings. Le Guin often subverted typical speculative fiction tropes, such as by writing [[People of color|dark-skinned]] protagonists in Earthsea, and also used unusual stylistic or structural devices in works such as the experimental ''[[Always Coming Home]]'' (1985). Social and political themes, including race, gender, sexuality, and [[coming of age]] were prominent in her writing. She explored alternative political structures in many stories, such as the [[Philosophical fiction|philosophical short story]] "[[The Ones Who Walk Away from Omelas]]" (1973) and the anarchist utopian novel ''[[The Dispossessed]]'' (1974).

Le Guin's writing was enormously influential in the field of speculative fiction and has been the subject of intense critical attention. She received numerous accolades, including eight [[Hugo Award]]s, six [[Nebula Award]]s, and twenty-five [[Locus Award for Best Novel|Locus Awards]]; in 2003, she became the second woman honored as a [[SFWA Grand Master|Grand Master]] of the [[Science Fiction and Fantasy Writers of America]]. The U.S. [[Library of Congress]] named her a [[Library of Congress Living Legend|Living Legend]] in 2000, and in 2014, she won the [[National Book Award|National Book Foundation Medal for Distinguished Contribution to American Letters]]. Le Guin influenced many other authors, including the [[Booker Prize]] winner [[Salman Rushdie]], [[David Mitchell (author)|David Mitchell]], [[Neil Gaiman]], and [[Iain Banks]]. After her death in 2018, critic [[John Clute]] wrote that Le Guin had "presided over American science fiction for nearly half a century",<ref name="Clute Guardian Obit" /> while author [[Michael Chabon]] referred to her as the "greatest American writer of her generation".<ref name="Fellow Writers" /><ref name=":0">{{Cite web |last=Chabon |first=Michael |date=November 20, 2019 |title=Le Guin's Subversive Imagination |url=https://www.theparisreview.org/blog/2019/11/20/leguins-subversive-imagination/ |access-date=November 24, 2019 |website=The Paris Review |language=en |archive-date=December 24, 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191224023023/https://www.theparisreview.org/blog/2019/11/20/leguins-subversive-imagination/ |url-status=live }}</ref>

== Life ==
=== Childhood and education ===
[[File:Ishi.jpg|thumb|right|Ursula's father, [[Alfred Kroeber]], with [[Ishi]], the last of the [[Yahi]] people (1911)]]
Ursula Kroeber was born in [[Berkeley, California]], on October 21, 1929. Her father, [[Alfred L. Kroeber|Alfred Louis Kroeber]], was an [[anthropologist]] at the [[University of California, Berkeley]].{{sfn|Spivack|1984|p=1}}<ref name="NYT obit">{{Cite news |last=Jonas |first=Gerald |date=January 23, 2018 |title=Ursula K. Le Guin, Acclaimed for Her Fantasy Fiction, Is Dead at 88 |work=[[The New York Times]] |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2018/01/23/obituaries/ursula-k-le-guin-acclaimed-for-her-fantasy-fiction-is-dead-at-88.html |access-date=January 23, 2018 |archive-date=January 23, 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180123221310/https://www.nytimes.com/2018/01/23/obituaries/ursula-k-le-guin-acclaimed-for-her-fantasy-fiction-is-dead-at-88.html |url-status=live }}</ref> Le Guin's mother, [[Theodora Kroeber]] (born Theodora Covel Kracaw), had a graduate degree in psychology, but turned to writing in her 60s, developing a successful career as an author. Among her works was ''[[Ishi in Two Worlds]]'' (1961), a biographical volume about [[Ishi]], an [[Indigenous peoples of the Americas|Indigenous American]] who had been studied by Alfred Kroeber. Ishi was the last known member of the [[Yahi]] tribe after the rest of its members died or were killed by white colonizers.{{sfn|Spivack|1984|p=1}}{{sfn|Cummins|1990|p=2}}<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Hallowell |first=A. Irving |date=1962 |title=Theodora Kroeber. Ishi in Two Worlds: A Biography of the Last Wild Indian in North America |journal=The Annals of the American Academy of Political and Social Science |volume=340 |issue=1 |pages=164–165 |doi=10.1177/000271626234000162|s2cid=145429704 }}</ref>

Le Guin had three older brothers: [[Karl Kroeber|Karl]], who became a literary scholar, Theodore, and Clifton.<!--The name "Clifton" is taken from Theodora Kroeber's writing: "Clifford" is incorrectly used by Spivack.-->{{sfn|Spivack|1984|p=2}}<ref>{{Cite book |last=Kroeber |first=Theodora |url=https://archive.org/details/alfredkroeberper00kroe_0 |title=Alfred Kroeber; a Personal Configuration |publisher=University of California Press |year=1970 |isbn=978-0-520-01598-2 |page=[https://archive.org/details/alfredkroeberper00kroe_0/page/287 287] |author-link=Theodora Kroeber |url-access=registration}}</ref> The family had a large book collection, and the siblings all became interested in reading while they were young.{{sfn|Spivack|1984|p=2}} The Kroeber family had a number of visitors, including well-known academics such as [[Robert Oppenheimer]]; Le Guin would later use Oppenheimer as the model for Shevek, the physicist protagonist of ''[[The Dispossessed]]''.{{sfn|Cummins|1990|p=2}}{{sfn|Spivack|1984|p=2}} The family divided its time between a home in [[Napa Valley]] during the summer and a house in Berkeley during the academic year.{{sfn|Cummins|1990|p=2}}

Le Guin's reading included science fiction and fantasy: she and her siblings often read issues of ''[[Thrilling Wonder Stories]]'' and ''[[Astounding Science Fiction]]''.
