==Reception==
[[File:CADAL02111774 李卓吾先生批評忠義水滸傳（二）.djvu|thumb|page=21|upright=0.65|A critical commentary of ''Water Margin'' by philosopher and writer Li Zhi (1527–1602)]]
[[File:CADAL06200337 古本小說集成：錘伯敬批評忠議水滸傳·二.djvu|thumb|page=306|upright=0.65|A critical commentary of the novel by Zhong Bojing, 1625]]
[[File:Jin Shengtan's edition of Water Margin.jpg|thumb|upright=0.65|A critical commentary on the novel by Jin Shengtan (1608–1661)]]
''Water Margin'', praised as an early "masterpiece" of [[Vernacular literature|vernacular fiction]],<ref name="Findlay">{{Cite book|title=Frae Ither Tongues: Essays on Modern Translations into Scots|date=2004|publisher=Multilingual Matters Ltd|editor=Bill Findlay|isbn=1-85359-701-5|location=Clevedon [England]|page=21|oclc=55630249}}</ref> is renowned for the "mastery and control" of its mood and tone.<ref name=Findlay/> The novel is also known for its use of vivid, humorous and especially racy language.<ref name=Findlay/> For the seventeenth-century scholar Dadi Yuren, ''Water Margin'' was to be acclaimed because it demonstrated the moral principles of loyalty (''zhong'') and righteousness (''yi'') which were crucial for the society.<ref>{{cite journal|last=Ge|first=Liangyan|title=The Mythic Stone in Honglou Meng and an Intertext of Ming-Qing Fiction Criticism|journal=The Journal of Asian Studies|volume=61|issue=1|year=2002|pages=57–82|doi=10.2307/2700189|jstor=2700189}}</ref> Some commentaries and sources from the late Ming and early Qing suggest that many ''Water Margin'' characters appealed to the literati readers of that time because of their symbolic power as the "[[Authenticity (philosophy)|genuine]]" and the "primitive", in which many literati found it unexpectedly refreshing.<ref>{{cite book |last=Huang |first=Martin W. |title=Negotiating Masculinities in Late Imperial China |publisher=University of Hawai{{Okina}}i Press |publication-place=Honolulu |year=2006 |isbn=978-1-4356-6553-8 |oclc=256489034 |pages=111-112 }}</ref>  Many Ming dynasty writers and scholars have lauded the novel, as [[Li Kaixian]] (1502–1568) writes:
{{Blockquote
|text=Cui Xian ({{lang|zh|[[:zh:崔銑 (明朝)|崔銑]]}}) [1479—1541], Xiang Guo ({{lang|zh|[[:zh:熊过|熊过]]}}) [1507—1581], [[Tang Shunzhi]], [[Wang Shenzhong]], and Chen Shu ({{lang|zh|[[:zh:陳束|陳束]]}}) [1508—1540] say that the ''Water Margin'' is filled with minute details and numerous veins that link up, and that only the ''[[Shiji|Records of the Grand Historian]]'' surpasses this book. Moreover, since ancient times there has never before been a book about a single event in twenty volumes (ce). One who would fault it for its treacherous banditry and deception knows nothing of methods for narrating events or of the subtleties of the study of history.{{sfnp|Gregory|2023|pp=64-65}}}}

On the other hand, ever since the novel became circulated in print, it has been received with profound ambivalence as a politically subversive and even potentially [[countercultural]] text.<ref name="knightener">{{Cite book |author=Roland Altenburger|title=A Companion to World Literature |year=2020 |publisher=Wiley |isbn=978-1-118-99318-7 | chapter=The Knight-Errant and the Good Fellow in Chinese Narrative: Water Margin and the Xia (Hero) Tradition|chapter-url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/9781118635193.ctwl0119|doi=10.1002/9781118635193.ctwl0119}}</ref> It has also been denounced as "obscene" by various critics since the Ming dynasty.<ref>{{cite book|title=Chinese literature|publisher=Foreign Languages Press, original from [[University of Michigan]]|year=1998|page=138}}</ref> Certain literati found ''Water Margin'' to be dangerous for readers who might rebel against imperial authority after reading this novel, given its images of rebellion in the conflict between the Liangshan fraternity and government forces.<ref name="transgression">{{cite thesis|degree=PhD|last=Lem|first=Henry|title=The Sixteenth-Century Novel Water Margin and the Tradition of Fiction Commentary and Sequels in Late Imperial China|year=2019|publisher=[[UC Irvine]]|url=https://escholarship.org/uc/item/5z32d0bs}}</ref>

{{blockquote|"These seduction cases are the hardest of all. There are five conditions that have to be met before you can succeed. First, you have to be as handsome as [[Pan Yue (poet)|Pan An]]. Second, you need a tool as big as a donkey's. Third, you must be as rich as Deng Tong. Fourth, you must be as forbearing as a needle plying through cotton wool. Fifth, you've got to spend time. It can be done only if you meet these five requirements."

"Frankly, I think I do. First, while I'm far from a Pan An, I still can get by. Second, I've had a big cock since childhood."
|source = Excerpt from the novel, translated by [[Sidney Shapiro]]<ref>{{cite web|url=http://asiaobscura.com/2011/11/the-goriest-raunchiest-chinese-classic-of-all-time.html#below|title=The Goriest, Raunchiest Chinese Classic of All Time|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150916175904/http://asiaobscura.com/2011/11/the-goriest-raunchiest-chinese-classic-of-all-time.html#below|archive-date=2015-09-16}}</ref>}}

The novel is widely acclaimed as among the finest of all the fictional works of the same period, and it has been subjected to more [[Literary criticism|scholarly critical]] attention than most other novels.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Goodrich |first1=L. Carington |author-link1=Luther Carrington Goodrich |title=[[Dictionary of Ming Biography, 1368-1644]] |last2=Fang |first2=Chaoying |author-link2=Fang Chao-ying |publisher=Columbia University Press |year=1976 |isbn=0-231-03801-1 |location=New York|pages=1204-1205|chapter=SHIH Nai-an}}</ref> According to Xu Yongqiang of the School of Humanities at Xi'an University of Electronic Science and Technology, there have been approximately 50 monographic series and over 1,000 research and analysis works on the ''Water Margin'' from the Ming and Qing dynasties to the present-day, demonstrating its immense influence and establishing "Water Margin Studies" as a prominent discipline of study.<ref>{{Cite web |script-title=zh:颜建国：小说《水浒传》人物原型再探源 |url=https://www.sohu.com/a/511362514_99904608 |website=Sohu |language=zh |access-date=2025-09-22}}</ref>

In his reading guidelines for ''Water Margin'', [[Jin Shengtan]] identifies fifteen literary techniques, including "advance insertion", "detailed and extended narration", "direct repetition", and "incomplete repetition of a topic", noting that ''Water Margin'' contains forms of diction, phrasing, sectioning, and the form of a work as a whole—all literary phenomena that fall under the category of visible and material [[dharmas]] known as [[rūpa]]. He asserts that "''Water Margin'' itself turns out to contain the methods for reading all the world's books".<ref>{{cite thesis|degree=PhD|title=The Genius of Form: Jin Shengtan's (1608–1661) Transformative Literary Program|year=2021|author=Alia Breitwieser|doi=10.6082/UCHICAGO.3415|publisher=[[University of Chicago]]}}</ref> Jin also claims that the author not only gave 36 different faces to the 36 major heroes in the novel, the author also created 36 different personalities as well, and points out that ''Water Margin'' emphasizes the construction of meaningful relationships between the characters.<ref>{{cite thesis|degree=PhD|title=Reading Bodies: Aesthetics, Gender, and Family in the Eighteenth-Century Chinese Novel Guwangyan (Preposterous Words)|year=2016|last=Ye|first=Qing|publisher=[[University of Oregon]]|hdl=1794/20508}}</ref>

[[Jaroslav Průšek]] wrote, "With its account of the bold deeds of the rebels, each told with fresh originality, with its apt characterization of their individual features, its precise yet poetic portrayal of the environment, this romance is a treasure of Chinese popular literature, and an inexhaustible source of ideas for the theatre and the story-tellers."<ref>{{cite book|last1=Průšek |first1=Jaroslav |last2=Słupski |first2=Zbigniew |year=1974 |title=Dictionary of Oriental Literatures: East Asia |publisher=Routledge |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=iYGDPwAACAAJ |isbn=9780415393539 |pages=157-158}}</ref>

Sinologist Lois M. Fusek framed the parallel between ''Water Margin'', which is revolutionary, glorifying bandits as divinely ordained agents of change; with the novel ''[[The Three Sui Quash the Demons' Revolt]]'', which tone more reformist and traditional, deriding such figures—depicted as humble peddlers like noodle-vendors and cake-sellers—as absurd pretenders to heavenly mandate. This mockery underscores a pro-establishment stance, emphasizing swift suppression. Other than that, the temporal momentum complements spatial allusions of ''Three Suis'' with ''Water Margin''{{'s}} iconic locales and archetypes creates a satirical mirror-world between those two novels.<ref name="LoisFusekWaterMargin">{{Cite book 
|title=The Three Sui Quash the Demons Revolt; A Comic Novel Attributed to Luo Guanzhong
|date= 4 August 2010
|publisher= University of Hawaii Press
|isbn= 978-0-8248-6070-7
|editor= Lois Fusek
|translator= Lois Fusek
|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=oYwBEAAAQBAJ
|pages= 188, 223
}}</ref>

==Themes==
===Religion===
[[File:Li County manual including several of the most famous heroes from Watermargin 01.jpg|upright=0.65|thumb|A Taoist manuscript from [[Li County, Hunan|Li County]], [[Hunan]] contains codifications of [[fulu|talismans]] for each of the 108 protagonists from ''Water Margin'', 19th century]]
The motif of pairings between 36 and 72 stars, possibly inspired from [[Dipper (Chinese constellation)|Dipper]], were common among Chinese mythologies and folk tales, including ''Water Margin'', which represented by the number of its protagonists.<ref name=fenfahenyanyi3>{{cite book |title= The Lady of Linshui Pacifies Demons A Seventeenth Century Novel
|date= 2008
|publisher= Stanford University Press
|isbn= 978-0-8047-4666-3
|author= Mark Edward Lewis
|author-link= Mark Edward Lewis
|translator= Brigitte Baptandier
|pages= 110, 132
|url= https://books.google.com/books?id=UeoSEAAAQBAJ
}}</ref> The religious theme of these 108 demons that incarnated into the 108 Liangshan bandits apparently drew inspiration from the [[List of gods in the Investiture of the Gods#Dipper Department|36 heavenly spirits and 72 earth fiends]] that also appeared in a later [[Written vernacular Chinese|Chinese vernacular]] novel titled ''[[Investiture of the Gods]]''. In that novel, the 108 demons were gathered by [[Jiang Taigong]] to fight against [[Di Xin]].<ref name=fengshenyanyi>{{cite book 
|title= Carpentry and Building in Late Imperial China: A Study of the Fifteenth-century Carpenter's Manual, Lu Ban Jing
|date= 1998
|publisher= Brill
|isbn= 978-90-04-10529-4
|author= Klaas Ruitenbeek
|page= 106
|url= https://books.google.com/books?id=KH2XJVKxgIMC
}}</ref> [[Liu Ts'un-yan]] added that the motif of 108 stars (36 spirits and 72 fiends representatives) constellation which appeared in both works were influenced by [[Buddhism]] and [[Taoism]].<ref name=fengshenyanyi3>{{cite book 
|title= Buddhist and Taoist Influences on Chinese Novels: The authorship of the Feng shen yen i, being a thesis approved for the degree of doctor of philosophy in the University of London, 1957
|date= 1962
|publisher= Kommissionsverlag, O. Harrassowitz
|author= Liu Ts'un-yan (Liu Cunren)
|author-link= Liu Ts'un-yan
|translator= Brigitte Baptandier
|pages= 110, 132
|url= https://books.google.com/books?id=uBppAAAAMAAJ
}}</ref> The organization of ''[[Flowers in the Mirror]]'' owes much to this orchestration of ''Water Margin''.<ref>{{cite book|title=The Beauty and the Book: Women and Fiction in Nineteenth-Century China|author=Ellen Widmer|isbn=978-0674021464|page=37|year=2006|publisher=Harvard East Asian Monographs|doi=10.2307/j.ctt1tm7fv5}}</ref>

Others analysed [[Li Kui (Water Margin)|Li Kui]], one of the most savage Liangshan bandit characters, in more religious aspects, by quoting from the words of Luo Zhenren (a Taoist immortal in the novel who comments on the characters' fates) and a famous line from [[Laozi]]'s ''Tao Te Ching'' (chapter 5): "{{lang|zh|天地不仁，以万物为刍狗}} ("Heaven and Earth are impartial and treat all beings as disposable "straw dogs" used in rituals"). This portrays the spiritual character of Li Kui as being representative of the chaotic force of nature, blending divine indifference with animalistic instincts.<ref name=likuiSymbolism1>{{cite journal |last=Qi |first=Yukun |title=Zhengque Kexue di Pingjia Li Kui |script-title=zh:正确科学地评价李逵|trans-title=A Correct and Scientific Evaluation of Li Kui |journal=Fujian Guangbo Dianshi Daxue Xuebao |script-journal=zh:福建广播电视大学学报 |trans-journal=Journal of Fujian Radio and Television University |year=2009 |publisher=Fujian Guangbo Dianshi Daxue (福建广播电视大学; Fujian Radio and Television University) |location=Fuzhou |language=zh}}</ref><ref name=likuisymbolism2>{{cite book |last=Zheng |first=Zhenduo |title=Zheng Zhenduo Wenji Disi Juan |script-title=zh:郑振铎文集第四卷 |trans-title=Collected Works of Zheng Zhenduo |volume=4 |publisher=Renmin Wenxue Chubanshe (人民文学出版社; People's Literature Publishing House) |location=Beijing |year=1988 |page=125 |language=zh}}</ref>

Furthermore, both [[Victor Purcell]]<ref name="boxer1">{{Cite book 
|title=The Boxer Uprising; A Background Study
|date= 3 June 2010 
|publisher= Cambridge University Press
|isbn=  978-0-521-14812-2
|author1=  Victor Purcell
|author1-link= Victor Purcell
|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=2MeUoD9G9xAC
|pages= 166, 223, 228–229, 231–232, 266
}}</ref> and [[Joseph W. Esherick]] have recorded that ''Water Margin''—along with ''Romance of the Three kingdoms'' and ''Investiture of the Gods''— were quite influential for the religious Belief of the radical [[Boxer movement]] in shaping their ideology,<ref name="boxer2">{{Cite book 
|title= The Origins of the Boxer Uprising
|date= 2004 
|publisher=University of Hawaiʻi Press 
|isbn=978-0-8248-2538-6 
|author1=  Joseph W. Esherick
|author1-link= Joseph W. Esherick
|url= https://books.google.com/books?id=jVESdBSMasMC
|pages= 13, 39, 45, 65, 294, 329
}}</ref> which became the reason for Qing government to ban the novel in 1799.<ref name="boxer1" />

[[Tao Chengzhang]] (d. 1911) attributed the surge of religious movements like the [[White Lotus Societies]] in north China and the ''[[Hongmen|Heaven and the Earth Society]]'' in the south was due to the influences of the novels ''Investiture of the Gods'' and ''Water Margin'' respectively. He writes: "Throughout the area of Shandong, Shanxi and Henan {{bracket|that is, the north}} there is no one who does not believe {{bracket|zunxin}} in the ''Investiture of the Gods'' story. Throughout the area of Jiangsu, Zhe-jiang, Fujian and Guangzhou {{bracket|the south}} there is no one who does not venerate {{bracket|chongbai}} the book, ''Water Margin''".<ref name=fengshenyanyi2>{{cite book 
|title= Unruly Gods Divinity and Society in China
|date= 1996
|publisher= University of Hawaii Press
|isbn= 978-0-8248-1724-4
|editor1= Meir Shahar
|editor2= Robert P. Weller
|page= 186
|url= https://books.google.com/books?id=gegRl__dR8EC
}}</ref> As [[Daniel L. Overmyer]] observes, northerners canonization of ''Investiture of the Gods'' and southerners veneration of ''Water Margin'', illustrates their symbiotic role in faith: a subversive tool empowering the illiterate through heroic divinity.<ref name=Kuan-yin />

In the novel, the Mount Liang bandits are under the aegis of a divine woman named [[Jiutian Xuannü]] (九天玄女 lit. "Dark Maiden of Ninefold Heavens").<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Liu|first1=Peng| title="Conceal my Body so that I can Protect the State": The Making of the Mysterious Woman in Daoism and Water Margin| journal=Ming Studies|date=2016| volume=2016| issue= 74| pages=48–71|doi=10.1080/0147037X.2016.1228876 |s2cid=164447144}}</ref> They need guidance from this "[[Mother goddess|great mother]]" to fight against the threat of death, as well as to pursue the value of life with others, instead of struggling for individual survival in a self-contained way.<ref>{{cite journal|language=zh-hant|title=《水滸傳》英雄的求生與再生─以女性為切入點|trans-title=The Trials of Heroes: the Female Figures in the Novel "Water Margin"|author=Pei-Huang Hsu|url=https://www.airitilibrary.com/Article/Detail?DocID=17278562-201303-201307080008-201307080008-143-170|year=2013|issue=50|pages=143–170|journal=Journal of Humanities College of Liberal Arts National Chung Hsing University|issn=1727-8562}}</ref> In Ming dynasty, lesser-known female deities surpassed the elite [[Queen Mother of the West]] in vernacular novels like ''Water Margin'' and ''Investiture of the Gods''. Rooted in [[Chinese folk religion]], likely inspiring syncretic sectarian icons such as the Venerable Mother [[Guanyin]]. These "post-menopausal" goddesses embody pure motherliness—nurturing wisdom without childbirth's mess or sexual desire's pitfalls—aligning with Confucian purity yet excising femininity's "negatives" like vulnerability and passion. However, this desexualized ideal reinforces gender binaries, reflecting Ming anxieties over female sexuality amid orthodoxy-heterodoxy clashes.<ref name=Kuan-yin>{{cite book 
|title= Kuan-yin; The Chinese Transformation of Avalokitesvara
|date= 22 March 2001
|publisher= Columbia University Press
|isbn= 978-0-231-50275-7
|author1=Chün-fang Yü
|page= 481
|url= https://books.google.com/books?id=TtlEr3tod18C
}}</ref>

=== Politics ===
[[File:颐和园长廊彩绘：林冲风雪山神庙.jpg|thumb|left|upright=1.15|[[Lin Chong]] ([[Summer Palace]] mural)]]

A major portion of the novel is made up of a series of connected stories, each recounting the making of a hero, his sufferings under an unjust social system and his resort to banditry as a relief from [[political persecution]]; hence, the expression {{zhp|p=bi shang Liangshan|c=逼上梁山|l=being forced to climb the Liang mountains}} or "being driven to rebel".<ref>{{cite journal|pages=1–15|publisher=[[University of Hawaiʻi Press]]|journal=CHINOPERL Papers|author=Samuel Hung-Nin Cheung|title=Structural Cyclicity in Shuihu Zhuan: From Self to Sworn Brotherhood|volume=15|year=1990|issn=2835-3188}}</ref> As [[Hŏ Kyun]] insisted, they were changed from the common people or blaming people to the resistant people.<ref>{{cite journal|language=ko|title=水滸傳 서사의 전환 하나, 黃泥岡 사건과 三阮의 등장 - 金聖嘆의 비평을 중심으로|trans-title=WongNaiGang Case and Appearance of Three Ruans, One of Change of the Epic ShuiHuZhuan(Outlaws of the Marsh)|year=2012|pages=305-336|issue=50|journal=한국한문학연구|author=이승수|issn=2733-4910}}</ref> [[Wu-chi Liu]] suggests the novel epitomizes human suffering and degradation at the hands of the [[ruling class]], and notes that there is little doubt where the author's sympathy lies: the bandit leaders are definitely the heroes of the novel and their uprising can only be attributed to government oppression and [[tyranny]].<ref name="taleofmarshes">{{cite book|pages=211-212|last=Liu|first=Wu-Chi|title=An Introduction to Chinese Literature|isbn=9780685162835|publisher=Indiana University Press|year=1966|author-link=Wu-chi Liu|location=Bloomington}}</ref> History and literature critic Shang Wei viewed ''Water Margin'' as a one of a kind novel which concerned about people's history ("petty history"), [[dynastic cycle]] topics, and among many others.<ref name=DerWeiWaterMargin>{{cite book |editor-last1=Wang |editor-first1=David Der-wei |editor1-link=David Der-wei Wang
|editor-last2=Wei |editor-first2=Shang |title=Dynastic Crisis and Cultural Innovation: From the Late Ming to the Late Qing and Beyond |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=qAD8EAAAQBAJ |publisher=Brill |year=2020 |orig-date=2005 |isbn=978-1-68417-414-0 |pages=14, 63, 408 |access-date=2025-11-07}}</ref>

The heroes' slogan—"Accomplish the Way for [[Tian|Heaven]]!" ({{lang|zh|替天行道}})—challenges an existing authority which subverts the Confucian ideal of government, and appeals to the moral sanctions that justify the replacement of an evil ruler by one who will reconstitute the moral order.<ref>{{Cite book|url={{google books |plainurl=y |id=7lBWH2rxRFsC}}|title=The Confucian Persuasion|editor-last=Wright|publisher=Stanford University Press|year=1960|isbn=9780804700184|editor-first=Arthur F.|location=Stanford, California|pages=3–20|chapter=Introduction}}</ref> The model of [[political action]] established in the novel stresses [[social solidarity]].<ref>{{cite book|author=Charlton M. Lewis|chapter=Some Notes on the Ko-lao Hui in Late Ch’ing China|editor=Jean Chesneaux|title=Popular Movements and Secret Societies in China 1840-1950|year=1972|publisher= [[Stanford University Press]]|location= [[Stanford, California]]|pages=97–112|isbn=9780804707909|lccn=70153816}}</ref> For the radical thinker [[Li Zhi (philosopher)|Li Zhi]], who esteems the fair-minded and honest outlaws as the arbiters of the correct course of the Chinese empire, their violent and conscientious resistance to [[political corruption]] and [[social repression]] proves their patriotism and loyalism in the "World Upside Down"—a world where authority has lost its legitimacy.<ref>{{cite book|page=28|publisher=University of Michigan Press|doi=10.3998/mpub.11564671|title=Writing Pirates: Vernacular Fiction and Oceans in Late Ming China|year=2021|author=Yuanfei Wang|isbn=9780472902484}}</ref> The book is also largely considered to reveal that "chaos works from the [[upper class]]" ({{lang-zh|t=亂自上作|labels=no}}).<ref>{{cite journal|language=zh-hans|year=2021|issue=2|pages=132–138|publisher=[[Qufu Normal University]]|issn=1001-022X|journal=Qilu Journal|title="乱自上作"与"儒自下毁"——《水浒传》与《儒林外史》中的"四进"开篇及其文化意蕴|trans-title="Chaos Works from Upper Class" and "Confucianism Destroys from Lower Class"——The Culture Meaning of the Beginning of the "Si Jin" in Water Margin and The Scholars|author1=Fan Qing-yan|author2=Si Ruo-lan|url=https://kns.cnki.net/kcms2/article/abstract?v=kn2pS460sONv4YVJ6jQScdUOjl9hAwcCTxvmCCDjP2ky870h9ps6XPqmbbaiQmWStsLZwfjCm9sSHK-h5ijEgbEhY_QVrhLa3_dja6sL7yOTJ7KOEufPKipOx43owpcAW1crrSnQ05Clda8RdyraIbS7RMHFoCSa08foWAJlHSqduiMQNVBbHA==&uniplatform=NZKPT&language=CHS}}</ref> [[Wei Jingsheng]] said the struggle of heroes in ''Water Margin'' was "exactly the kind of struggle aimed at winning equality of rights for man as a human being", and these heroic tales signified the historical continuity of the Chinese people's political struggle for recognition.<ref>{{cite journal|pages=47-59|journal=[[The National Interest]]|author=John Fitzgerald|title=China and the Quest for Dignity|year=1999|issue=55|publisher=[[Center for the National Interest]]|issn=0884-9382}}</ref>

In the Ming and early Qing periods, the argument centered on whether the novel's protagonists were "loyal and righteous" or "bandits".<ref name="sunlin">{{cite thesis|degree=PhD|author=Sun Lin|title=水浒忠义观的建构与解构|year=2019|publisher=[[Shandong University]]|doi=10.27272/d.cnki.gshdu.2019.000820|language=zh-hans|trans-title=The Construction and Deconstruction of the View of Loyaltyabout Water Margin}}</ref><ref name="sinica" /> By the time of the late Qing dynasty, [[bourgeois revolution]]aries began to interpret the novel from the point view of Western bourgeois thought such as liberty, equality, and human rights, seeing the book as "the beginnings of democracy and [[civil society]]".<ref name="randou">{{cite thesis|degree=PhD|publisher=[[Shandong University]]|language=zh-hans|url=https://kns.cnki.net/kcms2/article/abstract?v=CP5zkKmU_7fzjiYLWKLtTDTsCSSLjXEjbxgLYjvz1l9NVjZVkhPFiTSZbClkqP0pUmn3yRsvEwHkKsyFwseYpaFsc4-ISEQYTfBuUXprlImVnMzrWZkG2dkMIkcNSfb7pJRmDacKmXg3YHzgA_ozkyQSdKIZA0AnY-c-TpM7hlTPftYX0mDQafkg6EspBkB3&uniplatform=NZKPT&language=CHS|title=《水浒传》诠释史论|author=Zhang Tongsheng|year=2007|trans-title=On the Interpretation History of Water Margin}}</ref><ref name="sinica">{{cite book|doi=10.14277/6969-095-2/SV-3-6|language=zh-hans|author=Liu Yongqiang|year=2016|chapter=On the Three Stages of Contradictory Comments of The Water Margin|pages=81–92|series=Sinica venetiana|title=Linking Ancient and Contemporary: Continuities and Discontinuities in Chinese Literature|isbn=978-88-6969-098-3|editor1=Tiziana Lippiello|editor2=Chen Yuehong|editor3=Maddalena Barenghi|publisher=Edizioni Ca' Foscari}}</ref> Since the 1950s, the "Peasant Uprising" hypothesis has become one of the most influential and widespread interpretations in the study of the themes of the novel.<ref>{{cite journal|first=Zhaoming| last=Liu|volume=37|issue=6|year=2017|title=A Query about the "Peasant Uprising" and "Driven to Join the Liangshan Rebels" Hypotheses: An Analysis of the Identities and Occupations of the Heroes and Their Uprising Causes in Water Margin|pages=59–69|journal=Theoretical Studies in Literature and Art|issn=0257-0254|publisher=[[East China Normal University Press]]|url=https://tsla.researchcommons.org/journal/vol37/iss6/2}}</ref> Yet specialists continue to disagree about the [[political philosophy]] of ''Water Margin''.<ref>{{cite journal|last=Ivry|first=B.|year=2023|title=Book Review Bandits in Print: "The Water Margin" and the Transformations of the Chinese Novel|journal=Thai Journal of East Asian Studies|volume=27|issue=2|pages=137–142|url=https://so02.tci-thaijo.org/index.php/easttu/article/view/265106}}</ref> [[David Der-wei Wang|David Wang]] suggests that in the novel the heroes are torn between "total self-dedication and total self-betrayal" by first adhering to the code of chivalric fraternity against the authorities and then to the ideology of imperial loyalty.<ref>{{cite book|last=Wang|first=David|title=[[Fin-de-Siècle Splendor|Fin de Siécle Splendor]]|isbn=978-0-8047-2845-4|publisher=[[Stanford University Press]]|year=1997|page=123}}</ref> The book's challenging political implications have continued to exercise theorists in China even in recent times.<ref>{{cite book|page=352|editor=Brian Hook|title=The Cambridge Encyclopedia of China|location=Cambridge|publisher=Cambridge University Press|year=1982|isbn=0 521 35594X}}</ref> The literary critic and novelist Wang Zhongqi wrote in 1907:
{{Blockquote
|text=Since the birth of the society, there are no instances of an organization of government constituted one hundred people that are equal to one another. ''Water Margin'' is the only one. Had Shi Nai'an been born in the West, his work would be comparable to those of [[Plato]], [[Mikhail Bakunin|Bakunin]], and [[Leo Tolstoy|Tolstoy]]. Looking at its [[egalitarianism]], ''Water Margin'' is a work of [[socialism]]. Looking at its vengeance on the corrupted officials, it is a work of [[anarchism]]. All the organizations depicted in the ''Water Margin'' are complete in their functions. If we look at it this way, ''Water Margin'' is a [[political novel]].<ref name="pbtsap" >{{cite journal|journal=Asia Pacific Perspectives|title=Closing the Revolution: The Criticize Water Margin Campaign and the Politics of Surrender in Mao's China|author=Yaowen Dong|year=2025|volume=19|issue=1|pages=96–125|publisher=Center for Asia Pacific Studies, [[University of San Francisco]]|url=https://repository.usfca.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1097&context=asiapacificperspectives|format=pdf}}</ref>}}

[[File:厦门洪门腰牌.JPG|thumb|right|upright=0.85|Seal of the [[Hongmen]], the precursor of Tiandihui secret society, 19th century<ref>Alexander Wylie: Secret Societies in China, in  ''China Researches'', p131, 1897 Shanghai, reprinted in USA by Nabu Public Domain Reprints</ref>]]

According to [[:zh:李時 (弘治壬戌進士) |Li Shi]] (1471–1538), the authorial rationale behind the counterfactual victory of the Southern Song over the Liao at the end of the novel stems from the patriotic motivations of the novel's alleged authors, Shi Nai'an and Luo Guanzhong—both of whom lived during the Yuan dynasty.<ref>{{cite journal 
|title= "Shuihu zhuan" and the Military Subculture of the Northern Song, 960-1127
|year= 2006
|publisher= Harvard-Yenching Institute
|volume= 66
|issue= 2
|author= Paul Jakov Smith
|pages= 363–422
|journal=Harvard Journal of Asiatic Studies
|jstor= 25066819

}}</ref> Furthermore, ''Water Margin'' has been politically influential throughout subsequent Chinese history: while several emperors and Confucian elites banned the novel for its violent and rebellious content, the challengers of the established order, from [[Taiping Rebellion|Taiping rebels]] in the mid 19th century to [[Chinese Communist Revolution|Communist revolutionaries]], honored it for the same reason.<ref name="pbtsap" />

Some argue that the novel's theme of revolt against authority became popular during turbulent times of the [[Ming dynasty]], others argue that ''Water Margin'' became popular during the Yuan as the common people (predominantly [[Han Chinese]]) resented the [[Mongols|Mongol]] rulers.<ref name=InspirationWaterMargin>{{cite web |last1=Miyamoto |first1=Yoko |title=Water Margin: Chinese Robin Hood and His Bandits |url=http://www.demystifyingconfucianism.info/water-margin |website=Demystifying Confucianism |access-date=4 July 2018}}</ref> Zuo Maodi ({{lang|zh|[[:zh:左懋第|左懋第]]}}) (1601–1645), a Ming dynasty vice minister of war, viewed the ''Water Margin'' as a book that taught people to be criminals. He believed that if the book was not banned, it would impact the societal atmosphere negatively.<ref>{{cite web |author=Chen Weixing
|date=26 September 2013 
|title=明清时期《水浒传》禁毁情况考论
|trans-title=A Study on the Banning and Destruction of Water Margin in the Ming and Qing Dynasties |url=http://www.guoxue.com/?p=14929&u_atoken=68fba875-5a8c-12c7-97c3-bc8c8a14d42f&u_asession=01_SU3wHHWPn-F2dAcOyjqqzSrlw9udqoc0PJ2Mm0uUmmnyKpEX0qi83w1VB7WDEt5sr0mvdpkb8p6VWQHDYMEXG8evbUc49_OXyiOdDHywLab6xO2lZmK5tDapwFM4jOd&u_asig=05ieqWdNMTAm9Lsshuh83Rip5PQ-D0yBCPMG8Wd3G04hwJ_Ilx2KWsMQDNr4zWsSzk96m8tPvHUktjiUtlQVAQaelz9bYzZVeMRsbxCVGX2iC9WpwE3xSKhow3cdUZuaeAbX5LsBhw-N6nBFSVfEH8dWBk2oKiudZS6qKIpajFt4dFOXcStDLQ0IWIoKdg3XwitYCvOhmhMIoqrLDWYLoB5kGDaMXW141jG_zqKhDz_ONV1qzhjM-6HtsAB0YQPuFx3zQRFVRlED4dpM3mtmS8nbxEPu5uyQ2kWBPaGPsbxdz_8DYs7w33pIyefWv9VDvdBx9aYvVidezoJdO72Sl2Nw&u_aref=gJQvlOevJBhO4REygYD3Zi3kFjk%3D
|access-date=2025-10-24
|website=Guoxue.com 
|language=zh
|location= Sichuan
|publisher= Literature faculty, Chongqing Three Gorges University; School of History, Sichuan University |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210610023909/http://www.guoxue.com/?p=14929
|archive-date=2021-06-10}}</ref> [[Chongzhen Emperor]] of the Ming dynasty, acting on his advice, banned the book.<ref>{{in lang|zh}} [http://blog.sina.com.cn/s/blog_476624c9010008qf.html {{lang|zh|明代文学教案：第二章《水浒传》（之一）}}]</ref> In 1642, the Ming government ordered all its woodblocks and printed copies to be burned immediately.<ref name="transgression" /> Chen Chen, a Ming loyalist, saw the novel as an expression of Song resistance to the Mongol invaders in the Yuan dynasty.<ref name=JohnChristopherHamm />

Many [[Late Ming peasant rebellions|late Ming peasant rebel]] leaders were taking the names or nicknames of ''Water Margin'' heroes for themselves, and some [[Northern and southern China|northern]] brigand bands even organized themselves into thirty-six or seventy-two smaller troops after the numbers of major and minor ''Water Margin'' heroes.<ref>{{cite book |last = Hegel |first = Robert E. |author-link = Robert E. Hegel |year = 1981 |title = The Novel in Seventeenth-Century China |publisher = Columbia University Press| location = New York |isbn = 978-0231049283|page = 77}}</ref> Historian James Bunyan Parsons argues that ''Water Margin'' may have had some influence on [[Zhang Xianzhong]]'s rebellion. Based on Parsons' hypothesis, Mark R. E. Meulenbeld points out that  Zhang Xianzhong was recorded using the novels as a source for emulation, as he quoted an early Qing observer who ascribes Zhang's fondness with the novel, "The shrewdness of Zhang Xianzhong included him making people read books like ''Three Kingdoms'' and ''Water Margin'' every day..."<ref name=ZhangXianzhongWateeMargin>{{cite book 
|title= Demonic Warfare; Daoism, Territorial Networks, and the History of a Ming Novel
|date= 31 January 2015
|publisher= University of Hawaii Press
|author= Mark R. E. Meulenbeld
|pages= 191–192
|isbn= 978-0-8248-3845-4
|url= https://books.google.com/books?id=jB_HDwAAQBAJ
}}</ref> It was attested by citation from [[Perry Link]], that during the end of Ming dynasty period, rebels in [[Hebei]] used slogans such as "killing the rich to help the poor" and "carrying out the [[Dao (Chinese sword)|Dao]] on behalf of Heaven", which were popularized by both ''Water Margin'' and ''Romance of the Three Kingdoms'' as a form of "remedial protest".<ref name=WakemanWaterMargin />

The [[Jurchen people|Jurchen]] chief and Khan [[Nurhaci]] learned Chinese military and political strategies from ''[[Romance of the Three Kingdoms]]'' and ''Water Margin''.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Swope |first1=Kenneth M. |title=The Military Collapse of China's Ming Dynasty, 1618-44 |date=2014 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-1-134-46209-4 |page=16 |edition=illustrated |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=WRaoAgAAQBAJ&q=three+kingdoms+nurhaci+romance&pg=PA16}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last1=Mair |first1=Victor H. |last2=Chen |first2=Sanping |last3=Wood |first3=Frances |title=Chinese Lives: The People Who Made a Civilization |date=2013 |publisher=Thames & Hudson |isbn=978-0-500-77147-1 |edition=illustrated |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=agI7CwAAQBAJ&q=three+kingdoms+nurhaci+romance&pg=PT159}}</ref>

[[Yeongjo of Joseon|King Yeongjo]] of [[Joseon]], the first Joseon monarch to leave explicit records of reading ''Water Margin'', frequently cited the novel's plotlines and characters in court discussions between him and his ministers, and it exerted a tangible influence on the handling of Korean state affairs.<ref>{{cite journal|issn=1001-4667|journal=Journal of Nankai University (Philosophy, Literature and Social)|author=Sun Yongjin|trans-title=Fiction and Royal Power: A Historical Study of King Yeongjo's Reception of Water Margin|title=小说与王权：朝鲜英祖《水浒传》接受史考论|language=zh-hans|year=2026|issue=1|pages=112–124|location=Tianjin}}</ref>

Yu Wanchun instead gave his negative assessment as he saw its polemical tone and encouragement of brigandage and revolt as a potential threat to the state.<ref name=JohnChristopherHamm>{{Cite book |author= John Christopher Hamm |title=Paper Swordsmen Jin Yong and the Modern Chinese Martial Arts Novel |publisher=University of Hawaiʻi Press |year=2005 |isbn=978-0-8248-2763-2 |page=18 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=t1TOCXMakJEC |access-date=2025-09-24}}</ref> Late Ming dynasty scholar [[Jin Shengtan]] criticized Shi Nai'an as not motivated by traditional scholarly venting resentment through writing but as a way of leisure.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Yang |first=Chunshi |title=Introduction to Chinese Aesthetics |translator-last=Chen |translator-first=Haiming |translator2-last=Zhong |translator2-first=Xia |publisher=World Scientific |year=2025 |isbn=978-981-98-1529-6 |language=en |page=51 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=FOdyEQAAQBAJ |access-date=2025-09-24}}</ref> Jin also questioned the inconsistency of Song Jiang's characterization according to Confucian morality.{{sfnp|Gregory|2023|p=127}}

In the aftermath of Qing dynasty's [[Literary inquisition#Qing dynasty (1644–1912)|literary inquisition]] by [[Qianlong emperor]], the novel saw another boom of mass popularity and a wave of massive publications followed. This attracted the concern of a Qing official named [[Ding Richang]], who pointed out its polemical social effect, although he did not outright pursue banning the book.<ref>{{cite book |last=Ocko |first=Jonathan K. |title=Bureaucratic Reform in Provincial China: Ting Jih-ch'ang in Restoration Kiangsu, 1867–1870 |publisher=Brill |location=Leiden |year=2020 |pages=49–51 |isbn=978-1-68417-237-5 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=1gH8EAAAQBAJ |access-date=2025-10-31}}</ref> After the authorities issued numerous edicts against it because of its praise and support for rebels, in 1851 a group of Hunanese and Sichuanese [[Secret society|secret societies]] or, as the official documents call them, "religious bandits", was accused of owing many of their ideas to ''Water Margin'', with the result that yet another edict against the novel was promulgated.<ref>{{cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=7fxWKB9jijgC&pg=PA17|title=Chinese Theater: From Its Origins to the Present Day|date=1988 |editor=Colin Mackerras|isbn=9780824812201|publisher=University of Hawaii Press|pages=111-112}}</ref>

The ethics of outlaw loyalty permeated even the Post-1853 grand  [[Taiping Heavenly Kingdom]] shifted toward ''Water Margin''-inspired ethics, emphasizing blind loyalty to leaders and "yi"-style camaraderie. This suggests a tactical evolution from religious millenarianism to pragmatic, bandito-like solidarity, blending ancient monarchical fealty with subversive brotherhood.<ref name="Liu Kwang-chingWarerMargin" /> According to [[Frederic Wakeman]], the fraternal hierarchy which formed by Taiping leaders such as ''Heavenly King'' [[Hong Xiuquan]], ''East King'' [[Yang Xiuqing]], ''North King'' [[Wei Changhui]], and ''Wing King'' [[Shi Dakai]] was partly modelled on the brotherhood of the Liangshan outlaws from the novel.<ref>{{cite book |author1=Frederic Wakeman |author1-link=Frederic Wakeman |title=Fall of Imperial China |year=1977 |publisher=Free Press |isbn=978-0-02-933680-9 |page=149 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=ORBmFSFcJKoC}}</ref> {{lang|es|[[:es:Graciela de la Lama|Graciela de la Lama]]}} stated that the main concept of the politico-literary "model" which was borrowed by the Taipings was the concepts of "Loyalty and Fraternity" (忠義) which was followed by the Liangshan outlaws in the book.<ref>{{cite book |author1=Graciela de la Lama |title=China |volume=2 |year=1982 |publisher=El Colegio de México |page=239 |isbn=978-968-12-0103-6 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=EtZVAAAAYAAJ}}</ref>

[[Elizabeth J. Perry]]'s investigation with [[Anhui University]] scholars has concluded that the [[Nian Rebellion]]'s slogan banner, "Preparing the Way for Heaven, killing the rich to relieve the poor; Alliance Leader of the Great Chinese, Chang", which borrowed from the White Lotus sect, was inspired by the ''Water Margin'', emulating the outlaw heroes of Liangshan.<ref>{{cite book |author1=Elizabeth J. Perry |author1-link=Elizabeth J. Perry |title=Chinese Perspectives on the Nien Rebellion |year=1981 |publisher=M.E. Sharpe |isbn=978-0-87332-191-4 |page=63 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=SeBwAAAAMAAJ}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last=Perry |first=Elizabeth J. |title=Worshipers and Warriors: White Lotus Influence on the Nian Rebellion |journal=Modern China |volume=2 |issue=1 |pages=16–17
 |date=January 1976 |doi=10.1177/009770047600200102 |jstor=188811}}</ref>

The [[Baguadao]] sect used banners with the inscription "Entrusted by Heaven to Prepare the Way" during [[Eight Trigrams uprising of 1813]], a reference to the ''Water Margin'' novel.<ref name="Perk">{{cite book |last1=Perkins |first1=Dorothy |title=Encyclopedia of China: History and Culture |date=2013 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-1-135-93562-7 |page=141 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=KMQeAgAAQBAJ&q=eight+trigrams+rebellion&pg=PA141}}</ref>

Meanwhile, in the early-modern era, ''Water Margin'' has long and broad influence beyond its narrative as the inspiration for various subversive movements. The [[Triad (organized crime)]], enigmatic fraternal orders which were born in the Qing era's underbelly as a subversive force, blended messianic zeal (e.g., their slogan "Oppose the Qing and restore the Ming") with demonological rituals for political legitimacy. Their adoption of Water Margin's "yi" (unquestioning comradeship) rejects Confucian norms of duty and righteousness, positioning them as outlaw heroes. This unorthodoxy, combined with ritualistic elements, frames them as agents of political rebellion rather than mere criminals.<ref name="Liu Kwang-chingWarerMargin" />

Furthermore, Chinese revolutionary figure [[Song Jiaoren]] (1882–1913) idealizes the "heroes of the forest" (bandit archetypes from ''Water Margin'') as embodying Robin Hood-esque justice and chivalry. Despite critiquing their criminality and foreign alliances, he invokes ethnic Han solidarity ("fellow descendants of our Yellow Emperor") to humanize them, using the novel as a lens for nationalist empathy.<ref name="Liu Kwang-chingWarerMargin">{{Cite book 
|title=Heterodoxy in Late Imperial China
|date= 2004 
|publisher=University of Hawaiʻi Press 
|isbn=978-0-8248-2538-6 
|editor1=  Liu Kwang-ching
|editor1-link= Liu Kwang-ching
|editor2= Richard Hon-Chun Shek
|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=ihJ4exNdB2oC
|pages= 14, 16, 18, 326, 342, 451, 452
}}</ref> Novelist [[Zhang Henshui]] felt that ''Water Margin''{{'s}} emphasis on the patriotism as Liangshan outlaws join Song government troops against the Jin invaders, could inspire anti-Japanese feeling among the Chinese living in Shanghai.<ref name=恨水之夢>{{Cite book |author= Thomas Michael McClellan |script-title=zh:恨水之夢 : 改良舊體小說 |publisher=E. Mellen Press |date=15 May 2008 |isbn=978-0-7734-6087-4 |page=207 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=pDpkAAAAMAAJ |access-date=2025-09-24}}</ref>

[[File:三打祝家庄 苏州 场维顺.jpg|thumb|upright=0.85|''Three Attacks on Zhu Village'' ({{zhi|c=三打祝家庄}}), woodblock print, [[Jiaqing Emperor|Jiaqing]] Period (1796–1820)]]
Secret societies and criminal organizations during the [[History of the Republic of China|Republic era]] also adopted code like ''Water Margin''{{'s}} martial fraternity,  such as the [[Green Gang]] From [[Shanghai]]<ref name=greengangWaterMargin1>{{Cite journal 
|author= Ming Xia
|title= Organizational Formations of Organized Crime in China: perspectives from the state, markets, and networks
|publisher=Taylor & Francis 
|year=2008 
|volume=17
|journal= Journal of Contemporary China 
|issue= 54 |pages= 1–23
|doi= 10.1080/10670560701693039

 }}</ref><ref name=greengangWaterMargin2>{{Cite journal 
|author1= Jerome Ch'en 
|title= Secret Societies
|publisher=Johns Hopkins University Press 
|year=1966 
|journal= Ch'ing-shih Wen / Late Imperial China
|volume=1
|issue= 3 |url=https://muse.jhu.edu/pub/1/article/404446/summary
 }}</ref><ref>{{cite book |author1=Philip Ball |author1-link=Philip Ball |title=The Water Kingdom; A Secret History of China |date=2017 |publisher=University of Chicago Press |isbn=978-0-226-36920-4 |page=129 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=nZUtDwAAQBAJ}}</ref> and the [[Blue Shirts Society]], an unofficial secret police of the [[Chiang Kai-shek]] regime. One of the Blue Shirts founding members, [[Dai Li]], developed the organization based on the value of heroism and outlaw martial artists of the ''Water Margin'', where the recruits drawn from the lower strata of society: jugglers, wrestlers, itinerant entertainers, journeymen traders, jailers, executioners, thieves, and gangsters.<ref name=blueahirtWaterMargin2>{{Cite web 
|author1= Frederic Wakeman Jr.
|title= Chiang's Monster; Spymaster: Dai Li and the Chinese Secret Service
|publisher=University of California Press; The New York Review of Books
|date= 25 March 2004
|page=650
|website= ChinaFile |url=https://www.chinafile.com/library/nyrb-china-archive/chiangs-monster}}</ref> [[May Fourth Movement|May Fourth]] iconoclasts such as [[Mao Dun]] saw fit to transmit the novel's spirit without a trace of self-consciousness.<ref>{{cite journal|jstor=41490772|title=Kumarajiva's Foreign Tongue: Shi Zhecun's Modernist Historical Fiction|author=William Schaefer|year=1998|pages=25–70|issn=8755-8963|journal=Modern Chinese Literature|volume=10|issue=1/2}}</ref>
{{quote box|width=25em
|quote=There are many examples of [[Dialectical materialism|materialist dialectics]] in ''Water Margin'', of which the episode of the three attacks on [[Zhu Family Village|Zhu Village]] is one of the best.
|author=— [[Mao Zedong]], ''[[On Contradiction]]'', 1937<ref>{{cite book|title=Mao Zedong's "On Contradiction" Study Companion|isbn=978-2-491182-10-6|page=34|publisher=[[Foreign Languages Press]]|year=2019|author=Redspark Collective|url=https://foreignlanguages.press/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/N04-On-Contradiction-5th-Printing.pdf}}</ref>}}

''Water Margin'' also found its legs in the history of [[Chinese Communist Party]], where the novel enjoyed the party's endorsement since the 1930s for their political aim.<ref name="CJLim" /> [[Marxist literary criticism|Communist critics]] have invariably praised ''Water Margin'' as a great revolutionary novel, which "exposes the ugliness of [[Fengjian|feudal]] [[Bureaucracy|bureaucratic systems]], portrays the heroes' actions and minds, celebrates their rebellious spirits, and reflects the [[class struggle]] between the oppressed masses and the ruling class", and they conceive of the Liangshan band as the vanguard of a [[Class consciousness|class-conscious]] peasant force striving for enlightened political and economic revolution.{{sfnb|Hsia|2016|p=99}}<ref>{{cite thesis|title=Illustrating a New Nation: Shanghai Lianhuanhua in the Early Maoist Period|last=Lin|first=Chihho|degree=PhD|year=2021|publisher=[[UC San Diego]]|url=https://escholarship.org/content/qt8p28x5d8/qt8p28x5d8.pdf}}</ref> [[Liu Kwang-ching]] noted that ''Water Margin'' was one of [[Mao Zedong]]'s favorite readings.<ref name="Liu Kwang-chingWarerMargin" /> Mao chose to regard Song Jiang as a prototypic peasant leader and identified his rebellion as the uprising of the peasant classes of old China, and [[Maoism|Maoist]] authors regularly allude to such "declassed rebels" as "models" for the "people", claiming the revolutionary bourgeois and [[Petite bourgeoisie|petit-bourgeois]] of the novel constitute models "of the true hero in the hearts of the people".<ref>{{cite journal|jstor=1407255|author1=A. James Gregor|volume=40|issue=3|year=1978|title=Maoism and Marxism in Comparative Perspective|pages=307-327|author2=Maria Hsia Chang|journal=The Review of Politics|issn=00346705}}</ref>

During the [[Cultural Revolution]], Mao presented his ''Water Margin'' commentary on August 14, 1975, in response to a request from a teacher of Chinese literature at [[Peking University]], Lu Di, where Mao mentioned the novel as a political text "for learning by negative example, letting the people know the capitulationists". Within hours, the radical [[Gang of Four]] launched the Criticize ''Water Margin'' Campaign, which was prompted in part by that group's opposition to the rehabilitation of a number of prominent political
figures under the auspices of [[Zhou Enlai]]. The current Chinese official view, generally shared by Western observers, is that the gang deliberately "exploited" a few offhand comments by Mao. A flood of articles in the most authoritative Chinese publications denounced the book because Song Jiang - the leader of the peasant rebels - ultimately surrendered to the Emperor. Song is condemned as a renegade and the book is attacked on the ground that it glorifies him and his exploits, thus espousing "capitulationism". The chief targets of the campaign, [[Deng Xiaoping]] and Zhou Enlai, are thought to have corresponded to the arch capitulationist Song Jiang in the language of the campaign. However, the allusion campaign of the Gang of Four backfired, ending with Deng Xiaoping emerging victorious from the political struggle.<ref>Attributed to multiple references:

|title=Mao's Last Revolution
|date= 18 August 2006
|publisher= Harvard University Press
|isbn=  978-0-674-02332-1
|author1=  Roderick MacFarquhar
|author1-link= Roderick MacFarquhar
|author2= Michael Schoenhals
|author2-link= Michael Schoenhals
|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=ihJ4exNdB2oC
|pages= 401–407
}}
*{{cite journal|author=John Fitzgerald|title=Continuity within Discontinuity: The Case of Water Margin Mythology|year=1986|volume=11|issue=3|pages=361–400|journal=Modern China|issn=0097-7004}}
*{{cite news|work=[[The New York Times]]|author=Prank Ching|title=China Denounces Literary Classic|date=September 7, 1975|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1975/09/07/archives/china-denounces-literary-classic-historical-novel-that-mao-often.html|page=17}}</ref>

Another reason for Mao's criticism of the ''Water Margin'' was a move to curtail the possibility of armed coup by [[Lin Biao]]'s faction. As Mao said, "The rebels in ''Water Margin'' fought against dishonest officials but did not oppose the emperor. Later they capitulated. Take note, revisionism may emerge in China."<ref>{{cite book |author1=Li Gucheng |title=A glossary of political terms of the People's Republic of China |year=1995 |publisher=Chinese University Press |isbn=978-0-520-06459-1 |pages=417–418 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=J5QbQpQTegwC}}</ref>

=== Social ===
[[File:Porcelaine chinoise Guimet 281107.jpg|thumb|upright=0.85|Song Qing, Li Jun, and Ruan Xiao'er depicted in a Qing dynasty Kangxi period plate painting]]

A major social themes in ''Water Margin'' is {{zhp|p=yi|c=義|l=righteousness}},<ref name="Liu Kwang-chingWarerMargin" /> or "gallant fraternity", a moral code which [[Andrew H. Plaks]] translated as "good," "valor," "honor," "generosity," or "nobility".<ref>{{cite book | title=Three Yuan Plays by Yang Zi; In English Translation with Full Annotations
|isbn= 978-1-7936-5342-0
|date= 27 February 2023
|author= Hongchu Fu
| publisher= Lexington Books
|url= https://books.google.com/books?id=WZqvEAAAQBAJ
|page=79 }}</ref> Li Wenzhi concluded in his book, ''Popular revolts of the late Ming'',  that the concept of ''yi'' which was supposed to be a regulatory code for the   bandit chieftains, rebel and secret society leaders swore brotherhood together.<ref name=WakemanWaterMargin>{{cite journal |author=Frederic E. Wakeman jr. |author-link=Frederic Wakeman
|title=Rebellion and Revolution: The Study of Popular Movements in Chinese History |journal=The Journal of Asian Studies |volume=36 |issue=2 |pages=201–237 |date=February 1977 |doi=10.2307/2053720 |jstor=2053720}}</ref> This means the [[Youxia]] (Chinese knight-errant) motif in the novel expected one to focus on male bonding and unmoved by romance or sex.<ref>{{cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=D3vnDwAAQBAJ
 |title=The Chinese Political Novel; Migration of a World Genre 
|author=Catherine Vance Yeh
|date=11 May 2020
|isbn= 978-1-68417-555-0
|publisher= Brill
|pages= 123, 133, 139–140, 197, 241–242, 244–245
}}</ref> Its more complete form is {{zhp|p=zhong yi|c=忠義}}. Most of the existing editions of ''Water Margin'' in the Ming dynasty put "Zhongyi" in an obvious position, and {{zhp|p=zhong|c=忠|l=loyalty toward one's superiors}} requires one-dimensional "minister" obedience to "monarch", which is repeated many times in the text.<ref name="sunlin" /><ref name="mutual">{{Cite book |last=Vitiello |first=Giovanni |url=https://www.google.com/books/edition/The_Libertine_s_Friend/a0kGm8dGjBcC?hl=en |title=The Libertine's Friend: Homosexuality and Masculinity in Late Imperial China |publisher=[[University of Chicago Press]] |year=2011 |isbn=978-0-226-85792-3 |location=Chicago |pages= |language=en |oclc=880976492|page=68}}</ref> The critic Huang Moxi (1866–1913) contends that exerting oneself to the utmost for [[social good]] is called ''zhong'' (loyalty), putting this virtue into practice is called ''yi'' (righteousness), and loyalty to Heaven denotes a firm commitment to [[social justice]] and to people's well-being.<ref>{{cite book|pages=287-288|chapter=Use in Uselessness: How Western Aesthetics Made Chinese Literature More Political|author=Ban Wang|editor=Zhang Yingjin|title=A Companion to Modern Chinese Literature|publisher=John Wiley & Sons|year=2016|isbn=978-1-118-45162-5}}</ref>

Another theme is {{zhp|p=hǎo hàn|c=好漢|l=tough guy}},<ref name=AltenburgerWaterMargin />{{sfn|Ge|2001|p=160}} an [[antinomianism]] masculinity moral code. The ''hǎo hàn'' code values freedom and brotherhood above everything else, though it means one should sacrifice his own wife and children.<ref name="aftife" /> The indispensable personality traits of a ''haohan'' include a man's dedication to the code of brotherhood, ability and interest in gymnastic arts, [[generosity]] to friends, and "drinking wine in big bowls and eating meat in big pieces" ({{lang|zh|大碗喝酒，大塊吃肉}}) to show [[manliness]].<ref>{{cite book|last=Song|first=Geng|title=The Fragile Scholar: Power and Masculinity in Chinese Culture|publisher=[[Hong Kong University Press]]|year=2004|isbn=9789622096202|page=164}}</ref> This ideal of courageous manhood did not shy away from violence, and even gloried in it.<ref name="lizhisgpy">{{cite thesis|degree=PhD|title=The Making of "China" Through History: Li Zhi 李贄 (1527-1602) and the Shigang pingyao 史綱評要 (1613) in the Context of Late Ming Historiography|year=2023|hdl=10900/147833|last=Demuth|first=Sebastian|publisher=[[University of Tübingen]]|doi=10.15496/publikation-89174}}</ref> Portrayals of female ''hǎo hàn'' also existed in the novel, but they are often depicted as bloodthirsty as their male counterparts.<ref name="aftife">{{cite book | title=Asian Freedoms; The Idea of Freedom in East and Southeast Asia
|isbn= 978-0-521-63757-2
|date= 13 June 1998
|editor1= Anthony Reid
|editor1-link= Anthony Reid (academic)
|editor2= David Kelly
| publisher= Cambridge University Press
|url= https://books.google.com/books?id=nmgmgphLphQC
|page=98 }}</ref> As its non-[[elite]], and in some ways [[anti-elitist]], ''haohan'' infringes on the exclusive moral and political claims of the imperial order and [[scholar-official]]s from a Confucian perspective.<ref>{{cite book|isbn=978-0824834913|publisher=[[University of Hawaii Press]]|title=Gods, Ghosts, and Gangsters: Ritual Violence, Martial Arts, and Masculinity on the Margins of Chinese Society|author=Avron Boretz|page=48|year=2010}}</ref> In the words of Keith McMahon:
{{Blockquote
|text=
The ''haohan'' ideology is summed up by a number of key expressions which stress honor, duty, and comradeship. This comradeship is male-oriented, as indicated by the recurrent motto of "Within the [[Four Seas]], all men are brothers" ({{lang|zh|四海之內皆兄弟也}}). As for honor and duty, the general mission of the rebel band of ''haohan'' is to "enforce the True Way on behalf of Heaven" ({{lang|zh|替天行道}}) , that is, to enforce the higher good that bad rulers and officials disregard. In addition, there are ideals such as "upholding honor and belittling wealth" ({{lang|zh|仗義疏財}}) and "helping those on the wayside who have been wronged" ({{lang|zh|路見不平}}).<ref>{{cite book|page=52|last=McMahon|title=Causality and Containment in Seventeenth-Century Chinese Fiction|url=https://books.google.com.ni/books?id=RjaWNwaBa20C&printsec=copyright|first=Keith|year=1988|publisher=Brill|isbn=978-9004085459}}</ref>}}

[[File:Porcelaine chinoise Guimet 281106.jpg|thumb|upright=0.85|page=21|Song Jiang, Lin Chong, and Zhu Tong depicted in a Qing dynasty Kangxi period plate painting]]

[[Susan L. Mann]] writes that the "desire for male camaraderie" is "far from a mere plotline," for it is a basic theme of this and other classic novels. She places the novel's male characters in a tradition of men's culture of mutual trust and reciprocal obligation, such as figures known as the Chinese [[knight-errant]]. She finds such figures in this and other novels, such as ''Romance of the Three Kingdoms'' and ''[[Journey to the West]]'', all of which dramatized the "empathic emotional attraction between men who appreciate and play off against one another's complementary qualities."{{sfnb|Mann|2000|p= 1610}} [[Chen Pingyuan]] argues that ''Water Margin'' does not belong to the knight-errant tradition and classifies it under the category of dynastic heroes involved in preserving the state and its dominant ideology.<ref>{{cite book|year=2015|doi=10.2307/j.ctv47w7q9|title=The Chinese Political Novel: Migration of a World Genre|isbn=9780674504356|series=Harvard East Asian Monographs|volume=380|publisher=Harvard University Asia Center|last=Yeh|first=Catherine Vance|page=139}}</ref> Martin Weizong Huang stated that the problematic relations among the different aspects of the concept of ''yi'' (such as the private vs. the public) are explored in the novel in terms of subversion and parody, of which the most dramatized is the conflict between ''zhong'' and ''yi''.<ref>{{cite journal|pages=45–68|doi=10.2307/495223|jstor=495223|journal=Chinese Literature: Essays, Articles, Reviews|author=Martin Weizong Huang|title=Dehistoricization and Intertexualization: The Anxiety of Precedents in the Evolution of the Traditional Chinese Novel|volume=12|year=1990|issn=0161-9705}}</ref>

Licentious and treacherous women are another recurring theme. Modern critics have debated whether ''Water Margin'' is [[Misogyny|misogynistic]].<ref>{{cite book|script-title=zh:中国文学史新著|last=章培恒|date=2014|script-quote=zh:《水浒传》歌颂了男性英雄，却贬低了女性。在《水浒传》中没有真正意义上的对女性的描写，其中所写的女性大致可分两类，一类是孙二娘、扈三娘、顾大嫂这样的男性化了的女性，另一类是潘金莲、潘巧云、阎婆惜等"淫妇"。作者把潘金莲等女性写成天生的淫贱，既不顾及社会对妇女（例如潘金莲）的迫害以及由此引起的她们心理上的扭曲，又将对她们的迫害（例如石秀、杨雄的杀潘巧云）视作英雄的行为，这是其主要的历史局限。至其成因，则是我国封建社会长期流行着的对性爱的压抑和对女性的歧视。}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|script-title=zh:知堂回想录|last=周作人|date=1964|script-quote=zh:在这上面作者似乎无意中露出了一点马脚，即是他对女人憎恶的程度。}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.cuhk.edu.hk/rct/pdf/e_outputs/b01/v01p099.pdf|title=Renditions No.1|date=1973|quote= To be accurate, the world of The Water Margin does not hate the female sex as a whole. There are individual good women commended in the book; on the other hand, traits commonly held to be feminine shortcomings, such as pusillanimity, narrow-mindedness and naivete, have not been singled out for stricture. What is detested here is lascivious thought and behaviour. Women slain in the book have either committed adultery, or aided and abetted it. Slain too are the male offenders, e.g., Hsi-men Ch'ing and P'ei Ju-hai; when heroes like Li K'uei meet a pair of adulterous "dog and bitch", they put both to the sword without discrimination. This is actually fairer, and more respectful, to the fair sex than what often happens in the tales of Chaucer or Boccaccio and other medieval fabliaux, where the adulteress customarily gets away unscathed. However, owing to the distaste for carnality, women in the novel seldom combine beauty and virtue in their persons.}}</ref> Beautiful seductresses are frequently positioned as a danger to masculine heroes in the novel.<ref name="womanwarriors">{{cite web|publisher=[[University of Florida]]|author=Charles Sherwood|title=Woman Warriors of the Classic Chinese Novel Shuihu Zhuan|url=https://ufdcimages.uflib.ufl.edu/AA/00/07/71/82/00001/Sherwood_Charles_Thesis.pdf|access-date=May 21, 2026}}</ref> Especially notable is [[Pan Jinlian]], the sister-in-law of [[Wu Song]], who has later become an archetypal [[femme fatale]] and one of the most notorious villainesses of Chinese culture.<ref name="Yeh">{{cite book|last=Yeh|first=Wen-Hsin|title=Becoming Chinese: Passages to Modernity and Beyond|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Rn8GbgQpEeYC&pg=PA273|year=2000|publisher=University of California Press|isbn=978-0-520-22218-2|page=273}}</ref> Among women portrayed in a somewhat positive light, [[Gu Dasao]] and [[Sun Erniang]] are portrayed as extremely hideous and totally lacking in female charm, while the beautiful [[Hu Sanniang]] is married to a "short, ugly, and lustful" bandit.<ref>{{cite book|page=50|title=Images of Women in Chinese Literature. Volume 1|editor-last=Yu-ning|editor-first=Li|publisher=University of Indianapolis Press|year=1994|url=https://files.eric.ed.gov/fulltext/ED385489.pdf}}</ref> [[Sexual abstinence]] is seemingly required for membership in the brotherhood, as Song Jiang asserts that "in the gallant fraternity, anyone who 'wastes his marrow' (sex with women not for the purpose of reproduction) is a joke".<ref>{{cite journal|title=Masculinizing Jianghu Spaces in the Past and Present: Homosociality, Nationalism and Chineseness|journal=NAN NÜ|volume=21|issue=1|issn=1387-6805|pages=107–129|doi=10.1163/15685268-00211P04|publisher=[[Brill Publishers|Brill]]|year=2019|author=Geng Song}}</ref> The novel's theme tends to exclude the claims of family, especially those of women, and so it shows martial women (who fight for the interest of the group) prospering, and seductresses (who act for [[self-interest]]) meeting ghastly deaths.<ref>{{cite book |last=Wu |first=Yenna |title=The Chinese Virago: A Literary Theme |location=Cambridge, MA |publisher=Harvard University Press |year=1995 |page=106 |isbn=9780674125728 }}</ref>   

Critics offer various explanations for ''Water Margin''{{'s}} prejudice against women. Most common among modern Chinese critics is the [[Patriarchy|patriarchal society]] of the [[Imperial China]],<ref>{{cite journal|url=http://gb.oversea.cnki.net/KCMS/detail/detail.aspx?filename=CJZG200703024&dbcode=CJFD&dbname=cjfd2007|script-title=zh:另一种丑化——以扈三娘、孙二娘、顾大嫂为考察对象|last=解舒淇|journal=长江工程职业技术学院学报|date=2007|issue=3|pages=67–70}}</ref><ref>{{cite thesis|url=http://gb.oversea.cnki.net/KCMS/detail/detailall.aspx?filename=1013259231.nh&dbcode=CMFD&dbname=CMFD2013|script-title=zh:《水浒传》女性观探究|last=潘星晔|date=2013|publisher=曲阜师范大学|archive-date=23 May 2021|access-date=23 May 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210523023402/http://gb.oversea.cnki.net/KCMS/detail/detailall.aspx?filename=1013259231.nh&dbcode=CMFD&dbname=CMFD2013}}</ref> while Phillip S. Y. Sun of [[The Chinese University of Hong Kong]] argues that the hostility against women in the novel stems from a basic attitude that frowns upon amorous passion, and since passion is not good, charming women are received with suspicion and generally regarded as inauspicious.<ref>{{cite journal|url=https://www.cuhk.edu.hk/rct/pdf/e_outputs/b01/v01p099.pdf|author=Phillip S. Y. Sun|title=The Seditious Art of The Water Margin--Misogynists or Desperadoes?|pages=99–106|journal=[[Renditions (magazine)|Renditions]]|year=1973|issue=1|issn=0377-3515|location=Hong Kong}} Originally published as {{cite journal|author=孫述宇|journal=Chung-kuo hmeh-jen (The Chinese Schohrs)|issue=5|date=1973|title=水滸傳的煽動藝術|language=zh-hant|pages=75–101+ap4-5|doi=10.30187/CS.197307_(5).0006|publisher=New Asia College|location=Hong Kong}}</ref> On the other hand, some have noted that ''Water Margin'' actually made great progress in understanding women's emotions compared to Song and Yuan ''[[huaben]]'' fictional books.<ref>{{cite journal|doi=10.16393/j.cnki.37-1436/z.2024.03.010|title=男权视域下市井女性形象演变——从宋元话本到《水浒传》|trans-title=The Evolution of the Image of Ordinary Females in Cities from the Perspective of Patriarchy——From Song and Yuan Dynasty Scripts to The Water Margin|journal=Journal of Heze University|issn=1673-2103|pages=99–102|language=zh-hans|year=2024|volume=46|issue=3|author=Li Li}}</ref> According to Yenna Wu, ''Water Margin'' emerges as the first major Chinese novel that consciously uses extensive dream episodes as a literary and aesthetic device, and these dreams subvert the misogynistic tendencies in the narrative not only through their symbolic [[Femininity|feminine aspects]] but also through positive feminine figures.<ref name="feminine">{{cite journal|title=Outlaws' Dreams of Power and Position in Shuihu zhuan|journal=Chinese Literature: Essays, Articles, Reviews|year=1996|volume=18|pages=45–67|author=Yenna Wu|doi=10.2307/495625|issn=0161-9705}}</ref>

The novel is notable for its numerous violent plots and bloody and gruesome descriptions, including revenge killings, cases of indiscriminate slaughter, and the frenzied bloodlust of some heroes such as [[Li Kui (Water Margin)|Li Kui]].<ref>{{cite journal|language=zh-hans|issn=1674-0092|journal=Journal of Ankang University|doi=10.16858/j.issn.1674-0092.2025.06.009|author1=Feng Kaixing|author2=Lei Yong|title=《水浒传》中血腥描写的形成与接受|trans-title=The Formation and Reception of Bloody Descriptions in the Novel Water Margin|volume=37|issue=6|pages=54–59|year=2025}}</ref> When celebrating a victory, as educator William Sin writes, some protagonists sometimes "share their enemies' flesh piece by piece, an action combining [[Human cannibalism|cannibalism]] with ''[[lingchi]]''", the slow slicing of somebody to death.{{sfn|Sin|2017|p=106}} This type of violent imagery in the novel is mentioned in a "causal tone", with human flesh being eaten not just "in acts of revenge", but also "as a way of living".{{sfn|Sin|2017|p=105}} Noting that the outlaws celebrated in the novel were nevertheless widely regarded as "heroes and heroines" over centuries, he states that one cannot divide "the meanings of [their] actions" from "the cultural background under which they [were] performed" and that it would be "hasty" to project concepts and values of today "onto the situation of a distant culture" where they may not have applied.{{sfn|Sin|2017|pp=97, 107}} 
[[File:开膛破腹英雄雪恨.jpg|thumb|upright=0.85|A woodblock print collected at the [[Shanghai History Museum]] depicts Lu Junyi [[Disembowelment|disemboweling]] his steward and adulterous wife]]
Literary critic [[C. T. Hsia]] noted that, with all its affirmation of heroic ideals, its actual endorsement of savagery and sadism makes ''Water Margin'' a document of disturbing significance for the cultural historian of China.{{sfnb|Hsia|2016|p=97}} He stated that when such episodes were first told in the market place, they were meant to be entertainment, that the [[Pingshu|storytellers]] probably could see little difference between deeds of individual heroism and collective acts of sadistic punishment, and that its celebration of sadism is largely unselfconscious.{{sfnb|Hsia|2016|p=89}}
 
[[Liu Zaifu]] decries the novel as cultural poison, arguing that ''Water Margin'', together with ''Romance of the Three Kingdoms'', has sown people's "moral downfall".<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Sin |first1=William |title=''The Water Margin'', Moral Criticism, and Cultural Confrontation |journal=Dao |date=March 2017 |volume=16 |issue=1 |pages=95–111|doi=10.1007/s11712-016-9536-4}}</ref> There is also a popular anecdotal quip in China which says, "The young should not read ''Water Margin'' while the old should not read ''Romance of the Three Kingdoms''", criticizing its violent and machismo effects on young male audiences.<ref name="CJLim">{{Cite book 
|title= Once Upon a China
|date= 15 April 2021
|isbn= 978-1-315-40252-9
|publisher= Taylor & Francis
|author1= C.J. Lim
|author1-link= C.J. Lim
|author2= Steve McCloy
|chapter=The Margin of Water
|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=le8eEAAAQBAJ
|pages= 222–226}}</ref> By the late 19th century, the reformer [[Liang Qichao]] criticized ''Water Margin'' along with another novel, ''[[Dream of the Red Chamber]]'' as "incitement to robbery and lust".<ref>Leo Ou-fan Lee, "Literary Trends I: The Quest for Modernity, 1895–1927," in John K. Fairbank, ed., ''Cambridge History of China'' Vol. 12 Republican China 1912–1949 Pt I (Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1983): 455.</ref> Liangyan Ge called it a novel "full of scenes of brutality and sadism, representing only one extremity of Chinese culture".{{sfn|Ge|2001|p=55}} [[Yu Xiangdou]] and [[Li Zhi (philosopher)|Li Zhuowu]] justified the violence of ''Water Margin'' on political and moral grounds in their prefaces to the novel: Yu justified the actions of the heroes as righteous rebellion against the corruption of the Song dynasty officials, while Li centered on the notion that the novel was written "to give vent to deep indignation" at the historical tragedy that befell the northern Song.{{sfnb|Plaks|1987|p=358}}{{sfnp|Gregory|2023|p=92}}<ref name="lizhisgpy" /> [[Ryūnosuke Akutagawa]] in 1922 wrote:
{{Blockquote
|text="''Shuihu''-esque" is a kind of Chinese philosophical insight. It says that the 108 ''haohan'' weren't the loyal men of valor that [[Kyokutei Bakin|Bakin]], for example, made them out to be. No, they were just a bunch of hoodlums from start to finish. But they didn't come together just because they delighted in evil. … Among the Liangshan group there was a mind-set that said mere questions of good and evil were there to be trampled underfoot. Even a career military man like [[Lin Chong]] or a compulsive gambler like [[Bai Sheng]] could be a brother as long as they adopted that mind-set. It's a kind of "supramoral" philosophy that's not limited just to the characters in the novel. It has always had a strong root in the Chinese mindset—at least when compared with us Japanese.<ref>Hedberg, W. (2020). Civilization and Its Discontents: Travel, Translation, and Armchair Ethnography. In ''The Japanese Discovery of Chinese Fiction: The Water Margin and the Making of a National Canon'' (pp. 145-177). New York: [[Columbia University Press]]. doi:10.7312/hedb19334-007</ref>}}

==Authorship==
[[File:Shuihu5.PNG|thumb|200px|Illustration of a game of [[cuju]] from ''Water Margin'', from a 15th-century woodcut edition.]]

While the book's authorship is traditionally attributed to Shi Nai'an, there is an extensive academic debate on what historical events the author had witnessed that inspired him to write the book, which forms a wider debate on when the book was written.<ref name="methodology"/> Ming dynasty sources place Shi as a [[Yuan dynasty|Yuan]] writer from [[Hangzhou#History|Qiantang]] (modern Hangzhou), but reveal little about him, and there is a considerable gap between the assumed dates of the author and the earliest records about him.<ref>{{cite book | author=Y. W. Ma|chapter=Shih Nai-an 施耐庵|pages=699–700|title = The Indiana Companion to Traditional Chinese Literature | editor-first = William H. | editor-last = Nienhauser | location = Bloomington | publisher = Indiana University Press | year = 1986 |isbn = 0-253-32983-3 }}</ref> The first external reference of this book, which dated to 1524 during a discussion among Ming dynasty officials, is a reliable evidence because it presents strong [[falsifiability]].<ref name="methodology"/> Other scholars put the date to the mid-14th century, sometime between the fall of the Mongol-ruled Yuan dynasty and the early Ming dynasty.<ref name="methodology">{{cite journal|script-title=zh:关于《水浒传》成书时间研究的方法论思考|last=温庆新|script-journal=zh:清华大学学报哲学社会科学版|trans-title=Thoughts on the historiography of the methodology of dating the Water Margin|date=2014|url=http://www.lunwenstudy.com/gudaiwx/45439.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211019172129/http://www.lunwenstudy.com/gudaiwx/45439.html|archive-date=2021-10-19}}</ref>

Since fiction was not at first a prestigious genre in the Chinese literary world, authorship of early novels was often not carefully attributed and may be unknowable. The authorship of ''Water Margin'' is still in some sense uncertain, and the text in any case derived from many sources and involved many editorial hands. Recent scholars think that the novel, or portions of it, may have been written or revised by [[Luo Guanzhong]] (the author of ''[[Romance of the Three Kingdoms]]'').<ref name="Wilt">{{Cite book|last=Idema|first=W. L.|title=A guide to Chinese literature|date=1997|publisher=Center for Chinese Studies, University of Michigan|others=Lloyd Haft|isbn=978-0-89264-123-9|location=Ann Arbor|page=203|oclc=39106374}}</ref> Most modern Chinese critics see the novel as either written by Shi Nai'an, or written collectively.<ref>{{cite thesis|degree=PhD|last=Ryder|first=Amanda Jane|title=Narrative art in the Ming Dynasty novel, with special reference to Shuihu Zhuan, Xiyou Ji and Jin Ping Mei|year=1989|publisher=[[University of Leeds]]|url=https://etheses.whiterose.ac.uk/id/eprint/26092/1/236187.pdf}}</ref>

===Shi Nai'an===

Many scholars believe that the first 70 chapters were indeed written by Shi Nai'an; however the authorship of the final 30 chapters is often questioned, with some speculating that it was instead written by Luo Guanzhong, who may have been a student of Shi.<ref name=Wilt/> In the bibliographic entry in ''Baichuan Shuzhi'' ({{lang|zh|百川書志}}) compiled by the [[Jiajing Emperor|Jiajing]]-period author [[Gao Ru]] (高儒) in 1540, "Shi Nai'an from Qiantang" is credited with the original version of the novel, and Luo Guanzhong is credited with the finished form.<ref>{{cite thesis|degree=PhD|last=West|first=Andrew Christopher|title=Quest for the Urtext: The Textual Archaeology of the Three Kingdoms|year=1993|publisher=[[Princeton University]]|author-link=Andrew West (linguist)}}</ref>

In the earlier Ming dynasty ''Water Margin'' editions preceding [[Jin Shengtan]]'s, the title pages usually state "compiled by Shi Nai'an, edited by Luo Guanzhong" (施耐庵集撰 羅貫中纂修), but never any terms that denote original composition.<ref name="jstbrill">{{cite book|doi=10.1163/9789004279421_007|chapter=Appropriating Genius: Jin Shengtan's Construction of Textual Authority and Authorship in His Commented Edition of Shuihu Zhuan (The Water Margin Saga)|author=Roland Altenburger|isbn=978-90-04-27942-1|title=Authorship in East Asian Literatures from the Beginnings to the Seventeenth Century|series=East Asian Comparative Literature and Culture|volume=4|editor1=Christian Schwermann|editor2=Raji C. Steineck|pages=163–194|publisher=[[Brill Publishers|Brill]]|year=2014}}</ref> With the exception of the reference in ''Baichuan Shuzhi'', Shi was as a rule mentioned only in a subsidiary capacity, until Jin Shengtan's inclusion of an alleged preface by Shi in his edition established the claim of Shi's sole authorship for the succeeding centuries.{{sfnb|Plaks|1987|p=294}} Among philologists nowadays there has hardly remained any doubt about Jin's actual authorship of this preface, and Jin's contemporary [[Zhou Lianggong]] (1612–1672), in a short account about ''Water Margin'', noted that:
{{Blockquote
|text=Recently, Jin Shengtan cut away everything after chapter seventy which he considered a sequel added by Luo [Guanzhong]. For this reason he slandered Luo in extreme terms, moreover, he faked a Shi [Nai'an] preface which he placed in the front, [thus putting forward the view that] this book accordingly was Shi's. I say: Where in the world would there be someone who makes such a book! And back then he even dared to reveal his true name! This leaves open quite a few questions. I don't know on what basis the authorship of [Shi] Nai'an could be established.<ref name="jstbrill" />}}

===Luo Guanzhong===
Some believe that ''Water Margin'' was written entirely by Luo Guanzhong. Wang Daokun ({{lang|zh|汪道昆}}), who lived during the reign of the [[Jiajing Emperor]] in the [[Ming dynasty]], first mentioned in ''Classification of Water Margin'' ({{lang|zh|水滸傳敘}}) that: "someone with the family name Luo, who was a native of [[Wu (region)|Wuyue]] (Yue (a reference to the southern China region covering [[Zhejiang]]), wrote the 100-chapter novel." Several scholars from the Ming and [[Qing dynasty|Qing]] dynasties, after Wang Daokun's time, also said that Luo was the author of ''Water Margin''. During the early [[Republic of China (1912–1949)|Republican era]], [[Lu Xun]] and [[Yu Pingbo]] suggested that the simplified edition of ''Water Margin'' was written by Luo, while the traditional version was written by Shi Nai'an.{{citation needed|date=October 2017}}

[[Hu Yinglin]] (1551-1602) denies Luo a role in the composition of ''Water Margin'', as he considers ''Romance of the Three Kingdoms'' to be vastly inferior to ''Water Margin'', and therefore suggests that ''Water Margin'' was written by Shi Nai'an and that ''Romance of the Three Kingdoms'' was a poor emulation of it by Shi Nai'an's disciple, Luo Guanzhong.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://babelstone.co.uk/SanguoYanyi/TextualHistory/Authorship.html|title=The Textual History of Sanguo Yanyi : Authorship|website=[[Babelstone]]|archive-date=December 6, 2025|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251206185011/https://babelstone.co.uk/SanguoYanyi/TextualHistory/Authorship.html}}</ref> 

Huikang Yesou ({{lang|zh|惠康野叟}}) in ''Shi Yu'' ({{lang|zh|識餘}}) disagree with Wang Daokun's view on the grounds that there were significant differences between ''Water Margin'' and ''Romance of the Three Kingdoms'', therefore these two novels could not have been written by the same person.

[[Hu Shih]] felt that the draft of ''Water Margin'' was done by Luo Guanzhong, and could have contained the chapters on the outlaws' campaigns against [[Tian Hu]], [[Wang Qing (Water Margin)|Wang Qing]] and [[Fang La]], but not invaders from the [[Liao dynasty]].<ref>Hu Shih. ''Research on Water Margin'' ({{lang|zh|水滸傳考證}}).</ref>

===Shi Hui===
[[File:Shuihu7.PNG|thumb|200px|Illustration from a 15th-century woodcut edition]]
Another candidate is Shi Hui ({{lang|zh|施惠}}), a ''[[Nanxi (Chinese opera)|nanxi]]'' (''southern opera'') playwright who lived between the late [[Yuan dynasty]] and early [[Ming dynasty]]. Xu Fuzuo ({{lang|zh|徐復祚}}) of the Ming dynasty mentioned in ''Sanjia Cunlao Weitan'' ({{lang|zh|三家村老委談}}) that Junmei ({{lang|zh|君美}}; Shi Hui's [[courtesy name]])'s intention in writing ''Water Margin'' was to entertain people, and not to convey any message. During the [[Qing dynasty]], Shi Hui and Shi Nai'an were linked, suggesting that they are actually the same person. An unnamed writer wrote in ''Chuanqi Huikao Biaomu'' ({{lang|zh|傳奇會考標目}}) that Shi Nai'an's given name was actually "Hui", courtesy name "Juncheng" (君承), and he was a native of [[Hangzhou]]. Sun Kaidi ({{lang|zh|孫楷第}}) also wrote in ''Bibliography of Chinese Popular Fiction'' that "Nai'an" was Shi Hui's pseudonym. Later studies revealed that ''Water Margin'' contained lines in the [[Wu Chinese|Jiangsu and Zhejiang variety of Chinese]], and that ''You Gui Ji'' ({{lang|zh|幽闺记}}), a work of Shi Hui, bore some resemblance to ''Water Margin'', hence the theory that ''Water Margin'' was authored by Shi Hui.{{citation needed|date=October 2017}}

===Guo Xun===
Some early scholars attributed the authorship to Guo Xun ({{lang|zh|郭勛}}), a politician who lived in the Ming dynasty. [[Shen Defu]] ({{lang|zh|沈德符}}), a late Ming dynasty scholar, mentioned in ''Wanli Yehuo Bian'' ({{lang|zh|萬曆野獲編}}) that Guo wrote ''Water Margin''. [[Shen Guoyuan]] ({{lang|zh|沈國元}}) added in ''Huangming Congxin Lu'' ({{lang|zh|皇明從信錄}}) that Guo mimicked the writing styles of ''Romance of the Three Kingdoms'' and ''Water Margin'' to write ''Guochao Yinglie Ji'' ({{lang|zh|國朝英烈記}}). Qian Xiyan ({{lang|zh|錢希言}}) also stated in ''Xi Gu'' ({{lang|zh|戲嘏}}) that Guo edited ''Water Margin'' before.  [[Hu Shih]] countered in his ''Research on Water Margin'' ({{lang|zh|水滸傳新考}}) that Guo Xun's name was used as a disguise for the real author of ''Water Margin''. Dai Bufan ({{lang|zh|戴不凡}}) had a differing view, as he suspected that Guo wrote ''Water Margin'', and then used "Shi Nai'an" to conceal his identity as the author of the novel.{{sfnb|Ge|2001|p= 104-106}}
