{{chart bottom}}

The textual history of the novel is extraordinarily complex for there are early editions of varying lengths, different parts, and variations. The scholar Scott Gregory comments that the text could be freely altered by later editors and publishers who also could add prefaces or commentaries.{{sfnb|Gregory|2023|p=Introduction}} Not until the early 20th-century were there studies which began to set these questions in order, and there is still disagreement.{{sfnb|Li|2001|p=626-627}} The earliest components of the ''Water Margin'' (in manuscript copies) were from the late 14th century. A printed copy dating from the [[Jiajing Emperor|Jiajing]] reign (1521–1567) titled ''Jingben Zhongyi Zhuan'' ({{lang|zh|京本忠義傳}}, 'Capital edition of The Tale of the Loyal and Righteous'), is preserved in the [[Shanghai Library]].<ref>{{lang|zh|李永祜;《京本忠義傳》的斷代斷性與版本研究; 水滸爭鳴(第十一輯); 2009年.}}</ref><ref>{{cite web | url = http://www.nlcpress.com/ProductView.aspx?Id=10564 | script-title=zh: 容与堂刊忠义水浒传(全六册) | website = nlcpress.com | quote=(一)藏于上海图书馆，乃明正德、嘉靖年间所刻 ... }}</ref> The majority of scholars working in this field posit that significant changes were made to the text in the various 16th-century editions.<ref>{{cite journal|title=Shui-hu Chuan and the Sixteenth-Century Novel Form: An Interpretive Reappraisal|year=1980|volume=2|issue=1|author=Andrew H. Plaks|journal=Chinese Literature: Essays, Articles, Reviews|pages=3–53|doi=10.2307/495478|issn=0161-9705}}</ref>
[[File:MET 2013 715 a d a 02.jpg|thumb|300px|Pages of an illustrated woodblock version of ''Water Margin'' by [[Hokusai]], 1805–1838, from the [[Metropolitan Museum of Art]]]]
[[File:The Water Margin- Wang Qing Crossing the River MET DP-18167-001.jpg|thumb|300px|Illustrations in a 1610 edition of the novel depicting Wang Qing crossing the river, from the Metropolitan Museum of Art]]
[[File:NLC892-GBZX0301010873-252121 第五才子書水滸傳 七十五卷，七十囘 第6冊.pdf|thumb|300px|page=32|Pages from volume six of the novel in an edition collected by the [[Tianjin Library]]]]
The earliest extant complete printed edition of ''Water Margin'' is a 100-chapter version published in 1589.<ref>{{Cite book|last=Wilkinson|first=Endymion Porter|title=Chinese history: a new manual|date=2013|publisher=Harvard University Asia Center|others=Harvard University. Asia Center|isbn=978-0-674-06715-8|edition=2nd rev.|location=Cambridge, MA|page=413|oclc=792887523}}</ref> Its preface, attributed to Tiandu Foreign Minister, praises the novel as a "national medicine".<ref name="sunlin" /> He also claims that its text is a reconstruction of a Jiajing-era Guo Xun ({{lang|zh|[[:zh:郭勋|郭勋]]}}) edition, which was purportedly superior to other editions then circulating, and laments the poor quality of recent editions of the novel, the texts of which have been ruined by poor editing and the addition of spurious material by unnamed "village pedants".<ref>{{cite journal|title='The Wuding Editions': Printing, Power, and Vernacular Fiction in the Ming Dynasty|year=2017|volume=7|issue=1|journal=East Asian Publishing and Society|doi=10.1163/22106286-12341302|hdl=10150/625956|last=Gregory|first=Scott W.|page=1}}</ref> Recent researchers argue that the text of the Rongyu tang edition, thought to have been produced in the late [[Wanli era]] (1573–1620), could not be later than the Jiajing era, and is closest to the partially survived Jiajing edition, which now consists of chapters 47–55 only.<ref>{{cite book|page=269|isbn=9780231547581|title=The Spatiality of Emotion in Early Modern China: From Dreamscapes to Theatricality|date=May 2018|publisher=[[Columbia University Press]]|author=Ling Hon Lam|location=New York}}</ref>

Using the edition published by Guo Xun, the [[Chinese nobility|marquis]] of Wuding, [[Yu Xiangdou]] brought out a shorter version of the book in 1590 which included two new sections on the expeditions against the rebels Tian Hu and Wang Qing. These additions suffered drastic revision in subsequent, improved editions of the novel because they were "too inferior to occupy such a prominent place in the expanded version".<ref>{{Cite book |editor1=[[Luther Carrington Goodrich|L. Carrington Goodrich]]|author=Dell R. Hales |title=Dictionary of Ming Biography, 1368-1644 |editor2=[[Fang Chao-ying]] |publisher=Columbia University Press |year=1976 |isbn=0-231-03801-1 |location=New York|pages=1612-1614|chapter=YU Hsiang-tou}}</ref> The 120-chapter Yang Dingjian ({{lang|zh|楊定見}}) preface edition of the novel, published by Yuan Wuya ({{lang|zh|袁無涯}}), appeared in 1612 or slightly earlier under the title {{zhp|p=Shuihu quanzhuan|c=水滸全傳|l=The Complete Water Margin Saga}}.<ref>{{Cite book |author1 = Rolston, David L. |author2 = Shuen-fu Lin |name-list-style = amp |year = 1990 |title = How to Read the Chinese Novel |publisher = Princeton University Press |location = Princeton, NJ |isbn = 0691067538|pages=130, 356}}</ref><ref name="knightener" />

One of the most widely read [[Jin Shengtan#Major works|version]]s is a truncated recension published by Jin Shengtan in 1643, reprinted many times,{{sfnb|Li|2001|p=626-627}} which became a standard text for later editions and many translations.{{sfnb|Plaks|1987 |p=[https://archive.org/details/fourmasterworkso0000plak/page/292/mode/2up?q=292&view=theater 242]}} Jin provided three introductions that praised the novel as a work of genius and inserted commentaries into the text that explained how to read the novel. He cut matter that he thought irrelevant, reduced the number of chapters to 70 by turning chapter 1 into a prologue, and added an ending in which all 108 heroes are executed.{{sfnb|Li|2001|p=627}} There is general agreement that by casting aside the theme of the rebels' pacification, which dominates the dramatic action in the last fifty chapters, Jin revealed his own loyalist ideology and feudalistic moral sensibility.<ref>{{citation|first=Jing |last=Wang|publisher=Duke University Press |year=1992|isbn=0-8223-1195-X
|title=The story of stone: intertextuality, ancient Chinese stone lore, and the stone symbolism in Dream of the red chamber, Water margin, and The journey to the west
|url= https://books.google.com/books?id=49brOdOKlD0C | page=264}}</ref> A variety of ''Water Margin'' editions were made available for the "Criticize ''Water Margin'' Campaign" in 1975, including the Ming dynasty Rongyu tang edition republished by the [[People's Literature Publishing House]]. Since then, the 100- and 120-chapter versions have replaced the Jin edition as the most widely circulated editions for mass consumption.<ref>{{cite journal|last=Hegel|first=Robert E.|title=Traditional Chinese Fiction--The State of the Field|journal=The Journal of Asian Studies|volume=53|issue=2|year=1994|pages=394–426|doi=10.2307/2059840|jstor=2059840}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|date=April 9, 2018|language=zh-hans|url=https://m.voc.com.cn/xhn/news/201804/14491628.html|title=开启样书库，历数十几种人文版"四大名著"经典版本|work=[[Hunan Daily]]}}</ref>

There are two recensions of ''Water Margin'': the "full recension" and the "simpler recension".<ref>{{cite thesis|degree=MSc|title=Kyokutei Bakin's Eight Dogs and Chinese Vernacular Novels|author=Shan Ren|year=2019|doi=10.7939/r3-h2bw-cc78|publisher=[[University of Alberta]]}}</ref> The latter editions, edited for less sophisticated audiences, can contain all the events but in less detail. There is no way of knowing whether a simpler edition came before or was derived from another by adding or cutting text.{{sfnb|Li|2001|p=627}}

===Simpler recension===
The simpler-recension editions (簡本, ''jianben'' or ''chien-pen'') include stories on the outlaws being granted amnesty, followed by their campaigns against the [[Liao dynasty]], [[Tian Hu]], [[Wang Qing (Water Margin)|Wang Qing]] and [[Fang La]], all the way until [[Song Jiang]]'s death.

Known simpler recension of ''Water Margin'' include:

* A 115-chapter edition, ''Masterpieces of the Han and Song dynasties'' ({{lang|zh|漢宋奇書}})
* A 110-chapter edition, ''Register of Heroes'' ({{lang|zh|英雄譜}})
* A 164-chapter edition, combined with ''Sequel to Water Margin''
* A 109-chapter edition, ''2-Carved Heroes' Compendium''
* A 124-chapter version, ''Daodao Tang Edition''
* A 104-chapter edition, ''Water Margin Chronicles Commentary''

===Full recension===
The full-recension editions (繁本, ''fanben'' or ''fan-pen'') are more descriptive and circulated more widely than their simplified counterparts. The three main versions of the full recension are a 100-chapter, a 120-chapter and a 70-chapter edition. The most commonly modified parts of the full recension are the stories on what happened after the outlaws are granted amnesty.

* 100-chapter edition: Includes the outlaws' campaigns against the [[Liao dynasty]] and [[Fang La]] after they have been granted amnesty.
* 120-chapter edition: An extended version of the 100-chapter edition, includes the outlaws' campaigns against [[Tian Hu]] and [[Wang Qing (Water Margin)|Wang Qing]] (chapters 91 to 110).
* 71-chapter edition: Edited by Jin Shengtan in the late [[Ming dynasty]], this edition uses chapter 1 as a prologue and ends at chapter 71 of the original version, and does not include the stories about the outlaws being granted amnesty and their campaigns.

=== Non-English translations ===
''Water Margin'' has been translated into many languages, including German, Italian, Russian, [[Latin]], [[Mongolian language|Mongolian]], [[Uyghur language|Uyghur]], [[Kazakh language|Kazakh]], [[Lhasa Tibetan|Tibetan]], and Korean.<ref>{{cite thesis|degree=MSc|language=zh-hans|year=2023|publisher=[[Xinjiang Normal University]]|doi=10.27432/d.cnki.gxsfu.2023.000042|author=He Yanfei|title=目的论视角下《水浒传》中人物外貌描写的维译研究|trans-title=A Study on the Uyghur Translation of Characters' Appearance Description in Water Margin from the Perspective of Teleolog}}</ref> The book was translated into [[Manchu language|Manchu]] as {{MongolUnicode|}}[[Transliterations of Manchu|Möllendorff]]: Sui hū bithe.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Crossley|first1=Pamela Kyle|last2=Rawski|first2=Evelyn S.|date=June 1993|title=A Profile of The Manchu Language in Ch'ing History|journal=Harvard Journal of Asiatic Studies|volume=53|issue=1|page=63|doi=10.2307/2719468|jstor=2719468}}</ref> In 1753, the [[Qianlong Emperor]]'s imperial edict prohibited the translation of the novel into Manchu language for it and some other popular novels in Chinese that had been translated into Manchu "deteriorated the purity and nature of the [[Manchu people|Manchus]]". In the following year, at the suggestion of the [[Investigating censor]] Hu Ding ({{lang|zh|胡定}}, 1709-1789), the scope of the ban on the novel was further expanded to include all languages.<ref>{{cite thesis|degree=MSc|year=2024|last=Wang|first=Liguan|hdl=1903/33016|doi=10.13016/8a9d-awqm|title=The Formation and Evolution of Book Censorship in the Qing Dynasty: A Study of the Publishing Industry on Sibao|publisher=[[University of Maryland, College Park]]}}</ref> [[Jacques Dars]] translated the 70 chapter version into French in 1978, reprinted several times.<ref>''Au Bord De L'eau: Shui-Hu-Zhuan.'' (Paris: Gallimard, Bibliotheque De La Pleiade, 1983). 2 vols. {{ISBN|2-07-010910-0}} (v. 1) {{ISBN|2-07-010911-9}} (v. 2).</ref> The book was first translated into Thai in 1867, originally in [[Samud Thai]] (Thai paper book) format, consisting of 82 volumes in total. It was printed in western style in 1879 and distributed commercially by Dan Beach Bradley, an American Protestant missionary to Siam.

[[File:Shuihu.png|thumb|An illustration of the novel from an early Qing edition]]
Japanese translations date back to at least 1757, when the first volume of an early ''Suikoden'' (''Water Margin'' rendered in Japanese) was printed.<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=RJ4nUp-iOswC&pg=RA1-PA564|title=Early modern Japanese literature: an anthology, 1600-1900|date=2002|publisher=Columbia University Press|editor=Haruo Shirane|isbn=0-231-50743-7|location=New York|page=564|oclc=213305152}}</ref> In 1805, [[Kyokutei Bakin]] released a Japanese translation of the ''Water Margin'' illustrated by [[Hokusai]]. The book, called the ''New Illustrated Edition of the Suikoden'' (''Shinpen Suikogaden''), was a success during the [[Edo period]] and spurred a Japanese "Suikoden" craze.

In 1827, publisher [[Kagaya Kichibei]] commissioned [[Utagawa Kuniyoshi]] to produce a series of woodblock prints illustrating the 108 heroes in ''Water Margin''. The 1827–1830 series, called ''108 Heroes of the Water Margin'' or ''Tsuzoku Suikoden goketsu hyakuhachinin no hitori'', catapulted Kuniyoshi to fame. It also brought about a craze for multicoloured pictorial tattoos that covered the entire body from the neck to the mid-thigh.<ref name="tattoo">{{Cite book|last=Guth|first=Christine|title=Longfellow's tattoos: tourism, collecting, and Japan|date=2004|publisher=University of Washington Press|isbn=0-295-98402-3|location=Seattle|page=147|oclc=53477203}}</ref>

Following the great commercial success of the Kuniyoshi series, other [[ukiyo-e]] artists were commissioned to produce prints of the ''Water Margin'' heroes, which began to be shown as Japanese heroes rather than the original Chinese personages.

Among these later series was [[Tsukioka Yoshitoshi|Yoshitoshi]]'s 1866–1867 series of 50 designs in Chuban size, which are darker than Kuniyoshi's and feature strange ghosts and monsters.<ref>{{Cite book|last=Klompmakers|first=Inge|title=Of brigands and bravery: Kuniyoshi's heroes of the Suikoden|date=1998|publisher=Hotei Pub|others=国芳(1797-1861) 歌川|isbn=90-74822-08-8|location=Leiden|oclc=39162440}}</ref>
A recent Japanese translation is {{cite book|translator=Yoshikawa Kojiro |translator2=Shimizu Shigeru |script-title=ja:水滸伝 |title=Suikokuden|publisher=Iwanami Shoten|date=1998-10-16}}

===English translations===
In the late Qing Dynasty, missionaries and scholars in China such as [[Elijah Coleman Bridgman|E. C. Bridgman]], [[Alexander Wylie (missionary)|Alexander Wylie]], [[Samuel Wells Williams|S. W. William]], [[Herbert Giles]], [[Harry Parkes (diplomat)|Harry Parkes]] and others successively published introductions of characters or book reviews on the novel ''Water Margin''. In 1872–1873, the first partial English translation of ''Water Margin'' was serialized and published in ''[[The China Review]]''.<ref>{{cite journal|title=晚清时期《水浒传》在英语世界的译介与传播|trans-title=Translation, Introduction and Dissemination of Water Margin in English Speaking Countries in the Late Qing Dynasty|journal=Literature and Culture Studies|issn=1674-912X|language=zh-hans|doi=10.13896/j.cnki.wxywh.2026.02.012|location=Tianjin|author=Bian Haoyu|year=2026|issue=2|pages=126–135}}</ref>

====71-chapter version====

|author=— [[Pearl S. Buck|Pearl Buck]], [[1938 Nobel Prize in Literature]] lecture<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/literature/1938/buck/lecture/|title=Nobel Prize lecture |publisher=nobelprize.org }}</ref>}}

#[[Pearl S. Buck]] was the first English translator of the entire 71-chapter version. Titled ''All Men are Brothers'' and published in 1933.<ref>''All Men Are Brothers'' (New York: The John Day Co., 2 vols. 1933); reprinted: New York: Moyer Bell, 2010 {{ISBN|978-1-55921-303-5}}). The 71-chapter version, excluding the foreword by [[Shi Nai'an]].</ref>  It was revised in 1937 including the Introduction/Foreword attributed to Shi Naian. The book was well received by the American public,<ref>{{cite thesis|degree=PhD|last=Wang|first=Yunhong|title=A study of three English translations of Shuihu Zhuan|year=2016|publisher=[[Hong Kong Polytechnic University]]|url=https://theses.lib.polyu.edu.hk/handle/200/8729}}</ref> but also criticised for its errors,<ref>{{cite journal|title=Foreignization of Nicknames of Characters in All Men Are Brothers Translated by Pearl S. Buck|journal=BCP Social Sciences & Humanities|year=2022|pages=483–489|volume=19|author=Jiaxuan Lu|doi=10.54691/bcpssh.v19i.1733}}</ref> such as the mistranslation of [[Lu Zhishen]]'s nickname "Flowery Monk" as "Priest Hwa" and [[Sun Erniang]]'s "Female [[Yaksha]]" as "Night Ogre".<ref>{{cite web|url=https://ent.sina.cn/qt/2006-08-16/detail-iavxeafr9050960.d.html|title=稀罕与误读：四大名著在美国|language=zh-hans|work=[[List of newspapers in China#Jinan Daily|Jinan Daily]]|author1=Cheng Gang|author2=He Shenquan|date=August 16, 2006|via=[[Sina Corporation|Sina Entertainment]]}}</ref> [[Lu Xun]] argued that the title of the translation was unsuitable because "the idea of 'brothers' failed to accurately capture the precise meaning of the novel".<ref>{{cite thesis|degree=PhD|title=Pearl S. Buck as a bridge between the East and the West: a transpacific study of her non-fiction works|author=Linguo Ye|publisher=[[Complutense University of Madrid]]|year=2023|hdl=20.500.14352/101402}}</ref>
#In 1937, another complete translation appeared, titled ''Water Margin,'' by J. H. Jackson, edited by [[Fang Lo-Tien]].<ref>{{Cite book|author=Shi Nai'an|title=The water margin: outlaws of the marsh|date=2010|publisher=Tuttle Pub|translator=J. H. Jackson|others=Introduction by Edwin Lowe|isbn=978-0-8048-4095-8|edition=1st|location=North Clarendon, Vt|oclc=436027537}} The 70-chapter Jackson translation, which includes Shi Nai'an's foreword (1.5 pages) and prologue (nine pages), is estimated at about 365,000 words.</ref> A translation of Jin's Preface was published in 1935 by the Shanghai journal, ''The China Critic''.{{sfnb|Chin|1935}}

'''Unabridged'''
*The J. H. Jackson translation was revised, restored, and updated by Edwin H. Lowe in 2009 and published by Tuttle Classics.

====100-chapter version====
Later translations of the 71-chapter version include Chinese-naturalised scholar [[Sidney Shapiro]]'s ''Outlaws of the Marsh'' (1980) that also does not include the verse. However, as it was published during the [[Cultural Revolution]], this edition received little attention then.<ref>{{Cite book|title=Outlaws of the marsh|date=1981|publisher=Foreign Languages Press|author1=Shi Nai'an |author2= Luo Guanzhong |translator=Sidney Shapiro|isbn=0-253-12574-X|location=Beijing|oclc=6863157}}</ref> It is a translation of a combination of both the 71-chapter and 100-chapter versions.

====120-chapter version====
The most recent translation, titled ''The Marshes of Mount Liang'' (1994–2002), by Alex and John Dent-Young, is a five-volume translation of the 120-chapter version. It includes a prologue but omits the foreword by Shi Nai'an and some passages related to the official details of the Ming dynasty.<ref>Nai'an Shi, Guanzhong Luo, John Dent-Young and Alex Dent-Young. ''The Marshes of Mount Liang: A New Translation of the Shuihu Zhuan or Water Margin of Shi Naian and Luo Guanzhong.'' (Hong Kong: Chinese University Press, 5 Vols,1994–2002). Vol 1: {{ISBN|978-962-201-602-6}}, vol 2: {{ISBN|978-962-201-751-1}}, vol 3: {{ISBN|978-962-201-847-1}}, vol 4: {{ISBN|978-962-201-989-8}}, vol 5: {{ISBN|978-962-201-990-4}}.</ref>

====Differences====
These translations differ in the selection of texts and completeness. The Jackson and the revised Buck translations of 1937 contain the foreword attributed to [[Shi Nai'an]] as does the restored 2010 edition. The Shapiro translation incorporates the prologue into chapter 1 but omits the foreword and most of the poems. The Dent-Young translation omits the author's foreword and the passages concerning the Ming dynasty administration and the translators admitted to compromising some details and retaining inconsistencies in their ''Brief Note on the Translation''.

== Sequels and spinoffs ==
The number of published and circulated sequels to ''Water Margin'' that appeared from the Ming dynasty to the Republican period has reached sixteen, one of the highest numbers in the history of Chinese fiction.<ref>{{cite book|author=李忠昌|title=古代小说续书漫话|pages=3–5|language=zh-hans|year=1992|location=Shenyang|publisher=Liaoning Education Press|isbn=9787538216714}}</ref><ref>{{cite thesis|degree=MSc|language=zh-hans|author=唐海宏|title=《水浒传》续书研究|year=2009|publisher=[[Qinghai Normal University]]|url=https://kns.cnki.net/KCMS/detail/detail.aspx?dbcode=CMFD&dbname=CMFD2009&filename=2009161916.nh}}</ref> Some tell subsequent stories of the heroes fighting the [[Jurchen people|Jurchen]]-ruled [[Jin dynasty (1115–1234)|Jin dynasty]], infighting of the heroes, or moving to [[Siam]].<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.confucianism.com.cn/html/wenxue/1887695.html |script-title=zh:简述《水浒传》的成书过程与作者 |access-date=29 August 2010 |archive-date=11 March 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120311002210/http://www.confucianism.com.cn/html/wenxue/1887695.html |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref name=SourceSequelMargin0>{{cite web |script-title=zh:《水滸》縱橫談 |language=zh |url=http://chowkafat.net/Fiction1.htm }}</ref> There is also a so-called "sequel" attributed to [[Luo Guanzhong]], the 49-chapter ''Zheng Sikou'' ({{lang|zh|征四寇}} ''Campaigns Against the Four Bandit Groups''), which is actually the second half of the 115-chapter simpler-text version issued as a separate book.<ref>{{cite book | author1=Y. W. Ma|author2=Tai-Ioi Ma|chapter=Shui-hu chuan 水滸傳|pages=712-716|title = The Indiana Companion to Traditional Chinese Literature | editor-first = William H. | editor-last = Nienhauser | location = Bloomington | publisher = Indiana University Press | year = 1986 |isbn = 0-253-32983-3 }}</ref>

=== ''Jin Ping Mei'' ===
''[[Jin Ping Mei]]'' is an erotic novel of manners written under the [[pen-name]] Lanling Xiaoxiao Sheng ({{lang|zh|蘭陵笑笑生}}) ("The Scoffing Scholar of Lanling") in the latter half of the 16th century. The novel is framed as a [[spinoff (media)|spinoff]] of ''Water Margin'' based on the story of [[Wu Song]] avenging his brother in ''Water Margin'', but the focus is on [[Ximen Qing]]'s sexual relations with other women, including [[Pan Jinlian]]. The intervening sections, however, differ in almost every way from ''Water Margin''.<ref>Paul S. Ropp, "The Distinctive Art of Chinese Fiction," in Ropp, ed., ''The Heritage of China: Contemporary Perspectives on Chinese Civilization.'' (Berkeley; Oxford: University of California Press,  1990), pp. 324–325.</ref> In the course of the novel, Ximen has 19 sexual partners, including his six wives and mistresses, and a male servant.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Hinsch |first1=Bret |title=Passions of the Cut Sleeve: The Male Homosexual Tradition in China |date=1992 |publisher=University of California Press |isbn=978-0-520-07869-7 |page=135 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=2a0wDwAAQBAJ |language=en}}</ref>

Scholars generally consider the book as the first Chinese novel that was wholly the creation of one author and had no antecedent in the oral tradition.<ref>{{cite book |last1 = Schonebaum|first1= Andrew|first2 =Tina |last2 = Lu |year = 2012 |title = Approaches to Teaching the Story of the Stone (Dream of the Red Chamber) |publisher = Modern Language Association of America| location = New York |isbn = 978-1-60329-110-1|page = 63}}</ref> The influential author [[Lu Xun]], writing in the 1920s, called it "the most famous of the [[novels of manners]]" of the Ming dynasty, and reported the opinion of the Ming dynasty critic, [[Yuan Hongdao]], that it was "a classic second only to ''Water Margin''." He added that the novel is "in effect a condemnation of the whole ruling class."<ref>Lu Xun. ''A Brief History of Chinese Fiction'' (1923; Foreign Languages Press, 1959). Translated by G. Yang and Yang Xianyi. p. 232, 235.</ref>

=== ''Shuihu Houzhuan'' ===
[[File:《水滸後傳》書影.jpg|thumb|200px|An image of the novel ''Shuihu Houzhuan'' (''The Later Story of Water Margin''), published in the third year of the Kangxi reign of the Qing dynasty (1664)]]

A sequel to ''Water Margin'' titled ''Shuihu Houzhuan'' ({{lang|zh|[[:zh:水滸後傳|水滸後傳]]}}) (''The Later Story of Water Margin'') that authored by {{ill|Chen Chën|zh|陈忱}}, a writer from the early era [[Qing dynasty]] and native of [[Zhejiang]], was released In 1664.<ref name="司" />{{rp|155}}<ref name="魯">{{cite book|author=Lu Xun|script-title=zh:中國小說史略|trans-title=A Brief History of Chinese Fiction |url=http://www.bwsk.net/mj/l/luxun/zgxs/017.htm|publisher=上海古籍出版社|location=上海|year=1998|isbn=978-7-5325-8902-9|language=zh-hans|access-date=2021-08-27|archive-date=2021-08-27|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210827114838/http://www.bwsk.net/mj/l/luxun/zgxs/017.htm}}</ref>{{rp|102}}<ref name=SourceSequelMargin>{{cite web|script-title=zh:水滸後傳 |language=ja |url=https://zh.m.wikisource.org/w/index.php?title=%E6%B0%B4%E6%BB%B8%E5%BE%8C%E5%82%B3&uselang=ja}}</ref>

''Shuihu Houzhuan'' comprises 40 chapters, organized into two parts. Its plot diverges somewhat from the original ''Water Margin''. The first 30 chapters focus on the chaotic state of China, with the Liangshan heroes gradually assembling, reaching a total of 32 by the 29th chapter. The final 10 chapters depict the heroes' decision to journey to a foreign land, where they encounter a wise monarch and benevolent people, leading to a joyful conclusion.<ref name="司"/>{{rp|156}} ''Shuihu Houzhuan'' also introduces new characters such as [[Hua Rong]]'s son Hua Fengchun ({{lang|zh|花逢春}}), [[Xu Ning]]'s son Xu Sheng ({{lang|zh|徐晟}}) and [[Huyan Zhuo]]'s son Huyan Yu ({{lang|zh|呼延鈺}}).<ref name=SourceSequelMargin />

==== Plot ====
The story started with [[Ruan Xiaoqi]], falsely accused of treason by corrupt officials Tong Guan and Cai Jing after wearing Fang La's discarded dragon robe. Returning to Shijie Village, he kills Cai Jing's ally Zhang Ganban and flees, joining former Liangshan heroes like [[Hu Cheng]] and [[Luan Tingyu]] in banditry.<ref name="司"/>{{rp|155–156}}

Meanwhile, [[Li Jun (Water Margin)|Li Jun]] and seven others, disillusioned with China's chaos after the Northern Song's fall, sail to Siam (historical [[Thailand]]), conquer Jin'ao Island, and ally themselves with the royal family. Thirty-two surviving Liangshan heroes regroup in Shandong and Hebei and later join Li Jun in Siam during a siege.<ref name="司"/>{{rp|155–156}}
In the chapter 35, an army of 10,000 Japanese warriors embarked from [[Satsuma Domain]] and Ōsumi provinces aboard 300 warships to aid a usurper in Siam against the Liangshan heroes. The figure leading the Japanese army is called [[Sesshō&nbsp;and&nbsp;Kampaku|Kanpaku]]. The Kanpaku is depicted as eight shaku (approximately 2.4 meters) tall and riding an elephant. He also commands a naval warfare unit known as the 'Kurooni' (Black Ghosts). However, the entire army meets its end by freezing to death due to Gongsun Sheng's sorcery.<ref name=SourceSequelMargin /> The Liangshan heroes manages to defeat the usurper Gong Tao, and Li Jun becomes the king of Siam.<ref name="司"/>{{rp|155–156}}

Later, Li Jun rescues Southern Song Emperor [[Emperor Gaozong of Song|Gaozong]], who pardons the heroes and recognizes Li Jun's rule. Under Li Jun, Siam adopts Chinese influences, and the 32 heroes marry and settle happily.<ref name="司"/>{{rp|155–156}}

====English translation====
Chen Chen's sequel was translated as ''Water Margin Sequel'' by Valentin Saric and published in May 2026.<ref name="水滸後傳">{{cite book|author=Chen Chen |translator=Valentin Saric |title=Water Margin Sequel |location=[[Zagreb]] |publisher=Valentin Saric |year=2026|asin=B0H16QD2ST|language=en}}</ref>

==== Receptions and themes ====
The author, Chen Chen, was known for his resentment towards the rule of Qing and joined the Jingyin Poetry society, together with many loyal to Ming like [[Gu Yanwu]]. Later, he published the sequel in 1664.<ref name="司">{{cite book|author=Thomas Zimmer |trans-title= The Long Novel of Late Imperial China. Translated by Ge Fang et al. |script-title=zh:中國皇朝末期的長篇小說 |publisher=華東師範大學出版社|location=上海|year=2012|isbn=978-7-5617-6626-2|language=zh}}</ref>{{rp|155}} Chen Chen took the pen name "Yandang Shanqiao" and giving commentary for the published edition and claimed the original script was written by an anonymous "loyalist of Song" who lived during the early years of Yuan dynasty rule.<ref name="孫">{{cite book |editor1=Kang-i Sun Chang |editor1-link=Kang-i Sun Chang |editor2=Stephen Owen |editor2-link=Stephen Owen (sinologist) |title=The Cambridge History of Chinese Literature |volume=2 | publisher=三聯書店
|year=2013|isbn=978-7-108-04467-9|language=zh}}</ref>{{rp|242}}

According to [[Hu Shih]], the theme of this sequel work reflects Chen Chen's grief and anger about the fall of Ming dynasty, which he analogizes with the fall of Northern Song to the Yuan dynasty, which is the backdrop era of the ''Water Margin'' story.<ref name="胡">{{cite book|author=Hu Shih |author-link=Hu Shih |script-title=zh:胡適文存二集 |trans-title=&nbsp;"Two Prefaces to the Sequel to Water Margin." | pages=750–767|chapter=〈《水滸續集》兩種序〉|publisher=安徽教育出版社|location=[[Hefei]]|year=2003|isbn=7-5336-2217-0|language=zh-hans}}</ref>{{rp|755、759、760}}
The novel also continues to promote the themes of loyalty and resistance to foreign aggression through rebellion. However, the methods of these reformed Liangshan heroes in&nbsp;Siam&nbsp;are very different from that of&nbsp;the original group, as they resorted to less violence, held family happiness in high regard and showed awareness of the importance of civil government system; which followed by setting their end goal in establishing a state in Siam. In the end, the work expresses the hopes, fears and resentment of the Ming loyalists, and&nbsp;the anti-Qing&nbsp;movement.<ref name="孫"/>{{rp|242–243}}

Furthermore, the book's poems reveal the author's desire to establish a new utopia for Ming loyalists in a foreign land and may allude to&nbsp;their hopes for [[Zheng Chenggong]]'s regime&nbsp;in&nbsp;Taiwan.<ref name="趙">{{cite journal|author=Zhao Hong Jan |trans-title=Novel. Gender. History and Culture: An Interview with American Sinologist Professor Wei Ailian |script-title=zh:〈小說．性别．歷史文化——美國漢學家魏愛蓮教授訪談錄〉|url=http://www.zjujournals.com/soc/article/2018/1008-942X-48-2-194.html|journal=《浙江大學學報（人文社會科學版）》|year=2016|volume=48|issue=2 |pages=194–201|access-date=2021-08-18|language=zh-hans|archive-date=2020-07-28|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200728035612/http://zjujournals.com/soc/article/2018/1008-942X-48-2-194.html}}</ref>

Overall, Hu Shih does not rate this sequel work with high praise, with the exception of some of its chapters which stand out from others, such as "Zhongmu County's Elimination of Traitors" in volume 22. The book also described Yan Qing's visit to&nbsp;Emperor Huizong of Song&nbsp;, which was written in a sad and touching way, far surpassing the other chapters.<ref name="胡"/>{{rp|765、767}}
Sinologist Ellen Widmer believed that the literary value of the ''Shuihu Houzhuan'' was mixed and not enough to be included in the list of first-rate classics.<ref name="趙"/> The work directly influenced the 19th-century Japanese&nbsp;novel ''Chinsetsu Yumiharizuki'' (also known as ''Crescent Moon'' in English) by&nbsp;[[Takizawa Bakin]], who maintains that the ''Houzhuan'' makes sense of ''Water Margin'''s [[Ethical dilemma|moral disorder]], and proposes that readers think of the two novels as a single work.<ref name="趙"/>{{sfnb|Widmer|2004|pages=133–134}}

=== ''Dangkou Zhi'' ===
''Dangkou Zhi'' ({{lang|zh|蕩寇志}} ''The suppression of the bandits''), which also known for its alternate title ''Jie shuihu quanzhuan'' ({{lang|zh|結水滸全傳}} ''Terminating the Complete Saga of the Water Margin''),<ref name=AltenburgerWaterMargin /> is a novel written by Qing dynasty novelist {{ill|Yu Wanchun|zh|俞萬春}} ({{lang|zh|俞萬春}}) during the reign of the [[Daoguang Emperor]]. The story follows the end of original ''Water Margin'' runs im chapter 70. The book runs from Chapter 71 to Chapter 140, totaling 70 chapters, with a concluding chapter titled "The Conclusion to the Son".<ref name=SourceSequelMargin2 /> It took him 22 years to complete the book.<ref name=DangkouzhiTaiping>{{Cite book|author1=Takashi Matsumura |author2=Ken Komatsu|script-title=zh:[[図解雑学シリーズ|図解雑学]] 水滸伝|year=2005|publisher=ナツメ社|isbn=978-4-8163-3809-0|language=ja|pages=205, 208}}</ref>

Yu Wanchun disagreed that the Liangshan outlaws are loyal and righteous heroes, and was determined to portray them as ruthless mass murderers and destroyers, hence he wrote ''Dangkou Zhi''. As a result, he portrays the Liangshan outlaws here as the antagonists, only to be eliminated by the designated protagonists.<ref name=chenxizhen2 /> Yu and the ''Dangkou zhi'' commentators aim to shape ''Water Margin'' into a cautionary tale against rebellion by properly terminating the Liangshan "bandit resistance movement", with the effect of "rectifying" the meaning of ''zhongyi''.<ref>{{cite book|author=Henry Lem|title=Ming Qing Studies 2019|chapter=Fiction as Cautionary Tale: Rewriting "Rebellion" in Yu Wanchun's Dangkou zhi|year=2018|pages=57-85|editor=Paolo Santangelo|isbn=978-88-85629-71-4|publisher=WriteUp Books}}</ref>

The novel, which starts at the Grand Assembly of the 108 outlaws at Liangshan Marsh, tells of how the outlaws plundered and pillaged cities before they are eventually eliminated by government forces led by {{ill|Zhang Shuye|zh|張叔夜}} ({{lang|zh|張叔夜}}) and his lieutenants Chen Xizhen ({{lang|zh|陳希真}}) and Yun Tianbiao ({{lang|zh|雲天彪}}).<ref name=SourceSequelMargin2>{{Cite web |url=https://zh.m.wikisource.org/zh-hant/%E8%95%A9%E5%AF%87%E5%BF%97/%E5%BA%8F |script-title=zh:结水浒全传：前言 |access-date=2007-03-10 |trans-title="The Complete Water Margin" Preface
}}</ref> The protagonist of this novel is Chen Xizhen, a Taoist and martial arts master who turned outlaw, and ended opposing the Liangshan outlaws led by Song Jian.<ref name=chenxizhen2>{{Cite book |title=The Sword Or the Needle The Female Knight-errant (xia) in Traditional Chinese Narrative |author=Roland Altenburger |author-link=Roland Altenburger |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=jvihHb4qBTMC |year=2009 |isbn=978-3-0343-0036-0 |publisher=Peter Lang |pages=274–275 }}</ref>{{sfnb|Luo|2011|pp=884-885}} This reflects the contradictory and tangled psychology of Yu Wanchun, who was a fan of ''Water Margin'' and wanted to inherit Jin Shengtan 's ideas to attack the rebels.<ref name=chenCizhen>{{Cite book |script-title=zh:水浒书录|author=Ma Tiji|url=https://books.google.co.id/books?printsec=frontcover&vid=LCCN87177499&redir_esc=y |publisher=上海古籍出版社 |pages=146, 319, 325, 363 |language=zh}}</ref> As David Wang points out, contrary to ''Water Margin'', which advocates "bandit" loyalty as an alternative ideology to the imperial mandate, the novel advocates unconditional loyalty to the imperial court and seeks to mix Western [[epistemology]] with ancient Daoist beliefs, historical saga with [[supernatural]] fantasy.<ref>{{cite book |editor-first=David Dei-Wei |editor-last=Wang |title=A New Literary History of Modern China |date=2017 |publisher=[[Belknap Press]] |isbn=9780674978898|page=97}}</ref>

Due to its pro-establishment and anti-rebellion theme, this sequel was supported and endorsed by government of Qing. However, the [[Taiping Rebellion|Taiping rebels]] disliked the nuance of the novel and ordered the burning of the book in every place they occupied.<ref name=DangKouZhi>{{cite book
| last = Chuang
| first = Renjie
| script-title=zh: 晚清文人的風月陷溺與自覺
| trans-title = The Indulgence and Awareness of Late Qing Literati in Romantic Affairs
| url = https://books.google.com/books?id=IfQq9bcWc2UC
| publisher = Showwe Information Co., Ltd.
| year = 2010
| isbn = 978-986-221-431-2
| page = 61
| language = zh
| format = ebook
}}</ref><ref name=DangkouzhiTaiping /> ''Water Margin'' may also have inspired the novel ''[[Ernü Yingxiong Zhuan]]''.<ref name=AltenburgerWaterMargin>{{cite book |last=Altenburger |first=Roland |title=The Sword Or the Needle: The Female Knight-errant (xia) in Traditional Chinese Narrative |publisher=Peter Lang Publishing |year=2009 |isbn=978-3-0343-0036-0 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=jvihHb4qBTMC |access-date=2025-11-02 |pages=36, 273}} 
google.co.Idi</ref>

=== ''Can Shui Hu'' ===
A sequel novel which titled ''Can Shui Hu'', or ''Water Margin Finale'' ({{lang|zh|殘水滸}}), was written by {{ill|Cheng Shanzhi|zh|程善之}} (pen name of Cheng Qingyu, {{lang|zh|程慶餘}}; 1880–1942);<ref name=殘水>{{Cite web |url=https://zh.m.wikisource.org/wiki/%E6%AE%98%E6%B0%B4%E6%BB%B8 |script-title=zh:殘水滸|website=Wikisource|year=1933 }}</ref> a novelist associated with the Southern Society ({{lang|zh|南社}}) literary group. It was serialized in 1933 in the New Jiangsu Daily ({{lang|zh|《新江蘇日報》}}) under the pseudonym "Yi Su" ({{lang|zh|一粟}}), and reprinted by Heilongjiang People's Publishing House in 1997. The novel exists and is a well-documented sequel to the 70-chapter edition of Water Margin. It composed 16 chapters that followed the original simple ''Water Margin'' version of 70 chapters, spanning from chapter 71 to 86.{{citation needed|date=October 2025}}

The narrative picks up directly from [[Lu Junyi]]'s prophetic nightmare, followed by the split of the Liangshan brotherhood due to ideological rifts. the leaders divide into two camps over the issue whether they should surrender to the government and seek pardon, or keep being outlaws. Lu Junyi's faction (pro-surrender) seeks alliance with Northern Song border general named Zong Shidao ({{lang|zh|種師道}}). Song Jiang's faction, which composed of 36 core members, refused the integration aspiration by Lu Junyi, and clinging to their autonomy as outlaws. Some of the Liangshan heroes fell during the ensuing civil war, such as Li Kui's death by [[Hu Sanniang]] and [[Dong Ping]]'s poisoning by Cheng Wanli's Daughter. After Liangshan's defeat, Song Jiang's faction flees to Haizhou ({{lang|zh|海州}}), where they are captured by Zhang Shuye ({{lang|zh|張叔夜}}), the historical Song general who subdued Song Jiang in 1121 (per History of Song). 
Lu's faction, honoring old bonds, petitions the court to spare Song's life—sparing execution but dooming the remnants to further tragedy. The book culminates in total annihilation: Surrenders lead to executions or exile, battles claim the rest, and Song Jiang is ultimately also implied being killed.<ref name=殘水 />

With the exception of Zhang Shuye and Chen Xiuzhen (who also the protagonist of ''Dangkou Zhi''.), there are not many notable new characters in this novel. Yet, the personality of certain legacy characters are given more focus, such as Song Jiang 's cunning and Wu Yong's wisdom. Chen Xizhen and his daughter, Chen Liqing, were persecuted by the government, particularly by Gao Qiu and Gao Yanei. Both father and daughter were forced to fled the capital. However, Chen Xizhen also hated the Liangshan heroes and refused to join them. Later, Chen Xizhen occupied a village and gathered people to start an uprising, until he accepted the amnesty and surrendered to the government. He joined forces with Zhang Shuye and others in the suppression of Liangshan outlaws, until they manage to eliminate the group.<ref name=chenxizhen2 />

=== Other notable ''Water Margin'' sequels ===
''Hou Shuihuzhuan'' (後水滸傳; "A Sequel to The Water Margin") was written by pseudonymous writer Qinglian shi zhuren ({{lang|zh|青蓮室主人}}; "Master of the Blue Lotus Chamber") and published during the [[Qianlong Emperor|Qianlong era]] (1736–1795). The story revolves around the early Southern Song rebel Yang Yao ({{lang|zh|[[:zh:岳飛剿滅楊幺|楊幺]]}}; {{circa|1115}}–1135), who is described as the reincarnation of Song Jiang. He launched a peasant's revolt in the [[Dongting Lake]] to carry on and develop the career of Liangshan heroes.<ref>{{cite journal|doi=10.16393/j.cnki.37-1436/z.2006.03.016|issn=1673-2103|journal=Journal of Heze University|pages=76–80+119|trans-title=On the Heroine Images in the Novels of Shuihuhouzhuan,Houshuihuzhuan and Dangkouzhi|title=论《水浒后传》《后水浒传》《荡寇志》中的女英雄形象|language=zh-hans|author=Liu Xiangyu|year=2006|issue=3}}</ref><ref>{{cite thesis|degree=MSc|language=zh-hans|trans-title=The comparative study on Water Margin sequel After the Mass Water Margin and After the Water Margin|title=《水浒传》续书《水浒后传》与《后水浒传》比较研究|url=https://kns.cnki.net/kcms2/article/abstract?v=wGRGwcz8A0fAJn7L0rI3GXKwv_CqWshdvFHdZq8BwukRqsLCzgASWWZJOJM5pg-Y55uIG4evAoCOyjX04uQvcDuJqreKMJIas6iTkEy8S0jdCnQzcRWQCnXxbjU-YxYaD7eqA7xwMm0Fx76Lm0pTac19M8TdbkXuQncdTyy2qJaOKn6XKikv4deo1U5CP6pY&uniplatform=NZKPT&language=CHS|author=You Yedong|year=2010|publisher=[[Anhui University]]}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|language=zh-hans|pages=104–106+137|issn=1672-8572|journal=Journal of Eastern Liaoning University(Social Science Edition)|doi=10.14168/j.issn.1672-8572.2011.06.011|trans-title=Multiple Value of Hou Shuihuzhuan|title=Multiple Value of Hou Shuihuzhuan|author=Hou Zhongyi|year=2011|volume=13|issue=6}}</ref> Chapters 31 to 45 of the novel depict general [[Yue Fei]], portrayed as a ''divine general'', suppresses the rebels at Caibo Bridge. Defeated, the heroes ascend to heaven, enlightened by a [[karma|karmic]] epilogue emphasizing redemption through reincarnation.<ref name=SourceSequelMargin4>{{Cite web |url=https://zh.m.wikisource.org/zh-hant/%E5%BE%8C%E6%B0%B4%E6%BB%B8%E5%82%B3 |script-title=zh:後水滸傳 |access-date=2007-03-10 |trans-title=Water Margin Transmission}}</ref> Ellen Widmer wrote that the novel "evidently belongs to a lower cultural level" than even the ''Houzhuan'', but is more critical of the imperial system.<ref>{{cite journal|title=Review: [Untitled] Reviewed Work: The Margins of Utopia: Shui-hu hou-chuan and The Literature of Ming Loyalism by Ellen Widmer|author=Keith McMahon|volume=48|issue=2|year=1988|journal=Harvard Journal of Asiatic Studies|pages=545–550|doi=10.2307/2719323|jstor=2719323|issn=0073-0548}}</ref>

{{anchor|Xin Shuihu}}
[[Lu Shi'e]]'s humorous novel ''Xin Shuihu'' (''New Water Margin'', 1909) depicts the protagonists from the parent novel swiftly adjusting to the new world after hearing of "[[Late Qing reforms|political reform]]", leaving their stronghold and getting involved in various modern enterprises.{{sfnb|Huang|2004|page=34}}{{sfnb|Yang|2004|page=147}}<ref>{{cite journal|issn=1004-2253|language=zh-hans|journal=Zhejiang Social Sciences|doi=10.14167/j.zjss.2023.09.016|pages=143–149+161|trans-title=The Breaking of the Refurbished Novel Had Promoted the Modern Canonization of the Si Da Qi Shu|title="翻新小说"的破体与"四大奇书"的近代经典化|year=2023|issue=9|author1=Wen Qingxin|author2=Zhang Jingjing}}</ref>

The so-called 120-chapter ''Guben Shuihu zhuan'' ("Ancient Edition of Water Margin") first surfaced in 1933 with prefatory material by Mei Jihe (1891–1969) claiming that the manuscript on which it was based represented the entire novel as originally written by Shi Nai'an, with the first half being consistent with Jin Shengtan's version of and the second half continuing the story in accordance with the author's conception of Jin's attitude toward the rebels.<ref>{{cite book|page=39|title=Traditional Chinese Fiction and Fiction Commentary: Reading and Writing Between the Lines|isbn=9780804764957|author=David L. Rolston|date=April 1997|publisher=Stanford University Press}}</ref>

During the [[Second Sino-Japanese War]], [[Zhang Henshui]] serialized a patriotic ''Water Margin'' sequel, ''A New Tale of the Water Margin'' (''Shuihu Xin Zhuan'', 1940–1943), which follows the former bandits as they join Song government troops against the Jin invaders.<ref>{{cite thesis|degree=PhD|title=Zhang Henshui's fiction: attempts to reform the traditional Chinese novel|last=McClellan|first=Thomas M.|year=1992|hdl=1842/20003|publisher=[[The University of Edinburgh]]}}</ref>

==Influence and adaptations==
===Literature===
{{quote box||width=25em
|quote=These stories are told in articulate, vigorous language, its effectiveness well proven through a long process of oral tradition. … Only some of the Song-Yuan short stories can be compared with the ''Tale of the Marshes'' [''Water Margin''] in their skillful use of the colloquial, but the ''Marshes'' is the first sustained prose fiction that adopts the living language of the people as the medium of narration. It has set an example for all later novels and its influence is lasting and immense.
|author=— [[Wu-chi Liu]] on the literary influence of the novel<ref name="taleofmarshes" />}}
''Water Margin'' had a far-reaching impact on [[East Asia]]n narrative literature.<ref>{{cite thesis|degree=MSc|language=ko|title="수호전"의 조선어(한국어) 번역본에대한 번역학 연구|trans-title=A Study on the Korean Translation of "Water Margin" with Medio-Translatology Method|author=Li E|publisher=[[Yanbian University]]|year=2016|url=https://kns.cnki.net/kcms2/article/abstract?v=R4S5WDEiKcsXZeQoUM0ma3xSmuJIHSNtcoa_TpCh_hzsiUT3SPpqymOzV-d9YC6454WYqynYvEfHHcGMSus8orWobVIhFL-Nr8qN268o_eC0vgxWok_sIJwEGH9khlI8EZKJoT-SqyuJPNV1FK_9g34GHp-X4yBRbAyoOlupZSFIyxFyv977OJ2FkYfiXlBq&uniplatform=NZKPT&language=CHS}}</ref> It became an "inexhaustible" source of inspiration for the adaptation and recreation of works in various literary forms across the region for centuries.<ref>{{cite book|title=Concise Reader of Chinese Literature History|chapter=Novels in the Ming Dynasty|doi=10.1007/978-981-99-5814-6_33|author=Liu Qian|editor=Yuejin Liu|pages=413-428|publisher=China Social Sciences Press|isbn=978-981-99-5814-6|year=2024|translator=Min Xie}}</ref> Luo Yuming concludes that, because of its skillful use of the vernacular language, and the shifting towards a central focus on characterization in content, the novel "represented a record level in the progress" and "heralded the direction of the development" of fiction in China.{{sfnb|Luo|2011|p=651}} [[Herbert Giles]] stated that the modern Chinese novel followed a succession of great works including ''Water Margin''.<ref>{{cite book|author-first1=Herbert|author-last1= Giles|author-link=Herbert Giles|title=A History of Chinese Literature|publisher=Frederick Ungar Publishing|year=1967|orig-date=1st pub. London: W. Heinemann:1901|page=486}}</ref> Ellen Widmer calls ''Water Margin'' "noticeable for its rambunctiousness, its sense of structure, and its use of the spoken [[idiom]]", and each has played a role in the various texts it has influenced.  She mentions that the Korean novel ''[[Hong Gildong jeon]]'', which heavily draws from ''Water Margin'', is easily identified as a descendant of the novel.<ref>{{cite journal|title=Island Paradises : Travel and Utopia in Three East Asian Offshoots of Shuihu zhuan|author=Ellen Widmer|year=2000|volume=13|issue=1|pages=20–33|journal=Sino-Japanese Studies|issn=1041-8830|url=https://chinajapan.org/articles/13.1/13.1widmer20-33.pdf}}</ref>

Modern Chinese scholars have recognized ''Water Margin'' as one of the first great masterpieces in a long line of novels which began with mass entertainment and progressed to include some of the finest literary products of later ages.<ref>{{cite book|page=450|isbn=9780802150387|publisher=Grove Press|year=1965|last=Birch|first=Cyril|title=Anthology of Chinese Literature: Volume I: From Early Times to the Fourteenth Century}}</ref> [[Lee Fong-mao]] argues that the novel created a narrative mode of myths which marked the establishment of a literary genealogy of the unified formal structure in Ming-Qing fiction and inspired a trend in the writing of [[Gods and demons fiction|hagiographic novels]] on religious conversion.<ref>{{cite journal|author=Lee Fong-mao|language=zh-hant|title=暴力修行：道教謫凡神話與水滸的忠義敘述|trans-title=Religious Conversion through Violence: Taoist Myths of Banishment and the Discourse on Allegiance and Righteousness in Water Margin|year=2013|volume=19|pages=147–180|doi=10.24112/sinohumanitas.192182|issn=1562-2754|journal=Sino-Humanitas}}</ref> [[Victor H. Mair]] and Zhenjun Zhang wrote that, under the influence of ''Romance of the Three Kingdoms'' and ''Water Margin'', many [[historical novel]]s appeared in  the middle and late periods of the Ming dynasty, some of which inspired the well-received ''[[Romance of the Sui and Tang]]''.<ref>{{cite book|editor1=Victor Mair|editor2=Zhenjun Zhang|title=Routledge Handbook of Traditional Chinese Literature|year=2026|isbn=9781032231013|publisher=Routledge|lccn=2024042866|pages=505–506}}</ref> Richard James Havis in ''[[South China Morning Post]]'' described ''Water Margin'' as the most influential book in regards to [[Wuxia|heroic martial artists]].<ref>{{cite web|author=Richard James Havis|title=What martial arts storytelling owes to The Water Margin, wuxia novel from 14th century adapted for Japanese TV and by Chang Cheh for cinema, and how its themes and style still resonate|url=https://www.scmp.com/lifestyle/entertainment/article/3149074/what-wuxia-storytelling-owes-water-margin-martial-arts|work=[[South China Morning Post]]|date=September 19, 2021}}</ref>

With the rise of the [[Written vernacular Chinese#20th century reforms|vernacular writing movement]], the novel became an important model of vernacular writing, especially in schools where teachers used fragments from the book as instructional materials.<ref>{{cite journal|language=zh-hant|author=Lian-qian Guo|trans-title=Cultural and Educational Trends in Modern China and the Commercial Publication of the Outlaws of the Marsh (1919-1949)|title=中國近代文教趨勢與《水滸傳》的商業出版（1919-1949）|pages=157-218|issue=10|year=2013|journal=Tsing Hua Journal of Chinese Literature|issn=2218-8517|publisher=[[National Tsing Hua University]]}}</ref> The [[New Sensationists|Shanghai modernist]] writers of the early 1930s, most notably [[Mu Shiying]] and [[Shi Zhecun]], make [[Intertextuality|intertextual]] references to the novel in their writings.<ref>{{cite book|page=115|year=2017|publisher=[[Edinburgh University Press]]|title=On the Margins of Modernism: Xu Xu, Wumingshi and Popular Chinese Literature in the 1940s|isbn=9780748696376|author=Christopher Rosenmeier}}</ref> Shi Zhecun's short story ''Shi Xiu'' (1931) "shocked Chinese readers in the early 1930s" because it delved into the [[psychology of sexual desire]] and recast [[Shi Xiu]] as a [[Sexual sadism disorder|sadistic]] and [[Voyeurism|voyeuristic]] bandit.<ref>{{cite thesis|degree=PhD|author=Lin Qingxin|publisher=[[University of Hong Kong]]|title=Brushing history against the grain : constructing the Chinese new historical fiction as an oppositional discourse|doi=10.5353/th_b3124337|year=2001}}</ref><ref>{{cite thesis|degree=PhD|last=Peng|first=Tao|year=2022|title=The Emergence of the Modern Chinese Narrator: Studies of Lu Xun, Shi Zhecun, Sun Li, and Wang Zengqi|publisher=[[UC Riverside]]|url=https://escholarship.org/uc/item/2r07t1hp}}</ref> [[War novel]]s of the late 1940s in [[Communist-controlled China (1927–1949)|Communist-controlled China]] were largely modeled after ''Water Margin''.<ref>{{cite book|last=Wang|first=David Der-wei|title=The Monster that is History: History, Violence, and Fictional Writing in Twentieth-century China|year=2004|publisher=University of California Press|isbn=978-0-520-93724-6|pages=162-163}}</ref>
{{quote box||width=25em
|quote=Scholars have long noted the importance of ''The Water Margin'' to the literary and visual culture of greater East Asia—especially [[Edo period|Edo-period]] Japan, where the narrative was consumed  in  a  dazzling panoply of translations, adaptations, parodies, spinoffs, woodblock illustrations, and even board games based (often, very tenuously) on the Chinese original. … Commentators such as [[Mori Ōgai]] (1862–1922), [[Tokutomi Sohō]] (1863–1957), [[Masaoka Shiki]] (1867–1902), Kano Naoki ({{lang|ja|[[:ja:狩野直喜|狩野直喜]]}}) (1868–1947), and [[Akutagawa Ryūnosuke]] (1892–1927) informed their readers that ''The Water Margin'' provided a perfect "snapshot" of contemporary Chinese society, and the comparison between China and ''The Water Margin'' became ''de rigueur'' in Japanese literary travel documents of the period.
|author=— William C. Hedberg on the influence of ''Water Margin'' on Japanese culture<ref name="meijinature" />}}

''Water Margin'' has also been identified as one of the most influential works in the development of early modern Japanese literature.<ref name="D'haen">{{cite book|title=The Routledge Companion to World Literature|publisher=Routledge|year=2011|isbn=978-0-415-57022-0|editor1=Theo D'haen|pages=464–475|oclc=900201453|quote=During the Edo period (1603-1868), when early modern Japanese fiction was developed, its greatest influence came from Chinese vernacular fiction.|editor2=David Damrosch|editor3=Djelal Kadir}}</ref> Nan Ma Hartmann stated that in terms of the significance of its influence as a single work of foreign fiction, it is unrivaled by any other work in Japanese literary history.<ref name="nanma">{{cite thesis|degree=PhD|last=Hartmann|first=Nan Ma|year=2014|title=From Translation to Adaptation: Chinese Language Texts and Early Modern Japanese Literature|doi=10.7916/D8PK0DFW|publisher=[[Columbia University]]}}</ref> William C. Hedberg wrote that "It is difficult to exaggerate the importance of Chinese fiction and drama to the literary culture of early modern Japan&nbsp;... From a certain vantage point, the Chinese novel ''Shuihu zhuan'' [''Water Margin''] is a ubiquitous presence in the literary and visual culture of early modern Japan."<ref name=Hedberg1>Hedberg, W. (2020). Sinophilia, Sinophobia, and Vernacular Philology in Early Modern Japan. In ''The Japanese Discovery of Chinese Fiction: The Water Margin and the Making of a National Canon'' (pp. 25-53). New York: [[Columbia University Press]]. doi:10.7312/hedb19334.6</ref><ref name=Hedberg2>Hedberg, W. (2020). Histories of Reading and Nonreading: Shuihu zhuan as Text and Touchstone in Early Modern Japan. In ''The Japanese Discovery of Chinese Fiction: The Water Margin and the Making of a National Canon'' (pp. 54-94). New York: [[Columbia University Press]]. doi:10.7312/hedb19334.7</ref> The earliest extant copy of ''Water Margin'' in Japan is the 1592 edition collected by [[Tenkai]], abbot of the [[Tendai]] and adviser to the fledgling [[Tokugawa shogunate|Tokugawa regime]].<ref>{{cite thesis|degree=PhD|language=zh-hans|year=2017|author=冯雅|title=《水浒传》在日本的传播研究|publisher=[[Northeast Normal University]]|url=https://kns.cnki.net/kcms2/article/abstract?v=DgjXjbKQq8f0CTBtLYxzUa_vZ8nxH6XVpy0dSCO8FW1Z9PMcuhk-BujwVPDa6srcoEwglK7CH6o3IWgLCyh5a3qPLzuI0ldatUA1oXo8I32c7mZ3aR2sXpoF37RGkushz8o-3cyKd5jmXIt-FwiQlUQUMdtNOrvfg0a-SU02ZxJfTfy3Uyy-_Q==&uniplatform=NZKPT}}</ref> Conventional literary histories of Japan have regarded the novel as central to the emergence of ''[[yomihon]]''.<ref name="suikodenmono">{{cite journal|language=ko|title=근세 일본문학에서의 『수호전』과 <수호전물> - 요미혼의 형성과 지식의 확산을 중심으로 -|trans-title='Suikoden' and 'Suikodenmono' in Early Modern Japanese Literature — Focusing on the Formation of Yomihon and Diffusion of Knowledge —|pages=303–326|volume=134|year=2025|issn=1226-2552|last=Hong|first=Sung-Joon|journal=Journal of Japanese Language and Literature}}</ref> The earliest ''yomihon'' novels by the late Japanese ''yomihon'' representative writers, [[Santō Kyōden]] and [[Kyokutei Bakin]], all were references to ''Water Margin''.<ref>{{cite journal|volume=5|issue=1|year=2014|doi=10.15093/00000042|language=ja|title=京伝と馬琴の『水滸伝』 : 『忠臣水滸伝』と『高尾船字文』の翻案を中心に|trans-title=Kyoden and Bakin's all men are brothers : by the focus on modification and translation of Tyusinsuikoden and Takaosenjimon|author1=Na Zhou|author2=Shuang Liu|issn=2186-0483|journal=Study journal of Kyushu Kyoritsu University|pages=29–34}}</ref>

[[Haruo Shirane]] pointed out that as a result of the [[Kansei Reforms]] in the 1790s, writers and readers had to develop new forms, other than ''[[sharebon]]'' and ''[[kibyoshi]]'', that would avoid censorship. This need was answered by various Japanese adaptations of ''Water Margin'', beginning with {{ill|Takebe Ayatari's|ja|建部綾足}}'s ''{{ill|Honchō Suikoden|ja|本朝水滸伝}}'' (''Japanese Water Margin'', 1773).<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=jAf9aqjnnGMC&pg=PA313|title=Early Modern Japanese Literature: An Anthology, 1600-1900|last=Shirane|first=Haruo|year=2002|publisher=Columbia University Press|isbn=9780231507431|pages=886}}</ref> The group of adapted works is known as ''Suikodenmono'' ({{lang|ja|水滸伝もの}}).<ref name="suikodenmono" /> By the [[Meiji Restoration]], there were over twenty similar adaptations, the ''[[magnum opus ]]'' being ''[[Nansō Satomi Hakkenden|Hakkenden]]'' by Bakin.<ref name="bjwb">{{cite web|language=zh-hans|work=[[Beijing Evening News]]|date=September 24, 2025|title=《水浒》为何被"翻案"|author=Cai Hui|url=https://bjwb-app.bjd.com.cn/content/s68d382fce4b0221b9bed4e1f.html}}</ref>  [[Meiji era|Meiji-period]] Japanese readers hailed the gritty mimesis and dialogue of ''Water Margin'' as uncannily proto-modern attempts at peak Western literature-level "[[Naturalism (literature)|naturalism]]".<ref name="meijinature">{{cite journal|author=William C. Hedberg|title=Translation, Colonization, and the Fall of Utopia: The Qing Decline as Explained Through Chinese Fiction|pages=115–136|journal=Japanese Language and Literature|volume=54|issue=1|year=2020|issn=1536-7827|doi=10.5195/jll.2020.79}}</ref>

Notable Japanese ''Water Margin'' variations after the 1920s include [[Eiji Yoshikawa]]'s ''Shin Suikoden'' and [[Kenzo Kitakata]]'s {{ill|Suikoden (Kenzo Kitakata novel)|lt=''Suikoden''|ja|水滸伝 (北方謙三)}},<ref name="bjwb" /> the latter of which has sold more than 11.6 million copies in Japan, and its TV adaptation premiered in February 2026 on [[Wowow]] and [[Lemino]].<ref name="kkn">{{cite web|url=https://www.oricon.co.jp/news/2439873/full/|language=ja|title=織田裕二主演『北方謙三 水滸伝』世界観を支えるデザイン解禁 入門コンテンツもYouTubeにて無料配信|work=[[Oricon News]]|date=March 4, 2026}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|work=[[PR Times]]|url=https://prtimes.jp/main/html/rd/p/000000189.000048223.html|title=WOWOW×Lemino 連続ドラマ「北方謙三 水滸伝」公開記念 名古屋の人気ラッパーが集結するラップバトルイベント「連続ドラマ 北方謙三 水滸伝 presents 呂布カルマ RAP梁山泊」開催決定|language=ja|date=February 8, 2026}}</ref>

''[[The Water Outlaws]]'', a novel by [[S. L. Huang]], is a [[Gender flip|gender-flipped]] version of the story in which many of the outlaws are queer women.<ref>{{cite web|last1=Tor.com|access-date=2023-07-29|title=S. L. Huang's New Take on the Most Famous Chinese Novel You've Never Read in English: Announcing The Water Outlaws|url=https://www.tor.com/2020/10/15/book-announcements-s-l-huang-the-water-outlaws/|date=15 October 2020|website=Tor.com}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|access-date=2023-07-29|title=The Water Outlaws by S L Huang|url=https://www.publishersweekly.com/9781250180421|website=www.publishersweekly.com}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|access-date=2023-07-29|title=Sapphic Book Club: The Water Outlaws|url=https://www.solidstatebooksdc.com/events/2023/9/25/sapphic-book-club-the-water-outlaws|date=24 September 2023|website=Solid State Books}}</ref> ''Rise of the Water Margin''<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.amazon.com/dp/B09SNY8YY8|website=Amazon|title=Rise of the Water Margin: A Novel of the Near Future}}</ref> ({{lang|zh|水滸再起}}) is a cyber-thriller novel launched in 2022 by the American author Christopher Bates in which all of the Chinese characters and their approximate character arcs are 21st century modernizations of people in ''Water Margin''. [[Frank Chin]]'s novel, ''[[Donald Duk]]'', contains many references to the ''Water Margin''. Song Jiang and Li Kui make several appearances in the protagonist's dreams.

===Comics===
[[File:Suikoden.jpg|thumb|200px|[[Yang Lin (Water Margin)|Yang Lin]], a hero from the novel, from [[Utagawa Kuniyoshi]]'s series of woodblock prints illustrating the 108 Suikoden]]

''Water Margin'' is referred to in numerous Japanese [[manga]], such as [[Tetsuo Hara]] and [[Buronson]]'s ''[[Fist of the North Star]]'', and [[Masami Kurumada]]'s ''[[Fūma no Kojirō]]'', ''Otokozaka'' and ''[[Saint Seiya]]''. In both works of fiction, characters bearing the same stars of the ''Water Margin'' characters as personal emblems of destiny are featured prominently. A Japanese manga called ''[[Akaboshi: Ibun Suikoden]]'', based on the story of ''Water Margin'', was serialised in ''Weekly Shonen Jump''.

A Hong Kong [[manhua]] series based on ''Water Margin'' was also created by the artist [[Lee Chi Ching]]. A reimagined series based on ''Water Margin'', ''108 Fighters'', was created by [[Andy Seto]].

Inspired by the novel, the Italian artist [[Magnus (comic artist)|Magnus]] created the [[graphic novel]] ''I Briganti'' ("The Outlaws"), which had a great impact on the Italian mediascape.<ref>{{cite book|title=The Western Reinvention of Chinese Literature, 1910–2010: From Ezra Pound to Maxine Hong Kingston|editor1=Zong-qi Cai|editor2=Stephen Roddy|year=2022|publisher=Brill|pages=9-10|isbn=9789004515048}}</ref>

In 2007, Asiapac Books published a graphic narrative version of portions of the novel.<ref>{{cite book|title=Water Margin Compact Classic|year=2007|edition=reprint|last=Shi|first=Nai'an|author-link=Shi Nai'an|editor-last=Ng|editor-first=Keng Yeow|isbn=978-981-229-458-6|publisher=Asiapac Books|access-date=2018-08-22|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=7oPpAgAAQBAJ}}</ref>

===Film===
Most film adaptations of ''Water Margin'' were produced by Hong Kong's [[Shaw Brothers Studio]] and mostly released in the 1970s and 1980s. They include: ''[[The Water Margin (film)|The Water Margin]]'' (1972),<ref>{{Cite web|title=All about movies, games, gambling and martial arts|url=http://www.kungfucinema.com/|access-date=2021-06-15|language=en-US|archive-date=14 April 2005|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20050414031604/http://www.kungfucinema.com/}}</ref><ref>[http://www.dragonsdenuk.com/reviews/water_margin.htm Dragon's Den UK]</ref> directed by [[Chang Cheh]] and others; ''[[Delightful Forest]]'' (1972), directed by Chang Cheh again and starring [[Ti Lung]] as [[Wu Song]];<ref>{{IMDb title|qid=Q5253955|id=tt0068821|title=The Delightful Forest}}</ref> ''[[Pursuit (1972 Hong Kong film)|Pursuit]]'' (1972), directed by Kang Cheng and starring [[Yueh Hua (actor)|Yueh Hua]] as [[Lin Chong]]; ''[[All Men Are Brothers (film)|All Men Are Brothers]]'' (1975), a sequel to ''The Water Margin'' (1972) directed by Chang Cheh and others; and ''Tiger Killer'' (1982), directed by [[Li Han-hsiang]] and starring Ti Lung as Wu Song again.<ref>{{IMDb title|qid=Q11124379|id=tt0084922|title=Tiger Killer}}</ref>

Other non-Shaw Brothers production include: ''[[All Men Are Brothers: Blood of the Leopard]]'', also known as ''Water Margin: True Colours of Heroes'' (1992), which centers on the story of Lin Chong, [[Lu Zhishen]] and [[Gao Qiu]], starring [[Tony Leung Ka-fai]], [[Elvis Tsui]] and others;<ref>{{IMDb title|qid=Q11130278|id=tt0105400|title=All Men Are Brothers: Blood of the Leopard}}</ref> and ''[[Troublesome Night 16]]'' (2002), a Hong Kong horror comedy film which spoofs the story of Wu Song avenging his brother.

===Television===
Television series directly based on ''Water Margin'' include: [[Nippon Television]]'s ''[[The Water Margin (1973 TV series)|The Water Margin]]'' (1973), which was later released in other countries outside Japan;<ref>[https://web.archive.org/web/20121022063229/http://ftvdb.bfi.org.uk/sift/series/40004 BFI Entry]</ref><ref>[http://fabulousfilms.co.uk/site/Home/Index.htm "Originally screened on British TV in 1976"]</ref> ''[[Outlaws of the Marsh (TV series)|Outlaws of the Marsh]]'' (1983), which won a [[Golden Eagle Awards (China)|Golden Eagle Award]]; [[China Central Television|CCTV]]'s ''[[The Water Margin (1998 TV series)|The Water Margin]]'' (1998), produced by [[Zhang Jizhong]] and featuring fight choreography by [[Yuen Woo-ping]]; ''[[All Men Are Brothers (TV series)|All Men Are Brothers]]'' (2011), directed by Kuk Kwok-leung and featuring actors from mainland China, Hong Kong and Taiwan.

Animations adapted from ''Water Margin'' include: ''[[Giant Robo (OVA)|Giant Robo: The Animation]]'' (1992), an anime series based on [[Mitsuteru Yokoyama]]'s manga series; ''[[Outlaw Star]]'' (1998), another cartoon series which makes several references to the novel; ''[[Hero: 108]]'' (2010), a flash animated series produced by various companies and shown on [[Cartoon Network]]. ''Galaxy Divine Wind Jinraiger'', an anime in the [[J9 Series]] planned for a 2016 broadcast, has also cited ''Water Margin'' as its inspiration.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://jinraiger.com/story |script-title=ja:=銀河神風ジンライガー » Story |publisher=Jinraiger.com |date=2014-04-09 |access-date=2014-05-20 |archive-date=28 January 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200128100221/http://www.jinraiger.com/story }}</ref><ref name=otakuma>{{cite web|url=http://otakei.otakuma.net/archives/2014040810.html |script-title=ja:新J9始動！アニメ『銀河神風ジンライガー』制作決定、モチーフは水滸伝 {{pipe}} おたくま経済新聞 |publisher=Otakei.otakuma.net |date=2014-04-08 |access-date=2014-05-20}}</ref>

The 2004 Hong Kong television series ''[[Shades of Truth]]'', produced by [[Television Broadcasts Limited|TVB]], features three characters from the novel who are reincarnated into present-day Hong Kong as a [[Triad (organized crime)|triad]] boss and two police officers respectively.

===Stage===

''Water Margin'' has given rise to a large number of [[Theatre of China|theatrical]] pieces in the major forms, regional dramas, and different kinds of performing arts that elaborate on well-known episodes of the novel, usually those before the grand assembly.<ref>{{cite journal|author=Wang Jian-ke|title=论汉水流域的水浒戏及其传播特点|journal=Journal of Shaanxi Normal University (Philosophy and Social Sciences Edition)|year=2015|volume=44|issue=05|pages=68-76|language=zh-hans|trans-title=Plays of the Outlaws of the Marsh in the Reaches of the Han River and Characteristics of Their Dissemination|url=https://wap.cnki.net/touch/web/Journal/Article/SXSS201505010.html}}</ref> In the Ming and Qing dynasties, the ''Water Margin'' themes were repeatedly used in a fairly large number of ''zaju'' and ''[[Chuanqi (theatre)|chuanqi]]'' plays.<ref name="quyi">{{cite thesis|degree=MSc|language=zh-hans|doi=10.7666/d.y1701858|author=杨小娜|year=2010|title=明清时期《水浒传》传播研究|publisher=[[Yangzhou University]]|url=https://kns.cnki.net/KCMS/detail/detail.aspx?dbcode=CMFD&dbname=CMFD2011&filename=2010176247.nh}}</ref> Around the 1750s, the imperial court commissioned an enormous multi-volume drama entitled ''The Plan of the Stars of Loyalty and Righteousness'' (''Zhongyi Xuantu''), which was based on the various existing [[Kunqu|kunju]]-system ''Water Margin'' dramas and refashioned this "politically sensitive and morally damaging" story for Qing purposes.<ref>{{cite book|page=213|title=Opera and the City: The Politics of Culture in Beijing, 1770-1900|author=Andrea S. Goldman|isbn=9780804782623|year=2012|publisher=Stanford University Press}}</ref> [[Peking opera]] has a deep relationship with traditional novels, and there are over seventy plays based on ''Water Margin''.<ref>{{cite journal|journal=Saint John’s Journal|author=Xiangyu Liu|issn=0859-9432|year=2022|volume=25|issue=37|pages=99-115|title=Huwen and Intertextuality: Chinese Traditional Intertextuality and Western Intertextuality|url=https://sju.ac.th/pap_file/a6a7328ba33132e7f12fce4971b6e3b4.pdf}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://hlj.cri.cn/2020-07-23/fbd6e9d9-7c66-c7e0-1b2c-f9d71c1e6994.html|title=黑龙江省京剧院“云中戏苑”迎传统戏专场|language=zh-hans|work=CRI Online|date=July 23, 2020}}</ref>

''Song Jiang'', a 1921 [[civilized drama]] is regarded as the first ''[[huaju]]'' based on ''Water Margin''.<ref name="jiaosu">{{cite thesis|degree=PhD|language=zh-hans|title=20世纪中国水浒戏剧研究|year=2017|url=https://kns.cnki.net/kcms2/article/abstract?v=s7Ax9qbH24mgheZznJ2hlwxe2UnBXgy46M2G9717yJtUsAVjZOZg1Nx_jmRWN1w4rkz2DBjd6emPwABioaY0I9eCBRFTmjerT4nV82-MRaV0BEU1JrZt7A_9WRIloaI8J6cLSk05wTjEUM5cxA8JoIobgry-XVn5f-hbwKqYc9P0A6Ije-a7GfEwSaMgAGz5&uniplatform=NZKPT&language=CHS|publisher=[[Shaanxi Normal University]]|author=焦欣波}}</ref> Later [[Ouyang Yuqian]]'s five-act play ''Pan Jinlian'' (1926), which controversially recasts Pan as a "modern, [[Women in China#Developments in early 20th century|liberated]] woman in steadfast pursuit of romantic love", received wider acclaim.<ref>{{cite book|page=65-66|title=War and Popular Culture: Resistance in Modern China, 1937–1945|isbn=9780520354869|publisher=[[University of California Press]]|last=Hung|first=Chang-tai|year=1994}}</ref> In the early 1940s, two Peking opera plays with "new political content", launched by the Communists, were highly successful, both based on the novel: ''Three Campaigns against the Zujiazhuang Village'' was staged to inspire people in their resistance against [[Japanese aggression]] during the [[Second World War]]; the 1944 production ''Driven to Join the Liang Mountain Rebels'' (''Bishang Liangshan'') has been credited as, due to Mao Zedong's enthusiastic praise, "an epoch-making beginning of revolutionizing old theater" in the official discours.<ref>{{cite book|pages=103-104|title=Peking Opera|isbn=9787508502564|series=Cultural China Series|publisher=[[China Intercontinental Press]]|author=Xu Chengbei|translator=Chen Gengtao|year=2010}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|pages=4-5|location=Hong Kong|publisher=[[Hong Kong University Press]]|author=Xing Fan|title=Staging Revolution: Artistry and Aesthetics in Model Beijing Opera during the Cultural Revolution|isbn=978-988-8455-81-2|year=2020}}</ref>

In the "Seventeen Years" period (1949-1966), ''Water Margin'' drama became one of the most frequently created and adapted traditional dramas, and the image of Liangshan heroes was reconstructed to represent "typical revolutionary historical figures".<ref>{{cite journal|doi=10.6257/JOTS.201801_(21).069|author=Xin-bo Jiao|title=「十七年」戲劇中「梁山好漢」形象的文本再構|trans-title=Textual Reconstruction of the Image of "Liangshan Hero" in the Drama of the Seventeen Years|language=zh-hant|pages=69-87|issue=21|year=2018|journal=Journal of Theater Studies|issn=2070-2663}}</ref> Following the [[Socialist market economy|market-oriented transformation]] in the 1990s, various creators of ''Water Margin'' dramas worked to weaken political overtones and fit a [[kitsch]] aesthetic.<ref name="jiaosu" /> "108 Heroes", a three-part opera first shown in 2007 mixing Chinese opera, [[street dance]], [[cosplay]], and [[Rock musical|live rock music]], gained success.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.taipeitimes.com/News/feat/archives/2011/06/10/2003505396|title=Brave new sequel|work=[[Taipei Times]]|date=10 June 2011|author=Ian Bartholomew|url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110613155031/https://www.taipeitimes.com/News/feat/archives/2011/06/10/2003505396|archive-date=13 June 2011}}</ref>

===Video games===
Video games based on the novel include [[Konami]]'s console RPG series ''[[Suikoden]]'' and [[Koei]]'s strategy game ''[[Bandit Kings of Ancient China]]''. Other games with characters based on the novel or were partly inspired by it include: ''[[Jade Empire]]'', which features a character "Black Whirlwind" who is based on [[Li Kui (Water Margin)|Li Kui]]; [[Data East]]'s ''[[Outlaws Of The Lost Dynasty]]'', which was also released under the titles ''Suiko Enbu'' and ''Dark Legend''; ''[[Shin Megami Tensei: Imagine]]''. There is also a beat em' up game ''Shuǐhǔ Fēngyún Chuán'' ({{lang-zh|t=水滸風雲傳|l=Water and Wind}}), created by Never Ending Soft Team and published by Kin Tec in 1996.<ref>{{cite web|work=ぴこぴこ I Feel Alright! |url=http://blogs.yahoo.co.jp/rig_veda/60655515.html|script-title=ja:【MD/東亜】 アジア版 Mega Drive 用 ROMカートリッジ Vol. 2 (1989 年頃～) ≪非ライセンス≫}}</ref> It was re-released for the [[Mega Drive]] and in arcade version by Wah Lap in 1999.{{Citation needed|date=October 2020}} An English version titled "''Water Margin: The Tales of Clouds and Winds''" by [[Piko Interactive]] translated and released in 2015. Some enemy sprites are taken from other beat 'em ups and modified, including ''[[Knights of the Round (video game)|Knights of the Round]]'', ''[[Golden Axe (video game)|Golden Axe]]'' and ''[[Streets of Rage]].''{{Citation needed|date=July 2025}}

In the 8th [[canto]] of the 2023 video game ''[[Limbus Company]]'', there is a faction known as "The Pinky", based on the 108 heroes.<ref>{{cite web |title=The Pinky|url=https://limbuscompany.wiki.gg/wiki/The_Pinky#Members |website=Limbus Company Wiki |access-date=2 June 2025 |language=en}}</ref>

===Other===

In Chinese, the name "Li Gui" – from the character who impersonates the notorious Li Kui to rob people – is used as a synonym for [[Shanzhai|fake products.]]<ref>{{cite journal|author=Han Jianghua|title=The Meaning Construction of Idiom Based on Blending Model|pages=105–115|doi=10.26478/ja2019.7.10.7|journal=Macrolinguistics|volume=7|issue=1|year=2019|issn=1934-5755}}</ref>

The [[temple fair]] in Southern Taiwan [[Song Jiang Battle Array]] is based on the acrobatic fighting from ''Water Margin''.

Characters from the story often appear on [[Chinese playing cards#Money-suited cards|Money-suited]] playing cards, which are thought to be the ancestor of both modern playing cards and mahjong tiles. These cards are also known as Water Margin cards ({{lang|zh|水滸牌}}).

The trading card game ''[[Yu-Gi-Oh! Trading Card Game|Yu-Gi-Oh!]]'' has an [[archetype]] based on the 108 heroes known as the "Fire Fist" (known as "Flame Star" in the OCG) ({{lang|ja|炎えん星せい}}, Ensei) where the monsters aside from Horse Prince, Lion Emperor, and Spirit are based on those heroes.
