WIKIPEDIA ARTICLE: Recollections of Things to Come
======================================================================

{{Short description|1963 novel by Elena Garro}}
{{Use dmy dates|date=July 2026}}
{{Infobox book <!--See [[Wikipedia:WikiProject Novels]]-->
| image            = File:Recollections of Things to Come (Elena Garro) novel cover.jpg
| title_orig       = Los recuerdos del porvenir
| orig_lang_code   = es
| translator       = Ruth L. C. Simms
| author           = [[Elena Garro]]
| country          = Mexico
| language         = Spanish
| series           = 
| pages            = 295
| genre            = [[Magical realism]]
| publisher        = [[Joaquín Mortiz]]
| pub_date         = 1963
| english_pub_date = 1969
}}
'''''Recollections of Things to Come''''' ({{langx|es|Los recuerdos del porvenir}}) is a 1963 novel by Mexican writer [[Elena Garro]]. Inspired by her childhood in [[Southern Mexico]], the novel uses a nonlinear structure to explore themes of historical memory, national identity, and sexism. The fictional town of Ixtepec narrates the story of its military occupation during the [[Cristero War]], a conflict precipitated by attempts to secularize the country following the [[Mexican Revolution]] of 1910–1920. The town is able to recall events its inhabitants may not, while the rules of normal time do not always apply.

The manuscript was composed in 1953 and remained in a trunk for several years. Following its partial destruction in a fire, Garro rewrote portions and sent it to the publishing house [[Joaquín Mortiz]]. It received positive reviews at the time of publication, but attracted a wider audience only through the work of feminist writers toward the end of the twentieth century. A 1968 film adaptation directed by [[Alfredo Ripstein]], titled ''Memories of the Future'' in English, altered significant elements of the novel to avoid criticism of the Mexican government. 

[[Alfaguara]] issued a new Spanish-language edition with essays by contemporary authors including [[Guadalupe Nettel]] in 2019. The 2024 critical edition by Ediciones Cátedra, also in Spanish, contained over 100 pages of new analysis. The ''[[Chicago Review of Books]]'' describes Garro as "under-translated and under-appreciated".

== Background ==
[[File:Cristero-leaders-and-their-banner.jpg|left|thumb|220px|Cristero leaders with a religious banner during the Cristero War (1926–1929).]]
Garro wrote the novel based on her childhood in [[Iguala]], Guerrero.{{sfn|Garro|Esteban|Aparicio|2024|p=33}} Her family relocated to the city in 1926, at the start of the [[Cristero War]], a conflict sparked by elements in the [[Constitution of 1917]] limiting the influence of the Catholic Church. She witnessed religious persecution and grew to identify with the struggles of poor and Indigenous communities resisting military repression.{{sfn|Garro|Esteban|Aparicio|2024|p=16}} This experience formed the backbone of ''Recollections of Things to Come''.{{sfn|Cypess|2012|p=34}} It combines the Cristero conflict with an exploration of the interplay between Western and Indigenous worldviews, what Garro called the "duality" of the Mexican countryside.{{sfn|Balderston|1989|p=42}}

Garro composed the manuscript over a month in 1953 while hospitalized for [[myelitis]] in Bern, Switzerland. The draft was stored in a trunk for nearly a decade, surviving a fire and near-loss in a New York hotel before she reconstructed the lost parts.{{sfn|Garro|Esteban|Aparicio|2024|pp=32–3}}{{efn|The ''Enciclopedia de la Literatura en México'' notes that some sources give the date of writing as 1945–1948, when Garro would have been in contact with figures like [[Jorge Luis Borges]]. It says the context of the writing is the same and the difference in dates is not great.<ref name="elem">{{cite web |last1=del Ángel |first1=Diana |title=Los recuerdos del porvenir – Detalle de la obra – Enciclopedia de la Literatura en México |trans-title=Los recuerdos del porvenir – Detail of the work – Encyclopedia of Literature in Mexico |url=https://www.elem.mx/obra/datos/3408 |website=Enciclopedia de la literatura en México (ELEM) |publisher=Fundación para las Letras Mexicanas |access-date=10 July 2026 |date=5 December 2017 |archive-date=11 July 2026 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260711152133/https://www.elem.mx/obra/datos/3408 |url-status=live }}</ref>}} Her marriage to [[Octavio Paz]], a future winner of the [[Nobel Prize in Literature]], deteriorated while the manuscript was in storage. He filed for divorce in 1959 in [[Ciudad Juárez]] without Garro's knowledge. This was later ruled invalid, complicated by the fact that Garro was underage when they married.{{sfn|Barrera|2025|loc=The Divorce in Juárez}} Despite their separation and growing professional rivalry, Paz championed Garro's work, delivering the manuscript to Joaquín Díez-Canedo in 1963. His support ensured the novel's release through the publisher Joaquín Mortiz.{{sfn|Garro|Esteban|Aparicio|2024|pp=32–3}}

The ''[[Enciclopedia de la Literatura en México]]'' states that the novel's title originates from a line in the poem "Concierto breve" by [[Carlos Pellicer]].<ref name="elem" /> Rafael Olea Franco instead suggests that Garro adopted the name of a famous [[pulquería]] in Mexico City that was popular among her social circle in the late 1930s.{{sfn|Garro|Esteban|Aparicio|2024|pp=24–25}} It has also been observed that a bar in [[Alejo Carpentier]]'s 1953 novel {{Interlanguage link|Los pasos perdidos (novel)|lt=''Los pasos perdidos''|es|Los pasos perdidos (novela)}} (''The Lost Steps'') shares the name Garro chose.{{sfn|Balderston|1989|p=46}} 

The first Spanish edition of the novel was published in 1963 by [[Joaquín Mortiz]], while the English translation by Ruth L. C. Simms was released in 1969 through the [[University of Texas Press]].<ref name="elem" />{{sfn|Garro|Esteban|Aparicio|2024|p=28}} It has also been translated into Italian (as {{lang|it|I ricordi dell'avvenire}}), German (as {{lang|de|Erinnerungen an die Zukunft}}), and French (as {{lang|fr|La maîtresse d'Ixtepec}} and {{lang|fr|La Fête à Ixtepec}}).<ref name="elem"/>

== Plot summary ==
The town of Ixtepec opens the novel with the line "{{lang|es|Aquí estoy, sentado sobre esta piedra aparente. Sólo mi memoria sabe lo que encierra.}}" ("Here I am, sitting on this apparent stone. Only my memory knows what it encloses.") The first half of the story centers on the brutal General Francisco Rosas and his obsession with his mistress, Julia Andrade. Julia remains mentally and emotionally detached from his control. With the help of the mysterious Felipe Hurtado, she escapes during a magical suspension of time.

The second half tells of the town's efforts to conceal the local priest from persecution. Juan Moncada is killed and his brother Nicolás executed. Isabel Moncada realizes she is unable to give up her feelings for General Rosas, despite the devastation he has brought upon her family. She chooses Rosas over the desire for a spiritual cure and is transformed into the "apparent stone" from the beginning of the story. Her former maid, Gregoria, finds the petrified body and views the event as divine punishment. Isabel's voice ends the story: "{{lang|es|Aquí estaré con mi amor a solas como recuerdo del porvenir por los siglos de los siglos.}}" ("Here I will be alone with my love as a recollection of things to come for ever and ever.")

== Themes and style ==
=== Narrative structure ===
[[File:José Clemente Orozco - The Demagogue - Google Art Project.jpg|thumb|right|220px|''The Demagogue'' (1930) by [[José Clemente Orozco]].]]
''Recollections of Things to Come'', published in 1963, is regarded as a forerunner of Latin American [[magical realism]]. It evokes frequent comparisons to ''[[One Hundred Years of Solitude]]'', published four years later.<ref name="clarin">{{cite web |last1=Lojo |first1=María Rosa |title=Vuelve Elena Garro, la mujer que imaginó el realismo mágico antes que Gabo |trans-title=Elena Garro, the woman who imagined magical realism before Gabo, is back |url=https://www.clarin.com/cultura/vuelve-elena-garro-mujer-imagino-realismo-magico-gabo_0_TVfoOzNBhi.html |website=Clarín |access-date=7 July 2026 |language=es |date=27 March 2024 |archive-date=5 April 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240405192819/https://www.clarin.com/cultura/vuelve-elena-garro-mujer-imagino-realismo-magico-gabo_0_TVfoOzNBhi.html |url-status=live }}</ref><ref name="revista" /><ref name="excelsior" /> In their critical edition, Esteban and Aparicio review attempts to categorize Garro's work, including her frustration with the male-dominated [[Latin American Boom]] and her belief that similar techniques had existed in Mexico for centuries.{{sfn|Garro|Esteban|Aparicio|2024|pp=67–8}}{{efn|Garro distanced herself from the commercialization of magical realism. She once said, "{{lang|es|Perdóname que lo diga. Y nomás por no escribir entre esa banda de pendejos yo ya no quiero volver a escribir jamás nada mágico. Han echado a perder toda la posibilidad de novela en América Latina con tanto realismo y tanta magia.}}" (Forgive me for saying this. And just for not writing among that bunch of idiots, I don't want to write anything magical ever again. They've ruined every possibility of a novel in Latin America with so much realism and so much magic.){{sfn|Garro|Esteban|Aparicio|2024|p=67}}}} They situate Garro alongside [[Juan Rulfo]] and [[Laura Esquivel]] in "a distinctly Mexican conception of the convergence of different realities, normalized through an aesthetic and technical device that we might call magical realism".{{sfn|Garro|Esteban|Aparicio|2024|p=70}}

Ixtepec narrates events in a voice using both the first-person singular ("I") and the first-person plural ("we"). Its inhabitants exist outside of normal time, and only the interruption of external forces shifts their reality.{{sfn|Dauster|1980|p=61}} Memory serves as a vehicle for the town to identify itself. This focus on [[collective memory]] explores how one generation inevitably repeats the acts of the previous one, which renders conventional historical records problematic.{{sfn|Balderston|1989|pp=41–5}}{{sfn|Garro|Esteban|Aparicio|2024|p=94}}

The town's narration presents an alternative to Western views of history as a progressive sequence of unique events. Rather than unfolding as a linear progression, Ixtepec's experience of time allows the past, present, and future to overlap and coexist within a fixed present.{{sfn|Garro|Esteban|Aparicio|2024|pp=85–6}}{{sfn|Barrera|2025|loc=On Time and Memory}} Garro credited her understanding of time as a cyclical or simultaneous phenomenon to the influence of her father, who was familiar with [[Buddhism]], and the [[Nahuas|Nahua]] women who helped raise her.{{sfn|Barrera|2025|loc=Running Wild, On Time and Memory}} 

=== Historical context ===
The novel depicts the period of state-building that followed the [[Mexican Revolution]] of 1910–1920. [[Porfirio Díaz]] had ruled the country as a dictator in a period of relative peace known as the [[Porfiriato]] (1876–1910), and ''Recollections of Things to Come'' takes place in a time of uncertainty about the country's democratic future. It portrays revolutionary generals, entrenched landowners, and the Catholic hierarchy as conspiring to suppress the peasantry rather than implement land reform.{{sfn|Garro|Esteban|Aparicio|2024|pp=75–76}} The novel contains frequent references to historical figures such as [[Plutarco Elías Calles]] and depicts the impact of the 1926 [[Calles Law]], which led to the government-ordered closure of churches.{{r|mcmurray}}{{sfn|Bowskill|2009|p=440}} The narrative distinguishes between individual religious faith and the Catholic Church as an institution. While the hierarchy is shown as complicit with the ruling elite, local outcasts are often the only characters who demonstrate empathy for the persecuted.{{sfn|Garro|Esteban|Aparicio|2024|pp=75–77}}

The character of Martín Moncada mentions that the country has endured a "long night" of national turmoil since the assassination of President [[Francisco I. Madero]] in 1913. The narrative voice critiques the political maneuvering of the 1920s, suggesting that the conflict between the government and the Catholic Church was a distraction from the subject of land redistribution.{{sfn|Pascual Gutiérrez|2018|pp=127–8}} The military is depicted as committing acts of violence and murder against the peasantry, whether out of boredom or a sense of professional obligation.{{sfn|Dauster|1980|p=57}} Meanwhile, the town-narrator watches high-ranking Church officials play cards with the families of government officials.{{sfn|Bowskill|2009|p=440}} Esteban and Aparicio characterize the effect as a "petrified" experience of time, forcing the community to relive past violence as its only possible future.{{sfn|Garro|Esteban|Aparicio|2024|pp=77, 82}}

=== Gender ===
Unlike earlier literature on the Mexican Revolution, ''Recollections of Things to Come'' portrays women as active participants rather than passive figures.{{sfn|Dauster|1980|p=65}} Early in the novel, Isabel Moncada describes the cultural expectation of marriage as a "humiliation", and her dependence on General Francisco Rosas becomes a complex betrayal of both her family and her community.{{sfn|Garro|Esteban|Aparicio|2024|pp=107–109}} The novel thus challenges [[machismo]] by giving voice to the collective resentments of women living under patriarchal rule.{{sfn|Cypess|2012|pp=6, 11}} Garro described her work as feminist, saying that "the women are rebels and if a woman is a rebel then she is a feminist".{{sfn|Garro|Esteban|Aparicio|2024|p=100}}

Sarah E. L. Bowskill notes that the narrative resists categorizing women's transgressive behavior through archetypes such as [[La Malinche]], the Indigenous interpreter to [[Hernán Cortés]] associated with betrayal. While characters such as Gregoria use these myths to explain away female rebellion and re-establish male authority, the narrative voice keeps women's motives enigmatic.{{sfn|Bowskill|2009|pp=444–46}} Sandra Messinger Cypess puts the novel in dialogue with Octavio Paz's depiction of La Malinche in ''[[The Labyrinth of Solitude]]'' as a passive and violated [[La chingada|victim]].{{sfn|Cypess|2012|pp=ix, 27}} By presenting older archetypes as "culturally determined" rather than inescapable fates, the novel offers an alternative to narratives of female submission.{{sfn|Cypess|2012|pp=47–8}} Bowskill argues that female participation in the conflict disrupts traditional models of domesticity and social order.{{sfn|Bowskill|2009|p=452}}

== Reception ==
{{rquote|left|The Catholic followers of [[Porfirio Díaz]] and the atheistic revolutionaries were digging the grave of agrarian reform together.
—''Recollections of Things to Come'', translated by Ruth L. C. Simms, p. 148, as quoted by McMurray.<ref name="mcmurray">{{cite journal |last1=McMurray |first1=George R. |title=Review of ''Recollections of Things to Come'' |journal=The Americas |date=1970 |volume=27 |issue=2 |page=212 |doi=10.2307/980526 |issn=0003-1615}}</ref>}}
''Recollections of Things to Come'' shared the 1963 [[Xavier Villaurrutia Prize]] with ''La feria'' by [[Juan José Arreola]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Premio Xavier Villaurrutia de Escritores para Escritores |url=https://literatura.inba.gob.mx/premio-xavier-villaurrutia.html |website=Premio Xavier Villaurrutia |publisher=[[Instituto Nacional de Bellas Artes y Literatura]] |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250217152904/https://literatura.inba.gob.mx/premio-xavier-villaurrutia.html |archive-date=17 February 2025 |language=es |trans-title=Xavier Villaurrutia Prize for Writers by Writers}}</ref> A positive 1965 review in ''[[Books Abroad]]'' distinguished Garro's use of time from contemporaries like Arreola. "The author recognizes history and time, but refuses to concede them hegemony over man."<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Sommers |first1=Joseph |last2=Garro |first2=Elena |title=Los recuerdos del porvenir |journal=Books Abroad |date=1965 |volume=39 |issue=1 |pages=68 |doi=10.2307/40119397}}</ref> Writing in ''[[The Austin American]]'' in 1969, C. Richard King observed that Garro's background in theater and film was evident in the novel's structure, which he compared to a "pageant", though he felt some of the work's theatrical "music" was lost in the transition to paper.<ref name="King">{{cite news |last=King |first=C. Richard |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-austin-american-a-mexican-village/202112926/ |title=A Mexican Village |date=19 October 1969 |work=[[The Austin American]] |pages=96 |via=[[Newspapers.com]]}}</ref> Also in 1969, John S. Brushwood said that the first-person narration by Ixtepec "sometimes rings a bit false" but the mix of realistic and fantastical elements worked. He suggested that the novel "may be one of those sleepers that future generations will repeatedly enjoy discovering".<ref name="kcs1969">{{cite news |last=Brushwood |first=John S. |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-kansas-city-star-when-only-a-madman/202112895/ |title=When Only A Madman Is Rational |date=16 November 1969 |access-date=24 July 2026 |work=[[The Kansas City Star]] |pages=98 |via=[[Newspapers.com]]}}</ref>

Garro's reputation collapsed following the [[Tlatelolco massacre]] of 1968. Under pressure from the Mexican government, Garro accused left-wing intellectuals of inciting student violence. Her public statements and reports that she served as a government informant led fellow writers to label her a "snitch" (''delatora'') and she went into self-imposed exile.{{sfn|Cypess|2012|pp=131–132}}<ref name="elpais2016">{{cite web |url=https://elpais.com/cultura/2016/10/13/babelia/1476359923_131235.html |title=Elena Garro, una escritora contra sí misma |lang=es |trans-title=Elena Garro, a writer against herself |last=Martínez Ahrens |first=Jan |date=13 October 2016 |website=El País |access-date=24 July 2026 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250611194008/https://elpais.com/cultura/2016/10/13/babelia/1476359923_131235.html |archive-date=11 June 2025 |url-status=live}}</ref> During this time, Mexican literary juries were often hesitant to recognize her work for fear of offending her influential ex-husband, Octavio Paz. Their intertwined legacies remain a subject of debate.{{sfn|Cypess|2012|p=2}}<ref name="elpais2016" /> Garro remained known as a playwright in the 1970s, but her prose received little scholarly attention. A 1980 analysis called ''Recollections of Things to Come'' "notoriously subversive" for its cynical view of the post-revolutionary Mexican government while noting its obscurity.{{sfn|Dauster|1980|p=68}} 

Feminist writers brought ''Recollections of Things to Come'' and Garro's prose to greater attention toward the end of the twentieth century.{{sfn|Cypess|2012|p=4}}{{sfn|Garro|Esteban|Aparicio|2024|p=20}} A 1987 review in ''[[The New York Times Book Review]]'' positioned its "warping" and "stopping" of time within the tradition of magical realism and described the overall effect as "luminous and affecting".<ref name="NYT1987">{{cite magazine |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1987/01/25/books/fiction-in-short-688487.html |url-access=limited |last=Kirk |first=Deborah |title=Recollections of Things to Come |date=25 January 1987 |work=[[The New York Times Book Review]] |page=20 |issn=03624331 |access-date=24 July 2026|id={{ProQuest|426386206}}}}</ref> A review of the 2019 text in ''[[El Tiempo (Colombia)|El Tiempo]]'' said that the book had "not lost an iota of [its] originality" and questioned why Garro had not been included in the canon of Latin American literature. The author suggested that "the machismo of the intellectual world of her time" had left Garro in the shadow of Paz and her later lover, [[Adolfo Bioy Casares]].<ref name="Ortiz">{{Cite news |last=Ortiz |first=Maria Paulina |date=12 November 2019 |title=La repetición del pasado |trans-title=The repetition of the past |url=https://www.eltiempo.com/lecturas-dominicales/resena-de-los-recuerdos-del-porvenir-novela-mitica-de-la-mexicana-elena-garro-que-es-reeditada-432820 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260729172713/https://www.eltiempo.com/lecturas-dominicales/resena-de-los-recuerdos-del-porvenir-novela-mitica-de-la-mexicana-elena-garro-que-es-reeditada-432820 |archive-date=29 July 2026 |access-date=29 July 2026 |work=El Tiempo |language=es}}</ref>

In twenty-first-century scholarship, ''Recollections of Things to Come'' has been recognized as an important piece of Mexican literature from the second half of the twentieth century.{{sfn|Garro|Esteban|Aparicio|2024|p=56}} It has received the most scholarly attention of Garro's works,{{sfn|Cypess|2012|p=68}} with ''The Cambridge Companion to the Latin American Novel'' calling it her "masterpiece" and noting its importance as a once-neglected work by a woman writer.<ref>{{cite book |last=Davies |first=Catherine |chapter=Gender studies |editor1-last=Kristal |editor1-first=Efraín |title=The Cambridge Companion to the Latin American Novel |publisher=Cambridge University Press |date=2005 |edition=ebook |isbn=978-0-521-82533-7 |url=https://doi.org/10.1017/CCOL0521825334}}</ref> On its sixtieth anniversary in 2023, Olivia Vázquez-Medina told ''[[La Jornada]]'' that the book's gender commentary resonated with contemporary audiences more than other novels of the "boom" era. The author also felt that Garro's close connection to nature and refusal to "put the human at the center of the universe" had remained surprisingly relevant for an author of her time.<ref name="Jornada2023">{{Cite news |last=Flores Soto |first=Alondra |title=La Jornada: Analizan la vigencia de Los recuerdos del porvenir a 60 años de su publicación |trans-title=Analyzing the validity of Los recuerdos del porvenir 60 years after its publication |url=https://www.jornada.com.mx/2023/08/22/cultura/a03n1cul |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260721130257/https://www.jornada.com.mx/2023/08/22/cultura/a03n1cul |archive-date=21 July 2026 |access-date=29 July 2026 |work=La Jornada |language=es}}</ref>

== Legacy ==
[[File:Victoriano Huerta en 1912.jpg|thumb|right|220px|The film takes place during the dictatorship of Victoriano Huerta to avoid criticizing democratic factions in the Mexican Revolution.]] [[Alfredo Ripstein]] directed a film adaptation titled ''Los recuerdos del porvenir'' (''Memories of the Future'') in 1968.<ref name="zarzosa">{{cite book |last1=Agustín |first1=Zarzosa |title=The Sordid Image: The Naturalist Cinema of Arturo Ripstein and Paz Alicia Garciadiego |date=March 2026 |publisher=Northwestern University Press |isbn=9798899480140 |pages=13}}</ref> At the time, the Mexican government was attempting to glorify the Mexican Revolution and increase the country's cinematic prestige. To avoid the political and religious controversies associated with the [[Cristero War]], the film was set in 1913–1914, during the early revolutionary era.{{sfn|Pascual Gutiérrez|2018|pp=125, 129}} While Garro's original text depicts the post-revolutionary government repressing the townspeople, the film portrays revolutionaries being repressed by the brief military dictatorship of [[Victoriano Huerta]].{{sfn|Pascual Gutiérrez|2018|p=129}} Garro called the adaptation "horrible" and "garbage" ({{lang|es|porquería}}), saying it betrayed the novel.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Rosas Lopátegui |first1=Patricia |last2=Toruño |first2=Rhina |last3=Garro |first3=Elena |title=Elena Garro |lang=es |journal=Hispamérica |date=1991 |volume=20 |issue=60 |pages=59 |url=http://www.jstor.org/stable/20539597 |issn=0363-0471}}</ref><ref name="morelia">{{cite web |last1=Aviña |first1=Rafael |title=The mysteries of Elena Garro {{!}} Morelia Film Festival |url=https://moreliafilmfest.com/en/mysteries-elena-garro |publisher=Morelia Film Festival |access-date=9 July 2026 |language=en |date=2 May 2025 |archive-date=15 February 2026 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260215052514/https://moreliafilmfest.com/en/mysteries-elena-garro |url-status=live }}</ref> Iris Pascual Gutiérrez observes that even Ripstein considered the film a failure{{sfn|Pascual Gutiérrez|2018|p=125}} while Agustín Zarzosa calls it an "expensive flop".<ref name="zarzosa" />

In the late 2010s, [[Alfaguara]] began a project to increase Garro's visibility outside Mexico. Her ''Complete Stories'', published in 2016, included two unpublished works. The 2019 Spanish edition of ''Recollection of Things to Come'' included new essays by authors from Argentina, Chile, Colombia, Mexico, and Spain, among them [[Guadalupe Nettel]]. Mayra González Olvera, literary director of Alfaguara, said there would be 5,000 copies.<ref name="excelsior">{{cite web |last1=Bautista |first1=Virginia |title=Amplifican la voz de Garro; Alfaguara publica por primera vez 'Los recuerdos del porvenir' |trans-title=Garro's voice amplified; Alfaguara first publishes 'Los recuerdos del porvenir' |url=https://www.excelsior.com.mx/expresiones/amplifican-la-voz-de-garro-alfaguara-publica-por-primera-vez-los-recuerdos-del-porvenir |website=Excélsior |access-date=7 July 2026 |language=es |date=30 October 2019 |archive-date=7 July 2026 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260707184724/https://www.excelsior.com.mx/expresiones/amplifican-la-voz-de-garro-alfaguara-publica-por-primera-vez-los-recuerdos-del-porvenir |url-status=live }}</ref> Nettel felt that literary scholarship had failed to recognize Elena Garro and predicted that the book would be at the "head of that literary canon that we are reconstructing" by midcentury.<ref name="Jornada2023" /> For the novel's 60th anniversary in 2023, the [[Guadalajara International Book Fair]] organized a seven-hour public reading marathon and distributed free copies to participants.<ref name="Informador2023">{{Cite news |last=Martínez |first=Xochitl |date=23 April 2023 |title=Día Mundial del Libro 2023: Lectura pública en voz alta de "Los recuerdos del porvenir" de Elena Garro para celebrar el Día Mundial del Libro 2023 |trans-title=World Book Day 2023: Public reading aloud of Elena Garro’s "Los recuerdos del porvenir" to celebrate World Book Day 2023|url=https://www.informador.mx/estilo/Dia-Mundial-del-Libro-2023-Lectura-publica-en-voz-alta-de-Los-recuerdos-del-porvenir-de-Elena-Garro-para-celebrar-el-Dia-Mundial-del-Libro-2023-20230422-0083.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260729205706/https://www.informador.mx/estilo/Dia-Mundial-del-Libro-2023-Lectura-publica-en-voz-alta-de-Los-recuerdos-del-porvenir-de-Elena-Garro-para-celebrar-el-Dia-Mundial-del-Libro-2023-20230422-0083.html |archive-date=29 July 2026 |access-date=29 July 2026 |work=El Informador :: Noticias de Jalisco, México, Deportes & Entretenimiento |language=es}}</ref>

Ediciones Cátedra published a critical anniversary edition in 2024 with over 100 pages of new analysis by Ángel Esteban and Yannelys Aparicio. Aparicio presented their work at the [[Association of Academies of the Spanish Language]] and wrote in {{ill|Nueva Revista de Política, Cultura y Arte|es|italics=y}} that Garro's book "has gone unnoticed outside Mexico until very recently".<ref name="revista">{{cite web |last1=Aparicio |first1=Yannelys |title=Elena Garro y «Los recuerdos del porvenir» |trans-title=Elena Garro and ''Los recuerdos del porvenir'' |url=https://www.nuevarevista.net/elena-garro-y-los-recuerdos-del-porvenir/ |website=Nueva Revista |access-date=7 July 2026 |language=es |date=21 November 2024 |archive-date=21 November 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241121181742/https://www.nuevarevista.net/elena-garro-y-los-recuerdos-del-porvenir/ |url-status=live }}</ref> A review by Hana Riebová in ''[[Romanica Olomucensia]]'' praised the 2024 edition's intellectual rigor. It argued that Garro's style of magical realism was earlier and more "authentic" than that of most of her contemporaries, suggesting she be read alongside landmarks like Carpentier's ''The Lost Steps'' and Rulfo's ''[[Pedro Páramo]]''.{{sfn|Riebová|2025|p=413}}

In 2025, Two Lines Press published a translation of Jazmina Barrera's Elena Garro biography as ''The Queen of Swords'' and Garro's short story collection ''La semana de colores'' as ''The Week of Colors''. The 1969 Simms text remained the only English translation of ''Recollections of Things to Come'' at that time.<ref name="oldweiler">{{cite web |last1=Oldweiler |first1=Cory |title=Of Things to Come {{!}} The Legacy of Elana Garro |url=https://southwestreview.com/volume-110-number-4/of-things-to-come-the-legacy-of-elana-garro/ |website=Southwest Review |access-date=7 July 2026 |archive-date=13 July 2026 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260713175229/https://southwestreview.com/volume-110-number-4/of-things-to-come-the-legacy-of-elana-garro/ |url-status=live }}</ref> The ''[[Chicago Review of Books]]'' referred to Garro as "under-translated and under-appreciated" in a review of the short story collection.<ref name="chicago">{{cite web |last1=von Essen |first1=Leah Rachel |title=Traitorous Magic in Garro's "The Week of Colors" |url=https://www.chireviewofbooks.com/2025/12/10/traitorous-magic-in-garros-the-week-of-colors/ |website=Chicago Review of Books |access-date=7 July 2026 |date=10 December 2025 |archive-date=18 January 2026 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260118104113/https://chireviewofbooks.com/2025/12/10/traitorous-magic-in-garros-the-week-of-colors/ |url-status=live }}</ref>

WIKIPEDIA ARTICLE: The Rector of Justin
======================================================================

{{Short description|1964 novel by Louis Auchincloss}}
{{Italic title}}
{{DEFAULTSORT:Rector of Justin, The}}
{{good article}}
{{Use mdy dates|date=September 2025}}
{{Infobox book
| author            = [[Louis Auchincloss]]
| isbn              = 978-0-618-22489-0
| pub_date          = 1964
| publisher         = [[Houghton Mifflin]]
| name              = The Rector of Justin
| genre             = [[Psychological fiction]]
| language          = English
| image             = The Rector of Justin 1964 hardcover dust jacket.png
| caption           = Cover of the 1964 first edition
| alt               = Photo of the original front cover

'''''The Rector of Justin''''' is a 1964 [[psychological fiction]] novel by [[Louis Auchincloss]] about the headmaster (or "[[Rector (ecclesiastical)|rector]]") of a socially exclusive American [[boarding school]]. Over the decades, various narrators provide contrasting perspectives on rector Francis Prescott's charismatic personality and autocratic leadership style. Through the narrators' disagreements, the novel gradually unveils that [[White Anglo-Saxon Protestants|White Anglo-Saxon Protestant]] society—of which Prescott is a reluctant mascot—has lost its innocence and abandoned its Christian values.

The novel was a commercial hit and was warmly received by most contemporary critics. It was a finalist for the [[Pulitzer Prize for Fiction]] and the [[National Book Award for Fiction]], losing to [[Shirley Ann Grau]]'s ''[[The Keepers of the House|The Keeper of the House]]'' and [[Saul Bellow]]'s ''[[Herzog (novel)|Herzog]]'', respectively. Its loss to ''Herzog'' marked [[American literature#Post-World War II fiction|American literary fiction]]'s transition from realist [[society novel]]s about the [[American upper class]] to poetic prose, [[Avant-garde literature|avant-garde style]], and culturally diverse protagonists.

Upon its release, ''[[Harper's Magazine]]'' called the book "almost certainly the finest work ever written about an American [[College-preparatory school|preparatory school]]". It is often considered Auchincloss' greatest novel.

== Synopsis ==
The story is told through six narrators: [[Frame story|frame narrator]] Brian Aspinwall, a teacher at Massachusetts [[Episcopal Church (United States)|Episcopal]] boarding school Justin Martyr ("Justin" for short; named for [[Justin Martyr|the Christian figure]]), who is asked to write a biography of its founder Francis Prescott; and writings and interviews from five people who knew him.

=== Brian Aspinwall ===
In 1939, Aspinwall begins teaching English at Justin. Prescott's contradictions fascinate him. Prescott is an intellectual, but Justin is laddish and focused on sports. Prescott's oldest friend Horace Havistock is gay, but Justin is institutionally homophobic. The school claims to be more democratic than its peers, but its students are generally rich. After the [[Fall of France]], Havistock persuades Prescott to retire, arguing that their shared world is dying.

=== Horace Havistock ===
Havistock and Prescott went to boarding school together.{{Efn|The school in question borrows several details from [[St. Paul's School (New Hampshire)|St. Paul's School]], which was also located in New Hampshire and also had a strongly Episcopalian headmaster who looked down on other Christian denominations. In the novel, the headmaster warns students that "Unitarians or Baptists ... would occupy a lower social level in the hereafter".{{Sfn|Auchincloss|1964|p=62}} At St. Paul's, the equivalent dictum was that "in the life to come Presbyterians will not be on the same plane as Episcopalians".<ref name="Williams2016">{{Cite book |last=Williams |first=Peter W. |title=Religion, Art, and Money: Episcopalians and American Culture from the Civil War to the Great Depression |publisher=[[University of North Carolina Press]] |year=2016 |location=Chapel Hill, NC |pages=14}}</ref>}} A [[American Civil War|Civil War]] orphan whose family was respectable but not especially wealthy, Prescott resents rich boys like Havistock, who become targets for his cruel wit. Even so, Havistock befriends him. Prescott dreams of building a different kind of boarding school, focused on religious and [[civic virtue]]. He has a crisis of faith at [[University of Oxford|Oxford]], but reconverts to Christianity after experiencing a vision of his dead father. Havistock persuades his friend Eliza to break off her engagement with the re-energized Prescott, who will always put his career over his relationships.

=== David Griscam ===
The chairman of the Justin board, [[white-shoe firm|white-shoe lawyer]] David Griscam, both idolizes and dislikes Prescott. He appreciated Justin's family atmosphere, but admits that Justin's bullying and [[code of silence]] taught him to be "underhanded". Neither Griscam nor his wife share Prescott's Episcopal faith: Griscam is [[Agnosticism|agnostic]], while his wife, an [[evangelical Christian]], resents Justin's religious elitism. Griscam insists on sending his two sons to Justin anyway, but neither succeeds there.

Appealing to Prescott's ambition, Griscam encourages Prescott to solicit donations from men whose wealth he resents. Prescott wants to expel a donor's son for [[academic dishonesty]], but Max Totten, a cynical [[scholarship]] student, agrees to take the blame in exchange for a job at the donor's company. Although Max is expelled, he eventually takes over the family business and becomes one of Griscam's "most valued clients", while the son falls into alcoholism.

=== Cordelia Prescott Turnbull ===
Prescott's daughter Cordelia claims that Prescott started a boys' school due to his own repressed homosexual tendencies. She marries a Catholic to annoy him, but after Prescott gives his approval, she leaves her husband and moves to Paris, where she and her lover Charley Strong (a Justinian who loses his Christian faith in [[World War I]]) become part of the [[Lost Generation#In literature|Lost Generation of American expatriates]]. Her mother visits her in Paris and reveals a deep intelligence that was repressed at Justin. Before Strong's death, Prescott reconverts him to Christianity, infuriating Cordelia. She returns to America and marries vulgar businessman Guy Turnbull, but surprisingly, Turnbull befriends Prescott, who craves his respect as a businessman and is impressed by his shameless materialism. Cordelia divorces Turnbull. Prescott confides to Aspinwall that while he has loved his daughters inadequately, he has shown them devotion.

=== Charley Strong ===
In the last surviving chapter of a manuscript that Strong burned before his death, Strong recounts his hero worship of Prescott, which may be rooted in Prescott forgiving him for an early sexual indiscretion. He sees Prescott's Christian discipline as an alternative to the rootlessness of the Lost Generation.

=== Jules Griscam ===
In a memoir written before his death, David Griscam's son Jules implies that his father sent him to Justin because David worried that his materialism would spoil his children. Jules is a poor fit for Justin and Prescott eventually expels him for lying, but David gets Jules into [[Harvard University|Harvard]] anyway. Jules concludes that "an act of desecration" is the only real way to get back at Prescott. He vandalizes several school relics and is arrested.{{efn|This sequence was based on a real-life incident from 1930, when Auchincloss was a young student at [[Groton School]].{{sfn|Piket|1989|p=320}} Two Groton alumni got drunk while visiting their alma mater and vandalized various places on campus.<ref name=":15">{{Cite magazine |last= |date=February 23, 1931 |title=Education: Drunk |url=https://time.com/archive/6863615/education-drunk/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250423220110/https://time.com/archive/6863615/education-drunk/ |archive-date=April 23, 2025 |access-date=March 28, 2025 |magazine=[[Time (magazine)|Time]] |language=en}}</ref> The school's headmaster, [[Endicott Peabody (educator)|Endicott Peabody]], declined to press charges.<ref name=":15" /> Several years after the event, he helped officiate the wedding of one of the men responsible.<ref>{{Cite news |date=April 18, 1934 |title=Colorful Wedding for Miss Willets |url=https://virginiachronicle.com/?a=d&d=TFD19340418.1.1&e=-------en-20--1--txt-txIN-------- |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250423220036/https://virginiachronicle.com/?a=d&d=TFD19340418.1.1&e=-------en-20--1--txt-txIN-------- |archive-date=April 23, 2025 |access-date=March 28, 2025 |work=Fauquier Democrat |pages=1 |via=[[Library of Virginia]]}}</ref>}} When Prescott visits him in jail, Jules claims that Prescott uses religion to aggrandize himself, which wounds Prescott deeply. Jules drunkenly commits suicide, taking his lover with him.

=== Brian Aspinwall ===
After Prescott's successor softens religious discipline and accommodates practicing Catholics,{{Efn|Prescott admits that his policy of forcing students to attend Protestant chapel services also deters Jews from attending the school, but actually praises Jews for refusing to accede to his demands. Auchincloss wrote that the real-life Endicott Peabody was neither "a snob" nor "intolerant of other faiths", but sincerely believed that "a Protestant Episcopal Church School naturally excluded other faiths."{{sfn|Auchincloss|1974|page=39}}}} Prescott plots to oust him. Aspinwall dislikes David Griscam's combination of materialism and tightfistedness, but tips him off anyway. Griscam persuades Prescott to relent by introducing him to elitist and racist dissidents on the Justin board, showing that his successor is the lesser of two evils. Prescott bitterly remarks that Justin is no different from any other prep school. He dies of cancer eight months later. Aspinwall resolves to finish his Prescott biography, although he implies that to preserve the idealized memory of Prescott, it will be "in some part [a] work[] of fiction".

== Development ==

=== Concept ===
[[File:Louis Auchincloss with President Bush.jpg|thumb|Author [[Louis Auchincloss]] '''(center)''' received the [[National Medal of Arts]] in 2005. He stands between President [[George W. Bush]] and First Lady [[Laura Bush]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite news |last1=Noble |first1=Holcomb B. |last2=McGrath |first2=Charles |author-link2=Charles McGrath (critic) |date=January 27, 2010 |title=Louis Auchincloss, Chronicler of New York's Upper Crust, Dies at 92 |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2010/01/28/nyregion/28auchincloss.html |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190702153415/https://www.nytimes.com/2010/01/28/nyregion/28auchincloss.html |archive-date=July 2, 2019 |access-date=March 28, 2025 |work=[[The New York Times]] |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}}</ref>|alt=Refer to caption]]{{Further|Saint Grottlesex|White Anglo-Saxon Protestants|Episcopal Church (United States)#Influence}}
Louis Auchincloss was sent to his father's boarding school, [[Groton School|Groton]], and graduated in 1935.<ref name=":12">{{Cite journal |last=Beran |first=Michael Knox |date=Fall 2010 |title=Louis S. Auchincloss '35, P'76, '82 |url=https://issuu.com/grotonschool/docs/quarterly_2010-fall/75 |journal=Groton School Quarterly |volume=LXXII |issue=3 |pages=72–73 |via=Issuu |archive-date=April 23, 2025 |access-date=April 23, 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250423221111/https://issuu.com/grotonschool/docs/quarterly_2010-fall/75 |url-status=live }}</ref> Although he later delivered the school's centennial address,<ref name=":13">{{Cite magazine |last=MacFarquhar |first=Larissa |author-link=Larissa MacFarquhar |date=February 17, 2008 |title=East Side Story |url=https://www.newyorker.com/magazine/2008/02/25/east-side-story-2 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241224080805/https://www.newyorker.com/magazine/2008/02/25/east-side-story-2 |archive-date=December 24, 2024 |access-date=April 1, 2025 |magazine=[[The New Yorker]] |language=en-US |issn=0028-792X}}</ref> he maintained a lifelong ambivalence for the institution, explaining that his first two years of prep school were a "festering misery"<ref name=":16">{{Cite web |last=Butterworth |first=Trevor |date=September 21, 2007 |title='The irony of my life' |url=https://www.ft.com/content/1925961a-67e4-11dc-8906-0000779fd2ac |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240613051352/https://www.ft.com/content/1925961a-67e4-11dc-8906-0000779fd2ac |archive-date=June 13, 2024 |access-date=April 1, 2025 |website=[[Financial Times]] |language=en-GB}}</ref> and that he was "at first abysmally wretched and later moderately content".{{sfn|Auchincloss|1969|p=355}} He got the idea for ''The Rector of Justin'' from his high school English teacher, Malcolm Strachan,{{sfn|Auchincloss|1974|p=59-60}} whose wife was the publisher of the ''[[Atlantic Monthly]]''.<ref>{{Cite news |date=November 28, 1998 |title=Paid Notice: Deaths - Campbell, Marion Danielson |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1998/11/28/classified/paid-notice-deaths-campbell-marion-danielson.html |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250423220052/https://www.nytimes.com/1998/11/28/classified/paid-notice-deaths-campbell-marion-danielson.html |archive-date=April 23, 2025 |access-date=March 28, 2025 |work=[[The New York Times]] |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}}</ref> Strachan had become a close confidant of Groton's founder and longtime headmaster, [[Endicott Peabody (educator)|Endicott Peabody]], and planned to write a novel showing that Peabody's "theology was subtler and more complicated than any of us supposed."{{sfn|Auchincloss|1974|p=60}} After Strachan's premature death, Auchincloss resolved to write the novel his way.{{sfn|Auchincloss|1974|p=60}}

In 1960, Groton published a collection of essays from the school community to commemorate its 75th anniversary. In his essay, Auchincloss wrote that the alumni had many different impressions of their high school years, and speculated that the aging Peabody had been "troubled by the number of Grotons he seemed to have created and of how little any of them resembled his own."<ref name=":14">{{Cite book |last=Auchincloss |first=Louis |title=Views from the Circle: Seventy-Five Years of Groton School |publisher=[[Groton School]] |year=1960 |pages=243–244 |chapter=The Different Grotons}}</ref> In addition, although published by the school, the essays voiced several criticisms of Groton. [[Ellery Sedgwick]] wrote that despite Groton's high-minded rhetoric, "evil and good have entered into Groton careers in a proportion astonishingly similar to their proportion in any community".<ref name=":4">''Views from the Circle'', p. 25.</ref> [[George Biddle]] said that while seven of his classmates were listed in ''[[Who's Who]]'', "nearly twice that number could, I suppose, be listed as absolute failures".<ref name=":5">''Views from the Circle'', p. 126.</ref> Auchincloss later sent two of his three sons to Groton,<ref name=":16" /> although his biographer cautioned that, by that time, it was "a far more permissive place".{{sfn|Gelderman|1993|p=216}}

=== Timeline ===
Auchincloss had wanted to write a story about a boarding school headmaster for some time, although he was saving the idea "for [a] time when I should feel ready to handle it".{{sfn|Auchincloss|1968|p=4}} In 1938, just three years after graduating from Groton, he drafted a novel in which a headmaster seeks to raise students "with the ideals of public service and a sense of [[noblesse oblige]]", but realizes that he has failed, as most of his students chase lucrative jobs on Wall Street.{{sfn|Piket|1989|p=183}}

Over time, Auchincloss decided that the story would need to cover a long span of time and that it would need to be either a biography or autobiography. He discarded the idea of an autobiography because a fictional Prescott would have trouble describing his effect on other people from his own perspective.{{sfn|Auchincloss|1968|p=7}} In 1956, Auchincloss published a predecessor of the story in ''[[Harper's Magazine]]'' under the title "The Trial of Mr. M."<ref>{{Cite magazine |last=Auchincloss |first=Louis |date=October 1956 |title=The trial of Mr. M |url=https://harpers.org/archive/1956/10/the-trial-of-mr-m/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241009052829/https://harpers.org/archive/1956/10/the-trial-of-mr-m/ |archive-date=October 9, 2024 |access-date=March 28, 2025 |magazine=[[Harper's Magazine]] |language=en-US}}</ref> The story details a retired boarding school headmaster who considers opposing his successor's reforms, but ultimately concedes that the school must adapt to the real world. Auchincloss recycles the imagery of the headmaster's lament—comparing himself to a vaudeville act in which a clown is "remorselessly" followed by a spotlight<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Sullivan |first=Barry |date=1996 |title=Professions of Law |url=https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1560043 |journal=Georgetown Journal of Legal Ethics |volume=9 |issue=4 |pages=1272 n.162 |ssrn=1560043 |via=SSRN}}</ref>—for Prescott's final monologue in the novel.{{sfn|Piket|1989|p=184}}{{sfn|Dahl|1986|p=253}}

In Auchincloss' first draft of the novel, David Griscam was the frame narrator instead of Brian Aspinwall, and the book emphasized the rivalry between Griscam and Prescott. He discarded the idea because Griscam's "personality got out of hand".{{sfn|Auchincloss|1968|p=8}} He eventually came up with the idea of making the biographer a younger man who differed from Prescott in every way except their shared religious faith, which they both recognized was "almost totally lacking in the school, the faculty, the parents, and the trustees," who "care[d] only about the appearance of faith".{{sfn|Auchincloss|1968|p=8}}

Late in his life, Auchincloss (who said that he had been sexually abused by another student in high school, without the school's knowledge{{Sfn|Auchincloss|2010|p=63-64}}) admitted that he had considered broaching the topic of [[Sexual abuse in primary and secondary schools|sexual abuse]] in ''The Rector of Justin'', but ultimately left it out. He felt that the literary mores of the day would not permit him to address the matter with sufficient candor. He subsequently touched upon this theme in ''The Scarlet Letters'' (2003) ''and The Headmaster's Dilemma'' (2007), as well as his 2010 autobiography.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Beran |first=Michael Knox |date=November 20, 2021 |title=Michael Knox Beran Re-Visits Louis Auchincloss |url=https://airmail.news/arts-intel/highlights/full-frontal-louis-716 |access-date=April 22, 2025 |website=Air Mail |language=en}}</ref>

Auchincloss submitted a draft of the novel to [[Houghton Mifflin Harcourt|Houghton Mifflin]] in July 1963. It was published in July 1964.{{sfn|Piket|1989|p=181}}

=== Inspirations ===

==== The school ====
Auchincloss sought to build a composite narrative of the American boarding school between the [[Gilded Age]] and [[World War II]], explaining that it was "the great era of headmasters". He reviewed a series of headmaster biographies from various schools, including Peabody's Groton, [[St. Paul's School (New Hampshire)|St. Paul's]], [[St. Mark's School (Massachusetts)|St. Mark's]], and [[Lawrenceville School|Lawrenceville]], but dismissed them as "a dreary lot".{{sfn|Auchincloss|1974|p=35}} Nonetheless, the novel frequently draws from Auchincloss' experiences at Groton in the 1930s. One critic quipped that in one scene, "the Rev. Francis Prescott, founder and first headmaster of Justin Martyr, an Episcopal school 30 miles west of Boston, was speaking about the Rev. Endicott Peabody, founder and first headmaster of Groton School, an Episcopal-oriented school 30 miles west of Boston".<ref name=":1">{{Cite news |last=Shepard |first=Richard F. |date=January 10, 1972 |title='Rector of Justin' In a Harder Time |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1972/01/10/archives/-rector-of-justin-in-a-harder-time.html |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231018212433/https://www.nytimes.com/1972/01/10/archives/-rector-of-justin-in-a-harder-time.html |archive-date=October 18, 2023 |access-date=March 28, 2025 |work=[[The New York Times]] |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}}</ref>

The novel mirrors some of the compromises Peabody made to build Groton. According to one story, in 1891, Peabody financed Groton's main dormitory by allowing donors who contributed at least $5,000 (approximately $175,000 in 2025 dollars) to nominate one student for admission, notwithstanding the waiting list.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Kintrea |first=Frank |date=October–November 1980 |title='old Peabo' and the School |url=https://www.americanheritage.com/old-peabo-and-school |url-status=live |journal=[[American Heritage (magazine)|American Heritage]] |volume=31 |issue=6 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231017121337/https://www.americanheritage.com/old-peabo-and-school |archive-date=October 17, 2023 |access-date=April 23, 2025}}</ref> He later remarked that focusing on educating wealthy students was "one of the great mistakes that [he] made as Headmaster".{{Sfn|Aldred|2017|p=284}} For his own part, Auchincloss commented that Peabody had no other option, since "who else in 1881 was going to support a new school started by three young men?"{{Sfn|Auchincloss|1974|p=39}}

==== The rector ====
{{Multiple image
| total_width       = 350
| image1            = Peabodyheadmaster.jpg
| alt1              = Photo of Endicott Peabody, Auchincloss' boarding school headmaster
| image2            = LearnedHand1910a.jpg
| alt2              = Photo of Learned Hand, an influential federal judge
| footer            = Auchincloss based Francis Prescott on schoolmaster [[Endicott Peabody]] '''(left)''' and judge [[Learned Hand]].
}}
The character of Frank Prescott was often compared to Endicott Peabody, although Auchincloss protested that the two men "shared not a single characteristic".{{Sfn|Auchincloss|2010|p=194}} He explained that Peabody was "simple, straightforward, literal, and always sincere", while Prescott was "complex, arrogant, witty, cynical, intellectual", and "a bit of a charlatan".{{sfn|Auchincloss|1974|p=36}} He admitted that he had borrowed "certain facts and dates" from Peabody's life, but maintained that Prescott was based, at least "in part", on federal judge [[Learned Hand]],{{sfn|Auchincloss|1974|p=60}}<ref name=":0" /> who he described as "the greatest man whom I ever had the good luck to know".{{sfn|Auchincloss|1968|p=5}} However, he later recalled that [[Archibald MacLeish]] was the only person who recognized Hand's influence on Prescott.{{sfn|Parsell|1988|p=53}}

Even so, upon its publication, the book reportedly "caused uproar among Groton alumni who saw it as an attack" on Peabody.<ref>{{Cite web |date=February 4, 2010 |title=Louis Auchincloss: American lawyer and writer |url=https://www.thetimes.com/comment/register/article/louis-auchincloss-american-lawyer-and-writer-dsg27r8gcgr |access-date=March 28, 2025 |website=[[The Times]] |language=en |archive-date=April 23, 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250423220107/https://www.thetimes.com/comment/register/article/louis-auchincloss-american-lawyer-and-writer-dsg27r8gcgr |url-status=live }}</ref> Peabody's granddaughter [[Marietta Peabody Tree|Marietta]] consoled Auchincloss by telling him that the criticism reflected how little his critics understood Peabody.{{sfn|Gelderman|1993|p=155}} In addition, Peabody's biographer Frank Ashburn commented that Frank Prescott "only remotely" resembled his subject,<ref name=":24">{{Cite book |last=Ashburn |first=Frank D. |title=Peabody of Groton |publisher=[[Riverside Press]] |year=1967 |edition=2nd |location=Cambridge, MA |pages=320}}</ref> and [[Larissa MacFarquhar]] wrote that "Prescott is a far more convoluted and ambiguous character" than Peabody.<ref name=":13" /> One Groton graduate, [[Cass Canfield]] of the [[Harper and Row]] publishing house, publicly praised the book and Prescott's character in particular, but did not discuss the Peabody connection.<ref>{{Cite news |date=1964-12-06 |title=One That Got Away |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1964/12/06/archives/one-that-got-away.html |access-date=2025-10-06 |work=[[The New York Times]]}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |date=1986-03-28 |title=Cass Canfield, a Titan of Publishing, Is Dead at 88 |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1986/03/28/obituaries/cass-canfield-a-titan-of-publishing-is-dead-at-88.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250526191537/https://www.nytimes.com/1986/03/28/obituaries/cass-canfield-a-titan-of-publishing-is-dead-at-88.html |archive-date=2025-05-26 |access-date=2025-10-06 |work=[[The New York Times]] |language=en}}</ref>

Prescott's title (and thus the title of the book) also refers to Peabody. While Groton did not use the term "rector" for its headmaster (the term was instead used by [[St. Paul's School (New Hampshire)|St. Paul's School]]), the school community informally referred to Endicott Peabody as "''the'' Rector".<ref>''Views from the Circle'', p. 64.</ref>

==== Other characters ====
The character of Brian Aspinwall is modeled on Auchincloss' old mentor, Malcolm Strachan.{{sfn|Auchincloss|1974|p=61}} Auchincloss admitted that Aspinwall was "much weaker and less attractive ... than Malcolm had ever been", but rejected claims that the character was a veiled attack on Strachan.{{sfn|Auchincloss|1974|p=61}} He said that he wanted to make Aspinwall as different from Prescott as possible for dramatic effect.{{Sfn|Auchincloss|1974|p=60}}

Auchincloss based Prescott's friend Horace Havistock on [[University of Cambridge]] legal historian [[G. T. Lapsley]].<ref name=":12" /> Like Havistock, Lapsley was a gay man<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Annan |first=Noel |author-link=Noel Annan, Baron Annan |date=1990 |title=The Cult of Homosexuality in England 1850—1950 |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/23539516 |journal=[[Biography (journal)|Biography]] |volume=13 |issue=3 |pages=194 |issn=0162-4962 |via=JSTOR}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |last=Bell |first=Millicent |date=July 19, 1984 |title=Notes of a Friend and Brother |url=https://www.nybooks.com/articles/1984/07/19/notes-of-a-friend-and-brother/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250424065030/https://www.nybooks.com/articles/1984/07/19/notes-of-a-friend-and-brother/ |archive-date=April 24, 2025 |access-date=April 1, 2025 |work=[[The New York Review of Books]] |language=en |volume=31 |issue=12 |issn=0028-7504}}</ref> who left America for Europe.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Gaillard Thomas Lapsley |url=http://trinitycollegechapel.com/about/memorials/brasses/lapsley/ |access-date=April 1, 2025 |website=Trinity College, Cambridge |archive-date=April 23, 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250423215953/http://trinitycollegechapel.com/about/memorials/brasses/lapsley/ |url-status=live }}</ref>

== Themes ==
Auchincloss spent most of his career detailing the decline of [[White Anglo-Saxon Protestants]]' (WASPs) leading role in American society.{{efn|Auchincloss personally disliked the term "WASP" and preferred the term "Protestant."<ref name=":17" />}} Shortly before his death, he explained that while most of his WASP friends were ''richer'' in the 21st century than they had been growing up, "everyone has moved up", and the old-money elite had "lost their monopoly."<ref name=":17">{{Cite web |title=Louis Auchincloss: The Rector of Justin |url=https://americanlegends.com/Interviews/rector_of_justin.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250713114004/https://americanlegends.com/Interviews/rector_of_justin.html |archive-date=2025-07-13 |access-date=2025-09-27 |website=American Legends}}</ref><ref name=":18">{{Cite news |last=Garner |first=Dwight |author-link=Dwight Garner |date=2010-12-15 |title=A Man Who Knew the People Who Mattered, and Wrote About Them |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2010/12/15/books/15book.html |access-date=2025-09-27 |work=[[The New York Times]] |language=en |archive-date=January 20, 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250120015523/https://www.nytimes.com/2010/12/15/books/15book.html}}</ref> He added that "to have witnessed the disintegration of an economic ruling class in the 1930s from a front row seat ... was all a novelist could ask [for]."{{sfn|Gelderman|1993|p=167}} In an early chapter of ''The Rector of Justin'', Horace Havistock concedes that "the world of the private school" is necessarily tied up with "the world of personal honor and a Protestant God", and that "when a civilization crumbles, it crumbles all together."{{Sfn|Auchincloss|1964|p=63}}

=== The collapse of aristocratic values ===
[[File:Former head of New York Stock Exchange before Senate Committee. Washington D.C. Richard Whitney; former President of the New York Stock Exchange, was the first witness as the Senate LCCN2016871192 (cropped).jpg|left|thumb|259x259px|The public disgrace of [[Richard Whitney (financier)|Richard Whitney]] (pictured), the aristocratic president of the [[New York Stock Exchange]], shocked upper-class society.<ref name=":13" />|alt=Photo of Richard Whitney, a disgraced upper-class financier]]
''The Rector of Justin'' explores the erosion of the WASPs' self-belief that values instilled at schools like Groton entitled them to leadership roles in the corporate world and public service, and reflects Auchincloss' growing disillusionment with WASP society in the 1930s and 1940s. Auchincloss said that when he was growing up, the [[Eastern Establishment]] thought it "could be trusted to regulate itself".<ref name=":13" /> As an example of these values, the novel notes how after David Griscam's father went bankrupt and fled the country, his mother felt a "sacred duty" to pay off her absentee husband's debts, forcing the family to abandon its upper-class lifestyle.{{Sfn|Auchincloss|1964|p=130}} As a young man, Auchincloss resented the Groton-educated [[Franklin Delano Roosevelt]]'s use of government to enforce morality in the corporate sphere, reasoning that it was a repudiation of Establishment values.<ref name=":13" /> However, he eventually lost faith in the idea that WASPs were more moral than the general population. Another Groton alumnus, financier [[Richard Whitney (financier)|Richard Whitney]], shocked high society with his 1938 [[embezzlement]] conviction;<ref name=":13" /> Auchincloss explored Whitney's misdeeds in his next novel, ''The Embezzler'' (1966).{{sfn|Dahl|1986|p=125}}

{{Quote box
| quote = Pa and Mother, of course, were supreme at Justin, but from the beginning we knew that Justin was not the real world. ... [A]lthough [the real world] treated Pa and Mother with respect, it was the kind of respect that people might pay to the sovereigns of a small Pacific Island kingdom, more exotic than powerful, not quite to be taken seriously, perhaps even a bit ridiculous.
| author = Cordelia Prescott Turnbull
| source = in ''The Rector of Justin'' (chapter 12){{Sfn|Auchincloss|1964|p=179}}
| align = right
| width = 300px
}}

Over the course of the novel, an increasingly immoral WASP establishment begins hiding behind moral individuals like Francis Prescott to obscure its own failures. Auchincloss wrote that the basic idea of the novel was "to study a saint and to leave it up to the reader whether saints are good or bad."{{sfn|Auchincloss|1968|p=9}} By the end of the novel, Justinians have raised up an idealized version of Prescott to pretend that Christian values are still relevant to modern society, turning Prescott into "a symbol rather than a source of morality."{{sfn|Piket|1989|p=190}} Prescott's daughter Cordelia points out that the true elites have carefully sidelined her father, who was "not quite to be taken seriously".{{Sfn|Auchincloss|1964|p=179}}

Removing Prescott from the picture clarifies that while the American elite's "inviolable rules of conduct ... were once the glue that held together a stern, but deeply felt system of ethical values," by the 1940s they were "little more than useful justifications for preserving a selfish status quo."<ref name="Kakutani">{{Cite news |last=Kakutani |first=Michiko |author-link=Michiko Kakutani |date=1984-07-26 |title=Books of the Times |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1984/07/26/books/books-of-the-times-088814.html |access-date=2025-10-06 |work=[[The New York Times]]}}</ref> Auchincloss praised the writings of [[Oliver La Farge]], another unhappy Groton alumnus, which taught him that "Groton without Peabody" is "''just'' this 'dream', this stuffy little group of snooty, cruel boys".<ref name=":13" />{{Sfn|Gelderman|1993|p=51-53}}

Auchincloss' views evolved after the novel was published. After watching his high school classmates [[William Bundy|William]] and [[McGeorge Bundy]] lead America into the [[Vietnam War]], he concluded that the novel's take on Groton ("that its graduates were ... too shallow to aspire to the school's ideals") was fundamentally incorrect. He decided that "the ideals themselves were rotten",<ref name=":13" /> explaining that Groton taught the Bundys to never concede defeat, even when the war could not be won.{{Sfn|Auchincloss|2010|p=71}} In ''The House of the Prophet'' (1980), the novel's stand-in for [[Walter Lippmann]] comments that the danger of Groton was in its culture of "pugnacity".<ref name=":13" />

=== Elite decadence ===
[[File:Theodore Roosevelt by the Pach Bros.jpg|alt=Photo of Theodore Roosevelt, a supporter of Endicott Peabody|thumb|262x262px|[[Endicott Peabody (educator)|Endicott Peabody]]'s friend [[Theodore Roosevelt]] supported Peabody's goal to toughen up the children of American elites,<ref>{{Cite web |title=Endicott Peabody |url=https://www.theodorerooseveltcenter.org/Learn-About-TR/TR-Encyclopedia/Culture-and-Society/Endicott-Peabody |access-date=April 23, 2025 |website=Theodore Roosevelt Center |archive-date=April 23, 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250423220028/https://www.theodorerooseveltcenter.org/Learn-About-TR/TR-Encyclopedia/Culture-and-Society/Endicott-Peabody |url-status=live }}</ref> urging Peabody's students to avoid "the life of mere vapid ease."<ref>{{Cite web |last=Roosevelt |first=Theodore |date=May 24, 1904 |title=Address at the Prize Day Exercises, Groton School |url=https://americanliterature.com/history/theodore-roosevelt/speech/address-at-the-prize-day-exercises-groton-school |access-date=April 23, 2025 |website=americanliterature.com |archive-date=April 23, 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250423215943/https://americanliterature.com/history/theodore-roosevelt/speech/address-at-the-prize-day-exercises-groton-school |url-status=live }}</ref> However, some students questioned whether Peabody had been successful.<ref name=":4" /><ref name=":5" />]]
The novel reflects Auchincloss' disillusionment with American boarding schools' inability to live up to their founders' vision. In a 1968 essay,{{efn|Later reprinted as an afterword to the 2001 Modern Library edition of the novel.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Auchincloss |first=Louis |title=The Rector of Justin |publisher=[[Random House]] |year=2001 |edition=Modern Library |location=New York |chapter=Afterword: Origin of a Hero |pages=355–363}}</ref>}} Auchincloss explained that "the central problem in all New England Protestant church schools of [Peabody's] day was the conflict between the piety and idealism of their inspirers and the crass materialism of the families" that supported them.{{sfn|Auchincloss|1968|p=4}} As [[Gore Vidal]] ([[Phillips Exeter Academy|Exeter]] '43) put it, Auchincloss' books frequently trace "the collapse of the Puritan ethical system and its replacement by—as far as those of us now living can tell—nothing."<ref name=":22">{{Cite news |last=Vidal |first=Gore |author-link=Gore Vidal |date=July 18, 1974 |title=Real Class |url=https://www.nybooks.com/articles/1974/07/18/real-class/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250227225750/https://www.nybooks.com/articles/1974/07/18/real-class/ |archive-date=February 27, 2025 |access-date=April 22, 2025 |work=[[The New York Review of Books]] |language=en |volume=21 |issue=12 |issn=0028-7504}}</ref>

Like Prescott, the real-life Endicott Peabody sought to toughen up spoiled aristocrats through harsh discipline and simple living.<ref name=":3">{{Cite journal |last=Hicks |first=David V. |date=Autumn 1996 |title=The Strange Fate of the American Boarding School |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/41212553 |journal=[[The American Scholar (magazine)|The American Scholar]] |volume=65 |issue=4 |pages=525, 528 |jstor=41212553}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Bundgaard |first=Axel |title=Muscle and Manliness: The Rise of Sport in American Boarding Schools |publisher=[[Syracuse University Press]] |year=2005 |pages=111–120}}</ref> Auchincloss suggested that this mission was doomed to fail, recalling Peabody "as a [[David]] engaged in the seemingly hopeless struggle of preserving some degree of spirituality from the [[Goliath]] of materialism that re-invaded the school with each new form of prosperous youngsters."<ref name=":14" /> In the novel, Prescott contemptuously remarks that Peabody's Groton is "well equipped to train young men for the steam room of the Racquet Club".<ref name=":2">{{Cite news |last=Peterson |first=Virgilia |date=July 12, 1964 |title=A Crucible Covered with Ivy |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1964/07/12/archives/a-crucible-covered-with-ivy-the-rector-of-justin-by-louis.html |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220927102305/https://www.nytimes.com/1964/07/12/archives/a-crucible-covered-with-ivy-the-rector-of-justin-by-louis.html |archive-date=September 27, 2022 |access-date=March 28, 2025 |work=[[The New York Times]] |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}}</ref> Only at the end of his life does Prescott realize that his school is no different.<ref name=":1" />{{efn|[[Nelson W. Aldrich Jr.|Nelson Aldrich]] ([[St. Paul's School (New Hampshire)|St. Paul's]] '53) quipped that while Groton boys dismissed St. Paul's boys as decadent and unworldly, "Groton boys were described in the same terms by Exeter boys, and Exeter boys in (almost) the same terms by high-school boys, and so on ... [until the point where] all boarding-school boys are described, without distinction, as a bunch of fairies."<ref>{{Cite book |last=Aldrich |first=Nelson W. |author-link=Nelson W. Aldrich Jr. |url= |title=Old Money: The Mythology of America's Upper Class |date= |publisher=[[Vintage Books]] |year=1989 |isbn=978-0-679-72224-3 |location=New York |pages=125}}</ref>}}

Auchincloss' upbringing was a case in point. Auchincloss' own father sent him to boarding school out of concern that a child who grew up "in a woman's world of cushions and caresses ... would turn into a sissy".{{sfn|Auchincloss|1974|p=36}} But Auchincloss' brother—who was also sent to Groton—left a career in the [[United States Foreign Service|Foreign Service]] for "a life of pleasure and leisure",<ref name=":19">{{Cite news |last=Kaiser |first=Walter |date=March 24, 2011 |title=Inside the Fortress |url=https://www.nybooks.com/articles/2011/03/24/inside-fortress/ |access-date=April 1, 2025 |work=[[The New York Review of Books]] |language=en |volume=58 |issue=5 |issn=0028-7504}}</ref> and Auchincloss said that "I could have almost lived on what [he] expended on shirts and cufflinks."{{Sfn|Auchincloss|2010|p=96}} A lapsed [[Presbyterianism|Presbyterian]], he later wrote that most of his Groton classmates stopped going to church as adults, but hedged that while "the [[Ivy League]] of my day" may have been "godless ... it certainly did not lack ideals".{{Sfn|Auchincloss|2010|p=76-78}}

The ending of the novel emphasizes that the American aristocracy must reform to survive. Despite his early ambivalence for the reformist Franklin Roosevelt, Auchincloss later admitted that Roosevelt "was not a traitor to his class" but "its last great representative".<ref name=":13" /> [[Christopher Dahl (administrator)|Christopher Dahl]] writes that the novel's ending suggests "there remains some good in a flawed institution like Justin Martyr, and it is better to support [] mild reforms ... than to abandon the battle altogether."{{sfn|Dahl|1986|p=28}}

=== Internal contradictions and self-delusion ===
Despite Prescott's best intentions, he "does not see, and [Aspinwall] only dimly glimpses," that there is a "fundamental irony implicit in attempting to foster 'democratic' ideals in [an upper-class] institution" like Justin Martyr.{{sfn|Parsell|1988|p=49-50}} Auchincloss commented that he "wanted [Prescott] to express the agony of failing ridiculously when he wanted at the very least to fail magnificently".{{sfn|Auchincloss|1968|p=5}} He said that Endicott Peabody must have reached a Prescott-like epiphany about his school's failure, explaining that while Peabody must have known that "half the Groton family paid only lip service to his ideals ... and that he had failed to persuade his boys to receive Christ", nobody in the Groton community wanted to admit this to him.{{sfn|Auchincloss|1974|p=59-60}} Auchincloss implied that he had gotten this impression from Peabody's confidant Malcolm Strachan.{{sfn|Auchincloss|1974|p=59-60}} However, he also wrote that "if Dr. Peabody had his moments of despair, they didn't show."{{sfn|Auchincloss|1968|p=5}}

The novel's main characters personify the internal contradictions of WASP society. One of the novel's recurring themes is that "there is something about exclusive boarding schools that magnifies the most juvenile tendencies of adults."{{sfn|Pitofsky|2014|p=58}} Prescott is "a man of intellect and idealism who could be noble, generous and kind but also, by turns, cruel, callous and arbitrary",<ref name=":0" /> and "one of the central strengths of the novel" is that it supports "widely divergent conclusions" about Prescott, with Auchincloss "go[ing] out of his way to present the negative as well as positive aspects of Prescott's character".{{sfn|Dahl|1986|p=21}} Christopher Dahl notes that the novel repeatedly provides examples of Prescott's "goodness and spiritual strength, only to follow each of them immediately with an instance of his pettiness or meanness".{{sfn|Dahl|1986|p=21}}

[[Robert M. Adams (literary scholar)|Robert M. Adams]] suggested that the book did not make its point clear enough, expressing concern that no individual narrator clearly explained that "a private New England Episcopal prep school [is not a] very distinct alternative to a world of money and snobbery". As an example, he wrote that Aspinwall also displays some of the flaws of the racist and classist trustees who seek to claim Prescott as their own, and that the novel was ultimately "an analysis of a petrified old windbag, unwittingly revealed as such by his most devoted admirer".<ref name=":11">{{Cite news |last=Adams |first=Robert M. |author-link=Robert M. Adams (literary scholar) |date=July 9, 1964 |title=Saturday Night and Sunday Morning |url=https://www.nybooks.com/articles/1964/07/09/saturday-night-and-sunday-morning/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250423220008/https://www.nybooks.com/articles/1964/07/09/saturday-night-and-sunday-morning/ |archive-date=April 23, 2025 |access-date=March 28, 2025 |work=[[The New York Review of Books]] |language=en |volume=2 |issue=11 |issn=0028-7504}}</ref> Auchincloss agreed that Aspinwall was a flawed character, commenting that while Aspinwall ends the book resolving to write a biography of Prescott, "personally, I doubt if Brian would have been able to finish it."{{sfn|Auchincloss|1968|p=9}}{{sfn|Pitofsky|2014|p=61}}

== Contemporary reception ==

=== Commercial response ===
''The Rector of Justin'' was a major commercial success. It topped the [[List of The New York Times number-one books of 1964|''New York Times'' best-seller list]] for one week,<ref name=":32">{{Cite book |last=Bear |first=John |url= |title=The #1 New York Times Bestseller |date= |publisher=[[Ten Speed Press]] |year=1992 |isbn=978-0-89815-484-9 |location=Berkeley, CA |pages=91–94}}</ref> and competed for first place for thirty-five weeks.<ref name=":6" /> It was the sixth-best-selling fiction book of 1964,<ref name=":33">{{Cite book |last=Hackett |first=Alice Payne |title=70 Years of Best Sellers, 1895-1965 |date=1967 |publisher=[[R.R. Bowker]] |location=New York |pages=224, 227 |language=}}</ref> and had sold 2 million copies by 1966.{{sfn|Gelderman|1993|p=155}} However, the novel's chief competitor for end-of-year literary honors, [[Saul Bellow]]'s ''[[Herzog (novel)|Herzog]],'' spent 29 weeks at #1, finished third on the yearly rankings for both 1964 and 1965, and sold considerably more hardcover copies (142,000 to 80,000).<ref>{{Cite news |last=Leader |first=Zachary |date=April 17, 2015 |title=The five essential Saul Bellow novels |url=https://www.theguardian.com/books/2015/apr/17/the-five-essential-saul-bellow-novels |access-date=April 26, 2025 |work=The Guardian |language=en-GB |issn=0261-3077}}</ref><ref name=":33" /><ref name=":32" />

[[Walter Wanger]] [[optioned]] the film rights for [[MGM]].<ref>{{Cite news |date=October 18, 1964 |title=Spies and Schooldays |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1964/10/18/archives/new-york-previews-spies-and-schooldays-walter-wanger-to-film-2-new.html?searchResultPosition=5 |access-date=April 23, 2025 |work=[[The New York Times]] |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |last=Weiler |first=A. H. |author-link=A. H. Weiler |date=November 1, 1964 |title=New Horizons for Cukor, Niven and Hatfield |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1964/11/01/archives/new-york-previews-new-horizons-for-cukor-niven-and-hatfield.html |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250423220126/https://www.nytimes.com/1964/11/01/archives/new-york-previews-new-horizons-for-cukor-niven-and-hatfield.html |archive-date=April 23, 2025 |access-date=April 23, 2025 |work=[[The New York Times]] |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}}</ref> He recruited [[George Cukor]] to direct, [[Samuel A. Taylor]] to write the screenplay, and [[Spencer Tracy]] and [[Katharine Hepburn]] to play the leads. However, Tracy was in poor health and the film was never made.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Curtis |first=James |url= |title=Spencer Tracy |date=2011 |publisher=[[Hutchinson Heinemann|Hutchinson]] |isbn=978-0-09-178524-6 |pages=821–23 |language=en}}</ref>

=== Critical response and awards consideration ===
Critics generally praised the novel. It was a finalist for the [[Pulitzer Prize for Fiction]] and the [[National Book Award for Fiction]], losing to [[Shirley Ann Grau]]'s ''[[The Keepers of the House|The Keeper of the House]]'' and Bellow's ''Herzog'', respectively.<ref>{{Cite web |title=National Book Awards 1965 |url=https://www.nationalbook.org/awards-prizes/national-book-awards-1965/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210430155636/https://www.nationalbook.org/awards-prizes/national-book-awards-1965/ |archive-date=April 30, 2021 |access-date=March 28, 2025 |website=[[National Book Foundation]] |language=en-US}}</ref> Although Pulitzer jurors Lewis Stiles Gannett and [[Maxwell Geismar]] personally disliked ''Herzog'', they picked ''The Keeper of the House'' over ''The Rector of Justin'' in part because the latter was "precisely ... the kind of novel to which the prize has been awarded in the past".<ref name=":8">{{Cite book |last1=Fischer |first1=Heinz-Dietrich |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Yjj7FiO4p44C |title=Chronicle of the Pulitzer Prizes for Fiction: Discussions, Decisions and Documents |last2=Fischer |first2=Erika J. |date=February 14, 2012 |publisher=[[K. G. Saur Verlag]] |isbn=978-3-11-097330-3 |location=Munich |pages=282 |language=en |access-date=September 17, 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241208091428/https://books.google.com/books?id=Yjj7FiO4p44C |archive-date=December 8, 2024 |url-status=live}}</ref> Geismar also dismissed Auchincloss' work as insubstantial, explaining that while he typically gave Auchincloss favorable reviews, his books were "polished entertainment and nothing else".<ref name=":8" /> Auchincloss admitted that it was "silly of me to mind" losing the awards, but was wounded nonetheless.<ref name=":6">{{Cite news |last=Plimpton |first=George |author-link=George Plimpton |date=Fall 1994 |title=Louis Auchincloss, The Art of Fiction No. 138 |url=https://www.theparisreview.org/interviews/1759/the-art-of-fiction-no-138-louis-auchincloss |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250613170910/https://www.theparisreview.org/interviews/1759/the-art-of-fiction-no-138-louis-auchincloss |archive-date=June 13, 2025 |access-date=April 23, 2025 |work=[[The Paris Review]] |language=en |volume= |issue=132 |issn=0031-2037}}</ref>

Despite the award snubs, J.
